Historical Information:
Arthur Ralph Ditterich was a Shire of Flinders Councillor from 1961-1964.
A.R. & F. Ditterich are Life Members of the Main Ridge Cricket Club - Ralph and Frank Ditterich were keen cricketers and involved in community affairs. They were involved in the planning and building of the bowls club and other works associated with the grounds. Both had orchards and lived in Valley View Lane, Main Ridge.  Prior to 1926 Main Ridge was known as Main Creek and the name change was brought about by Frank Ditterich.  Seven acres (2.8 hectares) was bought from C. Rigby in 1932 for a recreation ground at Main Ridge for the sum of 50 pounds ($100). A 10 pound ($20) deposit was raised by the community funded in part by a 'sheep guessing competition'. The balance payable over 5 years was raised by community fundraising efforts.
In 1957 the gates were given as a gift by Mrs Lillian Adams of Main Ridge.
On 28th April 1959 the Shire President was invited to unveil a plaque in memory of Frank Ditterich.  Frank was born in Long Gully, Bendigo on 17th September 1895 and died on 28th December 1956 at Mentone. He married his wife Jessie in 1930. They had two sons Richard and David.
Ralph was born in St Arnaud on 4th July, 1893 and married his wife Margaret in Palmerston, New Zealand in 1926. Their son Allan was born in 1929 and died in 1947. Ralph died in Redcliffe, Queensland in 1974.
Councillor A. R. McNabb, Mayor of the City 1947-48.

Alfred Stephen Kenyon (1867-1943) was born at Homebush, near Avoca on 7 December 1867. He was an engineer, ethnologist, numismatist, historian and a writer. He was educated at St Stephen's Grammar School in Richmond and later at Ormond College and the University of Melbourne. in 1887 he entered the Public Works Department and joined the Victorian Water Supply Department the following year. Kenyon was appointed Engineer in Charge of Town Water Supplies in 1901 before becoming Engineer for Agriculture with the Department of Agriculture in 1906. 1911 saw him transfer to the State Rivers and Water Supply Commission where he was Engineer in Charge of Water Supply to the North West Mallee. His first major literary work, The Story of the Mallee, was published in 1915 and in 1918 he was asked to report on land settlement for the placement of returned soldiers. Part of the report recommended the development of Red Cliffs and he was placed in charge of developing the district. Circa 1928 he evolved what he termed the 'Ironclad' Catchment to be made of flat galvanized iron sheets laid on sloping grounds to discharge water from rainfall into watertight covered storages. Following a stint as Acting Commissioner, in 1932 he was appointed Commissioner of the State Rivers and Water Supply Commission. He was a member of many scientific and professional societies including The Institution of Engineers, Australia, the Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, the Historical Society of Victoria, the Field Naturalists' Club, the Royal Society of Victoria, the Anthropological Society of Victoria, the Australian and New Zealand Association for the Advancement of Science, and the Society of Genealogists, Australia. He was also a member of a number of scientific societies overseas.

Historical Information: Aberfeldie (Perthshire, spelt Aberfeldy, near where the Black Watch Regiment was formed in 1739). According to an article retrieved from Wikipedia in March 2007, the suburb takes its name from a property called 'Aberfeldie', located on the corner of Aberfeldie Street and Park Crescent, which its owner, Scotsman James Robertson, had named after a place in Scotland. When the property was sold in 1888 it became the name of the suburb. Barnes (1964) and Blake (1977), on the other hand, state that Aberfeldie was the name of an estate owned by the Napier family. Both explanations point to a Scottish origin.

Historical Information:
Acheron is the name of a river, a settlement, an Aboriginal station, gold diggings at Swamp Creek, a gap in the Great Dividing Range, a pastoral run, a ridge in the Black Range State Forest, and a scenic road called the Acheron Way (Sinnot 2003). Saxton (1907: 5) considered it was a 'Classical name'. According to Martin (1944: 5) Acheron Way 'was the name of a river in Epirus (north-west ancient Greece), regarded in awe as connected with the underworld'. Blake (1977: 22) commented 'in 1839 Fletcher and Coburn took up their stn [station] between Acheron and Rubicon rivers, naming it after ancient Greek river which reputedly flowed to underworld'. Massola (1968) does not assert that Acheron is an Aboriginal placename. Barry Blake (2001 in Clark and Heydon 2002) considers it is a distortion of the Aboriginal name 'Ngaragon'. Sinnott has argued that Les Blake (1977) was unaware of the Aboriginal (Taungurong) name for the river: Agaroon (Neumayer) or Nyaggeron. Barry Blake has suggested that the original Taungurong word was Ngaragon. However, Cockburn and Fletcher would have been well placed to modify the Taungurong name or names to Niagaroon and Acheron, as the two men were the first licensees (1839) of both pastoral runs. (Also, Europeans often failed to hear or record the initial ng- in Aboriginal words). Acheron is the Latin spelling of Greek Ackheron (Ã  Ã  Ã Â©Ã  Ã  Ã Â½) "River of Woe", from akhos (Ã Â±Ã  Ã Â¿Ã  ), distress. The Acheron was one of the rivers of the Underworld or kingdom of Hades, and also the name of a river in Epirus, Greece. (Sinnott 2003: 11)

This placename may be an example of polysemy, in that the first European settlers heard Ngaragon and used 'Acheron' in its place, or then again its similarity may be purely coincidental.

Historical Information:
This Creek is purportedly named after William Thomas 'Bill' Ah Chow. Bill Ah Chow was one of 10 children born to Thomas Ah Chow and Agnes (nee Mason), a Chinese father and Welsh mother. He was a well known local character in the Omeo and East Gippsland district. Bill was known to be around the Omeo region at an early age, having been documented as discovering the body of murdered Charlie Price at Scrubby Creek in 1912. While living in Orbost, WW1 began, so he enlisted in the army and was wounded on three occasions. After the war, he settled at Swan Reach, and married Myrtle Cox. They had three children, but the youngest died in infancy. Although Bill and Myrtle remained married, they apparently lead separate lives. Around 1943, Bill was given the job of as fire spotter on Mt Nugong. He needed good accommodation, so constructed a hut for himself on the flat of Bentley Plains, just over a mile from the lookout. Bill has reportedly said he named his new abode Moscow Villa because it was finished the same day that the Battle of Moscow was being fought in WW II. Soon after, Bill was paid an official visit by the Governor of Victoria and officials.  It was during the Cold War when anything Russian was suspect. The official visitors were not pleased with the name of the hut so Bill, being quick witted, created the acronym. 'My Own Summer Cottage Officially Welcomes Visitors Inside, Light Luncheon Available'. Bill loved his  Moscow Villa and the solitude of the mountains, but always welcomed visitors. Myrtle lived in a small cottage near the Ensay Recreation Reserve and when Bill came down from Bentley Plain for supplies he would stay at the cottage. At Ensay he used to pay for fruit to be delivered to the school. The Forests Commission thought the world of Bill; they called a creek Bill Ah Chow Creek. 
Bill died at Omeo, aged 74, in 1967.

Historical Information: town, parish, former railway station, former shire (1869 - 1994). A mining camp and settlement, starting with (Richard) Vining's Red Gate Shanty (on the site of the present library), sprang up as a result of gold being discovered in 1866 and 1867 in three areas nearby. The settlement was at first known as Red Gate (Diggings), from a gate in a fence just south of Ultima Thule Creek that was the boundary between the Mount Pleasant A and B pastoral runs, and was occasionally called the McKenzie Diggings (after Donald McKenzie of the Mount Pleasant A run). John Downey, who surveyed the town, planned to call the place Eglinton (after the pastoral run), but it was renamed (24 April 1867) in honour of "The Rose of Denmark", Princess Alexandra Caroline Marie Charlotte Louise Julie (1844 - 1925), who in 1863 married Albert Prince of Wales. (She became queen consort in 1901 when her husband became King Edward VII.) There is a marble statue of the Princess by Charles Summers (1827-78) in the Jack Shiel Gardens (q.v.). Alexandra is a feminine form of Alexander - Greek Alex-andros ('????-a?d???) "defender of men". See also Alexandra Timber Tramway and Museum, Lucky Mine Lookout, McKenzie Flora Reserve, McKenzie's Pinch and Ultima Thule Creek.

Historical Information:
The council purchased Alexandra Park for Ã¿Â£200 ($400) in 1896. This became the Mornington Football Club's home ground, and it is now home to Mornington Football Netball & Cricket Clubs. The Mornington Cricket Club was established in 1863.  By 1905 the reserve was fenced and charges were made for entry, half the proceeds going towards improvements.  It was listed among the civic assets by Cr F. Linley in his submission to the Railway Commissioners, noting then that money was being spent on football and cricket at the reserve. A further two acres (.8 hectare) were acquired there in 1948. 
Possibly named in honour of Queen Alexandra, mother of King George V who reigned between 1910-1936, and after who King Georges Ave in Mornington was named.

Alf Walker served as a member of the Brunswick Cycling Club Committee until his passing in 2016, providing 68 years as a continuous volunteer. During this time he assisted as Club Coach, Secretary and Treasurer. He was voted a life member of the club in 1958, and in 1986 was recognised as a life member of Cycling Victoria and Cycling Australia.

Named in recognition of  Alfred Deakin who was born in Fitzroy, Victoria, in 1856. He was a member of the Victorian parliament from 1880 - 1900 and was the member for Ballarat in Australia's first House of Representatives, and was Prime Minister three times.

Alfred Deakin retired from politics in 1913, and died in 1919.

Founded in 1871, The Alfred is the oldest Melbourne hospital that is operating on its original site. The hospital was built in honour of His Royal Highness, Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, who survived an assassination attempt in 1868 while visiting Australia. The people of Melbourne were so thankful for the safety of the Prince that they established a fund to build a hospital in his name.
Author: Alfred Health Victoria

Historical Information: Alfred Ingram was born in 1911. He owned a dairy farm in West Wodonga and part of McFarlane Hill. He supplied Wodonga businesses with wood obtained by ringbarking trees on the hill, chopping them down and carting them down the hill. In 1974, the Albury-Wodonga Development Corporation acquired his land.
Wodonga Pioneer was born in 1911 in Wagga and then move to Wodonga

Alfred Nicholas and his brother George developed the Aspro painkiller formula, becoming the first person to officially patent the formula after it was lost from general use after the First World War. He purchased the land in 1929 and proceeded to purchase subsequent land around it, extending the size of the property to 13 acres. The Burnham Beeches Estate is an Art Deco masterpiece, designed for Nicholas in the early thirties, and is somewhat likened to the lines of an ocean liner.

Nicholas traveled to many parts of Victoria and overseas to look for established trees to populate his gardens, designing it with a lake, rock pools, and ornamental designs. He hired an expert gardener to help with the creation of his prized garden.

The gardens were not finished before his death in 1937, although the majority of the planting had been finished. This then left his widow alone to look after the property, resulting in the garden falling into a state of deterioration.

The property has a long history of patronage and has gone through many phases and changes of ownership, including being a hotel, a Children's Hospital in the early 1940s, a research facility in the 1950s, with new extensions added to it in both the 1950s and 1980s.

After the property fell into a state of disrepair and became unused from the early 1990s, the Estate was purchased in 2010 to be upgraded and refurbished to modern standards.
Author: Yarra Ranges Tourism

Historical Information: Named for the proximity to the R.S.L Memorial Hall, and provides recognition of those persons who fought in World War I and World War II.

The Cairn was erected by Members of the Morwell, Yinnar and Boolarra sub-branches of the RSL, with assistance from the Morwell Shire Council.

Historical Information: In 1846 a schooner 'Apollo' sheltered in the bay on the way from Port Phillip to Portland. A township proposed to be named Middleton was surveyed on Apollo Bay. Farming began in 1864 along the Barham River flats, immediately south of the bay, by the Cawood family who in the next decade built a guest house. The combination of a relatively sheltered bay, the best of the limited flat land along the coast and the Cawood settlement finally stimulated the sale of town lots, renamed as Krambruk, in 1877. In 1898 the name Apollo Bay, by which the settlement was generally known, was formally adopted by the post office.

Historical Information: Arthur's Seat. This is possibly the oldest Scottish place name in Metropolitan Melbourne. Acting Lieutenant John Murray named the mountain when he entered Port Phillip Bay in the ship 'Lady Nelson' in January 1802, because it reminded him of Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh, his home city. The suburb subsequently took its name from the mountain.
Author: Ian Kendall

Historical Information: Arthurs Seat has long been a landmark on the Mornington Peninsula. It was named by Lieutenant John Murray in 1802. At the peak of Arthurs Seat is a hexagonal tower, built in 1936 for Victoria's centenary. It replaced the Eastern Shore Light, a timber structure originally located at McCrae and later moved to Arthurs Seat as a lookout. A plaque within the tower identifies that this point was used for trigonometric survey from as early as 1853, and was later used as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria. Arthurs Seat is significant as an early trigonometric survey point located on one of the earliest Port Phillip landmarks to be named by white colonisers. The tower that sits over the survey point and the surrounding area, has been assessed as being of State significance in the Flinders Heritage Study

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: Avondale Heights (Avondale in the Shetland Islands and Avondale Castle in Lanarkshire). Avondale is also found as a place name both in England and in Ireland. It has been suggested that the name of this suburb honours the Duke of Clarence and Avondale, the eldest son of the future King Edward VII, who died of pneumonia in 1892 (Barnes, 1964; Blake, 1977). If this is correct, then a Scottish connection could be claimed since Avondale is a noble Scottish title used occasionally by the British royal family. The royal title refers to Avondale Castle in South Lanarkshire, Scotland, also known as Strathaven Castle (now a ruin and a Scheduled Ancient Monument accessible to the public).

Historical Information:
Mount Alexander is a prominent, heavily timbered mountain just east of the main Melbourne-Bendigo road (Calder Highway) near Elphinstone. The original mark was a flagstaff supported by a stone pile. This was replaced in 1876 with the present structure, a circular cairn of mortared, granite blocks capped by a single course of stone. In form the cairn tapers slightly towards the top. It is about 2.7m high and 2.4m in diameter. The timber flagstaff was removed at some stage and a steel target on a timber post added. The last recorded repair to the cairn was the repointing of the mortar in 1966. Nearby are two transmission towers and associated buildings. One of only two examples of mortared stone geodetic triangulation station cairns, the other being at Macedon.
Alexander Geodetic Survey cairn was constructed in 1864, one of a series of survey points built as part of the Triangulation Survey of Victoria. This survey was designed to enable the survey of land throughout Victoria in response to a strong demand for freehold land. The Survey Department was unable to meet the demand using the marking of Geodetic Squares and a method using triangulation was proposed. This method would enable large areas to be rapidly surveyed. The geodetic survey process was directed by R.L.J. Ellery, starting in 1858 and completed by 1872. Alexander geodetic survey mark was built in 1864. Originally a wooden structure - a flagstaff supported by a pile of stones - by 1874 it was reported as falling into disrepair (2 Mount Alexander Mail, 19 Nov. 1874) In 1876 the original flagstaff was dismantled and a new granite cairn (extant) and flagstaff erected. A foundation stone was laid by a Miss Mathews, assisted by a Miss Richards, members of "several parties out enjoying the Queen's weather which prevailed on the anniversary of her birthday". Part of the original flagstaff was collected as a momento of the early days of the District's settlmenrt by a Mr Thornburn.(3 Mount Alexander Mail, 14 May,1876) It is not known if it survives.

Charles Daley and Edward Pescott, both former presidents of the Field Naturalists Club of Victoria and keen bushwalkers to out of the way places, had seen and were impressed by the 'jungles' of Mount Drummer; through them in 1924 and 1925 the club made representations to the Lands Department for the establishment of a reserve to protect this unusual plant community. The Minister for Lands, Alfred Downward, MLA, agreed to the request and 1358 ha of land on the south side of the highway was set aside for preservation of the scenery and native vegetation in January 1926. Later a further 832 ha to the north of the road was added mainly to preserve fine stands of Gippsland Waratah (Telopea oreades). Downward refused to have his surname used in the naming of the park, but agreed to it being called by his christian name, 'Alfred'
Author: Alan Farlay
Title: A Field Guide to the National Parks of Victoria

Historical Information:
Associated with the survey of the NSW - Victoria State Border. The Black-Allan line is a series of cairns and other survey marks that together enabled the survey of the NSW-Victoria state border. There are 41 known marks - 37 original. Each of the 41 marks are described
separately on this database. Of these, one is the site of a peg, four are blazed trees, 33 are stone cairns and three are concrete structures replacing earlier cairns. Three of the blazes are recent (Blaze Cairns 12/2 and 12/5, and Blaze Mound No. 9) as is one of the cairns (Border Cairn 12/5). These are associated with a survey to locate the original border survey marks and are of interest as a part of recent surveying history. A survey to determine the border of New South Wales and Victoria was undertaken in 1870-72, twenty years after the two colonies were separated. The need to define the border on the ground arose due to the increasing settlement in this mountainous country, especially the advent of gold mining around the Bendoc region. The eastern end of the border at Conference Point (Cape Howe) was established in 1868 by NSW Surveyor-General P.F. Adams and R.J.L. Ellery for Victoria. The western end, at Forest Hill, is the source of the Murray River. It was marked by Alexander Black in 1870. Black proceeded to undertake an eleven month survey to mark the border on the ground between
Forest Hill and Allan's Peg, a peg positioned near the Delegate River by Senior Geodetic surveyor Alexander Allan. To achieve the simple "straight line" border across mountainous country involved enormous hard work under difficult conditions. Ellery writing about the geodetic Survey of Victoria in 1891 described the survey as "a piece of
survey work which for difficulties and for the requirement of skills, anergy and endurance, as well as for accuracy attained I believe has never been surpassed". Black's survey traversed very difficult terrain, covering 61.5 kilometres over 11 months. Allan's survey was 114 kilometres long, extending over 18 months. Over 50 marks were built by the surveyors and their teams. Some were substantial stone cairns. The surveyors also had to dig trenches to indicate the direction of the border, and clear the line of vegetation. The Black-Allan line border survey is of state significance as evidence of an outstanding surveying feat, testing the endurance and skill of the survey parties, and providing a dramatic demonstration of the difficulties encountered by surveyors in the nineteenth century. Historically, the marking of the border between New South Wales and Victoria symbolised a step in the development
of Victorian as a separate, self-governing region.

Historical Information: Arthur Sfetcopoulos was born on 14 October 1919 on Opserina, Greece. As a young man he served in the Greek Army during the Second World War. In February 1951 he migrated to Australia, leaving his wife, Sofia, and three young children behind in Greece. He landed in Melbourne and worked in cafes or restaurants and on vegetable farms in the Werribee area for about two years. In January 1953, Sofia and their children joined him in Melbourne. They lived in Werribee where they shared farmland with his brothers in law, growing vegetables on the property. In June 1955, Arthur and his family re-located to Shepparton, where he worked on orchards until October 1958. Then, Arthur and his eldest son, Michael, purchased an orchard on Verney Road from the Robinett family. They worked the orchard together until 2004, when due to Arthur's old age, it was decided to follow his dream and subdivide the land to a family oriented housing estate. Arthur was a pro-active member of the local Greek community and the Shepparton Greek Orthodox church. Arthur passed away on 23 July 2006.

In honour of Arthur Sfetcopoulos, a local orchardist who owned the land that was subdivided to later become Arthur Park estate.  Arthur Sfetcopoulos was also a proactive member of the local Greek community.

Historical Information:
B.A. Cairns Reserve was developed in the 1880s as a sports venue for cricket and football, but was also used for gymkhanas and stock auctions.  In the 1970s it was named after Bertie Alexander Cairns (1895-1979), a member of the pioneering Cairns family, in acknowledgment of his tireless dedication to the care and maintenance of the sporting reserve.
Bert did so much valued service, especially for the Park and Cricket Club. He was also a very good golfer. As a General Carrier for many years, he transported fish and other produce to the markets and brought goods back for the farmers and residents.
He is buried with his wife in the Flinders Cemetery.
B J Hubbard was a Councillor for the City of Ringwood in 1960.

The change of the school's name appears to have coincided with the decline of mining, as the Welcome mine (1866) finally closed in 1910.

A written submision was made to Council by Mr & Mrs Pedretti.

Mr Donald Baidwyn noted that the park area which was land deemed for recreational use when the developer was given permission to develop the Orchard Circuit/Dunstan Court Estate as part of the planning for that estate, was undeveloped. He called on local residents in the area for their support and organised contact with local councillors to meet with residents at a park BBQ held on the site, which was met with a very positive response. Mr Baldwyn had plans drawn up for submission to council for their approval. The plans were adapted for what the park is now. He collected donations from residents for the purchase of trees/shrubs for the area in addition to what council gave so that the area would be well covered around the outer boundaries. Once these trees were purchased, and the land semi developed by council, he organised a working bee for the planting of these trees and shrubs. He also developed a roster for the watering and care of these plants to assist in their early establishment. To this day, he still tends to the park, inspecting the plants for care and the grassed area to see if it needs watering. The park is much used by families as an area to fly kites, kick the footy, play soccer and football, and is also used by some elderly as a walking area, where they may take a seat when they tire, or to just watch the world go by in a peaceful environment, thanks to his foresight in developing this area.

Historical Information:
In terms of dictionaries of Victorian placenames, there is a consensus that Ballan is a toponym transplanted from north Ireland. For example, according to Saxton (1907: 8), Ballan was named by 'Mr. Robt. Von Steiglitz [sic] after a property in the north of Ireland, where he was born'. The Ballan Times accepted Saxton's interpretation (Ballan Times, 21 November 1912 in Ballan Shire Historical Society 1989: 4). Thomas O'Callaghan (1918: 25) was more expansive 'The village of Ballan was surveyed in 1850 by Assistant Surveyor Malcolm. Mr. Hoddle, in forwarding the plan, wrote that His Honour the Superintendent had named the village "Ballan". That was the name of a pastoral station close to the village, and then owned by Robert von Stieglitz. He had named it after an estate in Ireland'. O'Callaghan identified his information sources as W. Thorn, Chief Draughtsman, Lands Department, and J.G. Saxton's (1907) publication. Later dictionaries, such as A.E. Martin (1944: 8) and L.B.J. Blake (1977: 30) are derived from Saxton and O'Callaghan and do not add any further information. Massola (1968) does not assert that Ballan is an Aboriginal placename. The possibility that Ballan may have an Aboriginal origin was first raised in Clark and Haydon (2002: 21), and revolves around Ballan being a contraction of Ballindyapp. Robert William von Stieglitz occupied a run he named 'Ballan' (Ballen), 4,836 acres on the right bank of the Werribee River at Ballan in April 1838, and his brother, John Lewis von Stieglitz occupied an adjoining run named 'Ballanee', 16,000 acres north of Ballan in 1838 (Billis and Kenyon 1974: 170). Emma von Stieglitz (nee Cowie), wife of John, has provided us with a pictorial record of early Ballan, and one water colour sketch is entitled 'First settlement at Balindyeapp, Ballan, 1839. Victoria'. A second sketch is entitled 'Balindyeapp, Port Phillip, Septr. 1839'. In an edited publication of Emma von Stieglitz's sketchbook, the editor K.R. von Stieglitz has noted that 'Robert von Stieglitz's original quarters on the Balindyeapp, Ballindyapp, or Ballan station (there were numerous spellings) stood on the crest of slope immediately west of the Werribee' (von Stieglitz 1964: Figure 1, n.p.).

Thus it is argued here that Ballan, which is a likely contraction of Balindyeapp, was favoured by von Stieglitz because of its similarity with his birthplace in Ireland. This may be an example of what Kostanski (2009: 177) has understood as 'Anglo-Indigenous placename production, wherein the primary aim of adopting an Indigenous name for colonial landscape identification reflected an imperialist vision, overlooking or little concerned with the true meaning of significance of the names', in this case, Balindyeapp. Thus Ballan may be another example of polysemy, or then again its similarity may be purely coincidental.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: The Ballarat Avenue of Honour is a memorial avenue of about 3,800 trees, extending about 22 kilometres north-west from Alfredton. In May 1917, Mrs Tillie Thomson (a director of the local textile company, E. Lucas & Co.) proposed that trees be planted in honour of the local men and women who enlisted during the first world war.  With practical advice and assistance from many, about 500 employees of the company (the Lucas girls) planted the first 1,000 trees on 3 June 1917, and the final trees on 16 August 1919.

Historical Information: Balnarring is a beach resort south of Bittern on the western shore of Western Port Bay. It is most probably a corruption of the name of the early pastoral run taken up by the Meyrick brothers (Alfred, Maurice) and their cousin Henry in 1840 called 'Ballanrong' (Billis and Kenyon 1974: 114). Variant spellings of the station name include 'Ballyrungen' (Meyrick 1939: 135); Ballanarong; Ballanrong; Ballarong; Ballyrangue; Ballerangan (Meyrick 1939: 171). Meyrick (1939: 171) is clearly of the view that it is an Aboriginal placename as he notes that 'Ball or Balla meaning a camp is very common' and cites his source as A.S. Kenyon. According to Massola (1968: 8), Balnarring is from Balbalnarring, bal = camp, narring = hair, beard. Blake (1977: 32) posits that it is 'possibly fr. Abor. bael, gumtree, and "narang", little, or fr. Ballymering, Irish bally for "land belonging to"'. Gardner (1996: 27) has translated the name as 'hair camp'. Barry Blake (1991: 82) notes that the east Kulin word for 'beard' is 'ngarrin'; 'hair' is 'yarra', 'camp' is 'yilam' or 'wilam' which also mean 'bark'; 'red gum' is 'bial', and 'little' is 'waigurrk' or 'wayibu'. The Aboriginal origin of the placename Balnarring is contested only by Les Blake, and given the weight of the evidence supporting an Aboriginal origin, Blake's Irish etymology may be regarded as spurious.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: The Meyrick brothers used the name, taken from Aboriginal words meaning "gum tree" and "little", for their pastoral station established in 1840. Historical Information:
The Barbers were one of Somerville's early well-known nursery families.
In the mid-1800s, Claude Barber settled on a property in Lower Somerville Road. He then bought a 60-acre (24 hectare) property in Eramosa Road which was the first property on the Mornington Peninsula with the name of "Western Port". The original drive into the homestead was located in the area of today's Jordan Street. Barber Reserve is part of a former paddock on the farm property.  The orchard covered approximately 40 acres (16 hectares).

Community consultation to name the park occurred in 2014. The name Barclay was suggested by the Greensborough Historical Society as an option. Their records indicate that in the 1940's this part of Greensborough comprised 5 to 10 acre farmlets, one of which was home to the Barclay family. Henry Barwell Barclay, his wife Dorothy and their six month old son Eric moved to a 10 acre holding at Grace Park, at the end of Henry Street where it intersects with Elder Street, Greensborough in 1938. This farmlet stood where Gladman Street in now located (approximately 350 m south of McKenzie Court). Henry Barclay worked locally, in the market garden at nearby Yallambie House, a mansion on large acreage that fronted the Plenty River, and the produce merchant Stubley's in Greensborough, where he loaded wheat. Henry Barclay died in November 1959.

Historical Information: Locality north-west of Nillahcootie. Large pastoral run (34,000 ha, 1840-72), north and north-west of Mansfield (originally part of Watson and Hunter's Run). Wells listed the name in 1848 as "Barjoog". The Barjarg Saw Mill (ca.1919) was owned by George Duncan Howes. Les Blake suggests Barjarg "possibly derives fr. Abor. baadjur, black woman, or bartja, wild cherry tree"; only if the Taungurong had European colonies! William Francis Hunter Arundel, licensee (1841-48) of the Barjarg run, came from Barjarg near Craigenputtock, Scotland [Mansfield Hist. Soc.]. (There are four Barjarg place-names in the Dumfries & Galloway area.) Gaelic bàrr, top, height, and dearg, red.

Historical Information: (1160 m alt.), Mount Torbreck. In the early 1940s grazier Victor Roy Newman had a cook-house and camp here; and the Forests Commission built a number of huts to assist with salvaging timber killed by the 1939 fires. John Aylmer Barnewall (1812?-99) acquired a grazing licence in the area in 1870, and his son, Sir John (Robert) Barnewall (1881 - 1936) had timber interests in the Rubicon forest. The surname was originally de Berneval, and derives from the French place-name of Berneval (Haute Normandie). [Sir Reginald Barnewall, Clem Earp, Brian Lloyd, Leonie Taylor]

In 1797 George Bass explored and named Western Port Bay. He noted that fresh water was obtainable from the creek on the eastern side, ie Bass River, and named the eastern cape of Phillip Island Wollamai. Samuel Anderson's homestead became the place for surveying a village in 1863. It was named Woolamai, and kept that name until 1896 when it was changed to Bass.

(548 m alt.), Mansfield. Hill, named (2 December 1824) by explorers Alexander Hume and William Hilton Hovell because it resembled a military earthwork or fortress. Also called Battery Hill and Mount Beolite. Aboriginal (Taungurong) name Bayolite (Robinson, journal, 12 May 1840); Clark & Heydon (D) give Bayolite and Baalwite (error?). Massola (1968) implies that Beolite was the Taungurong name for Mount Battery but other writers give Beolite as a Taungurong personal name. The Mount Battery pastoral run (about 14,000 ha, 1840 or 1846-66) was originally part of Watson and Hunter's Run. See also Beolite and Little Battery.

Historical Information: Named after Frederick Bayles (1884-1915), the first member of the Railway Construction Branch to be killed in World War One. Frederick arrived in Melbourne in August 1913, enlisted on August 20th,1914 and was killed in action at Gallipoli on May 8th, 1915. Bayles was the station on the Strzelecki line (opened June 29, 1922) for the Yallock Village settlement. The Bayles Railway Station closed February 1959.

Historical Information: The site was originally used as a quarry and was named Bayview Quarry. Later the site was acquired by BORAL (Bitumen Oil Refineries of Australia Ltd). Council has granted leases for parts of the site to SP AusNet, Reverse Art truck, and Telstra/Optus for the purposes of power generation, recycling, and telecommunications respectively. The site has now become a public reserve.

Historical Information: Named after Benjamin Disraeli, the Earl of Beaconsfield. Disraeli was the British Prime Minister 1868, 1874-1880. Some sources say that on the day he died in 1881 (April 19) a deputation waited on the Victorian Minister of Railways to have a station built at what is now Beaconsfield, however this incorrect as the railway station had opened December 1, 1879. The Post Office had opened on October 1st, 1878. Beaconsfield means "open land near a beacon or signal fire". The town was originally called Little Berwick.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: The site of Belmont was settled by Dr Alexander Thomson in 1836. Thomson, a pioneer preacher and pastoralist named his holding Kardinia. The area now comprising the Belmont Common was a lagoon, and Thomson's Kardinia homestead was situated on the edge of rising ground. Westwards the ground rises towards the Barrabool Hills, which may be the source of the name of Belmont, a word of French or Italian origin for a fine or pretty hill. In 1861 the Belmont town was proclaimed as a settlement south of the Barwon River.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information:
The Maw family donated the land to Council in 1964 and was proposed as one of 3 names for the reserve.

The reserve was named after Benbenjie who was of the Boon wurrung tribe which lived in the Wonga (McCrae) area during the McCrae's occupation and he is said to have taught the McCrae children how to hunt and fish.

Named in honour of local Boon wurrung man Benbenjie who lived in this area, known as the Wonga region.  Benbenjie taught the McCrae children how to hunt and fish, showing them how to make equipment such as boomerangs and spears.

The name was given by the Haughton family who owned land in the area in the early twentieth century.  The family name for their land was 'Glen Agnes Bend of Islands Estate' and later, 'Bend of Islands Estate'.

'The late J.E. Foreman, J. P., of St. Kilda, informed the compiler that when a boy he had been present when a fight occurred between two diggers to settle a question of alleged encroachment on a mining claim.  The smaller of the combatants won the fight, and was applauded by the 'diggers,' who cried out 'Bravo Bendigo, Bravo - we'll call this place Bendigo.' 'Bendigo' was then the sobriquet of an English prize fighter.  This occurred on Fenton's Station, as it was then called.  In December, 1852, the name was officially declared to be 'Castleton' ; but in January, 1953, it was renamed 'Sandhurst.' In 1891 the name 'Bendigo' was reverted to.'

Historical Information: 'The Committee is concerned at the lack of uniformity in the spelling of Bendoc/Bendock in relation to a mountain, river, parish and town near the Victoria/ New South Wales Border.  In a pamphlet entitled 'Back to Bendoc School' it was discovered that the name originated from Benjamin Boyd's pastoral station 'Ben's Dock'.  However, a letter received from the Shire of Orborst dated 20th September, 1966 informed the committee that local sentiment wished to retain the spelling Bendoc.  This desire was shared by the Progress Association.  The matter was finalised when the decision of the Minister of Lands was published in the Victoria Government Gazette on the 29th May, 1968, proclaiming the town to be spelt Bendoc.'
Author: Place Names Committee Files
Title: Letter

Historical Information: An Aboriginal name which, according to Blake (1977, p. 38), was formerly 'wagra bendoc' and means 'plain of the crows' or 'noise in the trees'.  'Bendock' was the name of John Hensleigh's station in 1842.  Benjamin Boyd (1796-1851) also had an outstation of that name in this district.  Suggestions that the name derives from Ben's dock (a yard for Ben's stock) cannot be true because the name was in use before Boyd took up a run in the area.  The mining town of Bendoc was originally surveyed and proclaimed as Wagra in 1872, but the name was altered to Bendock in 1886 (reflecting local preference) and the spelling was amended to Bendoc in 1951. [Research by I.D. Clark and D.A. Cahir, University of Ballarat, 2005.]

Historical Information: Also Bayolite. Parish south-east of Mansfield and north of Delatite. Beolite was proposed, but not adopted, for the town of Mansfield (q.v.). According to George Augustus Robinson, Biteruc or Bittertuc, leader (ngurangaeta) of the Yowung-illam-balluk band of the Taungurong, was called "Bay.er.lite . . . after the hill" (Mount Battery) by early Europeans in the Delatite River area. Other accounts say Biteruc or Beolite had a wife (or daughter-in-law) Delatite, and a son Barwite (Robinson's "Parg.wite"). Brough Smyth (1878) says that the place was also called Badlwite, but this seems like a mistake for Barwite. See also Barwite, Delatite, Mount Battery and Taungurong Creek.

Historical Information: Bernard Cox (1950-75) was the longest serving Border Stock Inspector at Wodonga. Bernie was also a Shire Councillor and was widely acknowledged as the "architect" behind the relocation of the saleyards. His role in the selection of the "McGeoch Site" was critical to the success of Council keeping the Saleyards within the Wodonga Shire despite the vigorous opposition of the Albury Wodonga Development Corporation. He was on the Saleyard's Committee for six years including the last two as Chairman (1969-1970). In 1974 Bernard Cox was appointed as part time Victorian Member for the Albury Wodonga Corporation until his death in 1977.

Historical Information: The school name reflects the name of the developer's estate "The Chase", giving the school a local identity supported by the community.

The site for the school was once part of a farm owned by WJT Clarke, a wealthy pastoralist and landowner.  The homestead on the farm was first known as 'The Springs' and later as 'Springfield'.  It was a model dairy farm and a significant example of Clarke's scientific farming methods.  'Berwick Fields' was chosen as the school name following community consultation.  It acknowledges the name of the area and the name of the original farm.

Historical Information: "Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the Lord delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married." Isaiah 62:4 was the inspiration the McKenzie family, devout  local Presbyterians, took when they named this tiny town Beulah in 1891.
Author: Aussie Towns

Historical Information: Beulah is a small town in the southern Mallee region of Victoria, some 395 km north-west of Melbourne. According to O'Callaghan (1918: 29), the placename is derived from the Biblical Beulah from Isaiah 62, 4. 'Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken, neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate, but thou shall be called Hephzi-bah and thy land Beulah, for the Lord delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married' (Martin 1944: 14). Massola (1968) does not assert that Beulah is an Aboriginal placename. According to L. Blake (1977: 39f), 'various meanings such as Abor. Belar, red ochre; Biblical, fruitful land; and Eng. Names, e.g. B. Spa in Norwood, have been given but first selector Alex McKenzie from Beauly, Scot'. Les Blake is the only source for the dissonant etymology, and it may be disregarded as mere speculation on his part.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information:
Bill Carroll spoke at the 1967 Annual General meeting of the Merricks Yacht Club, for the need of the young people of Merricks Beach to have a focal point in which to spend their evenings and leisure time, suggesting the need for a club house. Commodore Thiemeyer wrote to the Foreshore Committee and approval for the construction of a club house was given. A sum of $4,000 was raised and club house was commenced in November, 1968.

The Bill Carroll, or Palmers Hill Road Reserve is a small area of native vegetation at Merricks Beach. It was created in 1993 due to the interest of a group of Merricks Beach residents. A Committee of Management was formed to draw up a plan for submission to the Hastings Council and the area, which had formerly been grazing land, underwent a transformation to become a nature reserve.

Historical Information:
Billlimina shelter is an impressive rock overhang where Jardwadjali (Yard-wa-jali) camped from time to time and left many red paintings. Archaeologists who excavated this site in 1976 found stone tools and the remains of plant and animal foods. These materials demonstrated that groups camped here from late winter to early summer and caught kangaroos and small mammals such as bandicoots, possums and bettongs. They also collected emu eggs and freshwater mussles. 
The most interesting aspect of the paintings at Billimina is the many bars arranged in horizontal rows. These marked are believed to have been used to count events in retelling stories or to record the number of days spent at a place. While they are sometimes difficult to see, there are also emus, kangaroo and emu tracks, and 55 human stick figures painted here.

Historical Information: In 1839 an Aboriginal mission station was established about six kilometres south of Birregurra on the Barwon River. The station ceased in 1851. One of its overseers, a Captain Bowden, had his name given to the place (Bowden's Point) where the Cape Otway road crossed the river, and that place subsequently became Birregurra. It is thought that the name was derived from an Aboriginal word describing 'kangaroo camp' or (less likely) referring to a bend in the river.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: The Wadawurrung people were created by Bunjil, the spirit creator, at Kareet Bareet, now known as Black Hill near Gordon, not far from Ballaarat. Bunjil gathered clay from the mountain, and divided into two and placed it on sheets of bark, then formed it into the shape of two men. Bunjil's brother Palian, controller of the waters, began to thump the water with his hands, the water becoming thicker and thicker, taking on the shape of two women. The men were presented with hunting spears, and the women were presented with digging sticks, to dig edible roots and yams. This area was once covered in forest but is now largely a farming community, due to the rich volcanic soils. That is why the Wadawurrung are known as the red soil people.
Author: Bryon Powell

Historical Information: Ridge running north from Mount Murrindindi to the Strathbogie Ranges, but broken in the middle by the Goulburn River at Molesworth, between Mount Cunningham and Mount Concord. The Acheron Valley is lined on the west side by the Black Range, and on the east side by the Blue and Cathedral Ranges. Black Range may have been chosen as an allusion to the dark connotation of the word Acheron (q.v.), and Blue Range may be a pun on black ("black and blue"). The Black Range corresponds fairly closely with the territory of the Waring-illam-balluk band of the Taungurong, so it is just possible that the original name may have been the Blacks' Range.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: originally the Blacks' Spur. Forested ridge west and south-west of the Dom Dom Saddle (q.v.). The name is also used for the section of Maroondah Highway from Fernshaw (q.v.) to the Dom Dom Saddle (where it crosses the Great Divide) and a little beyond. There had long been an Aboriginal trail here, and it (or one close to it) was opened up as part of the early packhorse track to Woods Point. Massola says the name was adopted after some of John Carter and William Phillippe's teamsters met John Green (inspector for the Central Board to Watch over the Interests of Aborigines), William Barak, Simon Wonga (the elder) and a long line of Koories at the spur. Barwick writes that "Green had secured Board permission to cut a new track through the bush in a direct line from Yering* to the headwaters of the Goulburn River - to 'benefit the miners' who were now moving into this district in search of gold." E.E.H. (quoted by Mitchell), writing in 1934, said that Aboriginals guided some of the early miners over the spur. See also Acheron Aboriginal Station and Mount Dom Dom.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Cerberean Ranges. The Blue and Cathedral Ranges look blue in a painting by Eugene von Guerard (see under Cathedral Range), but the Blue Range is neither bluer nor blacker than the Black Range (q.v.). Blue might refer to the flowers of the abundant mint bush, Prostanthera melissifolia, but this occurs on the Black Range as well. For further comment on these names, see Black Range. Note that the South Blue Range, south of Mansfield, is sometimes called just the Blue Range; and there is a (North) Blue Range* north of Mansfield near Mount Samaria.

Historical Information: Originally in the 1850's the parkland was a quarry. As the area developed local identity John Barratt established a farm in the 1860s on top of the nearby hill in Harding Street. A copy of the auction notice confirmed the name 'Bluebell Hill' when John Barratt placed the farm on the market in 1868. The name also provides consistency alongside the existing tennis facility established in the reserve that has previously changed its name to Bluebell Hill Tennis Club.

Historical Information: Robert (Bob) Corbould was a well known local ornithologist and naturalist and long-time member of the Sunraysia Field Naturalist Club.  The area was previously known as Rifle Butt Swamp.
Bob Crosby built a successful machinery business and was a Wodonga councillor from 1991 to 1994.  He was Wodonga Hospital Board president and active in the Apex, Lions and local golf clubs.

In 1981 the Bob Pettitt Reserve, named in honour of the long-serving councillor R.W. Pettitt (27 years), was officially opened at Jan Juc on February 26. It was funded by a Government grant of $50,000, a local contribution of $10,000, and $60,000 from Council funds.

Historical Information: It was named after Mount Bogong (1986 m) which is 12 km north-east. Mount Bogong is one of several places of high elevation to which the bogong moth emigrates during the summer months. The moths were harvested and eaten for their high fat content by Aborigines. It is thought that the word bogong was derived from an Aboriginal word describing the moth.

Historical Information: Strathbogie Ranges. Locality at the junction of Bonnie Doon, Boundary and Upper Boho Roads. (There is also a parish of Boho*.) Massola (1968) regards Boho as Aboriginal, meaning "young wattle tree". If so, the word would be Taungurong. Les Blake, however, says it was named after Boho, Co. Fermanagh: in this case Irish Botha, huts, cottages. Halsall (1978: 69 - 74) reprints extracts from a history of Boho South, but this incorrectly mentions "a small group of islands off the coast of Northern Ireland". See also Strathbogie North.

Brankeet Inlet. Township, former railway stations; originally Doon (and occasionally called Brankeet as it is in that parish). According to both Martin and Reed (1973), named Doon by Thomas Nixon. Saxton agrees but adds "Suggested by Miss Dougald [sic] of Wappan", who was Mary Fraser Dougall, sister of Ann Bon. Leonie Taylor of Thornton supports this connexion (as do Chatham et al.). Joan Gillison says that Ann Bon wanted the name Bonnie Doon from the outset, but surveyor John Hardy insisted on just Doon. It was renamed in 1891, with the arrival of the railway, to distinguish it from Dooen* (near Horsham*). Most of the site of the original township is normally under the waters of the Brankeet Inlet. The railway station (closed 1978) and many houses were rebuilt on or moved to higher ground in 1955 because of the enlargement of Lake Eildon. The River Doon near Ayr, Scotland, is Gaelic: Dian, Dèan, probably the name of a Celtic goddess known to the Picts as Dewa or Dewona, and to the Romans as Divona. A ship called the Bonnie Doon plied between Melbourne and Hobart in 1854 (Les Blake). The words "bonie Doon" occur in three songs by Robert Burns, "Sweet Are the Banks", "The Banks o' Doon" and "Ye Flowery Banks".
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Rises in the Strathbogie Ranges, north of Golden Mountain, and eventually becomes the Brankeet Inlet. (The creek used to be a tributary of the Delatite River.) Jefferies (p. 11) mentions a Doon River and this, if not an error, may have been another name for the creek. Also recorded as Boranket Creek (Edward Barnett's survey of 1850). The creek originally fed a large swamp which was drained in the 1890s (government relief scheme). Gold discovered 1888; alluvial gold was worked in the 1930s (Chatham et al.). In the early 1860s a Ballarat mining company successfully mined a deeper lead, moving in the direction of Bowenvale, then known as Chinaman's Flat. In the 1870s Chinaman's Flat was named Bowenvale, after Sir George Bowen, Governor of Victoria (1873-79).

Historical Information:
A letter was received from Mr Morris Bradbury who wrote to council suggesting the Clover Avenue playground reserve was donated by his parents over fifty years ago. The information supplied by Mr Bradbury was confirmed via research by the Wodonga Place Names Committee (PNC), and showed rate records in 1948 had Elliott William Bradbury paying rates on 15 acres around the Clover Avenue area. 
Mr and Mrs Elliot and May Bradbury purchased a large parcel of land bounded by Chapple Street, London Road and the then Tallangatta Road (now Thomas Mitchell Drive) and in time subdivided it. Newspaper reports in 1951 refer to the development as Bradbury Estate. The Bradbury estate names included Gralen Street - named from two of their five sons Gra(ham) and Len, Glenview for a favored racehorse, Spring because it was fed by a small spring, Clover because it grew abundantly in the area, and Colman and Docking for Ted Colman and Bob Docking who bought land for their homes.
The Bradbury family lived in Chapple Street but set aside a block in Clover Avenue for use as a playground and recreational area still locally known as 'Bradbury's little park' by the older locals.
Elliott William Bradbury died in 1957 and his widow May remarried Clarrie Sutton. In the early 1970's May also donated the land in Chapple Street on which the St John Ambulance building was built.
'Named after James Charles Leslie Braddy.  Councillor 1943 - 1952 (9 yrs.)  Mayor 1948 - 1949.'

Historical Information: Parish, south of Brankeet Creek from Woodfield to Bonnie Doon. Aboriginal (Taungurong): the name of a local swamp (Les Blake). Massola (1968) says Brankeet was a swamp on "Borodomanin Creek", but he may have misinterpreted Brough Smyth's (1878) "swamp on Borodomanin" which probably refers to the pastoral run. Historical Information: Rises in the Strathbogie Ranges, north of Golden Mountain, and eventually becomes the Brankeet Inlet. (The creek used to be a tributary of the Delatite River.) The original name might have been Borodomanin Creek (see Borodomanin), though this may be a misunderstanding (see previous entry). Jefferies (p. 11) mentions a Doon River and this, if not an error, may have been another name for the creek. Also recorded as Boranket Creek (Edward Barnett's survey of 1850). The creek originally fed a large swamp which was drained in the 1890s (government relief scheme). Gold discovered 1888; alluvial gold was worked in the 1930s (Chatham et al.). See also Raspberry Creek (2).

Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: After migrating to Australia in 1949, Branko Palavestra opened a mixed business in Phillips St, Wodonga. His self-built corner store was the first delicatessen selling various imported goods sought after by the growing migrant community. He spoke seven languages and was always in high demand by migrants wanting him to translate for them.

Historical Information: The Education Department purchased the Wheatsheaf Road site in 1906, and in April 1908, 53 pupils moved into a new wooden building on the site. The first head teacher of the school was Miss Bridget Shortell. The appointment of a female to this position in that era was not common. Miss Shortell was the only female head teacher of the school on the site. Glenroy Primary School was amalgamated with the Glenroy North Primary School in July 2010, interestingly the first principal of the new school (Glenroy Central Primary School) is also a female.

Historical Information:
The Arboretum commemorates the men who were killed in a helicopter crash near Wandiligong in 1978, 

The Bright Memorial Arboretum is situated in Mountbatten Avenue, Bright. This area, originally a Forests Commission Victoria Pine Nursery, was converted into a Seed Garden in 1973 with the aim of supplying seed for the Forests Commission Victoria nurseries at Macedon and Creswick. A wide variety of trees were planted, not all were successful.

A helicopter carrying out a fuel-reduction burning operation crashed near Wandiligong on 19 April 1978, and two Forest Officers, Peter Collier and Stan Gillett and  the pilot, John Byrnes, lost their lives. It was decided to develop the former Seed Garden into a Memorial Arboretum in memory of those killed.

The Memorial Arboretum was officially opened on 14 December 1984.

Historical Information:
Henry Dendy, born in 1800 in Surry, had never been to Australia when he bought more than 5000 acres of land in Melbourne. Dendy inherited a fortune in farming assets from his father Samuel, sold up, and in 1841 put his name down for a big chunk of land at one pound per acre. He made the voyage to Australia with his wife and young son. Due to the increasing value of land in Melbourne, Dendy was now sitting on a huge fortune. But the colonial authorities in Sydney introduced new rules, and Dendy could only claim land further away from the city than expected. The area he claimed, first known as Waterville, quickly became known as Brighton after the seaside town in England. Dendy took on as his agent, the prominent colonial stockbroker, and politician Jonathan Binns, and together they built the beginnings of a village community. Brighton's central crescent streets were drawn up and there were plans to subdivide the land and realize the huge fortune that now seemed inevitable for Dendy. But fate intervened.

By the early 1840s, the wool industry had stagnated, widespread drought had hit the agricultural sector and a financial crisis in Britain scared investors away from the colonies. 1843 saw the collapse of the Bank of Australia and the economic outlet was grim. Henry Dendy's dreams of huge land sale prices in Brighton evaporated, along with a plan to sell plots to immigrants from Britain. The scheme was also hampered by the lack of a local freshwater supply and the area's distance from Melbourne. In the end, Dendy was forced to sell up to pay creditors. Much of the land ended up being sold to JB Were, to whom Dendy was also in debt. By the late 1840s, Dendy had started a brewing house in Geelong to recover the debt. 

His home was sold, and Dendy wandered to Yarra Glen with his wife where he ran sheep once the wool industry had recovered. For a while, he ran a mill at Eltham and eventually saved enough to travel back to England, but later returned to Victoria. His wife died and Dendy wound up living with his son, who drove a steam train at a gold mine in Walhalla. That's where Dendy died penniless in February 1881, in a modest bush shack, and was buried at Walhalla cemetery.
Author: Mitchell Toy
Title: Brighton founder Henry Dendy's rags to riches story

Historical Information: An anglicized version of Scot's Gaelic word Sruthan, meaning a 'small stream' or 'creek' used by Angus McMillian to describe the area where his exploration party camped at the confluence of Deep Creek and the Tambo River during his first expedition to the area in April 1840. 'An Sruthan' is the name of a town on the Isle of Skye 28km from Angus McMillian's birthplace of Glenbrittle and 14 km from Orbost, on the road to Berinsdale, which the Victorian town of Bairnsdale is named after. In Perthshire, 'Sruthan' is pronounced slightly differently, meaning 'stream-place'.

Historical Information: Buchan is the name of a village, river and tourist cave in Gippsland. Howitt (1904: 80) observed that Bukkan-munji is 'now written Buchan, and is supposed to be a Scotch name given by some early settler from North Britain. It should properly be spelled as I have written it, being the native name for the bag in which the Kurnai carries various articles. Bukkan-munji means bag there or the place of the bag'. George Augustus Robinson (Jnl 22/6/1844 in Clark 2000a) has suggested another etymology a propos another placename similar to Bukkan-munji: 'Fish are called munje, hence the compound Munberlemunje and so on'. William Thomas (in Pepper and De Araugo 1985: 120) considered it derived from Buccan 'stack of rocks with a hole in it'. This rendition is supported by Roberts (1977: 14) who locates Bukkan munji at the Buchan River and Tarra Creek junction where the rock folds. Saxton (1907: 13) in one entry asserts it has its origin in Scotland, however in 'Additions and Corrections' he notes 'Native name for the bag in which the Kurnai carries various articles. Buk Kan Mungi means bag there or the place of the bag. The Native Tribes of S.E. Australia, A.W. Howitt, 1904. Instead of Scotland' (Saxton 1907: 3). Martin (1944: 18) has recorded that 'Buk kan, natives' word for a bag they carried. Buk Kan Mungi was said to mean 'place of the bag'. According to Massola (1968: 14), Buchan is derived from 'Bukkan-munji, bag there, the place of the bag'. Blake (1977: 49) notes that in 1839 it was the name of Bayliss' station derived from buchan buchan, smoke-signal expert, or bukkan munjie, place of grass bag. Seddon (1994: 62) accords the meaning 'women's article'. The Buchan Sesquicentenary Committee (1989) translates mungie as water. Clark (1999) notes that bukin; bugin in Wiradjuri also refers to a medicine man of supernatural ability. Gardner (1992: 17) translates Bukkanmungie as 'place of the woman's bag'. This placename may be an example of polysemy, a toponym with multiple etymologies that was deliberately selected because of its polysemy.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: It has been argued that the word is a corruption of a local Kurnai Aboriginal expression "buchan buchan" meaning "smoke signal expert" or "bukkan munjie", meaning "the place of the grass bag". Equally some sources claim that George Robinson, the Protector of Aborigines, called the local area and the Aboriginal people "buckin" meaning "a mass of rocks with holes in it".

Historical Information: Buckley, an early Irish pioneer, came to Balnarring as a selector in 1861. He took up dairying and also raised pigs and potatoes. The 32 hectares of the reserve were once part of his selection and was set aside as a reserve in 1970
To commemorate a notable pioneer in the district.

Buckley Park High School commenced classes in 1963.  Its name was changed to Buckley Park Secondary College in the early 1990s.  Following consultation with the school community in 2001, a new name was proposed as part of a project to enhance the school's image in the local community.  The school takes its name from the nearby 'Buckley Park', which was named after a major landowner in the 19th century.

Historical Information: Traditional Name: Buluk Explanation: lake Discussion on Current Name: Buloke is the general word for 'lake' in Djadjawurrung, which is used here to refer to a specific lake. In this case, it can actually be shown that the general term took over from the specific one since the lake was known as Lake Banyenong (Hercus 1999),  Hartmann in Smyth 1878b: 176.
Author: Clark, Ian and Heydon, Toby

Historical Information: The shire's name came from Lake Buloke, near Donald. 'Buloke' is sometimes thought to have originated as the name of a tree known as bull oak, a species of Australian casuarina, and bull oak casuarina are found in the shire and around Lake Buloke. The connection, however, is probably incorrect, as the name of the lake is most likely to have come from the Aboriginal word of similar pronunciation meaning place of frogs (compare also, Lake Bolac, south of Ararat). In any event, Buloke Shire has both the lake and the similarly expressed Indigenous 'bull oak' as inspirations for its name.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: 'Buluk' is an Aboriginal language name meaning wetlands or swamp. It reflects the original natural environment where the primary purpose would have likely been as a food harvesting and gathering place for Aboriginal people.

Historical Information: Bundoora was first known as Springfield, the name of Irish immigrant William Forde Cleeland's nearby property. The area was also known as Prospect Hill and Janefield, which was derived from the field where James Miller Brock's wife was buried in 1851. Historical Information:
The first European tracks in this area linked the main pastoral properties, coming from Frankston via Carrup Carrup and Bunguyan to Coolart and also from Dandenong, via Bunguyan. A surveyor's map of 1858 shows "dray tracks" from both directions crossing at King's Bunguyan Cattle Station Pre-emptive Right, near the present site of Tyabb.
The Bunguyan or King's Cattle Station covered 15,000 acres (6.700 hectares) on the west side of Western Port when it was licensed to Martha Jane King in 1845.
Named after the 'Bunguyan' run held by Martha Jane King between 1845 - 59. 'Mrs. King was one of the very few women in this country to hold a run from original licence to land survey'.

Historical Information:
A. W. Howitt recorded the traditional name as Koi-wirp, 'called for the plentiful tea trees in old home [area]. The Richmond flats about Burnley'. 
This name was recorded by Alfred William Howitt, an anthropologist, from conversations he had sometime between 1897 and 1901 with William Barak, ngurungaeta (leader) of the Wurundjeri-willam, the traditional owners of what is now northern Melbourne, and Dick Richards, Barak's fellow Kulin countryman. Howitt has jotted down Aboriginal names, mostly in the Woiwurrung language once spoken in the Melbourne area, corresponding to landmarks and municipalities that arose in Melbourne town during Barak's lifetime (c.1824 to 1903).
Author: Jason Gibson, Helen Gardner, Stephen Morey
Page Title: Rediscovered: the Aboriginal names for ten Melbourne suburbs

Historical Information: Burnside and Burnside Heights - there are two places in Angus and one place in each of Fife, Moray, South Lanarkshire and West Lothian called Burnside. An explanation of the origin of the names of these western suburbs (two of Melbourne's newest, dating from the 1990s) has not been found. The location of these suburbs on the Kororoit Creek probably suggests a purely descriptive reason for the names, burn being a Scots and northern English word for a creek or stream.
Author: Ian Kendall

Historical Information: Mr Burnside and family farmed the area for many years, and were one of the first settlers in the West. Originally from Scotland, they pioneered the West,and were very active within the growing community of the time. Council named a street in Deer Park in memory of the Burnside family.

Big River State Forest. Locality and camping area north of Bulldog Flat, between a bend in the Big River and the Eildon-Jamieson Road. There is no bridge here now, but Horse Bridge, as the locals called it, stood here until it was burnt down [Ronald Soreng].

Historical Information: This refers to the Barham River, in south-west Victoria, near Apollo Bay. According to Massola (1968: 9), the name is a contraction of Burrum Burrum, meaning large, big. Blake (1977: 33) considers the name 'derives from Kent, England; however Barham may represent anglicising of Abor. n. for stream, burrum burrum, which possibly refers to big stones in river bed'. Pascoe (in Clark and Heydon 2002) suggests the name means muddy, presumably a corruption of 'burrum', seen elsewhere in western Victorian placenames such as Burrumbeep, Burrumbeet, and Burrumbite.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: Surveyors reserved a township on Gardiners Creek, sold in allotments in 1858 as Ballyshanassy, named after prominent politician Sir John O'Shanassy. Five acres (2 ha) were set aside for what is now Burwood Cemetery. Ballyshanassy never flourished and the Boroondara side of Boundary (Warrigal) Road did little better in the 1860s under the name of Norwood, with hotel, bakery, store and postmaster positioned there. In 1879 the Nunawading Shire Council renamed Ballyshanassy as Burwood, after Burwood Road, named after businessman and politician Sir James Palmer's residence Burwood House (now Invergowrie) in Hawthorn.

The Survey section of the Royal Australian Engineers was created soon after Federation and given the task of compiling contour maps of selected areas near capital cities to as part of defence planning. Initial survey work in Victoria included a large topographic triangulation covereing the area between Ballarat, Bendigo and Werribee. Their work became a high priority during the Second World War due to its closeness to Australia. Most of the surviving army beacons date from this period. The Baldhead beacon was built around 1939 by the Australian Army Survey Corp. Of regional significance as only one of only 5 known remaining examples in good condition of an Australian Army Survey Corp beacon, providing evidence of this important phase in the national coordination of the land survey system, the role of the Army survey corps, and the planning response to the anticipated need to defend Australia during the Second World War.

Historical Information:
The Baw Baw cairn is located approximately 1 kilometre east of the Mount Baw Baw village. The cairn is set within snow gums. It is built of roughly shaped stones, and is about 3 metres high and 3 metres in diameter. It is circular in form. There is no beacon on the cairn. The original cairn was a conical stone pile with pole and cross boards, the stone pile being 17 feet high, plus an additional 5 feet (1.5m) of pole. It is
assumed that the present cairn is the base section of the original cairn. A cairn was constructed at the summit of Mt Baw Baw in 1870 by surveyors A.C. Allan and W. Turton, one of many cairns constructed as part of the Geodetic Survey. Observations were taken later that year by surveyor McGeorge. A contemporary description by a visiting party in 1872 described the view from the cairn: "far away as the eye can reach, in every direction there are rolling forests - to the North, towards Woodspoint (sic) and the Upper Yarra - to the West, beyond the spurs of Mount Dandenong - to the East, over Mount Useful and the wild and almost unknown mountains of East Gippsland - to the South, past Toongabbie and Sale, down the coast of Bass' Strait , 100 miles away". Baw Baw geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of three examples remaining in the greater Melbourne region.

Historical Information:
V shaped mark within a blaze cut into the wood of a tree. The V appears to be black and the area where bark has been removed is white. Associated with the survey of the NSW - Victoria State Border. This mark was cut around 1988-90 by Bob Ross as part of a survey to check the State border survey marks. A survey to determine the border of New South Wales and Victoria was undertaken in 1870-72, twenty years after the two colonies were separated. The need to define the border on the ground arose due to the increasing settlement in this mountainous country, especially the advent of gold mining around the Bendoc region. The eastern end of the border at Conference Point (Cape Howe) was established in 1868 by NSW Surveyor-General P.F. Adams and R.J.L. Ellery for Victoria. The western end, at Forest Hill, is the source of the Murray  River. It was marked by Alexander Black in 1870. Black proceeded to undertake an eleven month survey to mark the border on the ground between
Forest Hill and Allan's Peg, a peg positioned near the Delegate River by Senior Geodetic surveyor Alexander Allan.
To achieve the simple "straight line" border across mountainous country involved enormous hard work under difficult conditions. Ellery writing about the geodetic Survey of Victoria in 1891 described the survey as "a piece of survey work which for difficulties and for the requirement of skills, anergy and endurance, as well as for accuracy attained I believe has never been surpassed". Black's survey traversed very difficult terrain, covering 61.5 kilometres over 11 months. Allan's survey was 114 kilometres long, extending over 18 months. Over 50 marks were built by the surveyors and their teams. Some were substantial stone cairns. The surveyors also had to dig trenches to indicate the direction of the border, and clear the line of vegetation. The Black-Allan line border survey is of state significance as evidence of an outstanding surveying feat, testing the endurance and skill of the survey parties, and providing a dramatic demonstration of the difficulties encountered by surveyors in the nineteenth century. Historically, the marking of the border between New South Wales and Victoria symbolised a step in the development of Victorian as a separate, self-governing region.

Bright and District Historical Society believes that this stone was the original datum point for the survey of Bright township, being originally placed on the corner of Wills, Camp and Howitt Streets c1862. It was moved in about 1985 for road widening, but has since been replaced close to its previous location. Research into government records of the survey of the Bright township show the township survey as having been undertaken by John Darbyshire, Acting District Surveyor c1865. The township plan records a number of existing buildings, including one on CA D5, Section F acquired by J D Prince on 29.8.1862. This plan does not show a datum stone, neither do subsequent surveys of this corner
in the 1880s, although a range of other points used in these surveys are noted. From existing information, it has not been possible to determine the likely purpose of this stone, or to confirm that it was associated with the original survey of the township.

Historical Information:
The Survey section of the Royal Australian Engineers was created soon after Federation and given the task of compiling contour maps of selected areas near capital cities as part of defence planning. Initial survey work in Victoria included a large topographic triangulation covering the area between Ballarat, Bendigo and Werribee. Their work became a high priority during the Second World War due to its closeness to Australia. Most of the surviving army beacons date from this period. The Budgeree beacon was built by the Australian Army Survey Corp, however the exact date has not been determined. Of local interest as only one of only 5 known remaining examples of an Australian Army Survey Corp beacon: this example is in poor condition, and
lacks integrity. It provides evidence of an important phase in the national
coordination of the land survey system, the role of the Army survey corps, and the planning response to the anticipated need to defend Australia during the Second World War.

Historical Information: Bunjil is a wedge-tail eagle, the creator spirit of the Wadawurrung and Kulin nation. In common with the other Kulin peoples, the Wadawurrung had a patrililineal kinship system, in which a person's skin-group (otherwise known as a moety) was inherited from their father. Clans belonged either to the Waa (crow) or the Bunjil (eagle-hawk) moiety. The park includes a large sculpture of a wedge-tail eagle at the entrance to symbolise Bunjil watching over the land. Bunjil's Nest encourages people to tell their stories and engage with the stories of others in a celebration of Aboriginal culture.

Calder Park (Calder in Highland and Renfrewshire, both minor rivers; Calder Water in North Lanarkshire gave its name to Calderpark in Glasgow, the site of the former Glasgow Zoo). There is also an important river in Lancashire, England called the River Calder. The Melbourne suburb no doubt takes its name from the Calder Highway on which it is situated. According to the Australian Dictionary of Biography, the highway was named after William Calder (1860-1928), roads engineer, who was born near Dunedin, New Zealand, only son of Arthur Calder and his wife Margaret Milne, nÃ¿Â©e Strachan. Victoria's modern network of highways has been described as Calder's greatest achievement. Considering his Presbyterianism, his parents' names and his place of birth in a particularly Scottish part of New Zealand, it is very likely that Calder's ancestry was Scottish.

Historical Information: Callawadda is the name of a pastoral district 29 km north of Stawell in the southern Wimmera region of Victoria. The locality formed part of John Robertson's 'Robertson's Station', some 22,400 acres on the Richardson River, north of Navarre; first taken up in February 1845 (Billis and Kenyon 1974: 272). Massola (1968) does not assert that Callawadda is an Aboriginal placename, however Blake (1977: 58), suggests the name is a corruption of an Aboriginal word for 'tall timber and plain', but fails to indicate his source. He posits that it 'may also be mis-spelling of Cadwallada which derives fr. Cadwaladr. Grandson in the fifth century of Cadwallan, ruler of North Wales'. Cadwalader or Cadwallader, which mean 'Battle Arranger' or 'Great General', are common names in Wales. Callawadda may be a transposition of Cadwallader, however until further research is undertaken, the etymology of Callawadda must remain unclear.

Historical Information: Timber mill and settlement near the Cumberland River, Marysville Woods Point Road. A portmanteau name, from Cameron + Barton + ville. A. Cameron and F. J. Barton established the mill to salvage timber from trees killed by the 1939 fires. There was also a school (1943-45, 1946-68), classified "as not suitable for a lady teacher" (VR). The mill closed in 1970, and in 1974 the area (28 ha) was added to the Cumberland Memorial Scenic Reserve.
