Historical Information: Until the 1850s the area was occupied for grazing, being described as 'light sandy country, timbered with gum and oak'. Roads were rudimentary, but at one point three roads intersected, and in 1853 an inn was erected at one of the corners. Its owner recollected that several roads converged at Camberwell Green, London, and he called it the Camberwell Inn. The intersection, known as the Burke Road or Camberwell Junction, is on the western boundary of Camberwell. All the district adopted the name of the inn.

Historical Information: Campbellfield - although there are no places in Scotland with this precise name, Campbell is a well-known Scottish family name. The Campbells were once the most powerful of all the Highland clans. The origin of the name is Gaelic - Cambeul -meaning 'crooked mouth'. It is uncertain as to which particular Campbell this suburb owes its name - Neil Campbell, J. D. Lyon Campbell or some other pioneer. The area became popular with Scottish settlers, with a Presbyterian Scots Church being built on Sydney Road (Hume Highway) in 1842. The bluestone structure, erected a little later in 1855, is now on the Victorian Heritage Register.
Author: Ian Kendall

Historical Information: Campbells Creek was named after William Campbell, pastoralist and politician. Campbell took up a small pastoral run, Tourello, near Clunes. In 1850 Campbell discovered gold on his brother-in-law's neighbouring property, entitling him to a reward as Victoria's first gold discoverer.

The locality is named after Capel Sound which is situated a short distance off the shore.

The historical entry for 'Capel Sound' reads as follows:

HMS Rattlesnake conveyed Capt William Lonsdale from Port Jackson to Port Phillip, arriving on 27 September, 1836. Taking advantage of the period required establishing a residence in the settlement for the Lonsdale family, Capt Hobson and his officers were able to survey the navigable areas of Port Phillip. In November, 1836 the ship anchored off Arthur's Seat to enable surveys to be made of that part of the coastline. It was during this time that Mount Martha and Mount Eliza were named by one of the lieutenants of the Rattlesnake, in compliment to Mrs.Lonsdale and Mrs. Batman, respectively. Although there is no available documentary proof to say that Capel Sound was named at this time, it was on the chart that was produced as a result of this survey that the name "Capel's/Capels Sound" first appeared. The Commander-in-chief of the East Indies Squadron of the British Navy was Rear Admiral Sir Thomas Bladen Capel, and it was him who sent the Rattlesnake to convey Capt Lonsdale to Melbourne. The following year, in 1837, HMS Victor named "Capel's Sound" in Victor Harbour, South Australia, after their Commanding Officer, Sir Thomas Capel. It is reasonable to conclude that Capel Sound in Port Phillip was named after Sir Thomas Capel, by the surveyors on board HMS Rattlesnake, in 1836.

Capel Sound was first named in 1836 during the survey of the Bay by HMS Rattlesnake. At that time the Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Navy's Far East Squadron was Admiral Sir Thomas Bladen Capel. Capel was an officer in the British Royal Navy whose distinguished service in the French Revolutionary War, the Napoleonic Wars and the War of 1812 earned him rapid promotion and great acclaim both in and out of the Navy. He was also a great friend of Admiral Horatio Nelson. On the 1836 survey it was shown as 'Capel's Sound' and on later charts as 'Capells Sound' and 'Capell's Sound'. By the 1860s it had stabilised in its current form of 'Capel Sound'.

Historical Information: Named after Caroline Chisholm (1808-1877). Caroline Chisholm worked tirelessly for female immigrants in NSW, as it was her belief that the best influences on colonial life were marriage and family life. She had continued this work on her return to England, and had encouraged poor people, especially young women, to leave the squalor of their homeland and emigrate to Australia. Her work in Victoria was in providing clean, cheap and safe accommodation to families or single people on the way to the Mount Alexander diggings. She pressured the government into a scheme to built ten shelter sheds, which would provide accommodation for single men, single women and families. While none of the sheds lasted, the park is in the rough area where the sheds were located.
Named by land developers after Mrs Caroline Chisholm who established shelter sheds to provide accommodation along the route to the goldfields, including one at The Gap.

Historical Information: Carrum Downs was in the Shire of Cranbourne but became part of the City of Frankston in the 1994 Council amalgamations. It takes its name from the Carrum Swamp, which was reclaimed when channels were created to take the waters of the Dandenong and Eumemmerring Creeks to the Bay. These creeks were connected to the man-made Carrum Outfall, now the Patterson River. The drainage works commenced in 1869. The Garem Gam run was taken up by Dr James Bathe and T.J Perry in 1840. This was also known as Gurn Gurn or Carrum Carrum. Garem Gam is thought to be Aboriginal for boomerang.

Historical Information:
Benjamin Chadd,  aged 15 years, from Bath, England was transported to Sydney on the convict ship 'Hive' arriving 11 June 1834. 

He was put to work labouring in irons on Goat Island in Sydney harbour, near the current suburb of Balmain East, a short distance west of the Sydney Harbour Bridge. He later worked on the Parramatta Road leading West from Sydney.

On 25 September 1837, Benjamin was part of a work party sent from NSW to Port Phillip (Melbourne) and put to work on public works for the foundation of Melbourne, then still part of NSW.

In 1839 Benjamin was a member of Henry Arthur's exploration of Diamond Creek (municipality of Nillumbik), 25 km North West of Melbourne. Henry Arthur was the nephew of Lieutenant-Governor George Arthur of Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) where he was the Collector of Customs at Launceston.

Henry Arthur followed the right hand fork of Diamond Creek, which was later named Arthur's Creek, and Benjamin Chadd the left fork and later named Chadd's Creek. Part of the land was surveyed and subdivided in 1845.

Currently, the site is named Chad's Creek ie, one 'D'. 

Sourced from James (Jim) Chadd a 5th generation descendent.

Chadstone Shopping Centre stands on the former site of the Convent of the Good Shepherd, part of which included land once occupied by Chadstone, an early weatherboard cottage on a small farm. Chadstone (cottage) was built for William Johnson in 1858, on 13 acres (5.2 hectares) of land at the corner of Chadstone and Dandenong Roads. In 1879 Johnson sold the property to John and Emma Evans, who used part of the land as an orchard, supplying plums, cherries, apples and pears to the local community. In 1888, following John's death in a riding accident, ownership of the property was transferred to Emma, who remained at Chadstone with her eight children. In 1909 the property was sold to the Convent of the Good Shepherd next door. The Good Shepherd Sisters demolished the cottage and used the land for market gardening and grazing cattle. Years later, this land was part of the land sold to the Myer family for Chadstone Shopping Centre. The Convent of the Good Shepherd opened in December 1883, for the purpose of 'training and educating poor and neglected children'. The Convent offered academic, domestic and commercial training for girls aged 11 to 13 who were deemed by the Children's Court to be in need of care, and also provided care for older girls and women. The Convent was renown for the quality of its embroidery. The Convent of the Good Shepherd was built in 1883 at the corner of Dandenong Road and Castlebar Road next door to Chadstone (cottage), on land originally owned by speculator Patrick O'Farrell. O'Farrell, a solicitor, had purchased 55 acres of land in October 1855 from the Crown. One of his clients was the first Catholic Bishop of Melbourne, James Alipius Goold OSM, to whom O'Farrell sold the land in 1856 for Ã¿Â£274. In 1881, in order to extend the work of the Convent at Abbotsford, Archbishop Goold invited the Sisters of the Good Shepherd to establish a convent and reformatory school on his land at Oakleigh (later known as Chadstone). In July 1881, Goold laid the foundation stone for the Convent, which was built with bricks made from clay quarried on the site and rendered with roughcast cement. The nineteenth century complex of buildings included the convent, chapel, reformatory school, laundry and priest's cottage. St Anthony's Primary School, established for the children of the Parish in 1899, closed in 1979. The foundation stone for a new French Gothic style Chapel, was laid by the Archbishop of Melbourne, His Grace the Most Rev. Dr. Daniel Mannix, in June 1930. The Chapel, with its graceful spire and clocktower, became a local landmark.
In 1958 and 1963, parts of the Convent land were sold for development of the shopping centre. In 1984, 3.2 hectares of land, containing the convent, chapel and other buildings of the Good Shepherd complex, were sold. The following year, amidst much controversy, the buildings referred to as 'a place of love, peace and shelter to countless numbers for over a century' were demolished in order to extend the car park at Chadstone Shopping Centre. Ken Myer returned from a visit to the United States of America with his vision for retailing and in 1958 part of the Convent land at Chadstone was purchased for Melbourne's first regional shopping centre. In less than two years, 30 acres of pasture were converted to the largest centre of its type in Australia.

Historical Information:
The Challis family selected Crown Allotment 167B of 80 acres on the Shelford-Cressy Road in the Leigh Shire, Parish of Doroq (west of Shelford) sometime in the 19th century.  In 1927 Thomas and Mary Challis (Bramley) and their three sons Joseph Edwin, Fredrick Thomas and Harry moved to the block.  They built a small fibro-cement house and in the following years a cluster of small farm sheds (that are still standing).  Subsequently two of the brothers Joe and Fred purchased more land in the vicinity and farmed there until their death, Joe in 1984 and Fred in 1989.  Harry moved out of the district.

Joseph Edwin Challis was a long time councillor of the Shire of Leigh - 1948 to 1968.  He was also Captain of the Shelford R.F.B. (1957 to 1977).  Both brothers were also on various local committees over a period of many years.

Historical Information: Chelsea Heights is situated on an ancient coastal sand dune, which was formerly surrounded by the Carrum Swamp. Parts of the area were leased for grazing, particularly during the summer in the 1850s, and one settler gave his address as the Islands of Wannark Laddin, a name which persisted at least until 1866 when it was printed on a hydrographic map of Port Phillip Bay.

Historical Information: 'The place from which this station took its name was at one time known as 'Two Acre Village.'  In 1853, Charles Whorral built an inn there, and called it 'Cheltenham,' after his native town in Gloucestershire, England.  As the settlement of 'Two Acre Village' (which was so named by Josiah Morris Holloway in 1850, or thereabouts) grew, the name of the inn was adopted by the township.'

Historical Information: The previous bridge was erected in 1856-7. A 210-foot span, ten-foot high, iron bridge with solid riveted iron walls had been designed to prevent Russian snipers from killing British troops during the Crimean War. The bridge was dismantled and reconstructed, with stone buttresses, in Richmond. The bridge was demolished in 1923, replaced with a bridge designed by Harold Desbrowe Annear and Thomas Ramsden Ashworth. The bridge was reinforced concrete which promoted the beautification of the city, and is named after Church Street.

The first families took up residence in late 1965. The town was first known as Hazelwood, but in February 1965, the government changed the name to Churchill to honour the English statesperson, Sir Winston Churchill. The local response was very negative and very vocal and it was November 1966 before the issue was definitely settled in favour of Churchill. A bronze coloured structure 102 feet high represents a cigar, symbolising the town's link with Churchill. The issue of the town's name re-emerged in 1987. After much lobbying, a survey was taken and a close result favoured retaining the name Churchill.

Historical Information:
In 1893-1911 a Dr john William Yorke Fishbourne turned his home into a school for mentally disabled children in Puckle Street, Moonee Ponds. 

St Aidan's was the first day school for mentally disabled children. St Aidan's School was operated by Dr Fishbourne and his daughter Leata, with two other daughters later joining the school as teachers. The school closed upon the death of Dr Fishbourne in September 1911.

In December 1911, Mrs Maude Nicol applied for registration for St Aidan's as a private hospital. Nurse Anderson took over St Aidan's in January 1917 and then in May 1923, the premises, which still stretched from Puckle Street through to Young Street, was purchased by Councillor G W Royle. In December of that year the Hospital was relocated to the corner of Ascot Vale Road and Bank street.

Shops were built in front of the house in Puckle Street, hiding it from view, glimpses of the buildings facade can still be seen from Puckle Street. The small arcade in Puckle Street is built inside the shell of the former home, school and hospital.

Historical Information:
The request to name the creek was submitted by McCrae Homestead Coastal Group Inc. The name recognises the long term historical association of the Coburn family to the area.

Mr William John Coburn migrated from Belfast to Melbourne with his wife Catherine Elizabeth in 1864. After living in Daylesford and North Melbourne, William Coburn built 'Springbank House' in 1891 which was unfortunately destroyed by fire in 1912. The Coburns rebuilt on the same site in 1925 and a second house is the current property of their descendant.

Historical Information: Coldstream (Scottish Borders). Coldstream is a descriptive name, applied by Kerr and Robert Black to their estate in the 1850s. Blake (1977, p. 69) notes that the name of this semi-rural suburb comes originally from a place on the English and Scottish borders. The Scottish village of Coldstream was the birthplace of the famous Coldstream Guards. Formed by General Monck in 1659, it is the oldest British regiment to have survived intact over time.

Historical Information: The Modewarre Football Netball Club and the Modewarre Cricket Club approached the Community Bank to provide the clubs $25,000 financial contribution in exchange for naming rights to their oval for three years.

A naming competition was held in May 2016. Rye Primary School participated and engaged 396 students and 50 children from the Rye Preschool contributed their suggestions to 'The Park with No Name Competition'. A panel of three judges included Kerryn Ladell, Manager Rye Beach Community House, Ginny Galbraith an Art Teacher with the Rye Beach Community House as well as Council's representative Cr. Hugh Fraser, who underwent a selection process to choose the student's winning suggestion and idea for the Rye Pocket Park's name and logo. The winning proposed name was from Rye Primary School student's aged 7 and 11 which was 'Community Grow & Play Gardens' with a logo of a tree with a purple bench.

Part of the traditional land of the Boonwurrung people prior to European settlement, 54 acres of land extending from Toorak Road to the Yarra River was acquired in the Crown land sales of June 1840. By 1847 a house was erected for Judge Edward Williams (after whom the road along the site's eastern boundary is named). Its lake and water vistas inspired Williams to name it after Lake Como in Italy, where he had proposed to his wife Jessie. Later owners John Brown and Charles Armytage kept the name. The lake became an unsightly swamp once the level of the Yarra River was lowered. Prahran Council purchased 35 acres from the Armytages in 1921, and spent thousands of pounds and many years of draining the swamp and re-grading the land, transforming it into a public park and recreation ground, laid out by curator William Greenwood. The extension of Alexandra Avenue, which began c1924, was stepped up during the Great Depression to provide 'sustenance work' for the unemployed, partially funded by Sidney Meyer. An Armstrong 40 pounder RBL gun, relocated from Rockley Gardens in the early 1930s, is listed on the Victorian Heritage Database as a rare surviving example of its kind. The opening of Como Park by the Governor of Victoria, Lord Huntingfield, in October 1934, was attended by 7,000 people. The Council-designed sports pavilion was opened by Mayor Cr Harry Landen in June 1939. Women's cricket matches were played here in the late 1940s, and the park remains a popular venue for sport and Christmas carols.

Historical Information: The lake, after which this station is called, was so named by the late Cecil Pybus Cooke.  In 1849 it bore the name 'Lake Condon', and was included in a cattle station known by the same name.  The station was purchased by Mr. C. P. Cooke in 1849 from Mr. Smyth.  In 1855 Mr. Cooke was told that 'Condah' was the native name for black swan, which birds were then plentiful on the lake.  Believing the statement, he changed the name to 'Condah', and when he found that he had been misinformed he thought it unnecessary to revert to the old name or to provide a new one.

Historical Information: It was named after Sir John Coode, an English harbour engineer who was engaged by the Melbourne Harbour Trust to select the optimum route for the canal as part of the Port of Melbourne. Coode chose the canal route so as to avoid dangerous tidal ebbs and inflows that would occur along one that went straight from the Yarra River docks to Hobsons Bay. The meander was known as Fishermens Bend or Humbug Reach. Later, Fishermens Bend came to be applied to the land opposite Coode Island on the other side of the canal and even to Sandridge Beach, Port Melbourne west. By the late 1930s the meander was almost abolished and the 'island' joined to West Melbourne, but the name continued to be used.

Historical Information: Cora Lynn was originally called Koo-Wee-Rup Central and renamed Cora Lynn on July 1st, 1907, when the Progress Association requested that the newly established postal service be established under the new name of Cora Lynn, to prevent the confusion of the name with Koo-Wee-Rup. Joe Dineen had recalled that it was the Head Teacher of the school, John McGibbon, who proposed the name, after the scenic rocky gorge and popular picnic area on the North Esk River, just out of Launceston in Tasmania. The name Cora Lynn comes from the Gaelic coire meaning cauldron or kettle and linn pool.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: There are two possible origins of the Cranbourne name. The Ruffy brothers were the first Europeans to settle permanently in the Cranbourne area, on the Mayune run, and they operated the Cranbourne Inn. The Inn was named after a town in Berkshire, England. Gunson suggests that Cranbourne was named for Viscount Cranborne (no u), the brother of the British Prime Minister. Viscount Cranborne was born in 1821 and developed blindness as a very small child. He died in 1865, and thus his brother succeeded to the title and then became the Marquis of Salisbury in 1868 when their father died. Salisbury was the British Prime Minister on three occasions between 1885 and 1902. The word Cranbourne means stream frequented by cranes or herons.

Historical Information: Rises between the Black Range and Strathbogie Ranges and flows into Pranjip Creek. Probably the V Mile Creek shown on Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847), but not the Five Mile Creek* between Violet Town* and Benalla*. The locality of Creighton's Creek is west of Wheeler's Hill. The Creighton's Creek state school (1884 - 1944) was destroyed by fire. The bushranger Henry Power (1820-91) held up a mail-coach in this area (the Longwood-Mansfield Road) on 22 May 1869. (North of the Hume Freeway are the Creighton Hills* and the locality of Creighton*.) Named after William Abraham Creighton or Crighton (d. 1849), licensee of the Five Mile Creek and Wanghambeham pastoral runs. The surname comes from either Crichton, 24 km south-east of Edinburgh (Gaelic crioch, border, and Middle English tune, farm, settlement), or Creighton, Staffordshire (Old Welsh creic, rock, and Old English tun, fence, enclosure, settlement).

The locality of Creighton's Creek is west of Wheeler's Hill. The Creighton's Creek state school (1884 - 1944) was destroyed by fire. The bushranger Henry Power (1820-91) held up a mail-coach in this area (the Longwood-Mansfield Road) on 22 May 1869. (North of the Hume Freeway are the Creighton Hills* and the locality of Creighton*.) Named after William Abraham Creighton or Crighton (d. 1849), licensee of the Five Mile Creek and Wanghambeham pastoral runs. The surname comes from either Crichton, 24 km south-east of Edinburgh (Gaelic crioch, border, and Middle English tune, farm, settlement), or Creighton, Staffordshire (Old Welsh creic, rock, and Old English tun, fence, enclosure, settlement).

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information:
The area that is now Croydon was initially called White Flats. Seen from the heights of the Yarra track, the valley appeared white because of the extensive growths of a silvery-white coarse grass called Danthonia pallida (Red-anther wallaby-grass).
In the early 19th century, the area now covered by the Croydon township was part of four large pastoral runs: Thomson's Warrandyte Run, the Anderson's Creek Run (owned by Lewis Robinson), William Turner's Stringy Bark Forest Run, and Gardiners Run, part of which now forms North Croydon. William Turner was the first European settler in the district. He came from England in 1837 and from 1840 to 1844 held Western Port, which stretched from present-day Mitcham to the Dandenong Ranges and from South Croydon to Mullum Creek. By 1860 he had built a house at the corner of present-day Dorset and Mount Dandenong roads.
When the railway from Melbourne was put through in 1882, the local station was called Warrandyte. The shire of Lilydale and the Railway Commissioners called for a more suitable name since the township of Warrandyte was 4 miles (7 km) away. As the railway line bisected Gregory Lacey's property, he suggested that the new name be Croydon after his wife's home town in England.
Author: Peter Baddeley

Historical Information: Yarra Ranges National Park. Named after Cumberland Creek (2). Established 1923 (Forests Commission tourist reserve) and 1929; the word Memorial was added to the name in 1994. A memorial, suggested by nursing sisters Bolam and McGowan [Mary Kenealy], to Australians who died during the First and Second World Wars and later conflicts. Includes the Cambarville picnic area, the Cumberland walking track, the Cumberland and Corra Linn Falls, lookouts, The Big Culvert, an historic water-race, fine stands of mountain ash and myrtle beech, the Big Tree (83 m high Eucalyptus regnans), and a Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis) marking the site of the home of George Loch, timber cutter and gold miner, who lived there until 1938. Leadbeater's possum was rediscovered in the area in 1961.

Historical Information: The feature was opened in 1937 but there is no record of it ever being officially named and gazetted. Over the years it has been known as various different names including Cunninghame Arm Bridge, Cunninghame Footbridge, Lakes Entrance Footbridge and simply The Footbridge. In 2009 the footbridge across Cunninghame Arm was replaced. This new structure was officially opened on 12 November 2009 and was opened as Cunninghame Arm Bridge in recognition of the fact that the structure catered for both pedestrian and emergency/official vehicular traffic. Again, this name was never gazetted. On 7 March 2011, 'Cunninghame Arm Footbridge' was proposed with the Office of Geographic Names (OGN) as the bridge traverses the body of water known as Cunninghame Arm, the township of Lakes Entrance was once known as Cunninghame and that anecdotally, locally the bridge is commonly referred to as Cunninghame Arm Footbridge or Lakes Entrance Footbridge.

Historical Information:
Cyril Edward Fox (1921-2006) left school at the age of 14 years and worked at the Islington Railway Workshops until World War II broke out. He then joined the Australian Navy in April 1940.  In 1946 Cyril was drafted to the Flinders Naval Depot to do a physical training course after which he was sent to New
Guinea. When he returned he was appointed to the Naval College as a Physical Training Instructor.  He retired from the Navy in 1961 after completing 21 years of service.
Cyril commenced a new occupation with the Education Department of Victoria as Physical Education teacher at Aspendale Technical School. He also taught at Dromana and Frankston before retiring from teaching.
He was a Hastings Shire Councillor, representing Bittern, and a Shire President.
He was on the Crib Point Swimming Pool Advisory Committee in 1980-81, the Hastings Red Cross Committee, and the Crib Point Primary School Committee in 1981.  C.E. Fox was also a Justice of the Peace.
The Cyril Fox Bushland Reserve is a 2.3 hectare reserve of high quality remnant vegetation adjacent to the Cyril Fox Recreation Reserve.

He served in the Royal Australian Navy for 21 years, including war service in the Pacific. He was a member of the Crib Point Football Club, Tennis Club, and the Devilbend Golf Club, as well as serving on the Council as Shire President and a number of community committees.

Historical Information:
Cape Bridgewater mark is located on a high point towards the southern tip of the cape and within private property. In 1941 it was recorded as being 2 m high with a pole. The mark was an arrow carved in stone below the cairn. A 1997 photograph shows a stone cairn built of unmortared field stone, with a timber post still held upright within the stone pile. It appears to have lost some stones and to have been reduced in height. Next to the cairn is a metal beacon supported on four steel poles. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The date of construction of this mark is not known. Recorded in the Angle Book as an "old ASC point". Cape Bridgewater geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of 3 examples remaining in the south-west of Victoria
(the other two being in the Grampians), and one of few examples to retain a timber centre pole.

Historical Information: Castle Hill is located north east of Licola, within the Wonnangatta-Moroka Alpine National Park. A stone cairn close to the present trig. station is thought to be what remains of the 1868 survey cairn. The Castle Hill cairn is approximately 2.3 metres high. It is built of loose stone and retains a wooden pole. The top of the pole was recorded as broken off in 1970, and repair work was undertaken to the cairn in 1979. At this time, the southern side of the cairn was found partially collapsed and was rebuilt and a new centre pole was cut and placed in the cairn vertically over the lower half of the original pole which was not disturbed during rebuilding. Castle Hill cairn is associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). This cairn was built c1868, and was partially rebuilt in 1979. Castle Hill geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of five examples remaining in the alpine areas of the East Gipplsand region of Victoria. Part of this cairn is intact and retains its original centre pole, one of few examples to do so.

Historical Information:
Cobberas No. 1 was used by A. Black for triangulation, setting out the Black-Allan border survey line. A stone platform, taken to be the old geodetic beacon site was recorded in 1987. It is described as a concial pile of stones, 2.5m high, with a centre pole. A later ground mark at Cobberas No. 1 - close to the old cairn - was recorded in 1985, and a geodetic plaque grouted to the surface. A beacon comprising a small rock cairn and centre pole beacon was replaced with a mortared cairn and steel pipe centrepole with vanes in 1987. The relative positions are shown in the OSG Angle Book 981. Cobberas No. 1 was constructed in 1869 as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria. Cobberas No 1 geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of seven examples remaining in the alpine areas of
Victoria. It was also used as part of the triangulation for the Black-Allan survey of the NSW-Victorian border in 1870-72.

The watercourse rises south-west of Yea, crosses the Goulburn Valley Highway and drains into the Goulburn River E.S.E. of Kerrisdale. The locality or small settlement is west of the creek at the junction of Homewood Road and Dairy Creek Road. A school, officially called Doogallook, but known locally as Dairy Creek, operated intermittently at the north end of Dairy Creek Road from 1882. It was moved further south in 1889, and officially renamed Dairy Creek. It closed in 1916, when the Homewood school opened after being moved to Dairy Creek Road. The creek may well have been named after the dairy near the Doogallook homestead in John Cotton's time.  See also Doogallook and Creamery Hill.

Historical Information: Parish; town; former pastoral run? The parish of Darlingford was originally on the south side of the Goulburn River on both sides of the Big River; it included a thin strip of land south of the Goulburn River between the confluences with the Goulburn of Jerusalem Creek and the Delatite River. The town (surveyed 1864) was on the Big River very near its junction with the Goulburn River, near the present Darlingford Reach and Darlingford Point (Point Knight). Named after Sir Charles (Henry) Darling (1809-70), governor of Victoria (1863-66). Darling is the Old English deorling, which had the same meaning a thousand years ago as now. The town was also known in its early days as The Junction or Big River Junction. Darlingford and Enoch's Point (q.v.) sprang up as a result of the discovery of gold on the Big River in 1854. There were schools at Darlingford from the 1860s, but there was also a Darlingford State School at Peachey's Bridge (q.v.). Darlingford township was submerged (ca. 1927), with much of the parish, by the filling of the Sugarloaf Reservoir, but see also New Darlingford. Spreadborough & Anderson's maps show a Darlingford pastoral run, but neither they nor Billis & Kenyon mention it in the text. The Borothat run, to the west of Darlingford on the map, looks too small. The Darlingford run may well be a mapping error for part of the Borothat run.

In 1852 a township was gazetted and named Darlington, possibly after the place of the same name in Durham, England.

Historical Information:
Darnum is the name of a small town south-east of Warragul in the Shire of Baw Baw. According to Saxton (1907: 21) it is a native name meaning 'parrot'. O'Callaghan (1918: 40), repeats Saxton's gloss and sources it from Bunce (1856: 33) and Smyth (1878 Vol. 2: 191); however I have not been able to substantiate the Smyth reference. There is a reproduction of Bunce's list in Smyth (1878 Vol. 2: 138). This definition is accepted by Massola (1968: 19) and Barry Blake (1991: 87). Copeland, in a local history of the Warragul Shire, noted the following:

Darnum is supposed to have acquired its name when the various small townships along the railway-line were taxing the ingenuity of official minds to christen and tabulate with appropriate names. This particular locality emerged from the unknown and un-named, it is said, from an exclamation of the late Sir Thomas Bent. This irascible old politician was annoyed with the suggestions made by different ones, when he expressed a desire to have the place called something it would be known by, and it was not clear whether he said Darn 'em or D___' em, but the milder expression appears to have been chosen, with a slight alteration and arrangement in spelling, to denote the little railway township. However, Darnum it has remained ever since. (Copeland 1934: 485)

Martin (1944: 29), asserts that 'it is generally believed that it was derived from an exclamation frequently used by Thomas Bent, Victoria's rugged premier' in 1904. Blake (1977: 79), believes the placename is the 'ancient n. for Doncaster, Eng., but is also Abor. word for parrot'. Gardner (1992: 12) suggests it almost certainly refers to the crimson rosella Platycercus elegans or the eastern rosella Platycercus exemius. This is an example where folk etymology has generated a popular explanation that is not grounded in the historical literature.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: Davey Richardson and his wife Trish migrated to Australia from Scotland in 1984 and first joined the Seaford Junior Football Club in 1988 as they had friends that were already involved in the club. Having no boys to play football did not discourage Davey and Trish from getting involved and Davey became a major sponsor of the club in 1989 - 2011. During his illness Davey asked Trish to set up a Hardship Fund for underprivileged players which is now in place. Davey was a builder by trade and had undertaken many improvements to the club's old rooms at East Seaford Reserve over the years. Davey passed away last June losing his battle with cancer. The club believes it to be fitting to recognize Davey's 21 years of volunteering and hard work.

Historical Information:
John Molison worked for a company called Fishburn and Morton who were contracted by the state government to build 21 miles of the railway line linking Gippsland with Melbourne. Fishbum and Morlon employed 900 men on this work and the death of John Molison was barely noticed and their track record of accidents was horrendous. ln 1874 a man was hurt during blasting while working on the Ballarat to Maryborough line. ln 1877 John was killed and two other men were seriously injured in separate accidents. ln 1881 and 1883 numerous men were injured or killed in incidents while working on the Mudgee railway line. The contractors might not have valued human life but they were given the contracts because of their ability to finish difficult jobs on or before time. They were also known to employ men who were not the savoriest of characters. At times the police would check the workforce looking for fugitives and known criminals, often
arresting a few in the ranks.

Historical Information:
A Balwyn historical society article from 2010 shows the history of Deepdene stretches back to the early 1880s.

An area of land, called Deepdene Estate, was first advertised for sale on November 3 1883. The land was on the southeast corner of what is now Burke and Whitehorse roads intersection. 

It comprised about 6ha and was subdivided into 35 building allotments. The land had previously belonged to the market gardener, Henry Finger, in 1858 and then, in 1870, to Harry Curtis, also a market gardener.

The advertisement for the sale of land said "the estate was so-called Deepdene after the celebrated estate of Mr (Thomas) Hope near London, in consequence of the extraordinary similarity of magnificent views from the two estates.

By 1889, architect David Askew built his home facing Whitehorse Road and named in Deepdene House.
Author: Gliddon, Greg
Title: History of Deepdene goes back to 1880s

Historical Information: Parish, settlement, county, former shire, former pastoral run. Aboriginal (Taungurong) personal or place-name. The Delatite pastoral run (1844-79) was of about 12,000 ha near Mansfield but south of today's settlement of Delatite; the homestead, associated especially with the Chenery and Ritchie families (M. R. Clark), still exists. The settlement or locality of Delatite is on the Delatite River upstream of Piries. The county includes Mansfield, Strathbogie and part of Euroa. The shire of Delatite was created in 1994 (by amalgamation of the shires of Benalla and Mansfield) but was subdivided in 2002 into the Rural City of Benalla and the (re-established) shire of Mansfield. The pastoral run was allegedly named in honour of a woman who was the wife of either the Taungurong chief Beolite or (less likely) his son Barwite. But both Martin and Saxton say the word means devil. A quite different origin is given by George Augustus Robinson: "Tal.la.tite is the name of the range south of Bayolite that leads to the Devils River near Waugh's" (journal, 12 May 1840): in other words, the South Blue Range, but not the Blue Range (near Rubicon) as stated by Clark & Heydon. See also Barwite, Beolite, Delatite River, Loyola (pastoral run), South Blue Range and Taungurong Creek.

Historical Information: Rises at Howqua Gap* (east of Mount Buller); the lower part was originally a tributary of the Goulburn River, but is now flooded to form the Delatite Arm of Lake Eildon. Near Mansfield it was occasionally called the Mansfield River. Most accounts say that Europeans at first called it the Devils' River, and there are at least three theories about this, involving members of George Watson and Alexander McLean Hunter's pastoral company: John Hunter and Hunter Campbell watching a corroboree (Gillison and, in part, Saxton), or Archibald Jamieson being awoken by a dog, or Andrew Ewan's fear of the Aborigines (Noble). However, Delatite appears to be the first name in print. It appears as a river name on Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix in 1847, and is listed by Wells in 1848 (without mention of Devils' River); but Devils' River persisted until the 1880s. It still occurs in Devils' Cove, Devils' River (creek) and Devils' River Hill (Mount Maintongoon). The river was named or renamed apparently after the pastoral run (see Delatite). The Yowung-illam-balluk band of the Taungurong probably called the river the Wappang. Brough Smyth (1976, 2: 196) also lists Callathera as a native name for the Devil's River (Woiworung galada means river), and Clark & Heydon (D, M) record Kalylatherer, Kay-lath-er-rer, Pappang (papa = mother) and Wapping, mother. See also Jerusalem Creek, South Blue Range and Wappan.

Historical Information: It was named after a Port Phillip Aboriginal man, Darrimart or Derrimut c1810-65, of the Boonwurrung clan. His people occupied coastal land from the Werribee district to Western Port. Derrimut is remembered for having on two occasions warned early white settlers, Fawkner and Aitken, of impending Aboriginal attacks. He was taken up by Fawkner and his portrait was painted in Hobart. His name was given to the Parish of Derrimut, south and west of Kororoit Creek and north of Werribee. He has a burial headstone in the Melbourne general cemetery.

Historical Information: Named after Desmond 'Des' Ignatius Custerson, a well known Dandenong identity and, with his wife Maureen, started the Chubbies Dance Band. They remained the core members of the band for 50 years. The Chubbies Dance Band played at the old Workingman's Club in Dandenong and was the first band to play there when it was renovated. The band was the heart and soul of the well-known Lyndale Dance and raised funds for the Dandenong and District Hospital for 28 years. The band also played at dances all over Victoria to raise funds for charities such as the Make-A-Wish Foundation, Yooralla, the Helicopter Search & Rescue Service and local churches and communities. Des played the last gig with the Chubbies Dance Band at aged 84. Des also had a long association with the St Mary's Parish Football Club (he coached the Midgets for almost 15 years) and the Dandenong Football Club, through his son Neil. Des and Maureen lived in Sunset Grove, Dandenong for over 25 years with their five children. They were well known and respected in the local community. Des and Maureen embraced the diversity of Dandenong and always welcomed new migrants to the area. He was a gentle and ethical man that shared his love of Dandenong and football with his neighbours. Des passed away in April 2016.
In recognition of Des Leonard, a member of the Glenlyon community who volunteered for numerous organisations for over 40 years including the Glenlyon Sports Club and the Glenlyon Fire Brigade.

Historical Information: Rises at Howqua Gap* (east of Mount Buller); the lower part was originally a tributary of the Goulburn River, but is now flooded to form the Delatite Arm of Lake Eildon. Near Mansfield it was occasionally called the Mansfield River. Most accounts say that Europeans at first called it the Devils' River, and there are at least three theories about this, involving members of George Watson and Alexander McLean Hunter's pastoral company: John Hunter and Hunter Campbell watching a corroboree (Gillison and, in part, Saxton), or Archibald Jamieson being awoken by a dog, or Andrew Ewan's fear of the Aborigines (Noble). However, Delatite appears to be the first name in print. It appears as a river name on Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix in 1847, and is listed by Wells in 1848 (without mention of Devils' River); but Devils' River persisted until the 1880s. It still occurs in Devils' Cove, Devils' River (creek) and Devils' River Hill (Mount Maintongoon). The river was named or renamed apparently after the pastoral run (see Delatite). The Yowung-illam-balluk band of the Taungurong probably called the river the Wappang. Brough Smyth (1976, 2: 196) also lists Callathera as a native name for the Devil's River (Woiworung galada means river), and Clark & Heydon (D, M) record Kalylatherer, Kay-lath-er-rer, Pappang (papa = mother) and Wapping, mother. See also Jerusalem Creek, South Blue Range and Wappan.

Historical Information:
Dexters Bush is named after Paul & Elizabeth Dexter in recognition of their efforts and the considerable time in nurturing and maintaining the bushland at the rear of their property in Dickasons Road Heathmont.
The Dexters purchased 5 acres of bushland, running from Dickasons Road to the Dandenong Creek in 1956. They gifted part of the land to Victoria Conservation Trust in 1988 and continued to be actively involved in preserving the bushland through their role on the committee of management, by assisting with plans, strategies and policies to promote the regeneration of the indigenous flora that was present in the soil and other significant species.   The Dexters stepped back from their role in the management of the bushland in 2015 and the land was transferred to Maroondah Council on 23 January 2018. The community and Council have always recognised the bushland as Dexters Bush.

Historical Information: John Dight of Campbell Town acquired portion 88, Parish of Jika Jika, County of Bourke, on 7 November 1838. Over the next few years, he constructed a brick mill on the site and began the production of flour. In November 1843, ownership of the land passed to John Dight and his brother Charles Hilton Dight. In 1864, the flour milling use was abandoned and the mill leased to Thomas Kenny. In the mid 1870s, the site was used by the Patent Safety Blasting Powder Co. The Dight family sold the mill site to Edwin Trennery in 1878 and he subsequently subdivided the land. The original mill on the river bank remained unoccupied until 1888, when flour millers Gillespie, Aitken and Scott, operating under the name of 'Yarra Falls Roller Flour Mills' constructed a new mill and associated buildings on the site. The mill race was rebuilt in much the same position on the site using bluestone blocks from Dight's old mill building, and a new mill and associated buildings were constructed some distance from the site of the original mill building. This enterprise was sold in 1891 to the Melbourne Flour Milling Company, run by the Hon. James Bell. In 1890, the founding Act of the Melbourne and Metropolitan Board of Works was established and the Board issued a licence to the company in 1895 for the construction and maintenance of the weir at the Falls. In 1909 The Melbourne Flour Milling Co sold ?its mill and plant on the banks of the Yarra at Abbotsford to Messrs John Darling and Son, the well known millers and wheat merchants of South Australia. John Darling and Son extended the lease with the Board of Works, but for a period of only three months. Within this time, however the mill suffered a disastrous fire and was destroyed. Most of what remained of the mill buildings was dismantled and removed from the site in the twenty years following the fire. The Melbourne and Metropolitan Board of Works has controlled and owned the site for most of the twentieth century. The site consists of the remains of the head race, tail race, turbine house, retaining wall and weir.

Historical Information: Before the arrival of white people into the district, the Aborigines called the area Watchegatcheca which had the meaning 'Wattle Tree and White Cockatoos'. The name 'Dimboola' has generally been accepted to have come from the Sinhalese word "dimbula" meaning 'Land of Figs'. The name came from the District Surveyor of the time John George Winchester Wilmot, who had previously lived in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). The relationship of the name to this area is suggested to have come from 'Upper Regions Station' where an abundance of fruit trees grew in the garden, many of which were figs.

Historical Information: The German community was named Waldau, but the name Doncaster gradually became commonly accepted. In 1854 John Robert Wilson, from Doncaster in Yorkshire, England, built the Doncaster Arms Inn on the track through the stringybark forest to the Warrandyte gold diggings. The track was later named Doncaster Road. An alternative derivation may be from William Burnley, a Richmond land developer, who sold land in Doncaster in the 1850s. He also was from Doncaster, England.

Historical Information: In 1859 the Dookie district was surveyed, taking in much of the Emu Plains pastoral run. Local lore has it that Mrs Turnbull, wife of the station's proprietor, was so unhappy at the prospect of survey and possible farm subdivision that the surveyor suggested a place name derived from the Singhalese word duka, meaning sorrow. Mrs Turnbull had lived in Ceylon. Duka was re-spelt Dookie.

Historical Information: Highlands. Parish; locality; school (Dropmore South, 1902-12); former pastoral run (1841-83 or later), of about 104 sq. km. Listed by Wells (1848). Les Blake suggests the Victorian name comes from Dromore, Co. Down. There is also a Dromore (Irish droim mór, big ridge) in Co. Sligo, but as there is a Dropmore in Buckinghamshire (England) - an ecclesiastical district south-west of Beaconsfield - this seems far more likely. At a guess, Old English deop, deep, and mor, fen, marsh, wasteland, upland. See also Nainbulbulla.

Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Drung Drung is the name of one of three lakes some 16 km south-east of Horsham. Samuel Wilson (in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 178) confirms that Drung Drung is a native name, but he does not provide a meaning. Saxton (1907: 22) considers it a native name meaning 'spoiling'. According to Martin (1944: 32) it is an Aboriginal name meaning 'much spoiled'. Massola (1968: 20) extends the meaning to 'spoiling, spoiled, ruined'. Blake (1977: 85) also notes that Drung is the name of an Irish village in County Donegal. Les Blake is the only source for the dissonant etymology, and it may be disregarded as speculation on his part.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: (two), Big River State Forest. (1) Rises from the Dudley Saddle and Weather Range Junction; tributary of the Torbreck River. Historical Information:
In 1929 two new Catholic centres were founded as part of St Anthony's Parish Glenhuntly, St Patrick's Murrumbeena and Holy Eucharist Murrumbeena North in Dandenong Road. The foundation stone at Holy Eucharist in Dandenong Road was laid by the Archbishop of Melbourne Dr Daniel Mannix in September 1929. The red brick building had a hall downstairs, which was used as a church on Sundays, with a sanctuary at one end. During the week the church seats were pushed aside and the building became a school. The early school, with an enrolment of sixty five students, was run by two Presentation Sisters. The Presentation Sisters staffed the school until 1973, when the first lay Principal was appointed. In 1936 the church was linked to St Mary's East Malvern and it was not until 1946 that the parish was separated from St Mary's and became a parish in its own right. In 1959 it was decided that the red brick church building was no longer adequate.
The new church, designed by architects Alan Robertson & Associates, and built by Holywood Constructions cost 55,000 pounds. It was officially opened by Archbishop Justin Simonds in 1962. Neighbouring East Malvern parishes Holy Eucharist and St. Mary's first partnered in 2008. In 2016 they formally became one Parish, 'Holy Eucharist and St. Mary's Malvern East'. The Holy Eucharist School closed in 2017 after enrolments dwindled to just 28 students.

DECKER, Lance Corporal Albert, 4092, 22 Infantry Battalion (10 Reinforcement Group). Age 18 years 3 months, Labourer, single. Born at Warragul, Victoria. Son of Jacob Elliott and Emily Decker (nee Jones) of Church Street, Warragul. Educated at Warragul State School. Served with the Senior Cadets prior to his enlistment. Brother of Company Sergeant Major 882 Jacob Elliott Decker, 8 Battalion; and Corporal 431 William Decker, 39 Battalion. On the Warragul War Memorial, and the Warragul State School, and Warragul Shire Honour Boards. Albert enlisted Melbourne 23 December 1915 and embarked at Melbourne on HMAT A18 Wiltshire 7 March 1916. Disembarked at Suez 10 April 1916. Embarked Alexandria 9 May 1916 and disembarked Marseilles 18 May 1916. Taken on the strength of 22 Infantry Battalion from reinforcements 31 July 1916. Wounded in action 1 August 1916 when he sustained shrapnel wounds to his shoulder and a gunshot wound to his leg and was admitted to 3 Canadian Stationary Hospital at Boulogne. Transferred to England on the Hospital Ship Cambria 8 August 1916 and admitted to 2 Western General Hospital, Manchester. Rejoined his battalion 24 November 1916. Appointed Lance Corporal 15 May 1917. Albert was killed in action 9 October 1917 during the ferocious fighting near Passchendaele, Belgium. During September and early October the Allies steadily drove the Germans back to the top of Passchendaele ridge. Through October and into November, wet weather and sheer exhaustion meant further attacks became hopelessly bogged down. Though the final ridge was eventually gained, no breakthrough was possible. Losses were horrendous on both sides. Official War Historian Charles Bean wrote: I have often thought that many a youngster when he was hit out there on the Passchendaele heights ... and he knew that the end had come - must have thought to himself: "well at least they'll remember me in Australia." Albert is buried at White House Cemetery (III.H.26), St. Jean-les-Ypres, West-Vlaanderen,
Belgium.

Mount Difficult cairn is located on the western edge of the Mount Difficult
Range (Grampians National Park) at the higest point on the range. The
surrounding terrain is rugged sandstone outcrops. The old geodetic survey stone cairn is located on the most prominent position on the outcrop with the trig approx 9.5 metres to the north. A metal tripod beacon was erected nearby in 1982. (Angle Book 472) The stone cairn is approximately 2.75 metres high by 3 metres diameter at the top. It is built of unmortared stone. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The Mount Difficult cairn was built c 1863. Mount Difficult geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an
example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of two examples remaining in the Grampians region (and one of three in south-western Victoria). Although it has lost its beacon, it retains its overall form and scale.

Historical Information:
A geodetic survey of the colony was proposed in the late 1850s by the Surveyor General Charles Ligar, with the aim of providing a sound framework for local surveys. Unlike the trigonometric surveys then underway, a geodetic survey would conform to parallels and true meridians. The proposal was to divide the whole colony into divisions, each being geographical "squares" of one degree each by longitude meridian and latitude parallel. Each division would then be divided into 100 blocks, each of around 24,000 acres, which would then be
further surveyed and subdivided by local surveyors. The geodetic survey began, and quickly faced practical difficulties with surveying geodetic lines of latitude and longitude. The lines could intersect anywhere, in swamps or gorges, and establishing line of sight between observing
stations was a problem. The first meridian (the 145th) was run from west Melbourne northwards to the Murray River, this meridian being chosen because of its closeness to the Williamstown Observatory. Thomas Pinniger's survey of the Shepparton-Dookie area is one of only two places in Victoria where evidence of the geodetic squares survey is known to survive. Pinniger was employed on the geodetic survey in 1859 as an assistant surveyor, later becoming a Geodetic Surveyor.
His work focused on the north-east of Victoria, where lines had been run nearly to the Ovens River. He established geodetic blocks from there to Seymour, Euroa and Mansfield. The work took many years. In 1863 Pinniger was working in the Longwood area and in the space of a year he had marked out fifteen blocks. In 1866 he was still in the same region, and by early 1867 had completed an additional eighteen blocks in the Seymour district. The Dookie post is certainly an example of his work. This post is one of only two places in Victoria where evidence of the geodetic squares survey is known to survive, the other being a series of survey marks and one geodetic Square Post established by Thomas Pinniger in the 1860s.

Historical Information: The Maggs family was one of the prominent early orchardist families throughout the foothills area east of Melbourne. James and Harriet Maggs arrived from Bristol, England, in 1852, and settled in what is now Springfield Road, Blackburn, in 1860. Maggs Street, Doncaster marks another Maggs orchard property. James and Harriet had 7 children. One of their sons, Samuel, was the first of the Maggs to settle near Burnt Bridge, on 43 acres, with a homestead Livilla". His son James (1880-1940) was at first an orchardist in North Ringwood, but then succeeded his father in the Burnt Bridge area. James had 9 children, one of whom, Douglas (1904-1977) was also an orchardist in the same area. Samuel's brother James (1862-1939) also had an orchard on Kalinda Rd, (Maggs St. Croydon), and another brother, Joseph, had 114 acres where Maroondah Hospital and Warrawong kindergarten now stand.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information:
In 1856, the Moravian missionaries, the Reverends Hagenauer and Spieseke, who had operated a mission at Lake Boga in Wembawemba country since 1850, were seeking an alternative mission site. They considered Lake Hindmarsh a suitable site, and in January 1859 they visited the region, staying with HC Ellerman at his Antwerp station. Ironically, they selected Banji-bunag, the site of an 1846 killing, as a suitable mission station site. They chose to cal this site Ebenezer. Ellerman actively encouraged the mission site and added a large area of his station to the 105 hectares granted by the government. Many Wegaia were attracted to the station, as the site was traditionally a corroboree ground and meeting place. One of the missionaries' first converts to Christianity was a Gur balug youth called Pepper. In August 1860, Pepper was baptised and chose Nathaniel as his Christian name. In 1862, the Hagenauers left Ebenezer and went to Gippsland to work. For a time, Nathaniel Pepper was taken to England. After the death of his wife in 1869, Nathaniel Pepper decided to leave Ebenezer and live with the Hagenauers at Ramahyuck, where he died in 1873. In 1871, 692 hectares were added to the Ebenezer mission station, and by 1873 the reserve had been fenced in and subdivided into grazing paddocks. Twenty-two stone and log cottages and huts had been errected there for the Wergaia. Under the terms of the Aborigines Protection Law Amendment Act 1886, 25 'half castes' were forced to leave Ebenezer. 
In 1902, the state government came to the decision that Ebenezer should be closed owing to the small number of Aborigines resident at the station. Accordingly, in 1904, the mission station was revoked and handed back to the Victorian Lands Department and made available for selection. The exception was the churchyard and small reserve left for the old tribespeople. Some of the Wergaia families had been forcibly removed to Lake Tyers, either under police escort, or because rations were withdrawn or children seized. Some Wergaia families, however, avoided removal and remained in the district.

Title: Scars in the landscape: a register of massacre sites in Western Victoria 1803-1859

Historical Information: Ecklin is the name of a swamp and a rural locality south of Terang, in western Victoria. Massola (1968: 21) noted that the Aboriginal name for Ecklin Swamp was Ecklin yalloack. This name was sourced from Lane in Smyth (1878 Vol. 2: 187), and contains yaluk the widespread Kulin word for creek. Blake (1977: 90) has raised the possibility that Ecklin is 'from Scot. L. Eck (linn, pool)'. Les Blake is the only source for the dissonant etymology, and may be disregarded as speculation.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: Edith Ileen Macpherson (1898-1984) bequeathed the park land to the Dandenong City Council. In life, she was always known as 'Ileen', her middle name. Her modest weatherboard house had been purpose-designed and built to accommodate her own special needs. This disability-access house served her for three decades, but in her will she specified that it be razed to the ground leaving no trace - and so it was. The playground of Edith Macpherson Park occupies the site of the demolished house. Ileen Macpherson and Ernesto Genoni's Demeter Farm operated for two decades (1934-1954). Ernesto and Ileen were both members of the Rudolf Steiner's Experimental Circle of Anthroposophic Farmers and Gardeners which was headquartered in Dornach, Switzerland. An imperative is to correct the name of the park from 'Edith Macpherson Park' to 'Ileen Macpherson Park'.
Author: Dr John Paull
Page Title: Edith Macpherson Park: Testament to a Pioneering Biodynamic Farmer

Historical Information:
Edythe McCallum (1917-2011) was the Senior Social Worker for the City of South Melbourne from 1962 to 1981. She made an extraordinary contribution to South Melbourne's reputation as a pioneer in social planning and community
development. She had a significant role in the preservation of housing for Iocal people in the 1970s and worked toward the establishment of the South Port Community Nursing Home. McCallum's work representing Victoria on a taskforce for the Australian Institute of Urban Studies regarding 'revitalising the cities' was featured in an article in The Age (23 0ctober, 1973, p.25): 'Mrs. McCallum points out that in any city, people must have access to the social infrastructure - that is, to the supportive networks within a community that help people to cope. Without such access, she says, people cannot help but feel alienated... It's the people that matter'. The Rotary Club of South Melbourne awarded her the Vocational Service Award for Outstanding Service in 1977.

Historical Information: (also Eglington, Eglintoun). Pastoral run (3,500 ha, 1845-81 or later), along the north side of Eglinton Creek (but see also Mount Pleasant run). Noble says that the run was named by Archibald Thom (licensee, 1845-48) after Eglintoun on the Tamar River, Tasmania (which the Thoms had left in 1834). The name is ultimately derived from Eglinton near Irvine in Scotland (from the Saxon name Ægelwine and Old English tun, enclosure). John Downey intended to use Eglinton for the town that became Alexandra (q.v.).

Historical Information: Parish, town. The first Eildon township, also called Eildon Reservoir, was built mainly on the east side of the Goulburn River, at its junction with Honeymoon Creek, just below the Sugarloaf Weir. Most of it, except for the cemetery, was obliterated by construction of the present Eildon Dam. The present town of Eildon dates from 1950-52, and was built almost entirely on the west side of the Goulburn. The street names (First, Second, Third, and so on) reflect its American planners, the Utah Construction Company. The new township was built for Eildon Dam construction workers and their families: a maximum of 1,780 workers were employed on the dam project in 1954, and the township housed about 4,000 people. During the construction period the new township was sometimes called "The Weir". Schools in the townships have been called Eildon Weir, Sugarloaf Waterworks and Eildon Primary (see also Upper Thornton). Eildon parish is on the north side of the Goulburn River, from its junction with the Delatite River west to Alexandra parish. The area south of the Eildon Pondage includes most of Upper Thornton, the former name for the area south of the Goulburn between Snobs Creek and Jerusalem Creek. Gold was discovered near the junction of the Goulburn and Delatite Rivers in 1854, and worked from 1864 onwards, especially in 1868 (Flett, 1970). For the origin of the name see also Eildon pastoral run.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: On Friday 7 December, 1951, a 49-year-old housewife named Mrs. Elsie Dorrington became the Shire of Mornington's first woman Councillor, when six hundred ratepayers decided to break with tradition of no women in the Shire Council. Cr. Dorringtons' first job was to urge the Council to set up a home-help scheme and she also went on to initiate a number of social welfare schemes in the Shire. Mrs Dorrington served three terms as Councillor until 1958. In 1960 Mrs Dorrington was appointed as Victorian Justice of the Peace and sat on the bench at Mornington's Magistrates Court. From 1961 to 1969, Mrs Dorrington worked for the Department of Mental Hygiene as the Manager of Moorakyne Girls Hostel in Hawthorn. Elsie Dorrington passed away on 1 June, 1995 in Mount Eliza.

Historical Information: Eric Juckert was a noted Australian potter who lives at Grossard Point, immediately next to the reserve.
Named after Eric Juckert (1918-2004), a noted artist and potter of Ventor, Phillip Island, who lived at Grossard Point adjacent to the reserve.

Eric Carl Juckert was born in the working class suburb of Richmond, Victoria on the 26th of October 1918. His father George Louis Otto Carl Juckert, (1884-1957) was then a Telegraph Mechanic and his mother was Ethel May Storey  (1895-1945).  They lived at 177 Coppin St Richmond.  The name "Juckert" is German in origin.  In 1919, the family moved to 34 Fitzgibbon Crescent, Balaclava. Eric was a prolific studio and commercial ceramic artist who began his extensive career with Una Deerbon (nee Darlot) at her studio at 5 Bray Street South Yarra in Melbourne, Victoria in 1936.  Then between 1937 and 1950 Eric set up his own business at his home at 34 Fitzgibbon Crescent, Balaclava, making a range of pottery that was sold by the Myer and David Jones department stores under the name Jacqueline.  Charles Wilton also worked with Eric at this time.   Eric's first advertised sales were at the height of the great depression at the 4th Floor, Bank Chambers (Centreway Arcade) 255 Collins Street Melbourne on the 8th of December 1937.  In 1939 at the start of the Second-World-War Eric, along with Charles  joined the RAAF as an Aircraftsman, he was discharged in 1946. Following a number of issues with the then Commonwealth Department of Employment and National Service, the pottery closed in 1950. For a time from early 1947, Eric was the proprietor of the Granthaven Gentlemans Country Home, near Healesville, Victoria.  He advertised Granthaven extensively during this year.  He also exhibited at the prestigious Kozminsky Gallery in Melbourne on the 20th of November 1947. In 1949, Eric was back in Melbourne, this time at 337a Balaclava Road Caulfield, not far from his old home in Balaclava.  The Electoral Roll lists him as being a potter.  He advertised pottery lessons from there on 29th November 1949.  This venture lasted until 1954 when he moved to Sandy Creek Road, Riddell, near Gisborne, north of Melbourne where he is listed on the electoral roll as a Farmer.  The Electoral Roll for Balaclava shows George, now a Toolmaker living with Norman and Isabel Juckert, Ethel is not there.  She died in 1945. Eric traveled to England for a time and is believed to have also traveled to Mexico, although there is scant evidence of this.  On his return to Melbourne, he then set up a studio at Point Road, Grossard point, Ventnor on Phillip Island, south of Melbourne in 1959 where he continued working there until 1992. His commercial works which were mainly made with a white spatter finish are incised 'Juckert' or 'Eric Juckert' to the base.  This spatter finish was used by a number of potters, most notably Premier, Rathjen and Raynham, but Eric was not restricted to this style. He was a magnet for other potters and was always available for advice.  People traveled from around the world to work with him.  Eric died on the 4th of January 2004 at the Warley Hospital, Cowes, Phillip Island.  He is buried in the Cowes Cemetery.  He was a popular local although it appears that he never married and had no children.
Author: The Rameking

Historical Information: Named after Eric Roberts. He farmed the land where the reserve is located. He also had significant achievements in the dairy industry over several years.

From the early 1900s, selectors were attracted to the area and established market gardens on the fertile red soil to supply Walhalla with produce. The district became known as Moondarra, and the area around present Erica as Upper Moondarra. In 1910, a narrow gauge railway was opened between Moe and Walhalla. The station at Upper Moondarra was renamed Harris, in honour of Albert Harris, the local parliamentarian who had promoted the line. But due to postal confusion with another town, in 1914 it was changed again to Erica, after nearby Mount Erica and the native heath.

Historical Information: A dairy farmer within the immediate area of the reserve, Ern Barker has had a long involvement with residents of the area from Hallam to Berwick. He provided support to Pony Clubs and equestrian activities throughout the area, and was also a member of the Berwick and District Agriculture and Horticulture Society. He was an Olympic-level equestrian for Australia.

Ern Hart was a field naturalist who discovered, photographed and painted many species of orchids and other native plants in the Wodonga area.  He taught many people about the values of the local natural environment, which led to the conservation of various patches.

Name acknowledges Ern Miles who was a member of the Kyabram Urban Land Care Group.  He dedicated many hours to revegetation works, including walking trails and seating, weed control, nesting boxes, school information days and hosting other land care groups. The reserve was previously known as the South Boundary Road Drainage Basin.

Ernie (Ernest) Condon grew up on his father's farm, Spreydon, approximately 5km from Wodonga. As a child, Mr Condon worked in a timber yard, working later in Jack Laughton's foundry in Albury. He was a self-taught engineer and inventor, starting his own engineering business next to his house in Osborne St.

Historical Information: Town, parish, pastoral run, former shire (1879 - 1994). The pastoral run (1840-82), of 32,000 ha, was also called Holdforth and Barton's (1842-44) or Urowa (named by James Kirkland ca. 1844), and was listed by Wells (1848, as Urowa). The name Euroa was assigned to the town in 1850 by Thomas Wedge, who surveyed the district. Ned Kelly (1855-80) and associates made an unauthorised withdrawal of £2,000 from the National Bank on 9 December 1878 (see also Faithfulls Creek). Aboriginal (Taungurong): eurawa, push, shake or thrust (Massola, 1968), yera-o, joyful (Saxton; Martin), or yera'o, joyful place (Reed 1973). The phrase "yera'o yea" was repeated in a "joy" song at local corroborees (Chambers).

Historical Information: Local historian, Frank McGuire, says that the Emerald diggings were so named at a meeting on March 12, 1859, on the basis that the discoverers of the gold diggings were predominantly natives of Ireland, the Emerald Isle. However, Helen Coulson, says the   town derived its name from nearby   Emerald Creek, which had been named after an early prospector Jack   Emerald. Emerald, the town, was first officially known as Main Ridge. Gold was found in the Emerald area in 1858. The first Emerald school, No.2110, was located on what is now Avon Road in Avonsleigh. The existing primary school, Emerald Township School, No.3381, was opened in 1901 and moved to the current site in 1909. In the 1871 Census, the Emerald gold field was referred to by Government officials as Irishtown to distinguish it from the township of Emerald. The lush vegetation apparently reminded some people of Ireland.

Historical Information: Rises in the Strathbogie Ranges between Marraweeny and Boho South; joins Seven Creeks south of Miepoll*. Named after George Faithfull and William Pitt Faithfull, "Overlanders" of 1838. Appears on Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847), and is listed by Wells (1848). Brough Smyth (1878) and Massola (1968) say that the Aboriginal name was Balmattum (q.v.). Also pastoral run (4,500 ha, 1841-79) east of Euroa. However, the Faithfulls Creek Pre-emptive Right was south of Euroa on the west bank of Seven Creeks, south of the Seven Creeks Pre-emptive Right (see Cropper's for explanation). In 1878 the Kelly Gang used the Faithfulls Creek homestead as a base for their raid on Euroa (q.v.).

Historical Information: In 1938 the State Electricity Commission of Victoria (SEC) began construction of the Kiewa hydroelectric scheme and by the end of World War II had established the Bogong village and a nearby power station. The full scheme involved the construction of two reservoirs on the Kiewa River's headwaters at Pretty Valley and Rocky Valley. The latter storage, the larger of the two, is 3 km upstream from Falls Creek. The Country Roads Board undertook road construction and apparently renamed a short stream, Horseshoe Creek, as Falls Creek because of its waterfall.

Historical Information:
With the support of the Congupna community the park name recognises the Farrell family.

The first generation of Farrell's in the district were William & Cecilia Farrell who moved to Congupna Road in 1889.

In 1924 their son William A (Bill) Farrell and his wife Ivy purchased land in Congupna. This was the second generation of the Farrell family in Congupna. William and Ivy had ten children. Nine of their children attended Congupna Primary School. Bill, Ivy and their children were active in the community.

The Farrell family still has connections with the Congupna community.

Historical Information: An area of Spring Creek (1) was surveyed by John Downey in 1869 for a township to be called Yarck, but it was not gazetted. Fawcett was first used for the area in 1885, possibly after John Fawcett, who apparently lived in the Eglinton Creek or Mount Prospect area in the late 1860s [Lyn Hampel]. The surname is derived from Fawcett, Yorkshire (Old English ford, ford, and [ge]sete, house, settlement) or Facit, Lancashire (Old English fag, fah, coloured, flowery, and side, slope). Residents also used the names of Durham Gully and Spring Creek. See also Koriella and Yarck.

Historical Information: Reserve and picnic area; former village, also called The Watts, Watts, Watts Bridge and Watts Crossing, between Healesville and the Dom Dom Saddle at the crossing of the Yarra Track and the Watts River. Surveyed 1865. The first school was (for reasons unknown) called Tooleen from 1871 to '72 and then renamed Fernshaw (presumably to avoid confusion with Tolleen*). The township's main industries were tourism and raspberry growing. As it was in a water catchment, the village was gradually bought up (1885-91) by the Victorian government and the buildings demolished or moved. The area was the scene of Louis Buvelot's painting, Near Fernshaw (1873). Named "by a north-country surveyor from the fact that the prominent features of the river banks were the 'shawes' of the ferns"  ("The Vagabond", quoted by Mitchell). The Scots (and probably northern English) term shaw, copse, wood, is derived from Old English sc(e)aga, thicket, wood. See also Maytown.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Prior to 1991, The Port Fairy Village Green was often referred to as the Fiddler's Green. In 1991 the Borough of Port Fairy officially named the area as the Village Green. With the construction of the permanent stage at the area, the Port Fairy Folk Festival are hoping to gain support for the renaming of the area as the Fiddler's Green. Fiddler's Green has a unique and special meaning and is associated with the history and culture of music, seafaring and fishing all of which are part and parcel of the history and culture of Port Fairy. The name Fiddler's Green has a mythical context and even has a folk song of that name that reflects the mythical context.
