Historical Information: Flagstaff Gardens is the oldest park in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia, first established in 1862. In 2005 it is one of the most visited and widely used parks in the city by nearby office workers and tourists. The gardens are notable for their archaeological, horticultural, historical and social significance to the history of Melbourne. The gardens are 7.2 hectares (18 acres) of Crown Land bounded by William, La Trobe, King and Dudley streets, managed by the City of Melbourne. On the south-east corner opposite is the entrance to Flagstaff railway station. Diagonally opposite stands the Victorian branch of the Royal Mint, established 7 August 1869. The former Royal Mint building is a well-preserved example of Victorian Gold Rush boom-period classical styled architecture. The facade features paired columns with scrolled capitals and the Royal Mint coat-of-arms. On the northeast corner over William Street, is the Queen Victoria Market. The park contains extensive lawns with a variety of mature trees, flowerbeds and wild animals including possums. The southern end is characterised by deciduous trees, while the northern end contains mature eucalypts. Avenues of elms shade pathways along with several large Moreton Bay Fig trees. The north corner contains a bowling lawn, rose beds, flower and shrub beds. Along William Street there are tennis courts, which also double as volleyball, handball and netball courts. Electric barbecues nearby provides a popular site for office parties in December. Scattered about the lawns and gardens are memorials and sculptures that illuminate some of the social significance of the area. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagstaff_Gardens
Author: Wikipedia

Historical Information: Originally called Burial Hill, this rise at the western end of the city grid was renamed when the flagstaff was erected in September 1840 for signalling shipping activities in Hobsons Bay. George Gordon McCrae reminisced that 'Bunting and great wicker balls' told what type of vessel was approaching and the port of origin. Marryat's code of signal flags was used to carry news from Williamstown. The advent of the telegraph rendered the flagstaff redundant and operation ceased on 1 October 1857. The signaller's store and dwelling were incorporated into the Flagstaff Observatory. At 130 ft (39.6 m) in height, and with better sight lines of Williams-town and the bay, Flagstaff Hill had been preferred to Batmans Hill as the observatory site. The Flagstaff Gardens were planted on the site in the 1860s.
Author: Judy Macdonald

Traditional name: Bongerimennin. Meaning: n/a

Bongerimennin overlooks Terrinalum (Mount Elephant) and Bonan Youang (Mount Buninyong). Buninyong and Terrinalum argued, and challenged each other to a fight. They came together at Pitfield; Terrinalum carrying a spear and Buninyong carrying an axe. Terrinalum pierced Buninyong's side with his spear, while Buninyong hit Terrinalum on the head and split it open. They returned to their campsites to rest, and turned to stone, their wounds still visible in the landscape.
Author: Bryon Powell

Historical Information: In the early station days it is said that a bucket of burning wood was hoisted to the top of a pole on the hill to guide bullock teams, hence the occasional name, Beacon Hill. The valuer for the Shire of Lowan, St Elroy D'Alton visited Wonga Lake Homestead at Lake Brimin in 1879-80 and reported: 'The homestead was the usual log hut type seated at the foot of a high sand hill, with a pole or flagstaff erected from the highest part'. The hill was burnt in 1946, and became seriously eroded by a combination of rabbits and visitors climbing up it, necessitating restricted access.

Historical Information: 'The is much difference of opinion as to the derivation of the name 'Flemington.'  Garryown, vol. 2, p. 721, says that it was named in compliment to Bob Fleming, a retail butcher who settled in that locality at an early date.  McCarron, p.57, says the place was named after John Wood Fleming, native of Melbourne, born 1837.  Herald, 8.9.13, agrees with McCarron.  The Argus, 5.6.96, on the authority of Thomas Kissock, says that the place was named by Mr. Watson (of Watson and Hunter, early pastoralists), in honour of his wife, whose father was manager of a Flemington estate in Scotland.'
Author: O'Callaghan, Thos
Title: Names of Victorian Railways Stations

Historical Information: Foxeys Hangout on the corner of Balnarring and Tubbarubba Roads, Merricks North has been a local landmark since the 1930's. It is reminiscent of the days when trapping of wild animals was essential for the farmers' livelihoods. The name was originally given to a conspicuous gum tree near the corner by neighbouring landowners who initiated a friendly contest between two trappers as to who took more foxes. The catches were hung from the tree and a tally was kept.

Historical Information: In the late 1850s,a Djargurd wurrung clan head, 'King Alick', was given several acres of land near Camperdown. When he died in 1860, 'Prince Albert' his son, sought to have this land transferred to his possession. However, given the urban expansion of Camperdown, the grant was cancelled, and another reserve in the worse accessible locality near Camperdown was proposed. The Framlingham mission station was established near Warrnambool in 1865 and this station became the home of many of the surviving Djargurd wurrung. A number of old people, however, refused to abandon their traditional country. By 1877, there were only two aged Djargurd wurrung men living in the Camperdown district. They lived near a brewery and were well cared for by local town residents, but would not go to Framlingham.

Historical Information: Frank Jones (1917-1988). Long standing local resident, spent 36 years living at 1 Simpson Street. He enlisted in the AIF in Sale on 4 November 1939, and served with distinction in Egypt, the Middle East, Greece and Crete. He was discharged medically unfit for active service on 9 December 1943 as a result of being severely wounded during the Battle of Crete. After the war he worked with the Sale Council in the sanitary department, then was employed on the construction of sewering Sale. Because of his size and strength he constructed all the manholes for the project.On the completion of this project he worked with the Victorian Railways for the last 20 years of his working life operating from the Sale Railway yards. He looked after the reserve area

Named by Surveyor George Smythe after Sir John Franklin, Governor of Van Diemen's Land in 1841, who requested that a lighthouse be built on Cape Otway.
Franklin died in 1847 on the expedition seeking a Northwest Passage through ice north of Canada. It is possible that this low headland had previously been named Point Danger by Lieutenant James Grant on the Lady Nelson 7 December 1800 (Grant 1803). Historical Information: Part Taylor's Overnewton/part Rockbank estates. Crawford Harvie's Union Inn was relocated to the eastern boundary of the area following the opening of the railway 1859 to accommodate Melton farmers forwarding butter to Melbourne. Overnewton Subdivision sale opened up area to influx of farmers engaged in hay making and cropping - among the first being the Fraser family whose son Hector achieved international renown as the World Champion Trap Shooter at the age of 19 years.
Named by explorers Hume and Hovell after a well-known convict surgeon in Sydney, William Bland; later known as Mount Fraser.  See also Victorian Historical Magazine Vol.1 No.3, Sept 1911.

Historical Information: Fred Lasslett served with the Royal Australian Navy aboard the HMAS Perth during World War II. The vessel sank in the Battle of Sunda Strait in 1942 and Mr Lasslett spent the remainder of the war as a Japanese PoW in Indonesia and Japan. He wrote letters in secret detailing his time as the camp electrician, failed escape attempts and facing a firing squad. Mr Lasslett survived and returned home safely. He and his family settled in Heidelberg shortly after where Mr Lasslett had been a prominent local identity for over fifty years, serving as President and dedicated member of the Heidelberg RSL sub-branch. Fred Lasslett died on July 10 2013, aged 94.

Historical Information:
A rock cairn marking one of the major instrument stations used by Alexander
Black to connect to the position of the spring identified as the source of the
Murray and in setting out the commencement of the north-west end of the Black-Allan line. A survey to determine the border of New South Wales and Victoria was undertaken in 1870-72, twenty years after the two colonies were separated. The need to define the border on the ground arose due to the increasing settlement in this mountainous country, especially the advent of gold mining around the Bendoc region. The eastern end of the border at Conference Point (Cape Howe) was established in 1868 by NSW Surveyor-General P.F. Adams and R.J.L. Ellery for Victoria. The western end, at Forest Hill, is the source of the Murray River. It was marked by Alexander Black in 1870. Black proceeded to undertake an eleven month survey to mark the border on the ground between Forest Hill and Allan's Peg, a peg positioned near the Delegate River by Senior Geodetic surveyor Alexander Allan. To achieve the simple "straight line" border across mountainous country involved enormous hard work under difficult conditions. Ellery writing about
the geodetic Survey of Victoria in 1891 described the survey as "a piece of survey work which for difficulties and for the requirement of skills, energy and endurance, as well as for accuracy attained I believe has never been surpassed". Black's survey traversed very difficult terrain, covering 61.5 kilometres over 11 months. Allan's survey was 114 kilometres long, extending over 18 months. Over 50 marks were built by the surveyors and their teams. Some were substantial stone cairns. The surveyors also had to dig trenches to indicate the
direction of the border, and clear the line of vegetation.  The Black-Allan line border survey is of state significance as evidence of an outstanding surveying feat, testing the endurance and skill of the survey parties,
and providing a dramatic demonstration of the difficulties encountered by surveyors in the nineteenth century. Historically, the marking of the border between New South Wales and Victoria symbolised a step in the development of Victorian as a separate, self-governing region.

Historical Information:
The name Gardenvale, initially spelt Garden Vale, came into use around the turn of the century. Sources suggest that it was a name derived from a family estate of the Lempriere family. When the family subdivided their local land (area between Elster Creek and Gardenvale Road and between Kooyong Road and the Point Nepean Road) they called it Garden Vale Estate. 

Alternatively the name Garden Vale may have its roots in the large number of market gardens, which had been located in the area.

Historical Information: The town was originally called Cannibal Creek. Renamed Garfield in honour of the assassinated American President, James Garfield, who was shot July 2nd, 1881 and died September 19th ,1881. Garfield Railway Station was originally known as Hopetoun, after Lord Hopetoun (1860-1908), the seventh Earl of Hopetoun and first Marquess of Linlithgow. Lord Hopetoun was the Governor of Victoria and later on the first Governor-General of Australia. The term Cannibal Creek is believed to refer to the killing of dogs by dingoes and was the name of an early cattle run, also called Coonabul Creek, based    around Mount Cannibal. Another interpretation is that the term comes from a corruption of the Aborignal  couna  meaning  forehead  and  bal  meaning he or she. This possibly referred to the shape of Mount Cannibal, which was thought to resemble a head.
Author: Casey Cardinia Libraries
Page Title: Place Names of Casey and Cardinia

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner

Historical Information: Gem stones were found in a creek by the Gembrook Mining Company. Albert Le Souef, part of the Company, named the creek Gem Brook. The town itself was pegged out in 1874. There have been five schools called Gembrook. Gembrook, No.2506, began in 1879 as the part time school No.2110 and became full-time in 1889. Classes took place in the Union Church from 1884 until it moved to the Main Street in 1906 and to the present site in 1915. Pakenham Upper School, No.2155, was called Gembrook South from 1879 until 1916. Gembrook West, No.3211, operated for just over a year from August 1894 until October 1895. The second Gembrook West School, No.4073, operated from 1921 until 1923. Finally, Gembrook South East, No. 3468, opened half time with Nar Nar Goon North in March 1904 and closed in December 1908.

Historical Information: Gerald Francis Mullane was born on the 11th of July 1927 to parents Thomas and Mary Mullane. He was raised at Ballan. He attended St. Bridget's Catholic School in Ballan until he was aged 12, when he went to work in Melbourne as a Telegraph Messenger. He returned to Ballan 12 months later and worked on the family farm, until he married Noreen Quinlan on the 29th of May 1951. They bought 420 acres at Navigators and farmed potatoes sheep and cattle. In 1951 he bought a Bedford truck and started livestock carrying. His interests included football, tennis, and cricket. He started playing football for Ballan in 1944 and played in their Premiership side. He then went to Bungaree where he played in two premierships. He was Chairman of Selectors at the Dunnstown Football  Club from 1970 - 1975. He joined Local Government on the 1/8/1980. He was Shire President of the Buninyong Shire in 1985. He became a member of the Ballarat Water Board in 1980. He was a member of the Ballan Fire Brigade for four years before joining the Mt. Buninyong Fire Brigade in 1951. He was made Captain in 1971 and retired in 1992. He is a life member of both the Mt. Buninyong Fire Brigade and the Victorian Rural Fire Brigade Association. He played A grade tennis at Navigators. He was instrumental in the development of the Navigators Community Centre where he served as a Committee member and President. He loved horses, and was a Committee member of the Agricultural Society. He was a steward at the Ballarat Show. He was a volunteer for 17 years with Riding for the disabled carting their horses each week and helping the children ride. He was a member of the Ballan Jockey Club.
Named in honour of Gerald Francis Mullane who farmed at Navigators and served as a councillor and shire president in local government, with local fire brigades and on the Ballarat Water Board.

Historical Information: (north-west of Yea). Major meeting place for the Taungurong; parish; former pastoral run; goldfield settlement. James Henry Campbell, first licensee, bestowed the name on the pastoral run (1838-70 or later) of about 6,000 ha. (The homestead still exists.) Listed by Wells (1848, as Ghinghin). Gold was discovered in August 1867, and three reefs worked. In its heyday the township had 13 houses, two shops and "innumerable shanties and huts built by the several thousand hopeful miners and fossickers who flocked there" (Blanks). The goldfield was sometimes called Palestine Creek (Flett, 1970). Ghin Ghin is Aboriginal (Taungurong): "deep dark waters" (Les Blake); "supposed to mean Green Grass" (Blanks); "meeting of the waters" (Jones & Jones: 1); "meeting of waters" (Clark & Heydon: M); but, because of the doubling of ghin, may mean very - or lots of - something (big meeting place?). See also Palestine Creek.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Gladstone Park - there are places called Gladstone and Gladstone Boreland in South Lanarkshire, and Gladstone Farm in Renfrewshire. Gladstone is a Scottish family name, well established in Lanarkshire by the thirteenth century (Herbert de Gledstan was one of the signatories of the Ragman Roll). The most famous bearer of this name was William Ewart Gladstone (1809-1898), one of Queen Victoria's Prime Ministers. Although he was born in Liverpool, his parents were both Scottish and he proudly claimed that "not a drop of blood in my veins is not Scottish." The name of this Melbourne suburb comes from a property owned by Thomas Gladstone between 1869 and 1883.

Historical Information: Glen Waverley and Mount Waverley - Waverley is the name of the main railway station in Edinburgh (see illustration). The station received its name in the 1850s, from the title of a series of novels by Sir Walter Scott (a monument to whom had been erected in Edinburgh near the future railway station in 1844). Sir Walter, in turn, had borrowed the name from Waverley Abbey, a Cistercian monastery in Surrey, England founded in 1128 but now a ruin. The Melbourne suburbs of Glen Waverley and Mount Waverley derive their names from that of an earlier township (now the suburb of Malvern East) which had been privately surveyed in 1853 and which was named Waverley by its owner after the Sir Walter Scott novels

Historical Information:
Billlimina shelter is an impressive rock overhang where Jardwadjali (Yard-wa-jali) camped from time to time and left many red paintings. Archaeologists who excavated this site in 1976 found stone tools and the remains of plant and animal foods. These materials demonstrated that groups camped here from late winter to early summer and caught kangaroos and small mammals such as bandicoots, possums and bettongs. They also collected emu eggs and freshwater mussles. 
The most interesting aspect of the paintings at Billimina is the many bars arranged in horizontal rows. These marked are believed to have been used to count events in retelling stories or to record the number of days spent at a place. While they are sometimes difficult to see, there are also emus, kangaroo and emu tracks, and 55 human stick figures painted here.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: Parish, township, pastoral run, goldfield. The Gobur pastoral run (about 2,400 ha, 1845-74 or later) was named by Henry Godfrey, licensee (1845-46), and was listed in 1848 by Wells (as "Gobier"). Aboriginal (presumably Taungurong): Les Blake gives goburr(a), kookaburra, and Clark & Heydon (M) gobur, kookaburra, but in closely related Woiworung, gurrborra means koala (Barry Blake). The township, once much larger than now, was also known as Godfrey's Creek, O'Brientown (Moyle & Davies) and Pennington(s) - after Ezekial Wilson Pennington (Flett, 1970). Waghorn (p. 6) gives a sketch map of Gobur in the gold-mining days which includes a number of features not named on survey maps. Some of these features can be located on modern maps with reasonable accuracy: see Burnt Hill, Cummins Hill, Mount Gobur and Stockade Gully; but three cannot be identified with certainty: Bald Hill (east to north east of Gobur), 82 Camp Hill (north of Bald Hill), and School Hill (south of Bald Hill).
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Rises in the forested ranges north-west of Woods Point, near Corn Hill, Bald Hill (3) and Frenchman's Gap; is dammed at Eildon and at Goulburn Weir* (near Nagambie*), and flows into the Murray River* above Echuca*. Named (1824) by Hamilton Hume and William Hilton Hovell in honour of Major Frederick Goulburn (1788 - 1837), colonial secretary in Sydney. (His surname was probably derived from the Old English name Golda, gold, and either byrgen, burial mound, or burna spring.) Also called the Hovell by Hamilton, Hume and Henry as there is another Goulburn River* in New South Wales (tributary of the Hunter*). Mentioned regularly by Wells (1848) in connexion with its tributaries, and also under Murray River and Western Port District, but not listed (its N.S.W. namesake is). Wells also refers to the "Bayungan or Goulburn river" (p. 420) and the "Goulburn or Bayungun [sic] or Twisden" (p. 276). Sections of the river have numerous Aboriginal names as it flows through Taungurong, Ngurai-illam-wurrung and Yorta Yorta (Jodajoda, Pangerang) language areas. "The Goulburn River they denominate Warring" - James Dredge, writing about the Taungurong in 1840 (HRV). Other Taungurong names include Boo-err-goen  (19 km above Yea), Koriella (at Koriella, q.v.) and beyond Seymour* Waaring*, Kai-el-a* (tribal name) and Kongoopka* (perch) (Massola, 1968). Brough Smyth (1878, 2: 198, 203) also lists Gila, Goyla ("Goulburn tribe") and Gungupnas* ("Murray tribe", probably Yorta Yorta), but emphasises that the last two are particular points on the river. Bayunga(n) (Wells) is presumably Aboriginal but may be a general term for river as it has also been applied to the Ovens* and possibly the Murray*. Clark & Heydon (M) also list Taungurong Bayyango and Waaring, Wahring, Warring ("big or large water"), and Taungurong or Ngurai-illam-wurrung Omio, Yorta Yorta Gaiyila* ("father of waters"), Gungupna* (from gupna, deep waterholes), and Koninner* at the confluence with the Murray*.

Historical Information: Gowanbrae - there are no Scottish towns or villages by this name. However, Gowanbrae is the name of a guesthouse, built in 1917, in Dufftown, Moray. In a communication received from its owners, it was stated that this guesthouse has always been known as Gowanbrae and that it receives many Australian visitors. Gowanbrae is one of Melbourne's newest suburbs (1990), which increases the chances that a visitor to the Scottish guesthouse may have named the suburb. Gowan is a Scots word for a daisy, more particularly the mountain daisy and the element 'brae' (pronounced bray) means a hill or hillside. It is interesting to note that most of the streets in this suburb are named either for flowers and trees commonly found in Britain or for places in Scotland (Balerno Circuit, Lanark Way, Lauder Court, Paisley Court, Perth Court, Rutherglen Crescent).

Historical Information: Named in recognition of Alex and Janet Gray who moved to Lake Boga in 1893 and established the town's first general store. [See 'The History of Swan Hill Shire' by Lesley Scholes.]

Alex & Janet Gray in 1893 moved to Lake Boga and established the town's first General Store. By 1897 Gray had land in the parish of Kunat and Boga.  Alex Gray died in 1903, his wife continued operating the store known as Alex Gray's Store, later in her own name.  Janet Gray's Store became one of the most highly respected in the shire, with suits made to measure, groceries, a timber and building supply yard and farming equipment.

Named after Lieutenant General Leslie James Morshead

Leslie Morshead won fame as the defender of Tobruk during the Second World War and is among the most renowned Australian divisional commanders of that war. He was born at Ballarat in Victoria on 18 September 1889 and became a teacher. Joining the AIF in September 1914 as a lieutenant, Morshead was posted to the 2nd Battalion. 

By the time he landed at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915 he was a captain; by August, when he fought at Lone Pine, he had been promoted to major. After Gallipoli he was promoted to lieutenant colonel and given command of the 33rd Battalion, which arrived in France in November 1916. Morshead led the battalion successfully through Messines and the Passchendaele campaign of late-1917, was awarded the Distinguished Service Order, and continued to command through the battles Villers-Bretonneux and Amiens in 1918. 

Morshead joined General Monash's staff for the demobilisation of the AIF and returned to Sydney in December 1919. He married Myrtle Woodside in November 1921. Having failed to make a success of a soldier-settlers' block in Queensland, Morshead returned to Sydney to work in shipping, gaining promotions and posts in several Australian cities and in England. 

He remained active in the militia, commanding two battalions and reaching the rank of temporary brigadier. In October 1939 he was given command of the 18th Brigade, sailing for Britain in May 1940. The following February Morshead was promoted to major general in command of the 9th Division, then in the Middle East. Reputed to be a tough commander who could be blunt with senior officers, Morshead led his division through the siege of Tobruk where his aggressive defence denied the Germans a breakthrough but earned him the ire of some subordinates concerned at the level of losses. 

His success at Tobruk was followed by promotion to lieutenant general and command of the AIF in the Middle East. Morshead, at the risk of alienating his British superiors, argued to keep the 9th Division together in the face of British demands to detach individual brigades. He led the division through the battle of El Alamein, where the 9th Division's contribution was considered vital to the victory. During the battle, he regularly visited both the front and the wounded behind the lines. 

Returning to Australia in 1943, Morshead took command of II Corps in October and then in November was elevated to command both New Guinea Force and the Second Australian Army. In May 1944 he was given command of I Corps, leading them through the final battles of the war in Borneo. After the war, he chaired a military court of enquiry into Major General Bennett's departure from Singapore in February 1942. 

Morshead refused offers of military and diplomatic posts, as well as the governorship of Queensland, returning instead to the shipping industry as manager of the New South Wales branch of the Orient Line; later he became its Australian general manager. He held a number of other directorships and civil appointments and was involved in right-wing politics before becoming ill with cancer in the mid-1950s. Morshead died in Sydney on 26 September 1959.

Historical Information: The name was applied in 1857 when Irish prospectors wanted to call their claim 'Great Eastern' to commemorate the ship of that name.  Mining warden Taylor preferred 'Great Western' because the claim was in the Western District.  Early settlers then apparently associated the name with the Great Western railway system in England, naming local streets after engineers and contractors associated with construction of the rail system.  A later attempt to change the name to 'Irvine' was rejected because Great Western wines were already well known.  See also Victorian Place Names Committee Card Index.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: Keith Greenham, aged 86, a long time resident of Pental Island, has been involved in a huge number of community committees over many many years. He was awarded the Order of Australia in 2006 for his service to the Swan Hill District 'through leadership within a range of organisations committed to community development.' At the time of receiving this award he had been Secretary of the Swan Hill Residents and Ratepayers Association since 1997; Secretary of the Swan Hill Association of Independent Retiree's Group since 1998; and Secretary of the Lake Boga Community Development committee between 1993 and 1997. He had been a member of the Victorian State Emergency Services for over 27 years; the Pental Island Warden since 1973 and was Deputy Chairman of the Pental Island River Management Board from 1983 until 1997 when the board was abolished. Between 1993 and 1997 Mr Greenham was also the Chairperson of the Mallee Regional Housing Council (Swan Hill Committee), and Branch Secretary of the United Dairyfarmers Victoria during the 1980's and 1990's. Also, a member of the Swan Hill Branch of the National Party, he had been its Secretary since 2000. Mr Greenham also served as a Councillor of the Swan Hill Shire from 1993 -1995, when the Council was abolished to become Swan Hill Rural City Council. He was a founding member of the Swan Hill Main Drain Community Action Group, and in 2000 he was awarded Swan Hill Rural City Council 'Citizen of the Year Award' for his years of Community Service. Mr Greenham is also the Swan Hill South Chief Flood Warden, and through his involvement with flood management since 1955, was of invaluable assistance during the 2010 and 2011 floods in the Swan Hill area.
Named 'Greenhill Lake' by Major Thomas Mitchell in 1836.

Historical Information: Name honours the contribution and legacy of Salvatore ('Sam') Guastelegname.  He arrived in Australia in 1952 and, with his wife, purchased land to develop an orchard. Historical Information:
Edward Fritz Guye, better known as Tom, arrived in Winchelsea in 1910. He was a veteran of the 1914-18 war who took part in the first landing at Gallipoli. He was a founding member of the Winchelsea RSL and held executive roles in the RSL from 1919 to 1937. He was elected a member of the Winchelsea Shire Council in 1939 and served until 1960. He served two terms as Shire President in 1945-46 and 1959-60. He also served as Chairman of the Winchelsea Water Trust in 1946.

'Tom' Guye was elected in 1940 to the seat of Polworth in the Legislative Assembly of Victoria and retired from that role in 1960.

Jack Guye, the son of 'Tom', was a member of the Winchelsea Shire Council from 1961 to 1986 and served two terms as Shire President in 1968 -69 and 1976-77.

Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information:
George Scolaro (1933- 2018) Arriving in Australia in 1959, he was one of the foundation members of the Italian Social Club of Werribee, providing immigrants with assistance and a home away from home. Werribee was to him the luckiest place in the world to be. George became a concreter in Australia. He built many landmarks in Werribee - Locally he built hundreds of house slabs, Council offices, Bridges, Buildings, Schools, Industrial sites, Avalon air strips, and RAAF Base piers. His saying "I came, I saw, I concreted". He would always drive my son around and show him how he helped build Werribee. He always put Werribee first, and believed in buying local whenever he could... and never wanted any of his daughters move out of Werribee. Family and Community was before anything else in life! He was the first to bring tenpin bowling to Werribee, and not because he loved it, but because he wanted families to have somewhere to go. He always said if he can help keep kids off the streets he was happy. In 1980 he raised a record amount ($35,000) for the Yooralla Society. Diversity was George's middle name! He had friends in all cultures and walks of life and assisted many communities in building premises or just through support. Above all Dad was a visionary and wanted to leave a legacy to the community. When you thought he was done, he was just getting started. Walking down Watton Street with George was a lot of fun, he knew everyone, and they knew him! What should have taken 5 minutes would take and hour but his pride in the community spirit was strong. His love of life, jokes, stories and memories of early Werribee will greatly missed and having a bridge named after him would ensure his spirit and legacy live on. He built most of the bridges in Werribee, inc Werribee St bridge (across river), the ford in Cottrell St, the underpass, and so many more. He also built the current Council Offices, Werribee Police Station, Ballan Rd, Avalon Airport back in the early 70's, lots of the MMBW sewer pools.

He also was one of the founders of the Italian Social Club back in the 70's.
Little known is how he represented the old Werribee Fisher Motors and Bridge Hotel at the Royal Melbourne Show in Tug of War. He was on Ch7 on World of Sport every Sunday as the Coach for the team.

Historical Information:
Green Hill, also called Eynebury, is one of three points from which the Geodetic Survey of Victoria was constructed. A quadripod survey beacon has been placed over the original geodetic survey mark at Green Hill. The geodetic survey mark is set in concrete and covered by a cast iron cover. Part of the Geodetic Survey Baseline.  Three permanent marks are associated with the establishment of the Victorian
Geodetic Baseline at Werribee in 1860 by Robert Ellery, Government
Astronomer and Supervisor of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria: South Base, North Base and Green Hill extension. Located on the east side of the Werribee River, north of the railway, the baseline was five miles in length. It was extended north-west to a total of nine miles to
Green Hill by triangulation. The baseline was measured using three ten-foot iron rods made in Victoria against the NSW standard originally obtained from the Ordnance Survey Department of South Hampton in England. The north and south ends of the five mile baseline 'were permanently marked with sunken masonry piers, having in their upper surfaces a piece of brass carrying a platinum dot indicating the termini of the measure. These marks were then covered with heavy cap stones'. The third mark, at the end of the extension to the north, on Green Hill, 'consists of a sunken bluestone block with a projecting iron spike. The South and North Bases, and the location of the third mark on Green Hill are shown on a 1915 Army Ordnance map of the area. Examining this map it is possible to follow the course of the baseline from the present day location of Hoppers Crossing, across the Tarneit Road to the North Base south of Sayers Road and close to the Werribee River, and then across the Werribee River to Green Hill within Staughton's Eynesbury Estate. The South Base is possibly the best known of the three permanent marks because of its location close to the Princes Highway and the various campaigns to ensure its preservation. A photograph of the South Baseline stone appeared in 'Trust News', after the National Trust had classified the three historic marks as 'physical evidence of an important element of the 19th century Geodetic Survey and consequently the earliest maps of Victoria'. Robert Lewis John Ellery was a physician as well as an astronomer. He was one of the founders of the Royal Society of Victoria, and was the foundation President of the Institute of Surveyors.

Historical Information: Harold Alexander (1902-1964) was Town CIerk of City of South Melbourne from 1936 to 1964. He was a pioneer who contributed to the creation of an environment that prioritised citizens' social welfare. On his death the Iocal paper, The Record, reported that 'he guided the destinies of his native city surely and safely and, through his innovations, placed it in the Iead in social service, a model and example to other municipalities not only in Australia, but overseas'. These innovations were many and included supporting the establishment of the Meals on Wheels service (in 1953, South Melbourne was the first municipality in Australia to offer this service), and the introduction of social workers and a maternal and child health doctor (in 1941 South Melbourne was the first Council in Victoria to employ a social worker). He lobbied for the current site of the Victorian Arts Centre to be set aside for a cultural purpose. He was president of the Iibrary board that oversaw the establishment of municipal and school libraries. At the Ordinary Meeting of Council on 30 January 2006, Council noted the requirement for demolition of the Harold Alexander Pavilion (at the former Middle Park Life Saving Club). At that Council meeting, it was identified that Harold Alexander should, in the future, be commemorated at a suitable site that would properly reflect his contribution to the community and the esteem in which he is held.

Harold Caterson was a member of Moorabbin Rugby Union Football Club's first committee, he was at the initial meeting in December 1964 that agreed to create a rugby club in Moorabbin to commence in season 1965. He was a long-term committee member (in various positions) and club member in the 60s, 70s and 80s and he was key in establishing a home for Moorabbin at Keys. Rd. Additionally, he was involved on the Management Committee of the Victorian Rugby Union over many years.
In the history of the club Harold Caterson and Jack McDavitt stand out as the two most influential club members who founded, developed and built Moorabbin Rugby Club from scratch.
Jack has, appropriately, had the extended clubrooms (originally built in 1978) named in his honour for his contribution to the club. The reserve was renamed in honour of Harold's contribution to the club.

Keys Rd ground was an old rubbish tip that had been filled and covered in a layer of soil. The surface was continually subsiding, in 1965 junior cricket was played on this ground and the oval was found unsuitable for cricket; it was actually a muddy paddock in winter and a corrugated concrete oval in summer. Cricket never returned to this oval.
Harold could see the potential in the Keys Rd Reserve and in 1967 donated the cost of a single car steel garage placed on a concrete slab, which was to become our first changing room/clubroom, and was later known as "the old tin shed". It had the nickname of "Mr. Cat's Cottage" on a sign above the door.
The following year a small extension was added that held a briquette hot water service and several showers.
As the Club grew over the years, Harold continued to be a committee member and also continued to liaise with Council regarding club matters. Whether it was gaining approval for further extensions to the shed (there were several extensions over the years), ground improvements, a second playing field, flood lighting and eventually Clubrooms were built in 1978.
Harold was the "go to person" in regard to Council. He developed a very good relationship with Mayor Bricker, who later became our Patron for many years and over time became one of the Rams strongest supporters.
Gaining significant funding for a sport that was practically unknown in the district, was not easy. The relationship between Harold and Cr. Bricker proved vital on several occasions as the councillor supported funding for the club which otherwise might not have been approved.
That the Rams are based at Keys Road can be put down to Harold's dedication to securing a permanent home for rugby union in Moorabbin.

The club's playing jersey is also a legacy from Harold Caterson's U18 Marlins team.
He was President in 1968 and 1971; Vice President in 1969, 1970 and from 1972 to 1981 inclusive. Ordinary Committee Member 1965 to 1967.
Harold was made a Life Member in 1977.
Additionally, he was the Moorabbin club delegate to the Victorian Rugby Union for many years; and he would collate the results and statistics for the VRU weekly magazine each week during the season.
His work with the club, Council and the VRU continued right up to his sudden death in 1981.
It is worth noting that four generations of the Caterson family have been involved in playing and administrating the Moorabbin Rugby Club since its inception in 1965.
Author: Ian Ray
Title: Life Member Moorabbin Rugby Club

Historical Information: Named in honour of Harry Lavery (1909-1977) who acquired the land known as Sailors Gully Estate in 1955 and had a great attachment to "the bush paddock".  The reserve was set apart to protect its bushland state. Harry Lavery was also a volunteer fireman, a Justice of the Peace and a newspaper correspondent.

The name recognizes Harry Lavery, who had a direct connection with the site from 1955 until his death twenty-two years later. Harry's great-grandfather emigrated from County Armagh, Northern Ireland, to become a pioneer of the Mount Bolton - Waubra area.  Harry was born at Waubra on 16 August 1909, the eldest son of a large family.  After leaving school at 12 years of age, he worked in a variety of jobs before finding permanent employment with the Victorian Railways, initially with a track maintenance gang, eventually becoming a heavy machinery maintenance worker, servicing the area from Rockbank to Ouyen. Harry was a volunteer fireman and Justice of the Peace as well as being involved in many local community projects.  He had a keen interest in politics and was an active member of the Australian Labor Party, serving as secretary and newspaper correspondent. Harry acquired the land now known as Sailors Gully Estate in 1955 and had great attachment to "the bush paddock", becoming custodian of the land.  He knew every inch of it, studied every bird and animal, kept gorse and blackberry in check and cleared debris and fallen timber when necessary.  He educated his children in the geology and history of the land and passed on to them the love and respect he had for it. Although Harry died on 10 March 1977, "the bush paddock" remained with his family until development of the Sailors Gully Estate began. Although Harry never looked for acclaim, it is fitting that his close attachment to and love of this land be recognized in its name.

Historical Information: In 1845 Mrs Martha King took up the Bunguyan pastoral run in the Hastings district and is considered to be the first white settler. Mrs King, a widow, had emigrated to Port Phillip in 1840. Her homestead was calledTyabb, and the first township surveyed was also called Tyabb, now Old Tyabb. Old Tyabb's position at the head of the Hastings Bight was not quite right, as already there was a fishing settlement about 2 km south, at a place favoured by deeper water. The place, known as Kings Creek, was renamed Hastings in about 1860, probably after the sea port of Hastings in Sussex, England.

Historical Information: The district of Hawksburn is named after Hawksburn House, one of the earliest houses in the area. The house, built in 1851 for James Cassell, the Collector of Customs, stood on a large estate of about 33 ha. The name is said to be derived from Cassell's sighting of a hawk in a wet gully (called a burn in Scotland) on his property.
It was named after Hawksburn House (situated near where the railway station was later built), which was so named when its owner saw a hawk near a stream which he likened to a Scottish burn.

Mark Hayes selected the land at Tooborac in August 1857 and the family lived in tenets on a little creek on the east side of the road (which is now the reserve in question) until the stone house 'Leicester House' was built.  This was finished and occupied by 1862.  The House was continuously lived in by members of the Hayes family, until the property was sold in the 1970's. Historical Information: 'The Hazelwood station was named after Mrs Hazel Bennett wife of William Bennett, and sister of Albert Eugene Brodribb, who were co-holders of the station from 1844 to 1852.  The Bennetts held it alone from 1852 - 60.  Mrs Bennett was the first white woman to live in the Morwell area.  The Bennett family played an important part in the early development of Gippsland.  The Revd. Francis Hales in his Diary, kept during his pioneering ministerial journey through Gippsland in 1848, states that he stayed a night at 'the comfortable Bennett home at Hazelwood.'  Bishop Perry and Mrs Perry called there in 1849.'

Historical Information:
Kulin name: Woo-rite. Meaning: not recorded. 
This name was recorded by A. W. Howitt, anthropologist, from conversations from sometime between 1897 and 1901 with William Barak, ngurungaeta (leader) of the Wurundjeri-willam, the traditional owners of what is now northern Melbourne, and Dick Richards, Barak's fellow Kulin countryman. The Kulin was an alliance of Aboriginal nations in central Victoria. Howitt jotted down Aboriginal names, mostly in the Woiwurrung language once spoken in the Melbourne area, corresponding to landmarks and municipalities that arose in Melbourne town during Barak's lifetime (c.1824 to 1903).

Page Title: Rediscovered: the Aboriginal names for ten Melbourne suburbs

Hedgeley Dene Gardens were formed along an early watercourse. Initially land had been purchased in this area by William Harwood in 1856. In 1877 solicitor, Edward Charsley bought both the Harwood land and the surrounding property naming his farm Hedgeley Dene after Hedgerley in England close to where he was born. The (Royal) Melbourne Golf Course was formed in 1891 and Hedgeley Dene's land was used for part of the 18 hole course. By 1902 the Maidment family owned a dairy farm on the land and its dam and waterhole, known as 'Maidment's Lake', formed watery obstacles along the 8th
and 9th fairways of the golf course. Golfi ng activity ceased in 1909. When Alfred Sydney Baillieu subdivided the dairy farm in 1911 the Maidments moved to Kardella Street. New streets, which would service 142 building allotments, were created. An area reserved for 'drainage' later provided land for the future gardens. The Malvern City Council also purchased land from the Estate, hoping to use it for tennis, bowling and croquet. A covenant on the title ultimately prevented this type of use. Soldiers returning from WW1 were given jobs planting trees, beautifying an area which had for a time been used as a quarry and a tip. In 1924 F.L. Reeves, Malvern Council's Parks Curator, put forward a comprehensive plan to fully develop the area as a park by planting native and exotic trees, redeveloping
the water-feature (adding an island and some rustic timber bridges), improving pathways and later adding electric lighting. During the Depression, garden projects provided work for the unemployed.
Another war and its aftermath saw manpower and resources diverted elsewhere. Hedgeley Dene Gardens fell into a long malaise until 1978 when it once again received some long overdue attention. The polluted lake was cleaned out, new trees planted and other necessary work done; resulting in a new lease of life which brought back not only the ducks, but fi lm crews, weddings and a happier public - winning the State Garden Competition in 1980. Hedgeley Dene Gardens is considered to be one of the most unique linear, Edwardian municipal gardens in Melbourne.
Author: Malvern Historical Society
Title: Stonnington Gardens - Hedgeley Dene

Historical Information: The Hedgeley Dene Gardens were formed along an early watercourse that was once part of a sixty acre estate first sold by the Crown in 1856. The same year a weatherboard cottage of two rooms was built and a brick house of four rooms was under construction in Wattletree Road for owner William Harwood. In 1877 more than forty acres, along with Harwood's cottages fronting Wattletree Road, were purchased by solicitor Edward Charsley for 500 pounds. Charsley named his farm after his English birthplace Hedgerley. Original trees, including poplars from the Hedgeley Dene farm still survive.

Historical Information:
In the November 1944, William (Bill) and Violet Hicks announced to the people of Wodonga and District that they had taken over the General Store from farmer & Son. They hoped by catering for their customers to merit a share of patronage.
Their sons, Lindsay, Harold, Ray, Oscar, Frank and Clem all at one time worked in the store, (some of them were away at the war when the store was taken over by the Hicks). The store was located in High Street, where the second hand car yard is now, on the southern side of Bond Lane. W. Hicks and Son was in business until the early 1960's. The store sold wine & spirits, clothing, drapery and groceries.

Five kilometres north-west of Wonthaggi, on the Bass Highway, there is Hicksborough. It had a railway station and a short lived school (1911-14). Hicksborough had census populations of 307 in 1921 and 274 in 1933, but apparently its census was reduced after then. Under 100 were recorded until 1961. The Hicksborough general store on the Bass Highway is a landmark. Another say is that it was possibly named after the Hicksborough Coal company from 1924.

Historical Information: Plateau, settlement. The rocky plateau is north of Yea and west of the northern section of the Black Range and includes the area around Caveat, Dropmore, Highlands settlement, Kobyboyn, Ruffy and Tarcombe. (No connexion with the Highlands* pastoral run near Mount Bogong*.) The settlement was originally called Fassifern, but in 1908 the inhabitants were asked to rename it (to avoid confusion with a similar name), and John McAlpin suggested Highlands, presumably after the Highlands of Scotland. The first name was probably after Fassifern (now Fassfern), Scotland (north-west of Fort William). Gaelic: fàsach a' fearna, which James Johnston translates as "forest of alders". Fàsach normally signifies a desert, a wilderness, or an area of luxuriant grassland (a prairie), but it can also mean a grove of trees (fàsach coille); clump of alders might give a closer meaning.

Historical Information: The Hopetoun district was settled as a pastoral run in 1846, and in 1877 the run was acquired by Edward Lascelles. He had farm and township blocks surveyed in 1889 and apparently persuaded the Victorian Governor, Lord Hopetoun, to visit his pastoral station in 1890. The naming of the township followed, and the first land sales occurred in 1891. Lascelles' residence, Hopetoun House was built in 1891.

Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: Parish, township, former shire, pastoral run. The parish (now partly submerged) was originally at the junction of the Howqua and Goulburn Rivers, south of Boorolite and north of Jamieson parishes. The township is on the south shore of the Howqua Inlet (primary school, 1941-57). The shire was established in 1874, with headquarters in Jamieson, and superseded the Howqua Roads Board; it ceased in 1919, becoming the Howqua riding of the shire of Mansfield. The former pastoral run (about 4,900 ha) was established in 1845 and was subdivided, 1863, into Goulburn Downs and Howqua Hills*. See also Howqua River and Howqua West.

L. Howqua, Mansfield Courier 7 April 1974 [Brian Lloyd]), Chinese surveyor and early resident of Melbourne*. Aboriginal (Taungurong) name: Pyerlite (Clark & Heydon: D, M).

midwife and bush nurse. During a long career she helped deliver and care for many
of Melton's early residents.
Born in Ireland in 1832, Hannah sailed to Australia with her first husband at 20 years
old. By the time she arrived she had already impressed many with her natural
ability, and she was still serving the Melton community until her death at the age of
89, in 1921.

Historical Information:
In the early 1860s, the residents of Sydney Flat (now Woodvale) were wakened by a series of mysterious explosions. Upon investigation, it became clear the explosions had been caused by a group of youths trying to blast out tree stumps to ready the local oval for the imminent cricket season. The leader of these youths was a fifteen-year-old local boy by the name of Henry Frederick (Harry) Boyle.
From his beginnings on this oval, Harry Boyle went on to play cricket at the highest level and to achieve great fame. Some brief highlights include being the first Australian to bowl W G Grace in December 1873. His form for Bendigo United Cricket Club got him invited to play for the East Melbourne Cricket Club which was pretty much the top Melbourne team of that era. Boyle became one of the best players for that team and captain of the club in 1875. He also represented Victoria and for many years was a selector for the Victorian Eleven. He was a member of the 1878, 80, 82, 84 and 88 Australian teams to tour England as well as managing the 1890 tour.
In March 2023, the community named the oval located on the grounds of the Woodvale Recreation Reserve the "Harry Boyle Oval".

The original Hill "E" mark os a loose pile of rocks approximately 1.5 m high. Hill "E" 1986 - a modern mark in the same hilltop area as the Old Geodetic Hill "E" - is located approximately 1.65 km from Border Cairn No. 4. A Geodetic plaque in a pre-cast concrete block (stamped 87801) and one post were noted during field observations in 1986. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). Hill "E" and the oTher alphabetically notated instrument stations, were used by Alexander Black as part of his survey methods in laying in, marking and checking the placement of the major cairns on the source of the Murray to Allan's Peg section of the Black-Allan line. Date of construction of this cairn is not known. Hill "E" geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local interest as an example of
the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of seven examples remaining in the alpine area of north-east of Victoria. This cairn is in poor condition and has lost its beacon and some of its form due to collapse of the stonework.

The Hill "G" mark comprises an unmortared stone structure, partially collapsed at the top, and retaining a timber centre post. The cairn appears to have been conical in shape, and is now approximately 1.6m high and 2.0m diameter. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). Hill "G" and the other alphabetically notated instrument stations, were used by Alexander Black as part of his survey methods in laying in, marking and checking the placement
of the major cairns on the source of the Murray to Allan's Peg section of the Black-Allan line. Date of construction of this cairn is not known. Hill "G" geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of seven examples remaining in the alpine area of north-east of Victoria. This cairn is in fair condition, but retains its centre pole and overall form and scale.

The Hoddle Reference Tree is located on the Kew Golf Course, close to where it abuts the Greenacres Golf Course and the Yarra River. The tree is a River Red Gum. Robert Hoddle was engaged on survey of Crown Land for subdivision and sale in the Kew area in April 1844. The tree was used as a reference tree in the survey. Robert Hoddle was the Officer-in-Charge of the Port Phillip Survey Department from 4 March 1837 to 15 July 1851 and the first Surveyor-General of Victoria from 1851 to mid-1853. he was the centralfigure in the development of land surveying in the early years of the Port Phillip colony. In 1929 two new Catholic centres were founded as part of St Anthony's Parish Glenhuntly, St Patrick's Murrumbeena and Holy Eucharist Murrumbeena North in Dandenong Road. The foundation stone at Holy Eucharist in Dandenong Road was laid by the Archbishop of Melbourne Dr Daniel Mannix in September 1929. The red brick building had a hall downstairs, which was used as a church on Sundays, with a sanctuary at one end. During the week the church seats were pushed aside and the building became a school. The early school, with an enrolment of sixty five students, was run by two Presentation Sisters. The Presentation Sisters staffed the school until 1973, when the first lay Principal was appointed. In 1936 the church was linked to St Mary's East Malvern and it was not until 1946 that the parish was separated from St Mary's and became a parish in its own right. In 1959 it was decided that the red brick church building was no longer adequate.
The new church, designed by architects Alan Robertson & Associates, and built by Holywood Constructions cost 55,000 pounds. It was officially opened by Archbishop Justin Simonds in 1962. Neighbouring East Malvern parishes Holy Eucharist and St. Mary's first partnered in 2008. In 2016 they formally became one Parish, 'Holy Eucharist and St. Mary's Malvern East'. The Holy Eucharist School closed in 2017 after enrolments dwindled to just 28 students.

This cairn is in poor condition and of low integrity, having been completely rebuilt in the 1960s.

Historical Information:
Jack Williamson, OAM, was a well known and highly respected Gippsland horseman. As a competitor and committee member, his service to the Maffra and District Show spanned in excess of 70 years, almost 60 of these with his equally dedicated wife and equestrian Nancy beside him. Jack joined the committee whilst still a jumps competitor, was an exemplary member and rarely missed a meeting.
For decades, Jack oversaw horse events at the show. He put days of thought, time and labour into marking rings. Jack spent over a week before each show delivering and setting up horse jumps and equipment. He oversaw the period when the show society went from hunting to Olympic style jumping. On show day, Jack was the main point of contact for show jumping. Jack and Nancy always sponsored jumps events at the Maffra Show, as well as the children's equestrian section at the Sale Show.
In later years Jack dedicated himself to Riding for the Disabled and continued to help with the show even when his health began to fail. Jack and Nancy were awarded OAM's for their service to Pony Clubs, and in 1990, Jack was made a Life Member of the Maffra Agricultural Society.
Jack Williamson died on March 11, 2011. With the recent building of a dedicated horse jumps arena, it was unanimously passed by the Show Committee that it be fitting that the arena be named the 'Jack Williamson Arena.'
With Nancy Williamson in her 94th year, an appropriate opening is planned for the show on October 27th.

Albert Jacka was born on 10 January 1893 at Layard near Winchelsea, Victoria, fourth child of Nathaniel Jacka and his wife Elizabeth, nÃ¿Â¿Ã¿Â©e Kettle. The family moved to Wedderburn when Albert was 5. After elementary schooling, Bert worked for the Victorian State Forests Department. 
Jacka enlisted in September 1914 as a private in the 14th Battalion, Australian Imperial Force. His unit spent two months training in Egypt before landing at Anzac Cove on 26 April 1915. On 19 May the Turks launched a massive counter-attack. Amid frenzied fighting at Courtney's Post some Turks captured a 11m section of trench, one end of which was guarded by Jacka. For several minutes he fired warning shots into the trench wall until reinforcements arrived and, after shouting his instructions, he and three others sprang out into the trench. All but Jacka were immediately hit so he leapt back into the communication trench. Two bombs were lobbed at the Turks while Jacka skirted around to attack from the flank. Amid the smoke and the noise he clambered over the parapet, shot five Turks and bayoneted two as the rest hastily retreated. For this action he received the Victoria Cross, the first to be awarded to the A.I.F. in the war.
Jacka became a national hero. He rose quickly through the ranks, passing officer training and was commissioned 2nd lieutenant in April 1916.
Jacka's platoon moved into the line near PoziÃ¿Â¿Ã¿Â¨res, France, on the night of 6-7 August 1916. German troops overran a part of the line at dawn. Jacka had just completed a reconnaissance and had gone to his dug-out when two Germans appeared at its entrance and rolled a bomb down the doorway, killing two men. Jacka charged up the dug-out steps, firing as he moved, and came upon a large number of the enemy rounding up some forty Australians as prisoners. He rallied his platoon and charged at the enemy, some of whom immediately threw down their rifles. Furious hand-to-hand fighting erupted as the prisoners turned on their captors. Fifty Germans were captured and the line was retaken. Jacka was awarded a Military Cross. The entire platoon was wounded, Jacka seriously in the neck and shoulder. He received further promotions. 
On 8 April 1917 Jacka led a night reconnaissance party into no man's land near Bullecourt to inspect enemy defences before an attack against the new German line. He penetrated the wire at two places, reported back, then went out again to supervise the laying of tapes to guide the infantry. The work was virtually finished when two Germans loomed up. Realizing that they would see the tapes, Jacka knew that they must be captured. He pulled his pistol; it misfired, so he rushed on and captured them by hand.For  this action he was awarded a Bar to his Military Cross.
He was wounded by a sniper's bullet near Ploegsteert Wood on 8 July. In May 1918 he was badly gassed at Villers-Bretonneux and saw no more action. In September 1919 he embarked for Australia where a large crowd, met him. He was demobilized in January 1920. Shortly after his return he formed an import export business with two former comrades. 
On 17 January 1921 Jacka had married Frances Veronica Carey, a typist from his office. They settled at St Kilda and later adopted a daughter. In September 1929 Jacka was elected to the St Kilda Council and became mayor a year later. He devoted most of his energies on council to assisting the unemployed. His own business flourished until 1929 when the Scullin government increased import tariffs and the company went into voluntary liquidation in September 1930. Jacka then became a commercial traveller with the Anglo-Dominion Soap Co.
He died on 17 January 1932. Nearly 6000 people filed past his coffin when it lay in state in Anzac House. The funeral procession, led by over 1000 returned soldiers flanked by thousands of onlookers, made its way to St Kilda cemetery where he was buried with full military honours.

Historical Information: Named after James Ford who held a pastoral lease at Point Nepean in the early 1840s where he raised horses, wheat and other farm produce for ships and the quarantine station.  He also ran a lime kiln and built the first Jetty at Portsea to load ketches with lime bound for Melbourne.  It is understood that he named the village 'Portsea' and established the first baths and hotel in the area.  Ford was also owner of the land which comprises the newly created subdivision that includes the reserve.

Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information:
In 1839, Thomas Napier acquired land on the west side of Dandenong Creek. This area is believed to have been where Jells Park is now located. He was Mulgrave's first settler. One year later he sold out to Alexander Scott. Scott died soon after taking over Napier's land and cattle. His wife, Madeline Scott moved to the property and remained there for several years.

It was known as Corhanwarrabul (the Aboriginal name for the Dandenongs). She later acquired land in the area known as Bushy Park. It is uncertain whether the actual land was in Bushy Park or closer to Jells Park. The cattle run she started ran through Jells Park.

Mrs. Scott sold out to the Drew family. The property was later subdivided and had several owners. One of these owners was Joseph Jell who rode over the land that is now Jells Park.

Historical Information:
Jim Crow Hill, this was an early name for Mt Franklin, and was the name of a creek, range, and goldfield north of Daylesford. 'Mt Franklin' named after Sir John Franklin's visit to the Loddon Protectorate station in 1843 displaced 'Jim Crow Hill'. According to Saxton (1907: 36) Jim Crow Hill was 'Named by Capt John Hepburn. Capt. Bacchus, who accompanied him, asked what name should the ranges have, and Hepburn replied: Jim Crow, after a popular song'. Morrison (1967: 41) explains that the origin of the name 'Jim Crow' has intrigued many for a long time.

Some believe it is the name of a former 'king' of the local Loddon tribe of Aborigines. Etymologically, the term "jim crow" was used for various implements, as for example, a "jemmy", which is a miniature form of a bent crow (bar) and, somehow, the idea of bending or twisting seems to be implicit in its derivation. A device for bending iron bars was one time termed a "jim crow". About 1835, an American negro, James Rice who was a rather popular "song and dance" comedian wrote and popularised a song, the chorus of which was: "Wheel about and turn about and do just so, Turn about and wheel about and jump Jim Crow". Set to a catchy tune it swept the world, as similar songs do today. ... There seems to be no reason, to doubt the accuracy of the story that the application of the term "Jim Crow" to this region, stems from a trivial incident wherein Capt. Bacchus, riding on horseback between "Lalgambook" and Koorocheang with Capt. Hepburn, called to his companion, "What do you think we should call these ranges?" Hepburn (perhaps with the maddening refrain churning in his mind) replied: "Call them Jim Crow!" (Morrison 1967: 41)

Quinlan has noted that Mount Franklin

which the early squatters called Jim Crow and the natives knew by the name of Lalgambook. John Hepburn used the name Jim Crow to refer not only to the mount itself but to the creek below it and to the district. Edgar Morrison who, in 1965, published the memoirs of Edward Stone Parker under the title Early Days in the Loddon Valley, believes that Jim Crow derives from the chorus of an American minstrel song, popular at the time of the first overlanders. It seems quite feasible, as he suggests, that the behaviour of this winding creek recalled to someone like the Mollison brothers the popular jingle, 'Hop a little, stop a little, jump Jim Crow'. Later, when the aboriginal station was established there, many took it for granted that the word referred to the natives. (Quinlan 1993: 99)

According to Blake (1977: 133), overlander Alexander Mollison's records list the district as 'Jumcra', 'Aboriginal name for which meaning not traced; "Jim Crow" was minstrel song from U.S.A. 1835'. Randell (1979: 222) in a history of the Coliban district explained that Mollison took up two stations in the vacant land immediately west of his Coliban station in early May 1840, naming the Loddon run 'Jumcra, probably an aboriginal name. The second run was called Boughyards. The men soon corrupted the first name into Jim Crow'. Tully (1997: 87) supports the view that Jumcra was corrupted to Jim Crow.

Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: River system and former pastoral run. Appears to be called Templeton's Creek in Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847), presumably after James Templeton, licensee (1838-43) of the pastoral run. Wells's entry (1848) for Templeton's Creek provides additional corroboration. Seven Creeks is the principal drainage system for much of the Strathbogie Ranges. It rises south of Too-rour (west of Bonnie Doon Road), flows through Euroa and joins the Goulburn River south of Mooroopna*. Sections of the river provide a breeding habitat for the endangered trout cod (Macculochella macquariensis). Halsall (1980, 1: 48) mentions about three explanations for the name, none of them convincing. Seven Creeks is supposed to refer to Main Creek (another name for the trunk channel) and six other tributaries, though there are in fact more. Tributaries upstream of Euroa include Bald Hill Creek, Coach Road Creek, Hatchells Creek, Mountain Hut Creek, Sheans Creek, Shingle Hut Creek, two with the same name of Spring Creek (2 & 3), Station Creek (2), Surveyors Creek, Watchbox Creek and Wombat Creek (2). Magiltans Creek is an indirect tributary. The principal tributary downstream of Euroa is Faithfulls Creek. The Seven Creeks pastoral run (28,000 ha,  1838-80) was licensed (1851-67) to William Forlonge (1811-90), whose grazing empire at its height amounted to 932,000 ha (9,320 sq. km) of land in Victoria and New South Wales (see also Forlonge Memorial and Cropper's). For Seven Creeks State School see also Gooram Gooram Gong.

Sam Lazarus, owner of 'Homebush' estate proposed the name 'Junor' after his wife's maiden name (Mary Isabella Junor), but it was rejected on the grounds it was too close to 'Junee' in NSW. The suffix 'toun' was then added to 'Junor', it was again submitted and accepted.

The original name of the Junortoun district was 'Homebush' after the 2,000 acre estate extending along the valley of Splitters Creek. The homestead on this estate was the Post Office for the district up until the early 1970s.

In the early years of the 20th century numerous complaints over mail being directed to Homebush, NSW and another Homebush in Victoria led to the postal authorities and the Victorian Government decreeing that the name had to be changed.

At a meeting of residents the late Martin Dole suggested that the name be 'short, quaint and original'. Mr Sam Lazarus, the then owner of Homebush estate, proposed the name 'Junor' after his wife's maiden name. The name 'Junor' originated in Scotland. This was submitted to the authorities, however was rejected on the grounds it was too close to 'Junee' in NSW. At a subsequent meeting the suffix 'toun' was added to 'Junor' and this was accepted.

premiership captain with the Mildura West Cricket Club. He coached junior cricket over many years and the club was like his second home. He was also a life member of the Sunraysia Cricket Association.

John was president of the Mildura West Cricket Club for over 25 years and was instrumental in the club moving to the Old Aerodrome sporting complex. John
orchestrated significant fund raising to assist in the construction of the facilities that exist today. No job was too large and he was never too busy to give tasks or people the time they deserved.

The Mildura West Cricket Club nickname "The Toads" is named after John, in recognition of a man that gave a lot more that he took. John sadly passed away 4

Historical Information: The island was first named "Lady Julia's Island" in 1800 by Lt James Grant after either the wife or daughter of Hugh Percy, 2nd Duke of Northumberland. In 1802 Matthew Flinders expanded the name to Lady Julia Percy's Island as he sailed past on his ship the Investigator. Also in 1802, Nicolas Baudin sailed past the island in his ship the Geographe, and recorded the island as Ile aux Alouettes, a name that has not persisted.

Historical Information: At the time of his death in 1874 William John Turner Clarke had become one of Australia's wealthiest landowners, with property in New South Wales, the Port Phillip District and Van Diemen's Land. It was in Van Diemen's Land in the 1830s that Clarke had begun to amass property and wealth and in the late 1830s or early 1840s he lent money to the Scotch Company, which was composed of a number of Hobart Town traders, for the purpose of establishing a run in the Port Phillip District. The run they set up, Bank Vale, lay some twenty miles north of Melbourne, to the east of the Deep Creek (or Saltwater River), and just beyond the site of the future village of Mickleham. The land comprised undulating open pastures and was well suited for sheep. In the early 1840s the Scotch Company was no longer able to maintain the venture and the run was subsequently taken over in early to mid-1841 by Clarke who quickly installed John Edols, a young overseer, in the vacated manager's hut. This was Clarke's first undertaking in a district where he was within less than two decades to own the freehold title to more than 100,000 acres.
