Historical Information: Kaniva is a town in the west Wimmera region. According to O'Callaghan (1918: 56), probably 'a corruption of Kanizba, the name of a town in Hungary. A large number of Germans and Austro-Hungarians were amongst the earliest land selectors in that locality'. Presumably O'Callaghan is referring to Nagy-Kanisva, a town in the county of Szala, in southwest Hungary. 'The aboriginal name for the place was Budjick meaning tomahawk'. O'Callaghan cites St Eloy D'Alton 'Notes on the early settlement of the Wimmera' as his source. D'Alton was an Engineer in the Dimboola Shire in the early 1890s and the first Dimboola Shire Secretary. Massola (1968: 27) confirms that Budjick means 'stone axe'. Blake (1976: 59) in a history of Nhill and west Wimmera, notes that the name Kaniva was conferred to the locality in 1881 by the Post Master General, after the name of a shepherd's hut on the old station which recalled Kinnivie, near Durham, England. Blake (1977: 139) states that station plans show Kinivae as 'n. of shepherd's hut on pre-emptive right; Kinnivie is locality SW of Durham, England'. Landt (1961: 14), in a local history of Kaniva, notes that 'Kinivae was six miles north-west of Kaniva's present site shown on early maps and was the name given to the Overseer's Hut on Tatiara, Woolshed Hill. Kaniva itself was originally called Budjik Hill. Professor Browne suggests that the hut took its name from Kanziba [sic] in Hungary, suggesting that perhaps a Hungarian shepherd may have named the hut'. The identity of Professor Browne is not known. Wesson (2001: 72) is the only source that suggests Kaniva is an Aboriginal word, meaning 'snake asleep'. I suspect Wesson has considered Kaniva to be a variant of Kaneira (see above). Although the non-Indigenous origin of this placename is contested, there is very little support for it having an Aboriginal origin.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: Locality; railway station (1890 - 1978); former pastoral run. The pastoral run (1842-74 or later), originally a portion of the Tarcombe run, covered about 12,000 ha of land between today's Kanumbra settlement and Fawcett. For most of its existence the run was known as Millers Ponds (the name alludes to a drowning), but it was changed (ca. 1874) to Kanumbra by the last joint licensee, Dr. David Edmund Stodart. The settlement was named by land officer John Hardy of Alexandra, presumably after the pastoral run. To begin with, Kanumbra probably signified a straggle of properties in the parish of Yarck along the road from Cathkin to Merton (today's Maroondah Highway). However, the coming of the railway (1890) resulted in the establishment of Yarck and Kanumbra stations, so the name Kanumbra gradually became restricted to properties nearer the more northerly Kanumbra railway station. Until 1895 the state school was called Millers Ponds, after the pastoral run. Probably Aboriginal (perhaps Taungurong): "possibly fr[om] Abor. karumba, light or human spirit" (Les Blake). There is also Woiworung karnamba, sleep [Barry Blake].

Historical Information: Until 2015, the centre located at 39 Thornhill Drive, Keilor Downs, was the location of a child care centre. Historical Information: Lake Eildon National Park. Flows into the Big River Inlet (not into Kelly Bay). After Edward Kelly (1835-83) who, with John Dunn and Charles Washington Beattie ("Black Charlie"), brought supplies to Darlingford by pack mule. Kelly and Dunn were later (1874) joint licensees of the Big River pastoral runs. The surname Kelly is Irish, Ó Ceallaigh, derived from an old given name, Ceallach, with translations varying from "troublesome" to "bright-headed", though ceallach can also mean a recluse or a churchman.

Historical Information: The Thomson family were long term residents in the City of Coburg. During that time, Kelvin Thomson and members of his family were prominent in local affairs. Kelvin was a Councillor and Deputy Mayor, and served on the major Council committees, as well as being the Chairman of a number of committees. He had a special interest in environmental protection in the area, supporting planting of native vegetation and air, water and noise pollution control.

Strathbogie Ranges. Post office (closed 1967); school (1904-70). Originally Mountain View, but renamed (1906) because of a similar name in Gippsland*. Vision and Realisation says that Kelvin was  "from the name of a wine shanty in the locality" (3: 732). Les Blake claims (more convincingly) that Mrs. George Charman chose the new name after her birthplace in Scotland. Gaelic: probably caol, narrow, and abhuinn, river. See also Charman's Falls.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Ex-Councillor Ken Browne served as a Councillor of the City of Berwick for a period of 9 years between 1974 to 1983, and as Council's representative on the Lysterfield Lake Park Advisory Committee. He was one of the forces behind the establishment of recreation facilities, particularly those on Fox Road, Narre Warren North. He was a driving force behind the establishment of the National Cancer Register.

Ken McArthur, previously Shire Engineer to the Shire of Avon, joined the Shire of Mornington as deputy Shire Engineer and later became Shire Engineer then Director of Engineering before he retired in 1987.
Ken was regarded as the driving force behind the development of The Briars Park and evolved the concept for the Wildlife Reserve and the creation of a series of artificial wetlands to create habitat and natural diversity. The Council honoured Ken by naming the Ken McArthur Wetlands in 1991 and conferred on him Life Membership of The Briars.
Ken's interest in the wetlands took him around the globe to study wildlife and wetlands. Back home, Ken became the Foundation President of the Victorian Wetlands Trust, established to help landowners manage and create wetlands on private property. He was also involved with several Government agencies on land protection issues and provided environmental consultations.
Since 1985, the wetlands have developed and improved, in no small part due to the earlier work done by Ken McArthur.
Ken passed away on 16 September, 2010.

Thomas Kenevan arrived in Sydney from Ireland and travelled to Heyfield by pack horse. A hotel was established by Kenevan around 1862 on the intersection of Rosedale-Heyfield Road and Traralgon-Maffra Road. Kenevan built a house for his family a short distance away from the hotel. The hotel was called the Junction Hotel. It was leased at some time by a man by the name of Smith and later another by the name of Aubrey. It is thought it closed in the 1880's after making a fortune from the gold rush days. The corner was always known as 'Kenevans Corner' although the hotel no longer exists as it was unfortunately burnt down.

Historical Information: Kenmare is a farming district near Lake Hindmarsh. Massola (1968: 28) asserts Kenmare is an Aboriginal word meaning 'kangaroo'. This seems unlikely as the local word for grey kangaroo was 'gure', red kangaroo 'bara', and black-faced mallee kangaroo 'gudji' (Hercus 1986: 269). Blake (1977: 140) argues that it is 'named after Eire estate near Lake Killarney, owned by Lord Kenmare in nineteenth century'. The etymology of Kenmare is unclear; however, Massola's interpretation is not supported by linguistic analyses.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski

Historical Information:
Named after Ethel Maude Kestle who was a landowner in the area with family descendants for approximately 84 years.
William Henry Penaluna's sister, Elizabeth Jane Penaluna married John Mansell Kestle. Their son, William James Kestle married Ethel Maude Smartt and then Ethel Maude Kestle purchased the balance of crown allotments 88 & 88A at the same time as William Henry Penaluna purchased the other portion of these crown allotments. Ethel Maude Kestle retained ownership of this land until 1937 when she sub-divided it into two parcels (what is now the Hospital land and the current Kestle land). She sold the Kestle Land to Leslie Savage in 1937 and she then sold the Hospital Land in 1940. 
In 1942, Ethel Maude Kestle's son, Albert William Alfred Kestle purchased the Kestle Land of Leslie Savage and settled there with his family. One of the current owners, Raymond Kestle, was born on the property and has spent his whole life living on this land. Albert Kestle died in 1972, but the land title remained in his estate for the benefit of his wife until 1998, when the title then passed to the current owners Raymond and Alison Kestle. This portion of Crown Allotment 88 created in 1882 has been held within the Kestle Family for 84 of the 131 years since its creation.

Parish, settlements. From 1862 two small settlements sprang up, one serving the Luck's All and Star of the West mines called Mack's Creek; the other was 1.5 km to the north on the Mansfield Woods Point Road around J. S. Garrett's beer house (today's Kevington Hotel). The Mack's Creek settlement was surveyed and renamed Kevington, after the village in Kent, but failed to prosper, and the name Kevington was readopted by the township on the main road. The last two syllables of Kevington are probably from Old English -inga(s), people, and tun, enclosure, homestead, village, (though the ing in -ington is sometimes just a suffix), in which case the first syllable will be an Anglo-Saxon personal name such as Cyfa or Cafa.

Historical Information: Parish; locality; ruins (north of Yea); school, 1927-37; former pastoral run (north, north-east and south-east of Yea). The pastoral run (16,000 ha), at first known as Cheviot Hills station, was formed either in 1838, perhaps by division of the Muddy Creek run, or in 1839, by division of the Murrindindi run; the licence was cancelled in 1883. Billis & Kenyon, writing about John Macfarlane, refer to "Macfarlane's Station, Devil's R[iver], 1840". This may not have been one of the Delatite river runs (Delatite, Loyola, Maintongoon, Mimamaluke, Preston, Wappan). James Dredge visited "Mr Macfarlane's station" in May 1839 (HRV), but this was almost certainly the Cheviot hills (later Killingworth) run (licensees 1840-42 James and Duncan McFarlane). The run was renamed by George Sherbrook Airey after Killingworth, Tyne & Wear, England, the home of General Sir Richard Airey. Old English Cyllingas, Cylla's people, and worþ, fence, enclosure, homestead. See also Muddy Creek pastoral runs.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information:
Melbourne-born Bruce Kingsbury worked in New South Wales and Victoria before enlisting in May 1940. Embarking with the 2/14th Battalion from Sydney, he served in Palestine and Egypt and took part in the invasion of Syria. He returned to Australia with the battalion in March 1942. 

In August the 2/14th moved to Port Moresby, hoping to halt the Japanese on the Kokoda Trail. Kingsbury's platoon had been holding a position for two days against continual enemy attacks and severe losses when he made the heroic assault that cost him his life. On his own initiative, he charged with a Bren gun, shooting from the hip against intense enemy machine-gun fire, causing many casualties. Alone, he continued to sweep the enemy with his fire until he fell, shot by a sniper. A senior officer said that Kingsbury's valour had inspired the battalion over the succeeding weeks, and demonstrated that the previously undefeated Japanese could be beaten. Kingsbury was buried in the Port Moresby (Bomana) War Cemetery.
Author: Australian War Memorial

Historical Information: The approximate site of the Fighting Waterholes Massacre of 1 April 1840, where numerous old men, women and children from the Konongwootong gundidj clan were killed. Survivors of the massacre left their country and ended up at the Lake Condah mission in the late 1860s.

Historical Information: Aboriginal for blackfish swimming. The railway station at Koo-Wee-Rup was named Yallock when it opened in 1890 and it was renamed Koo-Wee-Rup in 1892. There have been five primary schools called Koo-Wee-Rup and ironically the original Koo-Wee-Rup State School, No.2629, was actually called Yallock, until 1903 when it was changed to Koo-Wee-Rup. The Cora Lynn State School, No. 3502, was known as Koo-Wee-Rup Central when it opened in January 1907 and changed its named to Cora Lynn in September of that year. The Modella State School, No.3456, was known as Koo-Wee-Rup East when it opened in January 1904. The Koo-Wee-Rup North State School, No.3198, at Five Mile, was initially called Koo-Wee-Rup South when it opened in July 1894. Finally, the Iona State School, No 3201, was originally known as Koo-Wee-Rup North.

Author: Clark, Ian and Heydon, Toby

Historical Information: Locality; former railway station. There used to be a creamery and post office at the south end of Spring Creek Road, and a railway station beside the highway near the junction. There was also a school (Alexandra Road, 1873? - 1909). The line from Cathkin reached Ainsworth's Stump (after Alfred Bower Ainsworth, Alexandra shire engineer) in 1890, and this was renamed Alexandra Road Station. It remained the end of the branch line until 1909, when the line was extended to Alexandra. The settlement and station were renamed Lily (1909, from Lily Gully nearby), Rhodes (1910, after South African statesman Cecil John Rhodes, 1853 - 1902) and finally (1916) Koriella, which may have been chosen by someone who had seen the word listed by Brough Smyth (1878, 2: 196). The station closed in 1973. (AES 1998; AES 2002; Jones & Jones) [Ian Newman, R. K. Whitehead]. Aboriginal (Taungurong): a name for the Goulburn River in this area, allegedly meaning cockatoo (Massola, 1968; Noble), though Clark & Heydon (D) point out that this could be a confusion with the word corella (derived from Wiradhuri); Brough Smyth (1878) mentions just the Goulburn River.  See also Alexandra Timber Tramway and Museum.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Koroit's origins lay with the Tower Hill caldera, the collapsed summit rim of a large volcanic cone about 3 km south of the town. Inside the rim there is a lake, nearly forming a moat around several islands. A peak on the large island was seen by French sea explorers in 1802, and was identified by Matthew Flinders as 'Peaked Hill' in the same year. The resemblance of the caldera to a moat and castle probably inspired Crown Surveyor Pickering (1842) to name the peak Tower Hill. It is thought that the Aboriginal name of the large island was the origin of the name 'Koroit'.

Historical Information:
A tall sandstone tower located on the highest point in the Kangaroo Ground
area. The tower is square in plan with three main storeys, built of reinforced
concrete and faced with sandstone rubble, concrete quoins and dressings. A fire
spotters cabin was added in 1974. The tower is set within a park featuring a
simple landscape design dominated by cypresses. The Kangaroo Ground Tower was built in 1925-26 to commemorate the First World War, replacing an earlier war memorial on this site, a simple stone cairn. The tower was designed by Stephenson & Meldrum, a well-known Melbourne architectural firm, based on a sketch by artist Harold Herbert. Its history is well documented.

The Ringwood Cultural Centre was officially opened on 19 April 1980 by the Governor of Victoria, the late Sir Henry Winneke.
The site upon which the Ringwood Civic Centre and the Cultural Centre was constructed on was formerly an antimony mine reserve.
The Civic Centre, which officially opened on 7 February 1970, was positioned and orientated in such a way as to complement the future construction of a cultural and social centre.
An extensive study undertaken in 1973 by Urban Systems Corporation P/L, at the request of the City of Ringwood, confirmed the needs of the community for a cultural and social facility. The construction of the function centre and theatre commenced in December 1978.
When the Ringwood Cultural Centre was opened in 1980, the theatre (only) was known as Karralika. 
As part of an overall marketing strategy to overcome the inconsistencies of different names for both facilities within one building, the Ringwood Cultural Centre name was changed to Karralyka Centre in December 1996

Historical Information:
Kelly Koochew was a Warragul resident and business owner, founding member of Women in Gippsland, and committee member of the Warragul Farmer's Market and Baw Baw Food Movement. Kelly was involved in the launch and promotion of Waterford Rise Estate, including organising a public 'block party' attended by more than 1,000 people in 2014. Kelly worked for Kingbuilt Homes and Vin Rowe Farm Machinery prior to her unexpected passing in 2018. She is survived by her husband, Nick Rowe, and their daughters Issie, Zoe, and Lola. As required by the Naming Rules, Council Officers have contacted Nick Rowe, who has provided written support for Kelly to be commemorated through place naming. Kelly's parents Glenda and Ian Koochew have also indicated support for the proposal, and correspondence
from them is attached.

Kelly Koochew was widely respected in the community. In a Gippslandia obituary, it was noted that Kelly had a rare skill in gently guiding others to find their sense of agency. Not only was she working away from the limelight to motivate positive change in our region, but she was inspiring others to do so too. A Bereavement Motion moved by Council on 24 October 2018 described Kelly as a ...community catalyst who helped many to achieve more than they thought possible. Tributes to Kelly demonstrate her capacity to listen with compassion, act decisively, see the humour in life's challenges, and work with many people and businesses to improve our part of the world. Her contribution to the success of many businesses and community initiatives in Warragul and Baw Baw over the past 10 years have been significant.

Historical Information: King Billy No 1 is an unmortared stone cairn, approximately 1.5m high and 1.5m in diameter with a stick as a centre pole. The cairn is located on a mesalike formation at the headwaters of the Jamieson River, approximately 16 km south east of the Mount Buller alpine village. Also known as Great Divide No 1. The current King Billy No 1 trig station is located close to the old geodetic cairn. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The date of the construction of King Billy 1 is not known. King Billy 1 geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of seven examples remaining in the alpine area of north-east Victoria. This cairn remains substantially intact, retaining a centre pole and its overall form and shape.
Also referred to as Great Divide No 2.

Historical Information: Arrow cut in dead tree. The tree was apparently ring-barked at the time the survey mark was cut into the tree, enabling the mark to survive. Surveyors William John Wills and Frederick John Byerley prepared a Plan of Goldfields in the Parish of Kingower in 1857. The plan clearly shows a survey mark at the location of the tree. The plan also shows the Township of Kooyoora which was surveyed but never settled. A later survey was undertaken in this area in 1907. The location of this tree coincides with that of a reference tree from this later survey. Kooyoorah marked tree is of local significance as a rare surviving example of a survey mark from a land subdivision survey in the early years of the twentieth century.

Historical Information:
Traditional name: Gourkk. Meaning: Battle of Blood. 
Many years ago a very sharp bit of fighting took place on the site of the railway station at Lake Boga, between the Tyntynder and Boga tribes, and in consequence of the quantity of blood spilt it was called the 'Battle of Blood', or 'Gourrk' (Stone 1911: 462).
Author: Ian Clark
Title: Aboriginal Placenames: Naming and re-naming the Australian landscape
Editor: Harold Koch and Luise Hercus
Chapter Title: Reconstruction of Aboriginal microtoponymy in western and central Victoria

Historical Information: Stone recorded 14 Wemba Wemba names for the town Lake Boga, its various features and surrounding areas. Lake Boga itself was stated to be 'Muymer' and the Lake Boga region was 'Gourrm', which Stone translates as meaning 'breast of woman'. Saxton's toponymic work published in 1907 stated that Lake Boga was named by Thomas Mitchell after the 'Bogan tribe of NSW natives', and in 1977 Blake republished this same information. Blake also added that the original name was Gunbowerooranditch. In 1854 E.S. Parker's lecture, The Aborigines of Australia, stated that the traditional name for the lake was 'ggorm', but in the region the word 'boga' also existed and, translated, meant 'swim'. The translation of 'boga' to mean 'swim' presumably came from the early pidgin English word 'bogey', which came from the Dharuk Sydney language and meant 'to swim' or 'to bathe'. Thus, there is evidence that the name Boga was in fact derived from the Indigenous languages local to the Sydney region and placed upon the Wemba Wemba landscape by Mitchell.
Author: Laura Kostanski
Title: Spurious etymologies : Toponymic books and town name identities on the Murray river

Historical Information: At one time, long years ago, there was a very large redgum tree growing in the lake, and its branches supported a tremendously large nest, the property of an immensely large pair of wedge-tailed eagles (Nurrayil'). One fine day a young mother wandered carrying her baby, a long way round the lake, and far from the camp, when, feeling tired, she sat down and amusedly watched her baby playing in the warm sand, when suddenly, and without warning, the larger of the two eagles swooped down and, seizing the baby, carrying it away over the water to its eyrie in the red gum tree. The poor mother, seeing her baby suddenly lost to her for ever, commenced a mournful wailing, which the curlews or stone plovers ('Will') in sympathy took up, and have continued ever since. The disconsolate young mother then hurried back to the camp and reported the occurrence, upon which the doctor or medicine-man ('Barngnull') directed that every person with a canoe was to proceed to the tree, and after cutting it down to tear it into little pieces, and to boat it all away to the river, where it was to be thrown upon the water to be carried away. The doctor then decreed that no more trees should grow in Lake Boga. The tree is falling hollowed out with its branches a big depression near the river, which they called 'Geranyuk' (where the branches and leaves fell). The large gnarled lump on the tree trunk struck and hollowed out a big hole at the entrance to the lake, which they named 'Wherpook' (where butt fell). (Stone 1911: 461).
Author: Ian Clark
Title: Aboriginal Placenames: Naming and re-naming the Australian landscape
Editor: Harold Koch and Luise Hercus
Chapter Title: Reconstruction of Aboriginal microtoponymy in western and central Victoria

Historical Information: Lake Boga was named by the New South Wales Surveyor General, Thomas Mitchell, on 21 June 1836, during his Australia Felix expedition. The inspiration for the name was reputedly the colonially named Bogan tribe of Aborigines in New South Wales. Mitchell's account of his discovery of the lake includes mention of smoke rising from a native encampment disturbed by one of Mitchell's men, on horseback, near the lake.

Historical Information: Said by Kenyon in his Story of the Mallee 'to have been named by Morgan, the bushranger, after a favourite steed. He was in the habit of traversing the Mallee by the Pine Plains - Kulkyne Track when one place or the other got too hot for him. He was eventually shot in 1865m at Peechelba.' Massola says it is more likely the horse is named after the lake, and that the name comes from local Aboriginal mythology in which two brothers Bram-bram-bult are involved. The dam in the bed of the lake was excavated in 1962. The lake filled in 1976 causing seedling regeneration of River Red-gum along the high water mark.
Author: Geoff Dunham
Title: Wyperfeld. Australia's first Mallee National Park

Historical Information: Artificial reservoir created by damming the Goulburn River at its confluence with the Delatite River. The Sugarloaf Weir submerged 3,000 hectares of land and created a lake, sometimes called the Sugarloaf Reservoir, first filled in 1927, with a capacity of 377,000 megalitres. The second dam enlarged Lake Eildon, when full, to a surface area of 13,800 hectares, a capacity of 3,389,000 megalitres and a shoreline of 515 kilometres. The lake's shape is due to the flooded river valleys which it fills, for example, the Delatite and Goulburn Arms, and the Big River, Brankeet, Burnt Creek, Ford, Howqua, Jerusalem and Maintongoon Inlets. See also Eildon and Eildon Dam.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel

Historical Information: The name refers to the tarns, ponds and bogs near the summit, particularly at Echo Flat and south of the Jubilee Trail. The altitude of the mountain is normally given as 1432 or 1433 metres, at the Marysville Lookout, but other parts of the massif or alpine plateau are higher. A hill just south-west of Panorama Lookout is 1450 m alt., and a few hundred metres north-west of Boundary Hut (q.v.) a knob reaches 1476 m alt. A strip of land either side of Lake Mountain Road (to Gerratys) forms the Lake Mountain Alpine Resort. The rest of the mountain is in the Yarra Ranges National Park.

Historical Information: Drung Drung is the name of one of three lakes some 16 km south-east of Horsham. Samuel Wilson (in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 178) confirms that Drung Drung is a native name, but he does not provide a meaning. Saxton (1907: 22) considers it a native name meaning 'spoiling'. According to Martin (1944: 32) it is an Aboriginal name meaning 'much spoiled'. Massola (1968: 20) extends the meaning to 'spoiling, spoiled, ruined'. Blake (1977: 85) also notes that Drung is the name of an Irish village in County Donegal. Les Blake is the only source for the dissonant etymology, and it may be disregarded as speculation on his part.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: It was named, as the name suggests, because it was the entrance for ocean-going vessels to access the Gippsland Lakes which are the largest navigable inland waterway in Australia. It was originally known as Cunninghame after a family of squatters who settled in the area. The local Gurnaikurnai had a Dreamtime legend explaining the lakes: a frog swallowed all of the world's water. The other animals tried to make the frog surrender the water by making it laugh. All deliberate attempts at humour failed but the sight of the eel standing upright on its tail caused the frog to laugh, the water was disgorged and the subsequent flood is said to have created the lakes.

Historical Information: Carrington, the railway reached Lang Lang in February 1890 and Carrington was the original name of the Lang Lang Railway Station and the town that developed around the station. It was renamed Lang Lang in December 1890. Carrington was named after Charles Robert Carrington, the third Baron Carrington, who was Governor of New South Wales from 1885-1890. Carrington was later created the Marquess of Lincolnshire. Carrington had the honour of being the first living person, other than Queen Victoria, to ever appear on an Australian postage stamp. He and Governor Arthur Phillip jointly appeared on a New South Wales stamp in 1888.
Author: Casey Cardinia Libraries
Page Title: Place Names of Casey and Cardinia

Historical Information: The first store and hotel were built c.1867 by William Lyall and located on part of the Tobin Yallock (or Torbinurruck) squatting run on the junction of McDonald's Track and the Grantville Road (as the South Gippsland Highway was then called). This store and hotel became the nucleus of the town of Lang Lang, as it was officially known, though the locals called it Tobin Yallock. Tobin Yallock would eventually have a church, a Post Office, Mechanics' Institute and other stores. Its decline began with the coming of the railway when the station, called Carrington, was built east of Tobin Yallock. By about 1894 most of the businesses and public buildings had transferred to the new Lang Lang based around the railway station. There are two published meanings of Lang Lang. Blake says that the term Lang Lang comes from the Aboriginal word for group of trees. However, the VACL website states that Lang Lang is Aboriginal for stones or stony.

Historical Information: Langwarrin was the original name of Pearcedale. When the Mornington and Stony Point railway lines opened in the late 1880s, the railway station near the Military Camp (now a Flora and Fauna Reserve) was named Langwarrin. A new town developed east of the railway station and was locally called New Langwarrin. The name comes from the squatting run called Lang Waring or Long Waring, leased by William Willoby from 1843. Blake says the name Long Waring comes from long waiting as it took Willoby a long time to obtain his run. There have been three schools called Langwarrin. The Langwarrin Railway Station School, No.3023, was opened in 1890 on the corner of McClelland Road and Golf Links Road. The name changed to Mornington Junction in 1906 and finally to Baxter in 1919. It moved to the six cross roads at Baxter in 1954. Langwarrin, No.3531, commenced in 1907, moved to Warrandyte Road in 1913 and was known as Langwarrin North until 1955, when the North was dropped. Finally, Langwarrin School, no.2961, opened in 1889 in what is modern day Pearcedale, closed in 1892, re-opened 1902 and in 1908 changed its name to Pearcedale.

Historical Information: 'Formerly known as 'Duck Ponds.' It was here that Hume and Hovel terminated their journey in 1824, and rested a few days before returning.  The stream appeared on an early map as 'Hovell's' Creek, but some of the early settlers called it 'Duck Ponds.'  In the middle 'seventies' the name was changed to 'Hovell's Creek,' but public protest caused it to be re-chistened 'Lara'.  Traditional meaning: 'hut on stony ground.'
Author: O'Callaghan, Thos
Title: Names of Victorian Railways Stations

Historical Information: The explorers Hume and Hovell arrived at Lara on 16 December 1824, believing that they had reached Westernport Bay. They recorded that the Aboriginal people described the bay as Jullong and land as Corago, suggesting origins for the names of Geelong and Corio. Hovells Creek was first called Duck Ponds Creek when the area was settled in the 1840s, and the place where Lara was laid out was known as Duck Ponds. The name accurately described the nature of the waterway and the plentiful fowl found there. A plan for the village in 1853 named it Lara. The colonial government decided on Hovells Creek in 1872. Two years later, after local petitioning, the name Lara was settled on. It is thought that the name is derived from an Aboriginal word meaning stone or building of stones.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: Lascelles was named after Edward Lascelles (1847-1917), who promoted closer settlement and water management in the area. Lascelles, a partner in the wool broking firm of Dennys Lascelles, subdivided Mallee pastoral land into agricultural farm blocks around Hopetoun, Lake Coorong, where he built a large homestead. He was an ardent believer in the possibilities of the Mallee for grain growing and grazing, on land cleared with the heavy Mallee rollers.

Historical Information:
Thomas Charles Lee was born at Port Fairy on 12 December 1915, the youngest of four children.  He enlisted in the Australia Army (VX56307) on 20 May 1941.  He was taken prisoner by the Japanese at the fall of Singapore and remained a prisoner at Changi and other places until the end of WWII.  

He was discharged from the Army on 11 December 1945.  Tom married Shiela in 1948, they had three sons David, Peter and Raymond.  In 1955 the family took on the purchase/lease of a farm (Lot 23) on the Shelford Soldier Settlement Estate.  They farmed there until 1972, when the family moved to Geelong.  Tom died in 2007, aged 91.

Historical Information: The name was suggested by Major E.P. Hill at a meeting of settlers in the early 1920s. Like other soldier settlers, Hill had served at Gallipoli and had spent time at Lemnos, which had been a base for Gallipoli operations.  The name was chosen because the island was considered beautiful and was also use for fruit-growing.

Title: Place Names Committee File

Historical Information: Name honours Leo Dineen (1936-2005) who served as a councillor and Mayor of the former Shire of Keilor.  He was active in the development of local roads and infrastructure, and was regarded as a 'pioneer' of the Tullamarine area.

'According to the Council, the late Mr. Hoffman served on Council from 1962 to 1977 and was Mayor on two occasions.  Council has also advised that Mr. Hoffman 'contributed materially to sport and recreation in the district by a long association with its Recreation and Leisure Consultative Committee'.'

Title: Submission

Historical Information: To commemorate the late Leo O'Brian (1904 - 1983). Historical Information: 'Named 'Lillydale,' by Mr. Hodgkinson, who was a visitor at 'Yering,' the residence of Mr. Paul de Castella, at the time he (Hodgkinson) was surveying the township.  He named it after Mrs. Paul de Castella, baptized 'Elizabeth,' but known, familiarly, as 'Lilly.'
Author: O'Callaghan, Thos
Title: Names of Victorian Railways Stations

Historical Information: 'When Marian Aveling was researching for her book, 'Lilydale. The Billanook Country' a diary of Surveyor John Hardy revealed his account of how the name was given.' 'In part the quotation reads '...My chainman... had been singing some popular songs of which one was 'Lilly Dale'. By phonetic transition the oft repeated name in the song suggested a dale with lillies growing in the stream, as indeed there were pools of the creek.'
Author: Place Names Committee Files
Title: Submission

Historical Information:
Sir Patrick Lindesay (1778-1839), was acting Governor of the colony of New South Wales for a short time in 1831. He was devoted to his military duties and to promoting natural history and explorations.

His name is commemorated by many including by the botanist-explorer Allan Cunningham who named Mount Lindesay on the New South Wales and Queensland border as a tribute. Mount Lindesay State Forest and Mount Lindesay Highway later ensued.

Explorer, Sir Thomas Mitchell, also named an Australian peak in New South Wales, Mount Lindesay. A third peak in Western Australia was named Lindesay after his Regiment had served in Western Australia.

Charles Sturt was a captain in his regiment and Lindesay is commemorated by Sturt's naming of the Lindesay River. It is possible that Lindsay Point and Lindsay Island followed this same theme

Mr Holman Lindsay Williams (1914 -1993) who was the Shire of Springvale Secretary and became the City of Springvale's first Town Clerk from 1955 - 1977. In his role Mr H. L. Williams focused on the modernisation of Springvale by improving physical infrastructure, roads and footpaths.

Historical Information: The township was named Lockington in 1921, less than ten years after irrigation was extended to the district by the Waranga Western Channel, converting a dry farming area to orcharding and dairying. The district was first known as Pine Grove, the name of a pastoral run taken up by John Patterson in 1846. When irrigation came in 1909 the main settlement was Bamawm. The Elmore and Cohuna railway was opened through the district in 1915. The railway station was named Bamawm, and the post office was named Pannoo-Bamawm. Neither name was popular with the progress association, which suggested naming the township after Father William Lockington (1871-1948), a Jesuit priest, superior of eleven Jesuit communities, anti-Conscriptionist and noted author and lecturer. He was closely associated with Archibishop Mannix. The Railways Commissioners adopted the suggested name in 1921.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: The Lord Somers Camp at Somers was set up by the then Governor of Victoria, Lord Somers, in 1931. Lord Somers aimed to duplicate the success of the popular United Kingdom Duke of York Camps where up to 400 teenage boys from public schools and industry could meet and mix for a week. The Camp has been highly praised for its country club character, with its own sewerage system, hot water and electricity, reticulated fresh water and a open air cinema. Lord Somers had a remarkable career with a highly developed sense of duty and leadership. Career highlights included his distinguished World War 1 service, Governor of Victoria  from 1926 to 1931, grand master of the United Grand Lodge of Victoria and his long term involvement with the scout movement as the Victorian chief commissioner in 1932 and as chief scout for Great Britain in 1941.
Author: Graeme Butler @ Associates
Title: Hastings Heritage Study

Historical Information: 'The Committee is concerned at the lack of uniformity in the spelling of Bendoc/Bendock in relation to a mountain, river, parish and town near the Victoria/ New South Wales Border.  In a pamphlet entitled 'Back to Bendoc School' it was discovered that the name originated from Benjamin Boyd's pastoral station 'Ben's Dock'.  However, a letter received from the Shire of Orborst dated 20th September, 1966 informed the committee that local sentiment wished to retain the spelling Bendoc.  This desire was shared by the Progress Association.  The matter was finalised when the decision of the Minister of Lands was published in the Victoria Government Gazette on the 29th May, 1968, proclaiming the town to be spelt Bendoc.'
Author: Place Names Committee Files
Title: Letter

Historical Information: An Aboriginal name which, according to Blake (1977, p. 38), was formerly 'wagra bendoc' and means 'plain of the crows' or 'noise in the trees'.  'Bendock' was the name of John Hensleigh's station in 1842.  Benjamin Boyd (1796-1851) also had an outstation of that name in this district.  Suggestions that the name derives from Ben's dock (a yard for Ben's stock) cannot be true because the name was in use before Boyd took up a run in the area.  The mining town of Bendoc was originally surveyed and proclaimed as Wagra in 1872, but the name was altered to Bendock in 1886 (reflecting local preference) and the spelling was amended to Bendoc in 1951. [Research by I.D. Clark and D.A. Cahir, University of Ballarat, 2005.]

Historical Information: Parish. State school (1878 - 1912). Also known as Head Station (and possibly Home Station) when part of Watson and Hunter's Run (q.v.), and also Boorolite Run. Historical Information: Henry Mundy, a local shepherd noted that Lubra Creek derived its name from a wanton slaughter of several 'lubras' by an enraged band of squatters whose sheep had been stolen, slaughtered and eaten by the Aboriginal people. When anything of that kind happened, it was usual for the squatters to band together and hunt for the 'delinquents'. In the case of the Lubra Creek tragedy, it appears they could not find any men to shoot and, finding the women hidden in the scrub, ruthlessly shot them down. He recalled that in the early years of his employment at Caramut 'the bones were lying there as evidence in my time to testify to the carnage as the bodies had never been buried'.

Historical Information: The suburb name commemorates Mrs Eleanor Lucas, founder of the local textile company Lucas and Co. and the girls who worked there who became known as the Lucas Girls. In May 1917 Mrs Tillie Thompson, a director of E. Lucas and Co. proposed that trees be planted in honour of the men and women who enlisted for service during World War One. The employees of the company were enthusiastic and 500 of them, known as the Lucas Girls planted an avenue along the Ballarat - Burumbeet Road, now known as Remembrance Drive. The first 1000 trees were planted on the 3 of June 1917 and the final trees on the 16 August 1919. While the Lucas Girls did the actual planting, practical advice and assistance was provided by local gardeners, farmers, council staff, family and friends. The 22km Ballarat Avenue of Honour is beleived to be the first and longest such Avenue in Australia and possibly the world. Part of the Ballarat Avenue of Honour along Remembrance Drive forms the northern boundary of the new suburb.

Historical Information:
Lake Wellington army survey beacon is located on a sand hill on the eastern shore of Lake Wellington. The beacon is located within an area that has been developed as a caravan park. The sand hill is known as Mount Cunninghame. The beacon is one of two standard designs used by RASC. It comprises a steel quadripod and centre pole and black disc beacon. This design has a detachable centre pole to enable observations to be made from within the structure. The Survey section of the Royal Australian Engineers was created soon after Federation and given the task of compiling contour maps of selected areas near
capital cities to as part of defence planning. Initial survey work in Victoria
included a large topographic triangulation covering the area between Ballarat, Bendigo and Werribee. Their work became a high priority during the Second World War due to its closeness to Australia. Most of the surviving army beacons date from this period. The Lake Wellington beacon dates from 1936. Lake Wellington mark is of State significance as a rare example of a surviving RASC mark, one of only 5 examples known to remain in Victoria and the only example of this specific design to survive. It provides evidence of an important phase in the national coordination of land survey work, the role of the Army survey corps, and the planning response to the anticipated need to defend Australia during the Second World War. It is also significant for its innovative design which enabled observations to be made without moving the beacon.

Historical Information:
Jim Crow Hill, this was an early name for Mt Franklin, and was the name of a creek, range, and goldfield north of Daylesford. 'Mt Franklin' named after Sir John Franklin's visit to the Loddon Protectorate station in 1843 displaced 'Jim Crow Hill'. According to Saxton (1907: 36) Jim Crow Hill was 'Named by Capt John Hepburn. Capt. Bacchus, who accompanied him, asked what name should the ranges have, and Hepburn replied: Jim Crow, after a popular song'. Morrison (1967: 41) explains that the origin of the name 'Jim Crow' has intrigued many for a long time.

Some believe it is the name of a former 'king' of the local Loddon tribe of Aborigines. Etymologically, the term "jim crow" was used for various implements, as for example, a "jemmy", which is a miniature form of a bent crow (bar) and, somehow, the idea of bending or twisting seems to be implicit in its derivation. A device for bending iron bars was one time termed a "jim crow". About 1835, an American negro, James Rice who was a rather popular "song and dance" comedian wrote and popularised a song, the chorus of which was: "Wheel about and turn about and do just so, Turn about and wheel about and jump Jim Crow". Set to a catchy tune it swept the world, as similar songs do today. ... There seems to be no reason, to doubt the accuracy of the story that the application of the term "Jim Crow" to this region, stems from a trivial incident wherein Capt. Bacchus, riding on horseback between "Lalgambook" and Koorocheang with Capt. Hepburn, called to his companion, "What do you think we should call these ranges?" Hepburn (perhaps with the maddening refrain churning in his mind) replied: "Call them Jim Crow!" (Morrison 1967: 41)

Quinlan has noted that Mount Franklin

which the early squatters called Jim Crow and the natives knew by the name of Lalgambook. John Hepburn used the name Jim Crow to refer not only to the mount itself but to the creek below it and to the district. Edgar Morrison who, in 1965, published the memoirs of Edward Stone Parker under the title Early Days in the Loddon Valley, believes that Jim Crow derives from the chorus of an American minstrel song, popular at the time of the first overlanders. It seems quite feasible, as he suggests, that the behaviour of this winding creek recalled to someone like the Mollison brothers the popular jingle, 'Hop a little, stop a little, jump Jim Crow'. Later, when the aboriginal station was established there, many took it for granted that the word referred to the natives. (Quinlan 1993: 99)

According to Blake (1977: 133), overlander Alexander Mollison's records list the district as 'Jumcra', 'Aboriginal name for which meaning not traced; "Jim Crow" was minstrel song from U.S.A. 1835'. Randell (1979: 222) in a history of the Coliban district explained that Mollison took up two stations in the vacant land immediately west of his Coliban station in early May 1840, naming the Loddon run 'Jumcra, probably an aboriginal name. The second run was called Boughyards. The men soon corrupted the first name into Jim Crow'. Tully (1997: 87) supports the view that Jumcra was corrupted to Jim Crow.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: Named in honour of the famous Australian poet and writer, Dorothea Mackellar (1885-1968).

Named after Dorothea Mackellar, as the sub-division streets were named after poets. The name arose from the view of the school which looks across the Keilor Plains to the Great Dividing Range, and fitted Mackellar's poem 'My Country'. 
'I love a sunburnt country, 
A land of sweeping plains, 
Of rugged mountain ranges, 
Of droughts and flooding rains;
I love her far horizons, 
I love her jewel sea, 
Her beauty and her terror - 
The wide brown land for me.'

Historical Information: Proposal to change the name to McKellars Bridge in 1993 was rejected.  The proposal had been initiated by the Yole family in recognition of their forebear who had operated a ferry across the Snowy River in the vicinity of the bridge from the 1880s.  George McKillop had crossed the river at a point near the bridge when he and fellow cattlemen (James McFarlane and Alexander Livingstone) first moved cattle from the Monaro to the Omeo district in 1835.  McKillop's crossing point was used often from the 1840s.  The name change proposal was not supported by the local council.

Historical Information: Named after the MacPherson family, early settlers in Toolern Vale.

A ferry service between Survey Paddock Richmond and Grange Road Toorak operated from 1880 to 1934. It was named the Twickenham Ferry, after a ferry that crossed the Thames between Richmond and Kew in England. The ferry was owned and operated by the Barrow family, starting from 1865 when Jessie Barrow too out a 99-year lease of land on the north bank of the Yarra, where he built a boat shed and house and developed a large garden. After the death of Jessie Barrow, his son and grandson operated the ferry until the opening of the bridge. Sir Macpherson Robertson, philanthropist, entrepreneur and founder of chocolate company MacRobertson's, financed the building of the bridge, which was opened in 1934 by the Premier of Victoria, Hon. Sir Stanley Argyle; and called the Centenary Bridge after the Victorian Centenary. It was extended in 1969, when the name was changed to Mac.Robertson, in recognition of the financier.

Historical Information: The name Wallermeryong was given to the Creek on Commander H.L. Cox's Charts of the area after he surveyed it in 1865, although the Bunurong People, who walked the Creek, already used this name. The name Main Creek appears on a Certificate of Title issued in 1872. A map of the Parish of Wannaeue from 1949 shows 'Main Creek' but a map of the Parish of Fingal printed in 1961 shows 'Wallermeryong or Main Creek'. The 'meryong' part of Wallermeryong means 'happy place' and the 'Waller' part of the name is the name of an animal species. The Bunurong Land Council is still researching what kind of animal. www.mornpen.vic.gov.au/Files/Governance_Minutes/031905om.pdf

Historical Information: Parish, between Brankeet and Eildon parishes to the north and south, and between Yarck and Wappan parishes to the west and east. School (1886-95, 1901-03). Pastoral run (occasionally called Devils' River Station), established 1838, of 11,650 ha along the Delatite River north of Eildon; subdivided, 1861, into Maintongoon East and West (q.v.). Aboriginal (presumably Taungurong). According to Les Blake from matong, great, strong, and ngune, you; but these words have probably been taken from Reed (1969), and ngune is given by Reed as South Australian. Gillison says the name means large lagoon, and was at first spelt Maitongoon. This spelling occurs in a map of ca. 1866, though an earlier map (1856) gives Maitongorn. The last syllable just might be from gurnung, river or creek in Taungurong and Woiworung.

The lake and ocean shore provided plentiful food for the Aboriginal inhabitants. Trade and ceremonies sometimes attracted Aboriginal people from neighbouring areas.

Historical Information:
Kulin name: KÃ¡Â¹Â»rnan/w. Meaning: not recorded. 

This name was recorded by A. W. Howitt, anthropologist, from conversations from sometime between 1897 and 1901 with William Barak, ngurungaeta (leader) of the Wurundjeri-willam, the traditional owners of what is now northern Melbourne, and Dick Richards, Barak's fellow Kulin countryman. The Kulin was an alliance of Aboriginal nations in central Victoria. Howitt jotted down Aboriginal names, mostly in the Woiwurrung language once spoken in the Melbourne area, corresponding to landmarks and municipalities that arose in Melbourne town during Barak's lifetime (c.1824 to 1903).

Historical Information: 'J. S. Manfield and brother John climbed the mountain via Goldies Spur and are said to have led the first party to the top and from the Horn to the Gorge in 1856.  Manfield family records claim that the Surveyor-General (Sir Andrew Black) had a cairn erected in 1866 (no longer evident) to commemorate the climb via Goldies Spur in 1856.  Manfield Chalet (Grannys Place) was run by Alice Manfield in the late 1880's.  Alice is also the author of 'Lyre Birds of Mt. Buffalo'.  Bronze plaque unveiled in 1965 at Bents Lookout by the Harrietville Historical Society in memory of the Manfield family.'
Author: Place Names Committee Files
Title: Submission

Historical Information: Manja (manya) meaning hands, has some of the best examples of hand stencils in Victoria. A total of 90 stencils have been recorded at these two shelters. It is believed that hand stencils were used to record a visit to a site, and to renew the ties a person had to a particular place. At this site there are also animal tracks and many human stick figures.

Traditional Name: Manja Explanation: hands Discussion on Current Name: rock art site containing hand stencils of adults,  given that the hands are stencilled in red pigment, Clark and Harradine (1990:58) recommended the n be changed to the local Aboriginal words for 'red ochre hands'. This is Wab Manja,  Clark and Harradine 1990: 57.
Author: Clark, Ian and Heydon, Toby

Place Name: MANNA GUM FAMILY AND CHILDREN'S CENTRE
Historical Information: Manna Gum is one of the most prominent Eucalypt trees in the region. The others include Candlebark, Black Wattle, Snow Gum or Black Gum. The Indigenous translation of Manna Gum is Wurun or Wurundjeri. The name is linked to the traditional owners of the land and also reflects the local flora. Trees sprouting from seed in the early beginning stage also ties in with the Maternal Child Health service.

Historical Information: Town, parish, shire, former railway station. A settlement, at first called The Battery (after nearby Mount Battery), grew up around a forge built by Alfred Chenery for a blacksmith named Deedy. The town was renamed in 1856 either after Edward Eyre Mansfield (resident in 1841) or, more likely, at the suggestion of Charles Dickens (manager of the Preston pastoral run), after Mansfield, Nottinghamshire (from Maun, Celtic river name, and Old English feld, clearing). Beolite was proposed but not adopted. Rail services arrived in October 1891, and finally ceased in November 1978. The railway station is now a visitors' information centre. The shire of Mansfield, first created in 1866, was incorporated into the shire of Delatite in 1994 but re-established in 2002.

Historical Information:
Named in recognition of Cecil Solomon Marks, an early settler, to the Hallston area. He was a dairy farmer & among the first in the district with a steam-powered milk pump, a wireless and a car.  The family farm was near the bridge & the house overlooking the bridge has long gone.  At  aged 39, he volunteered for the 2nd Pioneers. Being a farmer, and rather old, he was exempt from conscription, but chose to go regardless. His service records show how warfare in France broke him over three years before he was repatriated - suffering from the shell shock that haunted him for the rest of his life.  He was always the one asked to give the Anzac Day address locally post-war.
Here's some official details that have been compiled in the interim: http://emhs.org.au/person/marks/cecil_solomon

Historical Information: The name The Rings was developed with Council's branding agency Blaze in association with the naming for the new Aquanation facility. The Rings was an existing basketball stadium, known as the Maroondah Indoor Sports Centre, and a range of colloquial names such as MISC and The Maroondah Stadium. While undertaking the branding development work for Aquanation, Council undertook a review of the naming and branding of its existing 5 other facilities to ensure a new and consistent image for the Maroondah Leisure family. The name also tied in with the suburb name of Ringwood.

Sourced from records of the Melbourne and Metropolitan Board of Works:  'At the opening ceremony of the reservoir it was revealed that the name had been chosen to replace "Watts", the name of the river on which the dam was situated.  It was explained that the area was a tribal ground of the Aborigines known as Maroondah, the origin of which would not be divulged by them.'

Historical Information: Mars Stadium was recorded as the sponsorship name for a duration of 5 years from June 2017.

Its neighbouring area is Breakwater, and was included in that area before gaining a separate name. The Breakwater area was used for tanneries, fellmongeries and animal by-product industries. Many of them were located there to take advantage of the saltwater Barwon River, south of the artificial breakwater that was built in 1837. By the mid-1850s Thomas Marshall, a Geelong wool merchant, established a wool scouring works near the breakwater, and the place was named after him.

Historical Information: Father Pooley, a Catholic Priest, established Maryknoll as a rural community based on the principles of religion, family life and co-operative enterprise. Maryknoll means Mary's hill or knoll.

Historical Information: Parish; locality (1160 m alt.), junction of the Warburton Woods Point Road and Walhalla Road. Gold discovered, 1861. The township began (1863) as Emerald Hill, but was renamed (1864 or '65) after Matlock, Derbyshire - Old English mæþ(e)l, meeting, council, moot, and ac, oak - to avoid confusion with the Melbourne suburb of Emerald Hill* (later South Melbourne*). A number of "suburbs" or satellite settlements sprang up, including Alhambra (q.v.), Harper's Creek, Mutton Town* and Toorak (after the Melbourne suburb; Woiworung or Bunurong Turrak*: reedy swamp, reedy grass, or weed in lagoon). Toorak was soon renamed Thackeray (after writer William Makepeace Thackeray). A bushfire in 1873 wiped out almost all the buildings and, as the road to Woods Point had been rerouted away from the hill, Matlock was rebuilt at the new crossroads on the site of the former Thackeray. The old site became or was renamed Matlock Hill (q.v.). Just south of Matlock are the headwaters of B.B. Creek* which (further down) had its own goldfield and settlement. (B.B. probably stands for Bare Buttocks, as the creek's vegetation was reputedly very rough on miners' clothing.) See also The Springs.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: In 1862 and 1863 gold mines were opened either side of the Dividing Range about 2 km apart, near the future site of Matlock. By the end of 1863 a township had developed, called Emerald Hill. Because there was already an Emerald Hill in South Melbourne, the Board of Land and Works changed the name to Matlock in 1864, by when about 1000 miners were working the area.

Mr. Max Gray was born in Essendon in 1924 he joined the police force in Melbourne in 1950, spending time at Montague and North melbourne also some time on the patrol Cars. His appointment as C. I. B. Detective, the first for Wodonga was in 1958. He settled in William Street, where he still resides, his family consist of Marie whom he married at St Monica's in Moonee ponds in 1949. He retired in 1984 having served 34 years in the police force. But during this time served the community as a police man known for his compassion and good sense. He also served on the Vermont court Hostel Board and many other community projects.

Historical Information: Proposal to change the name to McKellars Bridge in 1993 was rejected.  The proposal had been initiated by the Yole family in recognition of their forebear who had operated a ferry across the Snowy River in the vicinity of the bridge from the 1880s.  George McKillop had crossed the river at a point near the bridge when he and fellow cattlemen (James McFarlane and Alexander Livingstone) first moved cattle from the Monaro to the Omeo district in 1835.  McKillop's crossing point was used often from the 1840s.  The name change proposal was not supported by the local council.

Historical Information: Parish, settlement, railway station (1890 - 1978). The Ryan brothers found gold about 1.5 km south-west of the village in June 1870 (Flett, 1970). Old English: mere, lake, pool, and tun, enclosure. Martin suggests  it was named after Merton Place, Surrey, which Lady Hamilton bought for Admiral Lord Nelson, or Mertoun, Scotland (near Wigtown), family home of squatter Benjamin Boyd. Wylie prefers Merton, Devon (near the border with Cornwall), an area from which many miners came.

Historical Information: 'Mr. M. Laffan was a resident of Sunshine for well in excess of 50 years. Historical Information:
In 1947 brothers Hugh and Bushby Jamieson obtained a depasturing licence for leasehold from Melbourne and named the property 'Yerre Yerre'. The name was later changed to 'Mildura' in 1858. They built the homestead cottage around 1850
In 1886 George Chaffey was in Mildura at the invitation of Victoria's Minister for Water Supply, Alfred Deakin, who had recently inspected the work done by the Chaffey Brothers in California, USA.
George Chaffey was so impressed with the opportunities he saw in Mildura that he immediately invited his brother, William Benjamin, known as WB, to sell up and come out.
The homestead garden later inspired George Chaffey to select Mildura as the site for his irrigation colony.
The Chaffey families lived at the homestead until WB Chaffey moved to Rio Vista House in 1892.
On 31 May 1887, the Indenture was signed by the Chaffey brothers and the Victorian Government and the Mildura Irrigation colony was born.
The first irrigation pumping for grape vines occurred at this site.
The homestead has been known as several names over the years including, Jamieson Homestead, Mildura Homestead and Mildura Station Homestead.

She suggested the creation of a reserve at the Minne Ha Ha Falls for picnic sports, boarded the local school teachers, supported the bush nurse, and helped with a range of community events.

Historical Information: There are various theories as to the meaning of Modella. Blake says it is from the Aboriginal word for "strike you". The name Modella was taken from Modella Park, a farm owned by James Douglas. One interpretation is that the name is a corruption of "model" because Modella Park was a "model" farm, and another theory is that is comes from the name of a famous race horse of the time. The Modella School, No.3456, and the area itself, were initially known as Koo-Wee-Rup East. The school name changed in February 1905.

Historical Information: Parish. Former pastoral run (6,500 ha, 1851-77) on the west bank of the Acheron River west and north-west of Buxton. Also called Jones's Station after Stephen Jones (licensee, 1856-60?). All or part of this land became the second and possibly third sites of the Acheron Aboriginal Station (q.v.), and thereafter was sometimes also called the Blacks' Station. Kenyon's map shows the Mohican run too far north, and makes the adjoining Taggerty run too small. Spreadborough & Anderson's maps show the Mohican run correctly (perhaps extending a bit too far south). Mohican persists as a parish name and in the Mohican Plantation. Les Blake thinks the name was probably taken from James Fennimore Cooper's novel, The Last of the Mohicans (1826); if so, the word is a variant of the North American tribal name Mohegan (Algonquian maingan, wolf), a subgroup of the Pequot, and probably their relatives the Mahican (Muh-he-con-ne-ok, people of waters that are never still) (Waldman). The Victorian name might be a squatterese version of an Aboriginal word or name.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Parish; village, surveyed in 1864 by John Downey; former railway station (1889 - 1978). Named in 1855 by government surveyor Thomas W. Pinniger, either after Sir William Molesworth (1810-55), British M.P. and colonial secretary (1855), or after Lieutenant James Molesworth (died Malta, 1854) of the 7th Royal Fusiliers - Colonel Yea's regiment (see also Yea). A much less likely candidate is Victorian solicitor-general Sir Robert Molesworth (1806-90). Blanks favours the lieutenant; Jones & Jones prefer Sir William. The surname is either from Molesworth, Cambridgeshire (Old English Mulesworð, Mul's enclosure) or Molesworth, Cheshire (Old English molda, top of a head or hill, and worð, enclosure). The new name took a while to be generally accepted, and the township was often referred to as Sloan's Punt. Because the parish boundary here runs along the Goulburn River, Cathkin and the Pig and Whistle area are in the parish of Molesworth, but the main part of the village of Molesworth is in the parish of Whanregarwen! See also Pig and Whistle settlement and Sloan's Punt Ford.

Historical Information:
The name chosen for this particular area is Monte Christo Bushland Reserve, from the nearby reef and gold mines. The South Monte Christo mine was within the reserve, while the Monte Christo, New Monte Christo and North Monte Christo were between 500 and 1000 metres further north.
Although it has not been possible to confirm exactly when these mines began and ceased operation, newspaper reports and notices in the Victoria Government Gazette show that:
Ã¢ Â¢	the Monte Christo Company was "paying expenses by crushing the surface reef" using their 16 head stamper at the beginning of January 1861,
Ã¢ Â¢	the manager of the New Monte Christo mine was "fined 40s and costs for neglecting to affix safety appliances to a cage working in a shaft at the mine" in May 1885, 
Ã¢ Â¢	the North Monte Christo Company issued a call on shares in 1888.  It was also one of nearly 1000 companies that were struck off the Companies Register in August 1964, in what appears to have been a purge to remove defunct companies from the register.
Between them, the four mines produced 424 kilograms of gold, worth almost $17 million at today's prices.  The area appears to have been particularly rich, with several nearby mines also yielding significant quantities of gold.

Named after a group of gold mines in the area - Monte Christo, New Monte Christo, North Monte Christo and South Monte Christo, active from 1860s to 1880s.  [Note consistently spelt 'Christo', not 'Cristo'.]

Historical Information: 'Moondarra run was taken up in the early 1850's by Henry Dutton and David Okeden.  It later changed hands twice before being cancelled in 1861.  Moondarra township was gazetted in 1891 and surveyed in 1899.  A Survey plan was published in 1917.  Successive revocations of the township led to its extinction by 1952.  It is understood that the name is Aboriginal, Mundara meaning 'plenty of rain' or 'thunder'.'

Historical Information: The pastoral property was originally called Morangourke, believed to be derived from the Aboriginal word 'Murrangurk', the name of a native that was bestowed on the English convict William Buckley, who escaped captivity and lived with the Wathaurong people for many years. Legend has it that Buckley was found by the Wathaurong people carrying a piece of broken spear that had been placed on the grave of Murrangurk. Thus Buckley was identified with Murrangurk and, 'as one returned from the grave', received his name. Moranghurk is understood to have several meanings, two of which are 'stone axe handle' and 'reincarnated warrior'.

Historical Information: Goulburn State Forest. Joins the Goulburn River at Woods Point. Named after the lucrative Morning Star gold mine, discovered by Joseph Corry and Ditmer Behrens, and initially developed by Colin and Duncan McDougall. Duncan McDougall arrived in Australia aboard the ship Morning Star in 1858 [Brian Lloyd]. Marked as the Left Hand Branch on Butler's map (1865). The headwaters of the creek near Alhambra were also called Killers Creek (WPMA). Incorrectly given as Big River State Forest on Matlock 1:25000 survey map.

This is the name of a river and township in the La Trobe Valley in Gippsland. Legg (1992: 28) has documented that the first variant 'Morewell' dates from 1844. Massola (1968: 36) claims that it is derived from 'More willie', meaning 'woolly possum'. Blake (1977: 180) accepts Massola's position. Gardner (1992: 16) considers it is a Gunnai word that means 'inhabitants of the swamp' and he believes it is unlikely that the name is derived from one of a number of places in England on the Tamar River near Plymouth including Morwell Rocks and Morwell Abbey. Stephen Legg (1992: 28-29, 32) in a history of Morwell Shire has undertaken a detailed analysis of the name and documents five interpretations - that it is derived from the name of a nearby hotel; that it is a corruption of Maryville; that it is named after the town of Morwell on the Morwell River in Cornwall; that it has an Aboriginal origin; and finally, that it gets its name from Morwell Street in London. Legg concludes that the Aboriginal explanation has the most integrity and is the only one that can 'survive critical examination'. He concludes that it is derived from 'morewill' meaning 'woolly possum' and he considers this 'a fitting tribute to the Ganai who pioneered the land' (Legg 1992: 34). The only difficulty with this bon mot is that the Ganai word for possum is 'wadthan' (see Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 96) and not 'wile' or 'wollert' which are Kulin words, a situation that Legg (1992: 32) was cognisant of.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: (1260 m alt.), Yarra Ranges National Park: south of Lake Mountain. No explicit origin of this name has come to light, but when the Pastoral and Agricultural Society of Australia Felix was founded in Melbourne* on 2 January 1840, its directors included William Ryrie, Peter Snodgrass and Thomas Arnold. At the first meeting (13 May 1840) in Melbourne* to agitate for the separation of Port Phillip from New South Wales speakers included W. Ryrie and T. Arnold (Garryowen 1: 427; 2: 906). Alexander, Donald and William Ryrie held several pastoral runs in the Lilydale* and Healesville area, and would have been well placed to suggest that the mountain be named after Thomas Arnold. Thomas Arnold, "A.C.G." (assistant commissionary general?), is also listed in Kerr's 1841 Almanac (pp. 173, 236) as resident in Lonsdale Street, Melbourne*. Arnold can be derived from either Germanic (arn, eagle, and wald, rule) or Old English (earn, eagle, and halh, nook, hollow). See also Arnold Creek, Mount Arnold Saddle and Snowy Hill.

Historical Information: An Aboriginal name which, according to Blake (1977, p. 38), was formerly 'wagra bendoc' and means 'plain of the crows' or 'noise in the trees'.  'Bendock' was the name of John Hensleigh's station in 1842.  Benjamin Boyd (1796-1851) also had an outstation of that name in this district.  Suggestions that the name derives from Ben's dock (a yard for Ben's stock) cannot be true because the name was in use before Boyd took up a run in the area.  The mining town of Bendoc was originally surveyed and proclaimed as Wagra in 1872, but the name was altered to Bendock in 1886 (reflecting local preference) and the spelling was amended to Bendoc in 1951. [Research by I.D. Clark and D.A. Cahir, University of Ballarat, 2005.]

'The Committee is concerned at the lack of uniformity in the spelling of Bendoc/Bendock in relation to a mountain, river, parish and town near the Victoria/ New South Wales Border.  In a pamphlet entitled 'Back to Bendoc School' it was discovered that the name originated from Benjamin Boyd's pastoral station 'Ben's Dock'.  However, a letter received from the Shire of Orborst dated 20th September, 1966 informed the committee that local sentiment wished to retain the spelling Bendoc.  This desire was shared by the Progress Association.  The matter was finalised when the decision of the Minister of Lands was published in the Victoria Government Gazette on the 29th May, 1968, proclaiming the town to be spelt Bendoc.'

However, a letter received from the Shire of Orborst dated 20th September, 1966 informed the committee that local sentiment wished to retain the spelling Bendoc.  This desire was shared by the Progress Association.  The matter was finalised when the decision of the Minister of Lands was published in the Victoria Government Gazette on the 29th May, 1968, proclaiming the town to be spelt Bendoc.'

Historical Information: (1224 m alt.), Yarra Ranges National Park: north-east of Mount Donna Buang. According to Les Blake, named "after drought-resistant shrub boobialla"; this is doubtful. The Aboriginal word bubiala or booby-aloe is from the Oyster Bay language of Tasmania, and was interpreted or borrowed by Europeans in Tasmania to mean the coastal wattle Acacia sophorae; in Victoria it is used for shrubs and trees of the genus Myoporum (especially M.. insulare), with small, succulent, often purplish fruits. Species of Myoporum are unlikely to occur on Mount Boobyalla, but the related genus Coprosma, with red fruits, certainly might. The mountain may have been named after the Boobialla River* in Tasmania, rather than directly after any plant.

Historical Information:
According to Saxton (1907: 13) named 'After Charles Buller of the Colonial Office'. According to Martin (1944: 18), 'christened by Mitchell, 1835, after an official in the Colonial Office. Natives knew it as Marrang'. Smyth (1878 Vol. 2: 196) lists Marrang as the Aboriginal name for Mount Buller. Massola (1968: 14) confirmed that Marrang meant 'the hand', or 'an edible root'. Presumably he is referring to the eastern Kulin marnang or marnong = hand (Blake 1991: 8), and murnong the eastern Kulin word for the daisy yam Microseris lanceolata (Gott and Conran 1991: 6). Blake (1977: 182) posits the Aboriginal name is 'Bulla Bulla, i.e. two'. However, Blake (1991: 96) has given bulabil or bindjirri as the eastern Kulin word for two. Robinson (Jnl 11/5/1840 in Clark 2000a) provides the name Marinebut (sometimes transcribed as Warinbut), as the Daungwurrung name for Mount Buller, although Smyth (1878 Vol. 2: 196) lists Warrambat as the Aboriginal names for Mount Timbertop and Mount Terrible. Presumably Marine and Marrang are cognate. Robinson (1844 in Clark 2000b: 201), notes that buller is the Dhudhuroa word for mountain; however Clark and Heydon (2002) acknowledge that the similarity with Mount Buller may be purely coincidental. Sinnott has the following entry:

Named by Sir Thomas Mitchell in 1835 after Charles Buller, a friend in the Colonial Office. Claims that it was named by Baron Ferdinand von Mueller in 1853 (first European to climb it) are unfounded as Mount Buller appears on Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847) and is listed by Wells in 1848. Aboriginal (Taungurong) names: Marrang (Smyth, 1878), Warrinbut (Clark & Heydon). Les Blake mentions another Aboriginal name, Bulla Bulla, meaning two: this is dubious). Clark & Heydon point out that buller is also a Dhudhuroa word for mountain. (Sinnott 2003: 103)

The non-Indigenous origin of the placename Mt Buller is well attested, and its similarity with an exogenous Aboriginal word for mountain is probably coincidental.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information:
Wadawurrung name: Bonan Youang. Meaning: man with knees raised. 

Buninyong (Bonan Youang) and Terrinalum (Mount Elephant) were two warriors who argued, and challenged each other to a fight. They came together at Pitfield; Terrinalum carrying a spear and Buninyong carrying an axe. Terrinalum pierced Buninyong's side with his spear, while Buninyong hit Terrinalum on the head and split it open. They returned to their campsites to rest, and turned to stone, their wounds still visible in the landscape.
Author: Bryon Powell

Historical Information:
Mount Cope located in the Bogong High Plains was purportedly named after Thomas Spencer Cope, 1821 - 1891.

Although the source biography is not published it can be verified through internet searches of Newspaper clippings on Judge Cope. For example there were many Obituary news articles in Victorian newspapers at the time of his death in 1891.

The earliest reference noted to Mt Cope is in 1872 http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/other/vic_gazette/1872/70/1872_1961.pdf
Author: Damaris Brodie Pearce
Title: Thomas Spencer Cope 1821-1891

Historical Information: Named after Thomas Spencer Cope (1821-1891) in the early 1870's, in recognition for his contribution to the early development of the Victorian Colony during the Gold Rush years, his successful pro-bono legal defence (as a leading member of the Defence team of Barristers) of the Eureka Stockade miners, his ten years' service as Judge of Court of Mines and County Court and Chairman of General Sessions for the district of Beechworth, and his commitment to the local region and community as evidenced by his active role in many community and Church organisations. Mt Cope was noted in Vic. Gov. Gazette in 1872

Historical Information: (1250 m alt.), Yarra Ranges National Park and scenic reserve. Aboriginal (Woiworung). Alan Gross (ADB 5) says that Joseph Anderson Panton (see also Panton's Gap), who mapped the Yarra Valley, first named this place Mount Acland but renamed it after learning the Aboriginal name. By contrast, Les Blake claims that Panton first used the name Mount Ackerley, then changed it in favour of daana buong, an Aboriginal phrase for the Dandenong Ranges*. However, Les Blake also gives Dandenong* as Tanjenong, "Abor. word for lofty mountain". Gross's account is more plausible as Panton's uncle, Lt.-Col. Joseph Anderson (see also Mount Juliet) served under Colonel (later Lt.-Gen.) Sir Wroth (Palmer) Acland (1770 - 1816) at the Battle of Maida (Italy, 1806). Martin also gives Mount Acland as the first name. Massola (1968) gives Dthonn-e-youang, the body of the mountain, for Donna Buang, and lists other derivations (including Tanjenong) for Dandenong* and Mount Dandenong*. Clark & Heydon (M) give yawang as Eastern Kulin for mountain.

Historical Information:
Wadawurrung name: Terrinalum. Meaning: place of the sea terns.

Buninyong (Bonan Youang) and Terrinalum (Mount Elephant) were two warriors who argued, and challenged each other to a fight. They came together at Pitfield; Terrinalum carrying a spear and Buninyong carrying an axe. Terrinalum pierced Buninyong's side with his spear, while Buninyong hit Terrinalum on the head and split it open. They returned to their campsites to rest, and turned to stone, their wounds still visible in the landscape.

Historical Information: Named after the parish in which it is located.
Previous name Mt Eliza. Changed due to duplication, named after the parish name of Kerrie.

Captain William Hobson RN was commander of the British man-of-war, HMS Rattlesnake, which had brought the governor's party from Sydney and undertook surveys of the Port Phillip Bay area. Hobson's wife was Eliza, nee Elliot, only daughter of a West Indian merchant of Scottish origin, whom he had married at Nassau on 17 December 1827. His mother was Martha, nee Jones, from an Anglo-Irish family prominent in church and state. It would appear that he wished to honour two women dear to him who had contributed significantly to advancing his naval career, the one with her dowry, the other with her establishment connections. Neither of them had further connection with Australia, although Eliza and the family accompanied William Hobson to his New Zealand appointment in 1839.
Author: Susan Priestley
Title: Charting Some Port Phillip Myths
