Historical Information:
Jim Crow Hill, this was an early name for Mt Franklin, and was the name of a creek, range, and goldfield north of Daylesford. 'Mt Franklin' named after Sir John Franklin's visit to the Loddon Protectorate station in 1843 displaced 'Jim Crow Hill'. According to Saxton (1907: 36) Jim Crow Hill was 'Named by Capt John Hepburn. Capt. Bacchus, who accompanied him, asked what name should the ranges have, and Hepburn replied: Jim Crow, after a popular song'. Morrison (1967: 41) explains that the origin of the name 'Jim Crow' has intrigued many for a long time.

Some believe it is the name of a former 'king' of the local Loddon tribe of Aborigines. Etymologically, the term "jim crow" was used for various implements, as for example, a "jemmy", which is a miniature form of a bent crow (bar) and, somehow, the idea of bending or twisting seems to be implicit in its derivation. A device for bending iron bars was one time termed a "jim crow". About 1835, an American negro, James Rice who was a rather popular "song and dance" comedian wrote and popularised a song, the chorus of which was: "Wheel about and turn about and do just so, Turn about and wheel about and jump Jim Crow". Set to a catchy tune it swept the world, as similar songs do today. ... There seems to be no reason, to doubt the accuracy of the story that the application of the term "Jim Crow" to this region, stems from a trivial incident wherein Capt. Bacchus, riding on horseback between "Lalgambook" and Koorocheang with Capt. Hepburn, called to his companion, "What do you think we should call these ranges?" Hepburn (perhaps with the maddening refrain churning in his mind) replied: "Call them Jim Crow!" (Morrison 1967: 41)

Quinlan has noted that Mount Franklin

which the early squatters called Jim Crow and the natives knew by the name of Lalgambook. John Hepburn used the name Jim Crow to refer not only to the mount itself but to the creek below it and to the district. Edgar Morrison who, in 1965, published the memoirs of Edward Stone Parker under the title Early Days in the Loddon Valley, believes that Jim Crow derives from the chorus of an American minstrel song, popular at the time of the first overlanders. It seems quite feasible, as he suggests, that the behaviour of this winding creek recalled to someone like the Mollison brothers the popular jingle, 'Hop a little, stop a little, jump Jim Crow'. Later, when the aboriginal station was established there, many took it for granted that the word referred to the natives. (Quinlan 1993: 99)

According to Blake (1977: 133), overlander Alexander Mollison's records list the district as 'Jumcra', 'Aboriginal name for which meaning not traced; "Jim Crow" was minstrel song from U.S.A. 1835'. Randell (1979: 222) in a history of the Coliban district explained that Mollison took up two stations in the vacant land immediately west of his Coliban station in early May 1840, naming the Loddon run 'Jumcra, probably an aboriginal name. The second run was called Boughyards. The men soon corrupted the first name into Jim Crow'. Tully (1997: 87) supports the view that Jumcra was corrupted to Jim Crow.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: (952 m alt.), south-south-east of Marysville. Named after Field Marshall Earl (Horatio Herbert) Kitchener (1850 - 1916). The original name, bestowed by "a patriotic German splitter" (Symonds) "at the time of the Franco-Prussian war" (Saxton), was Mount Bismarck, after Prince Otto Eduard Leopold von Bismarck (1815-96). There are no prizes for guessing when the change was made! The earlier name survives in the Bismarck Track round nearby Mount Edgar (q.v.). Kitchener means what it suggests, a cook or kitchen worker. Bismarck is from a place in Germany, first recorded as Biscopesmark, the boundary of a bishop or bishopric.

Historical Information: (1200 m alt.), Marysville State Forest. Ann Thomas (1986) claims the mountain was named after Lady Margaret Stanley (née Gordon) to mark her visit to Marysville in 1919 with her husband, Sir Arthur Stanley (5th Baron of Alderley), Governor of Victoria (1914-20); but Mount Margaret already appears on a tourist map of 1913. Libby Kotschet thinks the name might refer to a member of the Keppel family. Maurice F. Keppel's wife was Margaret, née Stevenson [Mary Kenealy], but she was alive in the 1940s and the mountain was probably named fifty or more years earlier. Another possible contender is Eleanor Margaret Panton, née Fulton, wife of J. A. Panton. Aboriginal (Bunurong?) name: Wort (Clark & Heydon: D, M). See also Mount Gordon and Panton's Gap.

Historical Information: Captain William Hobson RN was commander of the British man-of-war, HMS Rattlesnake, which had brought the governor's party from Sydney and undertook surveys of the Port Philip Bay area. Hobson's wife was Eliza, nee Elliot, only daughter of a West Indian merchant of Scottish origin, whom he had married at Nassau on 17 December 1827. His mother was Martha, nee Jones, from an Anglo-Irish family prominent in church and state. It would appear that he wished to honour two women dear to him who had contributed significantly to advancing his naval career, the one with her dowry, the other with her establishment connections. Neither of them had further connection with Australia, although Eliza and the family accompanied William Hobson to his New Zealand appointment in 1839.

Historical Information: (1514 m alt. + 2 m cairn), Torbreck Range and Rubicon State Forest. Les Blake suggests Welsh twr, rocky peak, and either Italian breccia, rock wall, or French brèche, mountain defile. If the first part were Welsh, then Welsh brych, mottled, would seem far more likely for the second part. However, as there is a village of Torbreck, 4 km S.S.W. of Inverness, Scotland, what about Gaelic tòrr, heap, pile, tower, and breac, speckled, spotted? The Taungurong name seems to have been lost, but Aboriginals used the mountain for collecting Bogong moths (O'Rourke) and for initiation ceremonies. The cairn at the summit was built by surveyor Thomas Pinniger and his party, and forms part of Pinniger's Line (q.v.). An R.A.A.F. Avro-Anson bomber crashed into the mountain in May 1940, killing all four crew members. The wreck was not found until January 1941. The area around Mount Torbreck, the Barnewall Plains and Conn Hill has been designated the Mount Torbreck Natural and Scenic Features Reserve.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel

Historical Information: Glen Waverley and Mount Waverley - Waverley is the name of the main railway station in Edinburgh (see illustration). The station received its name in the 1850s, from the title of a series of novels by Sir Walter Scott (a monument to whom had been erected in Edinburgh near the future railway station in 1844). Sir Walter, in turn, had borrowed the name from Waverley Abbey, a Cistercian monastery in Surrey, England founded in 1128 but now a ruin. The Melbourne suburbs of Glen Waverley and Mount Waverley derive their names from that of an earlier township (now the suburb of Malvern East) which had been privately surveyed in 1853 and which was named Waverley by its owner after the Sir Walter Scott novels.

Historical Information: Mt. William has a great historic value and reputation as the site of an Aboriginal quarry. The diabase found at Mt. William is extremely hard and probably the best example of high quality axe stone in Australia. Large quantities of flakes and chippings are still to be found on the site. Axes from Mt. William have been found in Western Australia and in Queensland. As there is another Mt William in Victoria, a name change was suggested, however this was refused due to the identification of the site with the quarry. The suggested names were Mt Dunlop or Mt Morrision after the selector and managers of a pastoral run in the area.

'Mount William is widely known by that name and has always been regarded as being one of the principal areas from which Aboriginals obtained the stone used in their axes and this fact has been recorded in reference books for the past century.'

Historical Information: Named by Thomas Livingston Mitchell, explorer and Surveyor-General of NSW, after King William IV, the reigning sovereign of the day during Mitchell's journey though 'Australia Felix' [Western Victoria].  'I ventured to connect this summit with the name of the sovereign in whose reign the extensive, valuable, and interesting region below [the summit] was first explored.'  The name was first published in 1838 after the King had died and the new sovereign was Queen Victoria.  Original manuscripts written by Mitchell and Stapylton (second-in-command on the journey) record other names including 'Mt Blue', said by Stapylton to be a reference to Mont Blanc, and reflecting what a cold night was spent on the summit on 14 July 1836.  See also G.W.C. Stapylton [1836] Stapylton with Major Mitchell's Australia Felix expedition 1836, Blubber Head Press, Hobart, 1986, Alan Andrews (editor).
Author: Mitchell, Thomas L.
Title: Three Journeys into the Interior of Eastern Australia Vol.2

Historical Information: Brankeet Inlet, Lake Eildon. Named after Scottish-born Ann Fraser Bon née Dougall (1838 - 1936, nom-de-plume "Sylvia", nicknamed "The Widow of Wappan"). She compensated for her innate shyness by becoming a formidable champion of the Taungurong and other Aboriginals, demanded an investigation (1881) into conditions at Coranderrk (q.v.) and served on the board of inquiry. She was founder of a school for Chinese children (in Melbourne*), a benefactor of the Austin Hospital (Melbourne*), and an advocate of humane treatment for the mentally ill. (A.D.B. 7.) See also Wappan. Bon is an Old French name derived from Latin bonus, good.

Historical Information: Rises from the northern slopes of Highlands, south of the Longwood-Gobur Road; forms an anabranch* and joins the Goulburn River south-west of Arcadia*. This is probably the IX Mile Creek of Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847). Only the headwaters are in the area covered by this book. There is also a parish of Pranjip*. Les Blake says the name is Aboriginal "branjep, possum-skin cover worn by men after undergoing initiation ceremony". If indigenous, the word is probably Taungurong. Barry Blake lists barndjip, Taungurong and Woiworung for apron. Clark & Heydon (D) have pointed out the similarity of Pranjip and Brankeet.

Historical Information: 'In 1968, following an enquiry from the Art Gallery of new South Wales, the Committee identified the 'Murchison Falls' and the 'Strath Falls' on the Queen Parrot Creek as being the ones depicted by the Melbourne artist, Eugen von Guerard, in 1862.  Later, in April, 1975, the Forests Commission suggested that the name 'Murchison Falls' be changed to 'Strath Creek Falls'; and that the name 'Strath Falls' be changed to either 'First falls' or 'Little Falls': it seems that a Miss J. E. lade, a resident of the area (her family having lived in the vicinity for about 100 years), is of the opinion that the Murchison falls should properly be called the 'Strath Creek Falls'.  Miss Lade contends that the name 'Murchison' is a misnomer, as the squatter Murchison took up land between Murchison Gap and Kerrisdale.'

Historical Information: Named Hume River in 1824 by Hamilton Hume after his father. He had crossed it with William Hovell near the future site of Albury. Historical Information: An Aboriginal word of the Gunnai language of unknown meaning.  The prefix could refer to the coastal tribe adjoining the Bidawal, and the suffix could be derived from 'gunni' meaning 'man', thus giving 'a man of the Murrung tribe'.  Or the prefix could be derived from 'muraty' meaning 'sick', giving 'a sick man'.  Blake (1977, p.195) suggested "a big hill where men lived'.  But this is regarded as incorrect.  [Research by I.D. Clark and D.A. Cahir, University of Ballarat, 2005.]

It was proposed that the site should have two names combined. Yarra Flats has historical significance as the former name for Yarra Glen. A local historian and author Mr Mick Woiwood has numerous references to the name of Murrup Brarn which he believes relates to the billabongs on the river flats in the Yarra Glen area. Purportedly the English translation is 'spirit water'.

Historical Information: 'This station was called after the township at the foot of Mount Macedon.  The mountain was named by Major Mitchell, 1836.  He wrote - 'I gave it the name of Mount Macedon, with reference to Port Phillip.'
Author: O'Callaghan, Thos
Title: Names of Victorian Railways Stations

Historical Information:
Mount Macedon Cairn is a large stone structure constructed of shaped and mortared stone. It is approximately 8m high, tapering from 4m diameter at the base to 2m diameter at top. This stone was replaced at the top of the cairn during repair work in June 1983. One of only three examples of mortared stone geodetic triangulation station cairns, the others being Alexander and Warby North. The original Macedon cairn is said to have been constructed in 1853, and to have been the point from which all surveys in the district originated. OSG information confirms that Mt Macedon and other prominent hills in the vicinity
of Melbourne were marked and cleared around 1853 by a team of British engineers who were experienced in the Ordnance Survey of Great Britain. A cairn was constructed by the Royal Engineers under the supervision of Captain Clarke. But it was not until August 1860 that the Macedon station was observed from the main geodetic triangulation and not until January/February the next year that  observations were taken at Macedon. The Superintendent of the Geodetic Survey R J L Ellery is said to have observed angles in February 1861 at Mount Macedon, and visited again March 1864. Macedon geodetic triangulation station cairn is of state significance as a rare example of a large mortared stone cairn, the largest example of only two nineteenth century examples in Victoria, and remaining substantially intact. It is significant as a fine example of the construction work of the Geodetic Survey and demonstrates the scale of their endeavour. Along with a number of other surviving examples of geodetic cairns, it provides evidence of the challenge of land survey in a rapidly growing colony. The Macedon cairn may be of social significance, given the popularity of Mt Macedon from the nineteenth century until today.

John Butler Maling lived in the Balwyn-Canterbury-Surrey Hill area in the 1800s. Maling was a carpenter, mostly building houses, and had connections to local government, schools and churches in the area. He built the original St Barnabas' Church in Balwyn in 1872 and extended the nave in the 1880s with his sons. His son William carved the pulpit in 1907 and the church was finished by the family in 1930. Part of Maling's land became Chatham Primary School.
He was also associated with the building of Pentridge Gaol.

Maling was a councillor for 29 consecutive years from 1886-1916, President of the Shire of Boroondara in 1887/88, 1897/98, 1904/05 and the first Mayor of Camberwell 1905/06, when it was officially gazetted as the Town of Camberwell in 1906.

Historical Information:
The 'Maroondah Federation Estate' is a community, cultural and arts facility located at 32 Greenwood Avenue Ringwood, based on the former Ringwood Primary School site.
When the school closed in 1998, Maroondah Council purchased the school site and developed the area.
The 'Maroondah Federation Estate' was jointly funded by Maroondah City Council, the Victorian Government's Community Support Fund and the Federal Government's Federation Fund and was a Centenary of Federation project.
The 'Estate' incorporates a Cultural Centre, which has been developed in the original school buildings and a Lifestyle Centre, which is contained in the extensive addition to the school building. The concept behind the refurbishment was to preserve its historical value and provide a new outlet for the development of artistic expression and to provide a purpose for use by community groups.
'Maroondah Federation estate' was officially opened by the Maroondah Mayor Cr Peter Gurr, the Premier of Victoria, the Hon Steve Bracks MP and the Federal Member for Deakin, Mr Phillip Barresi MP on Wednesday 31 January 2001

Named after Frederick McCubbin, the well-known Australian landscape artist.

Frederick (Fred) McCubbin (1855-1917), painter and art teacher, was born on 25 February 1855 at 165 King Street, Melbourne, third son of Alexander McCubbin, baker from Ayrshire, Scotland, and his English wife Anne  McWilliams. Educated at William Willmott's West Melbourne Common school and St Paul's School, Swanston Street, at about 14 he was placed in a solicitor's office. He soon joined the family business and drove a baker's cart before being apprenticed to a coach-painter. In 1869 he enrolled at the Artisans' School of Design, and later studied drawing at the National Gallery of Victoria. He completed his coach-painting apprenticeship in 1875 but next year his hopes for furthering his studies at the gallery were curtailed by the death of his father and the need to assist with the family business. McCubbin continued in the school of design and joined the school of painting. Tom Roberts and Mackennal were fellow students. He was awarded the trustees' first prize in the first of the annual students' exhibitions in 1883. He also studied and exhibited at the Victorian Academy of Art, showing in their annual exhibitions of 1876 and 1879-82, selling his first painting, 'View Near Fisherman's Bend', from the 1880 exhibition. In 1882 he was awarded a silver medal for figure drawing in the academy life-class and was elected an associate.

When Roberts returned from overseas in 1885, he and McCubbin went on painting trips, camping at Housten's farm at Box Hill, at Mentone on Port Phillip Bay and later in the Heidelberg area. Here they were joined by Arthur Streeton, Charles Conder and others, these first camps marking the beginning of what came to be called the Heidelberg school. Nicknamed 'The Proff' because of his philosophizing, McCubbin was a strong advocate of the particularly national element in the work of the school, drawing his inspiration both from the earlier traditions of colonial art and the growing sense of nationalism of the time. In 1886 he was appointed drawing master of the school of design and held this position for the rest of his life. A group of professional artists led by McCubbin, Roberts, John Ford Paterson and others broke away from the Victorian Academy of Art in 1887 and formed the Australian Artists' Association. A committee-member, McCubbin participated in the association's exhibitions until it amalgamated with the academy in 1888 as the Victorian Artists' Society. McCubbin served as a councillor of the society from the beginning and was president in 1903-04 and 1909. He contributed regularly to its annual exhibitions until 1912, when he resigned to join with seven other artists to form the Australian Art Association as its first president.

In 1889 he had joined Roberts, Streeton, Conder, C. Douglas Richardson, R. E. Falls and Herbert Daly in the exhibition of 9 x 5 impressions at Buxton's Galleries. He occasionally participated in the Society of Artists' exhibitions of the late 1890s in Sydney, was represented in the 1898 Exhibition of Australian Art, Grafton Galleries, London, and held one-man shows in Melbourne from about 1904. He had married Annie Lucy Moriarty at St Ignatius Church, Richmond, on 5 March 1889. On the death of Folingsby in 1891 McCubbin was acting director of the National Gallery until the appointment of Bernard Hall in 1892, and was so again in 1903 and 1905. He visited Tasmania in 1899, and in 1907 was given leave from the gallery to visit England and Europe, staying with his old friend Roberts and visiting numerous galleries and art schools. He was given further leave in 1916 owing to ill health and he died of heart disease on 20 December 1917 at South Yarra, and was buried in Brighton cemetery. His wife, four sons including Louis and two daughters survived him.

The Melbourne Observatory comprises a complex of buildings, most built by the Public Works Department, including the original Observatory (1862-3 with additions), giant telescope (1868-9), equatorial and heliograph complex (c1874), Magnet House (1876-7), Gatehouse (c1880), astrograph (1889), astronomer's residence (1889-90), and Meridian Mark. The buildings are generally intact however most of the original fittings and library have been dispersed. The Dome in the 1862-3 building which housed a 120mm telescope has been demolished. Parts of the giant telescope complex have been demolished. The Melbourne Observatory was built in 1861-63 as a replacement for the
Williamstown Observatory (that is the Timeball Tower). A residence for the Government Astronomer was later built nearby in 1890. Robert Ellery, Government Astronomer, joined the Surveyor General's
Department in 1858 to start the preparations for the proposed geodetic survey of Victoria. Ellery took charge of the Observatory in 1863, occupying the adjoining residence he built in 1890. As well as his responsibilities for the geodetic survey, Ellery fulfilled the role as Astonomer until 1895. The Observatory had many important roles in the developing city, providing scientific data essential for the smooth running of the city - from the setting of clocks, meteorological data, surveying, positional astronomy and star mapping, astrophysics and geophysics.The Observatory closed in 1944. In terms of land surveying, the Melbourne Observatory played a central role. From it observations could be made to the Green Hill end of the Werribee geodetic survey baseline, to Station Peak, Mt Macedon and other hilltop trigonometric points in the Melbourne region. The first method tried during the Geodetic Survey involved the marking of a grid across Victoria, each square being one degree of latitude and longitude. The Melbourne Observatory is of national significance as the focus of astronomical observation in the Southern Hemisphere, the centre of the Geodetic Survey process and as the State Authority on timekeeping and
meteorology. This reputation came from the service given by R L J Ellery, Government Astronomer from 1853-1895 and from the observatory equipment, including the world's largest telescope. from the persepctive of land surveying, the Melbourne Observatory (like the Williamstown Observatory before it) played a central role, being the headquarters for Ellery who directed the survey and an important observation point.

Small earth mound with central pile of field stone. A survey to determine the border of New South Wales and Victoria was undertaken in 1870-72, twenty years after the two colonies were separated. The need to define the border on the ground arose due to the increasing settlement in this mountainous country, especially the advent of gold mining around the Bendoc region. The eastern end of the border at Conference Point (Cape Howe) was established in 1868 by NSW Surveyor-General P.F. Adams and R.J.L. Ellery for Victoria. The western end, at Forest Hill, is the source of the Murray River. It was marked by Alexander Black in 1870. Black proceeded to undertake an eleven month survey to mark the border on the ground between Forest Hill and Allan's Peg, a peg positioned near the Delegate River by Senior Geodetic surveyor Alexander Allan. To achieve the simple "straight line" border across mountainous country involved enormous hard work under difficult conditions. Ellery writing about
the geodetic Survey of Victoria in 1891 described the survey as "a piece of survey work which for difficulties and for the requirement of skills, energy and endurance, as well as for accuracy attained I believe has never been surpassed". Black's survey traversed very difficult terrain, covering 61.5 kilometres over 11 months. Allan's survey was 114 kilometres long, extending over 18 months. Over 50 marks were built by the surveyors and their teams. Some were substantial stone cairns. The surveyors also had to dig trenches to indicate the
direction of the border, and clear the line of vegetation.  The Black-Allan line border survey is of state significance as evidence of an outstanding surveying feat, testing the endurance and skill of the survey parties,
and providing a dramatic demonstration of the difficulties encountered by surveyors in the nineteenth century. Historically, the marking of the border between New South Wales and Victoria symbolised a step in the development of Victorian as a separate, self-governing region.
Named after Anthony Cottrell, one of 15 members of John Batman's party, which was the first official European settlement in the Melbourne/Port Philip area.

Historical Information:
Mt Bogong cairn is located around 12 kms from Mt Beauty township, on the top of Mt Bogong, Victoria's highest mountain. The mountain has a rounded bare top, snow covered throughout winter. Stone cairn recorded in 1980 as being 2.5 metres high by 3.0 diameter with steel centre pole. The cairn was constructed c1860 by the Geodetic Survey and rebuilt in 1938 by the State Electricity Commission. A new station was formed alongside by the Army Survey Corps, but is presumed to have been since destroyed. Mt Bogong geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of seven examples remaining in the alpine area of north-east Victoria. Dating from 1860 and rebuilt in 1938 by the SECV, this cairn remains substantially intact to the date of rebuilding, and is assumed to retain an overall form and shape consistent with the original. The association
with the SECV is of historical interest, given their importance in the
development of the hydro-electricity industry in this area.

Drystone cairn built of shaped blocks. The cairn is approximately 3m high, and 4m diameter at the base, tapping slightly towards the top. One side of the stonework has collapsed. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The Mt Burrowa cairn was built c1860. Mt Burrowa geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local interest as an
example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of seven examples remaining in the alpine area of north-east Victoria. Dating from 1860, it is one of the earlier cairns built during the survey, however it retains only part of its form due to a major collapse of the stonework.

Mt Gibbo cairn is located on the summit of Mt Gibbo, a massive hill located midway between Benambra and Corryong. The cairn is constructed of unmortared field stone, 1.5 metres high by 2 metres diameter with timber centre pole and metal vanes. Mt Gibbo is associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872). The
date of construction is not known. The centre pole and vanes were placed more recently by SMA. The Angle Book also notes that Gibbo 1985 was established to densify the 2nd order net. Mt Gibbo geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local interest as an example of the drystone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria
(1858-1872), one of five examples remaining in the alpine area of eastern Gippsland. The cairn has probably been completely rebuilt as part of the installation of a new centre pole and vanes.

The Major Mitchell Memorial Cairn is located a short distance from the Mt Greenock trigonometrical station. The cairn is 4.9m high and 2.8m square at the base and constructed of mortared stone. A new brass plaque reads " Major Thomas Mitchell 26th September 1836 ". The original plaque read "Hereabouts on 26 September 1836 stood Major (Sir) Thomas Mitchell Discoverer of Australia Felix". The cairn commemorating the memory of Major Sir Thomas Mitchell was
unveiled on 28th March 1930. The cairn, located on the top of Mount Greenock, marks (as closely as could be ascertained) the place where the explorer stood in September 1836 and made a sketch of the surroundings. Dr Charles Fenner is recognised as the person who initiated the idea for the memorial cairn, with a Mr Hutchings and a committee undertaking the planning and development. The cairn cost 36 pounds to construct, with the funds coming from public donations. The unveiling speech by Sir James Barrett noted that Mitchell's journey would be marked by a series of stone cairns, and that every
school along the route where a cairn was erected would receive a copy of a diary of Mitchell's travels. (Talbot Leader 5.4.1930) This ceremony was one of many similar ceremonies across Victoria to
commemorate Mitchell's explorations. (Talbot Leader 5.4.1930) The Major Mitchell cairn on Mt Greenock is one of many examples throughout the State constructed to commemorate the explorations of Major Thomas Mitchell. It is of local significance. The cairn is not a survey mark and has no direct association with land surveying, although Major Mitchell's explorations were part of an overall process of identifying land for settlers

Historical Information:
Conical shaped stone cairn 3.6 high, tapering from 3.6 diameter at the base to 1.8 diameter at the top. The stonework uses large boulders at the base, tapering to smaller, shaped stones towards the top. Small rock pieces have been used to wedge between the boulders in place of mortar and the whole structure is remarkably sound. Some damage to the top of the cairn has resulted from the collapse of a nearby tree. Depressions near the cairn indicate areas where rocks were quarried from the ground, and remains of early glass bottles indicate that this area has been used as a campsite. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The Mt Juliet cairn was built c 1860. (1) Mt Juliet was selected for its height and visibility and was able to be aligned with cairns on Mt Tallarook, Mt Eliza, Mt Dandenong, the
Melbourne Observatory, Station Peak and Mt Macedon.  Mt Juliet developed as a popular destination for walkers visiting Healesville in
the early 1900s. Nicolas Caire, writing in J W Lindt's visitor's guide, described the view as an "...extended panorama of the surrounding country. Melbourne, the bay, Macedon, and the You Yangs being easily seen on a clear day". Mt Juliet cairn is a fine example of a geodetic triangulation station cairn, remaining remarkably intact and retaining some evidence of quarrying for stone to build the cairn and of early camping on the site. It is of at least regional significance as an example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), and is one of only two examples remaining within the greater Melbourne region, the others being Mt Baw Baw and Mt Macedon. It was a popular destination for walkers from the early
twentieth century, and can be expected to have some social significance for its long association with tourist and local visits to the area

Mount Trawool cairn is a small stone cairn, substantially collapsed. It was
described in 1973 as a small cairn, hollow 6' x 6', approx 2' high and made from local rocks. No ground mark was visible. Another small cairn was noted approx 20 m away. It is located within land reserved for a trig station within privately owned grazing land.

Mt Wellington cairn is located on the highest point of the northernly extension of the Razorback ridge, 8 km north of Gable End. It was originally built as a conical stone pile 20 feet (6 m) in both height and diameter. An illustration exists in OSG records. The cairn remains today in a partially dismantled state. It now measures approximately 10 metres in diameter by 3 metres high. A pre-cast concrete trig. block was cemented into the centre of the partially dismantled cairn. During
these works some pieces of rotting wood were found, probably remains of the old centre pole. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The date of the construction of the Mt Wellington cairn is not known. Mt Wellington geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local interest as an example of the large dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of five examples remaining in the alpine area of Gippsland. This cairn has been altered, and now retains only some of its original form. Once an example of a large cairn, it is now substantially depleted in size.

Leonard Roger Napthine was elected to the Winchelsea Shire Council in 1971 and served on the council until 1982. He was Shire president for one term 1979-80.
During his period on Council, he chaired a committee to determine the recreational needs of the community and was largely responsible for the construction of the Winchelsea Leisure Time Centre which was opened in 1978. 
The Winchelsea Historical Society was formed in 1980 with Cr, Len Napthine as president.
In 1974 Len was elected Deputy State president of the Young Farmers Club.
Theresa Napthine, Len's wife, was appointed as the first District Young Farmer President in 1974. She was also chair of the first meeting held in 1977 to launch the Winchelsea Star newspaper which has continued to this date. Theresa was also the initial Chairperson of the Social Development Committee which was formed in1977 and which was instrumental in the establishment of many social support facilities and groups during the following years.

Historical Information: Narbethong is the name of a township some 87 km north-east of Melbourne. Saxton (1907: 49) notes that it is a native name, meaning 'cheerful, lively, humorous'. According to Martin (1944: 63), it is an Aboriginal word meaning 'cheery'. Massola (1968: 38) agrees with Martin, adding the gloss 'lively'. Blake (1977: 198) notes that it was named 'by surveyor John Wrigglesworth in 1865 as Nar Be Thong; Abor. word for cheerful or a cheerful place'. Bunce (1856: 8, 27) records Narbethong as meaning cheerful and lively. Bunce (in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 144) in a list of east Kulin vocabulary, includes 'Narbeethong - Lively; Narbethong - Cheerful, fun, levity; Karbeethong - Mirth' (Bunce in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 140), and Carbeenthon or carbethon - Gay, cheerful, hilarity, humorous, play, to sport, to chuckle, to laugh, glad, gleeful, merry (Bunce in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 137). Blake (1991: 98) lists 'narbethong' as the east Kulin word for 'lively'. Sinnott (2003) accepts that Narbethong is an Aboriginal word. John Green, the superintendant of the Coranderrk Aboriginal station at Healesville informed John Mathew (Papers) that it is 'not a local Aboriginal word' but it is difficult to know what Green means by this comment as Bunce's vocabulary covers east Kulin which includes the Narbethong district. Green may be suggesting that it is not a placename. Symonds (1982: 54), in a history of Healesville acknowledges that the name is said to have come from the Aboriginal word for 'A cheerful place' but a local claims that the name derives from Narbeth, Wales, from where the Fisher family originated from. Sinnott (2003: 114) dismisses this claim.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: Parish (usually spelt Nar-Be-Thong) and township. Named in 1865 by surveyor John Wrigglesworth (Les Blake), but (according to Symonds) at first known as Fisher's Creek or Starvation Creek. Site of an internment camp during the Second World War. Aboriginal: cheery (Martin); lively, cheerful (Massola, 1968); but more likely to be Woiworung or Bunurong rather than Taungurong: in the 1850s Bunce listed narbeethong, lively, narbethong, cheerful, fun, levity, carbeenthon, gay, cheerful, and karbeethong, mirth, so Wrigglesworth probably took the name from Bunce. There seems no reason to believe the claim (quoted by Symonds) that the name derives from Narbeth, Wales, from where the Fisher family originally came. See also St. Fillan's.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: There are three interpretations of the origin of Narre Warren. One definition is that it is a corruption of the Aboriginal words for "little hills". Another definition is that it is a corruption of the Aboriginal words for "no good" from the belief that the creek water was brackish and "no good" for drinking. The VACL website suggests that it comes from the word meaning "red ochre". Narre Warren originally referred to the township of Narre Warren North, which was surveyed around 1860. This was later known as Old Narre Warren to distinguish it from New Narre Warren which developed around the Railway Station.The name was used in the area as early as 1837 when the Native Police Force was established at Nerre Nerre Warren, this area later became an Aboriginal Protectorate to protect the Aborigines from the white settlers. It is now the Dandenong Police Paddocks Reserve. Narree Worran is a Parish name in the County of Mornington.
Author: Casey Cardinia Libraries
Page Title: Place Names of Casey and Cardinia

No better explanation has emerged as to the source of the name Nathalia.

Historical Information: Apart from the Lorquon pastoral run (1851), a farm settler at Netherby occupied land near a swamp in 1884. It was known as the Rupeal or Warraquil swamp, and until 1886 the settlement which arose was named Warraquil. It was changed to Netherby in 1886 to avoid confusion with a similar-sounding town in eastern Victoria. The inspiration for Netherby was the name of a place in the poem Young Lochinvar by Walter Scott.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: In 1844 during a journey of exploration in the Wimmera, C.F. Belcher of Geelong and Dougald Macpherson found a swamp by which a number of Aborigines were camped.  The explorers used a young interpreter called Davey to ascertain that the place was called 'nyell' meaning 'abode of spirits', referring to vaporous mists over the water in the early mornings.  Macpherson wrote 'Nhill' in his notebook.  A pastoral run was selected shortly after and named Nyill in March 1849, and a homestead built near where the meeting occurred.  The township began to grow from about 1879.  See also Les Blake, Place Names of Victoria, p.202.

Historical Information: Parish. A former forestry district with headquarters at Taggerty (q.v.). Former pastoral run (originally 6,500 ha) east of the Whanregarwen run and west of the Acheron run and the Acheron River; established 1839; subdivided, 1864, into Niagaroon (cancelled 1881) and Riversdale No. 1 (q.v.). The Niagaroon run probably extended further south than is shown in Spreadborough & Anderson's maps. Les Blake has suggested that Niagaroon may allude to Niagara Creek (see under Snobs Creek) to the east, but it is in fact an Anglicised form of the Taungurong Nyaggeron (or Ageroon), probably adopted by the first licensees Ouseley Cockburn and Dr. Dougald Fletcher, who also (according to Les Blake) named the Acheron River (q.v.).

Historical Information: Niddrie (Edinburgh and Longniddry in East Lothian). The name comes from the Brythonic (a form of Welsh once spoken in that part of Scotland) 'newydd' meaning "new", and 'tref' a "house" or "hamlet". There are two theories concerning the origin of the name of this suburb. The first is that it took its name from a property called Niddrie that had been built between 1869 and 1871 by Henry Stevenson, and which he had named after the Edinburgh suburb (article on Niddrie, retrieved from Wikipedia in March 2007). Blake (1977), on the other hand, is of the opinion that the suburb was named for Niddry Castle in West Lothian, owned by the Earl of Hopetoun, Governor of Victoria from 1889-1895.

Historical Information: Honours Norm Jardine who served the Bruce Park Cricket and Football Club for 35 years and played over 400 games with the club.

Norm Jardine has been a member of the Heatherhill Cricket Club for almost 40 years, a committee member for 35 years and is also involved with the Mornington Peninsula Cricket Association which he has done so for almost 12 years. 

Norm volunteers his time to run the Under 13 Country Week for the Mornington Peninsula Cricket Association. This involves taking leave of absence from his work for a week at a time; at personal cost to himself, and organising equipment, selection of teams, ground allocation and the general running of the cricket matches. This would generally take Norm about 60 hours and he has volunteered his time to do this for the last 10 years. Norm also took the Under 15 Mornington Peninsula Cricket Association on a tour to England in 2005 and went again in 2007.
 
Norm has also coached junior representative cricket sides for the Mornington Peninsula Cricket Association for some 10 years, and coached juniors at Heatherhill Cricket Club for 11 years.
 
Norm coached junior football teams at Karingal Football Club for 8 years before coming to Frankston Rovers Junior Football Club and coaching there for a further 6 years.
 
Norm has volunteered his time for Clean up Australia Day between 2001 and 2005 and has also collected money for various charities over the last 10 years including the Heart Foundation, Royal Children's Hospital, McGrath Foundation (Pink Stumps Day) and the Leukaemia Foundation.
Norm Pietila left Finland in 1956 and formed the company, Nordcon Pty Ltd, one of the largest private land owners and developers in the Albury-Wodonga Region.
Name commemorates Private Norman Talintyre, a soldier aged 19 when killed in action at El Alamein in North Africa on 23 October 1942.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information:
Kulin name: Yern-da-ville. Meaning not recorded. 
This name was recorded by A. W. Howitt, anthropologist, from conversations from sometime between 1897 and 1901 with William Barak, ngurungaeta (leader) of the Wurundjeri-willam, the traditional owners of what is now northern Melbourne, and Dick Richards, Barak's fellow Kulin countryman. The Kulin was an alliance of Aboriginal nations in central Victoria. Howitt jotted down Aboriginal names, mostly in the Woiwurrung language once spoken in the Melbourne area, corresponding to landmarks and municipalities that arose in Melbourne town during Barak's lifetime (c.1824 to 1903).
Author: Jason Gibson, Helen Gardner, Stephen Morey
Page Title: Rediscovered: the Aboriginal names for ten Melbourne suburbs

Historical Information: Separated from the City of Melbourne in 1859 and initially called Hotham, its name was changed to North Melbourne in 1877. During the 1880s land boom it became the most densely populated part of the city. Although the town hall is still an Errol St landmark, in 1905 North Melbourne was taken back into the City of Melbourne as the Hopetoun ward, named after a former Governor of Victoria and Australia's first Governor-General, Lord Hopetoun.

Historical Information: Named after the Nunan family who settled in the Muckatah area, on the property east of the bridge where the channel runs through. In 1877,  Thomas Nunan was involved with activities in the Muckatah area, particularly the Muckatah Race Club, the Muckatah Recreation Reserve, Muckatah Football Club and the Cobram Agricultural Society.  The current generation farmed the property unit December 2001, ending 124 years of continuous family farming.

Reputedly from an Aboriginal word 'numphawading' meaning ceremonial ground or battlefield.  The name was first applied to a wide area.  Then the name 'Tunstall' was adopted for the locality, making reference to the famous Staffordshire pottery;  similar clay had been found locally and brick-making became a significant local industry.  Nunawading was adopted as the locality name after the second world war and with the growth of residential subdivisions. [See also Wikipedia.]

Historical Information: Nunawading derives its name from a local Aboriginal word translated variously as "meeting place", "battlefield" and "ceremonial ground". The name first described the local parish in 1854, two years after the area was first surveyed and in 1857 the Nunawading District Road Board was established. In 1872 the board was replaced by the Shire of Nunawading, but the central area was officially known as Tunstall after the famous English pottery region, until the City of Nunawading was created in 1945.

Historical Information: The name was chosen after a merger between the Nambrok and Denison Primary Schools.

The original Nambrok School was opened on the 16th September, 1909, in a hall near the present hall and recreation oval, in Hall Road.  The school moved from this site to its present site around 1923.

An early teacher at the school in Hall Road, which was known as 'The Pines', was a Miss Showers, who commenced teaching there in 1912.  She later married a Mr. Bermingham, and many of their descendants are still in the district and still attend our school. 

Up until the school closed during the war, in 1942, it was a one teacher school averaging twenty to thirty children, who studied to grade eight or as it was in those days, the Merit Certificate.  Children often rode horses to school which were kept in a small paddock on the other side of the Maffra-Rosedale Road to the school.

The school re-opened, as No. 3626, in 1955 on its present site to accommodate the children of the soldier settlers for whom the district was opened up in the early 1950's.  Later in the decade, with all the soldier settlement farms being taken up, the enrolment figure exceeded one-hundred, so two new rooms were added to the original building, also the site was enlarged to include a football oval and general play area.

In 1987 a re-organization between Nambrok and Nambrok West (No. 3648) Primary Schools took place.  Nambrok West Primary School's site was on the corner of Nambrok Road and Ross Road.  When Nambrok West amalgamated with Nambrok Primary School, all ten students attending Nambrok West transferred to the Nambrok site along with all their equipment and resources.  The 'newer' classroom and corridor from Nambrok West was also re-located onto existing buildings here.  In 1989 the original Nambrok West classroom was relocated here.  This room is known as the 'West Room' and is currently used as a Multi-Purpose Room.  The school population increased from an average in the early 1980's of around forty to just over sixty in 1988.  The school also went from being a three teacher school to a four teacher school. 

In early 1993 the State Government initiated many changes to the education system. The local result was that the Nambrok and Denison Primary Schools were merged on the Nambrok Primary School site for the commencement of the 1994 school year. School No. 5395, Nambrok-Denison Primary School as we now know it, was established.

The Denison School was originally known as Wandocka but in 1923 re-opened as Denison, No. 4168.  In 1964, sixty-four pupils were in attendance at the school, its highest attendance.   When the school closed on the 17th December, 1993, most student resources, the two Denison classrooms, corridor, and office area, were moved to the Nambrok site.  In 1994 the newly formed Nambrok-Denison Primary School had a population of ninety students, with a staff of five teachers.
Author: Nambrok-Denison Primary School

Historical Information:
Nino Arrigo (18/05/1950 - 27/11/2016) was very well known within the Wyndham community and contributed so much of his time and effort in to helping people throughout. He was an active member of the Werribee Rotary club for over 40 years, during which time he rode a bicycle from Perth to Melbourne raising $160,000 for cancer research. He went to school in Werribee, played football for Werribee and Hoppers Crossing, and then went on to start, and operate for 42 years, Werribee Glass and Glazing (a business that remains in his family today). Sadly, Nino lost a personal battle with cancer. He made selfless contributions he made the to Werribee community, and those beyond. 

Nino was born 18th May 1950 in Werribee and passed away on 27th November 2016 in Melbourne.

His parents owned some property near the bridge on which they ran some cattle and in his later years travelled this road regularly to get to his beloved getaway on the Murray River in Echuca.

Historical Information: The origin of St Arnaud's was the discovery of gold at a sandy knoll later called Bakery Hill, St Arnaud north, in January 1855. The resulting goldfield was known as New Bendigo, and mining spread into several hills and gullies. In 1856 a town was surveyed about 6 km east of the goldfield. It was named St Arnaud, after a French military commander in the Crimean War. Because of the town's distance from the goldfield the survey was cancelled and a township developed around the mining activity. The community readily adopted the proposed name, and sales of township lots occurred in 1858.
Author: Victorian Places

In 1845 the land in the Snowy River valley was sold to Norman McLeod, a Scot who named the area Orbost after a place on the Isle of Skye, where he was born, in Scotland. No one is sure why he named the town Orbost. There a number of possible explanations. Some suggest it was the name of a town on the Isle of Skye. Others claim it was the McLeod seat on the island. Other sources claim it is a Gaelic word meaning 'winged island'. And still others that it was the birthplace of McLeod. None of these are incompatible. It could have elements of all four explanations.
Author: Aussie Towns

Historical Information: When the first party of overlanders arrived at the bank of the wide Snowy River, they were puzzled how they should get to the other side. One of them, Cameron by name, said he would get across 'Or Bust'. So when they did get across, they called the place 'Or bust'.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information:
Reginald was born in 1895 in Colac to Charlotte (nÃ¿Â©e Harmer) and James Summers Olney. He was the first son and oldest of their five children. A younger sister died in infancy. His father was a Senior-constable with the Victorian Police and the family moved for his postings. The Olneys were Methodist. He joined the Lands Department as a clerk in May 1911.  Reginald was engaged to Em Keller. 
Reginald attempted to enlist on 16 occasions and was rejected 15 times for dental issues.  He was finally successful and joined the AIF on 24 July 1915 at 20 years old. He was allocated as a Gunner with the Artillery, and left Melbourne for Egypt in September. On arrival he was transferred to the Australian Records Section, where he worked until he became ill in late November and was taken to hospital. His illness was serious enough to require medical evacuation to England in December. He returned to Egypt in March 1916 and joined the 23rd Battalion as a Bombardier. He then left for France, where he joined the 21st Field Artillery Brigade. 
In May he was taken to the Casualty Clearing Station with influenza and trench fever, a common illness caused by the unsanitary conditions in the trenches. Once recovered he returned to his unit and attended the 1st Divisional Gas School. He was shot in the head on 11 August in Belgium and evacuated to England for treatment. He returned to Belgium in January 1918. In April he began to experience lung issues, believed to be related to gas exposure. He was initially diagnosed with pleurisy; in May it was confirmed as tuberculosis and he was sent home. On 13 January 1918 Reginald died at the Military Sanatorium, Macleod. 
Reginald was buried at the Coburg Pine Ridge Cemetery with military honours. He was 23 years old.  The Secretary of Lands expressed the great pride the Department felt in him.  As the first enlistee from the Department's Mallee branch, a parish in Mildura was named in his honour.
Author: Rebecca Russell
Title: Honour Roll 1914-1918 Department of Crown Lands & Survey & Office of Titles

Historical Information: Paine Reserve was named after the long standing Councillor of Victoria Ward, City of Williamstown, George A Paine. Councillor Paine served the residents of Victoria Ward, which stretched from Victoria Street in Williamstown to Mason Street, Newport and served as Mayor for the City of Williamstown for two terms between 1929 and 1931. As Councillor he oversaw the construction of many prominent civic buildings within Williamstown including the Williamstown Cricket Pavilion and the Ballroom at the Williamstown Town Hall. Councillor Paine was at the centre of many turbulent Council disputes in the early 1930s and was well known for his fearless oratory. He was also a founding member of the Newport Bowling Club that currently sits within the park named in his honour. George A Paine died on 6 January 1960.

Historical Information: Before its 1920s subdivision, Park Orchards was part of the orchard country covering Doncaster and Warrandyte. In 1902 the prominent orchardist, Tom Petty, purchased nearly one square mile of the Park Orchards district, converting it to 80 orchard blocks with wind breaks of pine trees and natural bush. Another orchardist, a nephew of Petty's, bought 100 acres north of Petty's holding. In 1925 Australis Sharp and John Taylor, South Melbourne timber merchants, bought 600 acres (including Petty's land), and had it subdivided by Saxil Tuxen and Miller. Tuxen had worked with Marion Mahony and Walter Burley Griffin on the Ranelagh estate, Mt Eliza and the Glenard estate, Heidelberg. Sharp and Taylor had owned the Ranelagh estate, and Park Orchards was designed on the same 'country club' principles. The circular street pattern is distinctively Mahony-Griffin-inspired.

The Mornington Cricket Club was established in 1863.  By 1905 the reserve was fenced and charges were made for entry, half the proceeds going towards improvements. In the late 1870s professional fishers moved to McMillan Strait, the settlement being known as Toonalook, supposedly an Aboriginal word meaning plenty of fish. Their catch was taken by steamer to Sale and railed to Melbourne. In 1879 Captain Payne, Harbour Master and Inspector of Fisheries, visited the area to select a site for a wharf. The settlement was renamed Paynesville in his honour, although the name was not officially adopted until 1888.

Historical Information:
The earliest c.1850s timber bridge over the Thomson River was near the end of its useful life when swept away in the 1891 flood. A temporary crossing was then erected, and a new timber bridge, designed by architects Anderson, Kernot and Thomas, was built in 1893-94, and then partly reconstructed in 1943. At that time a timber and steel superstructure, with road deck, was built atop the existing piles, using rolled steel joists instead of timber stringers. The timber decking ran counter (rather than parallel) to the diagonally-placed cross-beams, an approach developed by the Country Roads Board in the 1930s to address the uneven surface of transverse decks and vibrations caused by faster-moving motor vehicles. The works also increased the height of the superstructure, raising the new deck 420mm (16 Ã Â½"). The catalyst for the works may have been another flood in November 1942, which washed over the approaches to the bridge.

The bridges over the Thomson River have variously been known as Pearson's Bridge, after prominent local nineteenth century pastoralist and politician William Pearson; Warruk Bridge, after a reference in the Gippsland Times in 1893; and the current name, Thomson River Bridge.

In 1961-62, the Sale Causeway was constructed to span both waterways and the flood plain between. The new Thomson River concrete causeway bridge was built on an earlier road alignment and reputedly over the footprint of the 1850s bridge, of which remnant timber piles remain. With the relocation of Princes Highway traffic, the 1890s bridge was initially retained as a stock crossing, and in the 1980s incorporated into the Warruk-Sale bicycle and pedestrian pathway. The bridge was demolished in 2010 and replaced with the current pedestrian bridge, which represents the fifth bridge on or very near this location.

Suggested by Baw Baw Developments. The park is named after William Henry Penaluna who was a landowner in the area with family descendants of approximately 49 years.
William Henry Penaluna was born in Cornwall UK in 1853. He settled in Boolarra around 1878 and built the first hotel in Boolarra, the Settlors Arms. He married in 1881, had seven children, and died in Mirboo North at the age of 88 in 1941. 
He purchased the property at Warragul in 1924 from John Arnold Holden and it remained in his estate after his death until 1943 when it transferred to his children Emily Jane Lord, Laura Louisa Lushby, and Mary Annabella Anderson. The property was retained by the children until 1945 when it was sold to Leslie Grant Marrabel.
Recognises ceramic penguins incorporated in the park as part of a work-for-the-dole program.

Historical Information: Pentridge Prison was established in 1851 as a result of increased pressure on the Penal system due to the gold rush and the need for a place to hold those convicted of serious offences. The first stage was the 1850-1857 Pentridge Stockade Complex, a relatively ad-hoc group of structures built by prison labour and using predominantly local materials. The second phase undertaken in the late 1850s and early 1860s was the construction of Inspector General William Champ's model prison complex, based on British exemplars and incorporating a relatively sophisticated system of prisoner classification and penal reform. The main structures constructed at this stage and still surviving are the Entrance Building, Warder's residences, Prison Hospital, Panopticon B Division, F Division, a Workshop building (now known as the Laundry) and most of the prison walls. These were all constructed of bluestone. The prison was gradually expanded and developed in stages, reflecting both developments in penology as well as broader Government policies relating to the operation of the prison system. Following the Stawell Royal Commission of 1870 an extensive work program for prisoners was introduced as part of the system at Pentridge and a complex known as the Industries was constructed. These included a timber yard, a woollen mill, carpenters' and blacksmiths' workshops completed in 1879 and tailors' and bootmakers' workshops completed in 1886. A female prison was constructed on the site between 1860 and 1865 which is now known as A Division. This was superseded when a new female prison was constructed on the site between 1887 and 1894 in order to provide completely separate accommodation for women. This section is now known as D Division. Pentridge remained the main female prison until it was replaced by the new women's prison, HM Prison Fairlea in 1956. Pentridge was also the location of reformatories for both girls and boys, established following the findings of the Stawell Royal Commission of 1870. The Jika Reformatory for Boys was accommodated in an existing building (F Division), between 1875 and 1879, while a purpose built reformatory was constructed for the Jika Reformatory for Protestant Girls (G Division), which operated between 1875 and 1893. In 1900 labour yards for A Division were completed. During the 1950s these yards were later converted to a high security block which became known as H Division. In 1924 Pentridge replaced the Melbourne Gaol as the main remand and reception prison for the metropolitan area. The bodies of a number of prisoners executed at the Melbourne Gaol were exhumed and relocated to Pentridge, where they were reburied, possibly just east of D Division. Pentridge also became the venue for all subsequent hangings, until the last Victorian prisoner to suffer the death penalty, Ronald Ryan was executed in D Division in 1967. In April 1995 the Office of Corrections ordered that the six main towers at Pentridge be closed, since most of the high security prisoners from the gaol had been relocated to Barwon as part of the downgrading of Pentridge to a medium security prison. The prison was finally closed in 1996.

In honour of Captain Percy Cherry. Captain Percy Cherry was born in Drysdale on 4 June 1895 and lived in Drysdale until he was 7. In 1915 Captain Percy Cherry enlisted in the Australian Imperial Forces and was posted to the 26th Battalion. On 26 March 1917, Captain Percy Cherry's company was ordered to storm Lagnicourt and he quickly found himself in the lead when all officers became casualties. His conspicuous bravery in securing the village for Australian forces under fierce enemy fire won him the Victoria Cross. Captain Percy Cherry was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross and the Military Cross for valour on the same day for capturing two enemy machine-gun posts. Captain Percy Cherry was killed on 27 March 1917 during the German counterattacks.

Historical Information:
The Strathewen Cricket Club and the Strathewen Recreational Reserve Association suggested this newly built pavilion, located at the Strathewen Recreational Reserve, be named to honour the late community member Peter Avola.
Mr Ayala lived in Strathewen for 39 years before losing his life on the Strathewen oval during the Victorian bushfires in 2009. He helped to establish the reserve in the early 1980s and from then on gave his time, machinery and fuel to voluntarily maintain the oval and surrounding areas.
Mr Avola was a Life Member of the Strathewen Cricket Club and served on the club committee for over 20 years, including several years as president. Mr Avola was also a member of Strathewen Landcare Group since it was formed in 1992 and supported the development of the first Catchment Management Plan in 1994.
Peter was an active member of the Arthurs Creek & Strathewen CFA for over 20 years from the mid-1970s. As well as taking up his position on the brigade roster, he gave his own time to do brigade demonstrations and information events with junior brigade members.
Mr Avola showed dedication and passion for his community. He generously gave his time and efforts to set up and maintain the recreation reserve and cricket club at Strathewen. Naming the pavilion in his honour would serve as a valuable reminder of Mr Avola's significant contribution to the Strathewen community.

A submission was received by the Nillumbik Shire Council on 6 June 2011 from the Strathewen Recreation Reserve Association and the Strathewen Cricket Club requesting that the newly built Strathewen Pavilion, located at the Strathewen Recreation Reserve be formally named the Peter Avola Memorial Pavilion.

Peter Avola lived in Strathewen for 39 years and perished in the Victorian Bushfires of 2009 at the Recreation Reserve. Peter was heavily involved with getting the reserve set up in the early 1980's and, from then on, Peter took on the job of maintaining the oval and surrounding areas. He did this on a voluntary basis for nearly 30 years using his own time, machinery and fuel.

Council, at its 27 March 2012 meeting, resolved that it approve the naming of the Strathewen Pavilion as the Peter Avola Memorial Pavilion.

Following approval of the name by the Registrar of Geographic Names, notice of the registration of the name was published in the Victoria Government Gazette on 17 May 2012 with a subsequent Notice of Corrigendum published on 24 May 2012.

Historical Information:
The Reserve and immediate surrounding land is the site of the former Phoenix Wool Scouring Works established in 1919. The Phoenix Wool Scouring Works played a significant role in the development of the woollen industry within Geelong and was the first business in Victoria to make a separate industry of this kind of work. In more recent times the land has been associated with use as a quarry, a landfill site and been disused until 2011. In June 2011 the site was landscaped and revegetated using native species into a treed area that now provides a new community space, new habitat for native fauna and is acting as a carbon sink. It also creates an additional habitat and recreational linkage from the Barwon
River to Balyang Sanctuary.

Historical Information: (Alternative history)  Reputedly named during a storm, from Hindu words for 'wind' and 'blower'.  Previously known as Ovens Crossing.  [Note that Thomas O'Callaghan, Names of Victorian Railway Stations, 1918, p.78 recognises two possible origins of the name.]
Author: Blake, Les
Title: Place Names of Victoria

Historical Information:
According to O'Callaghan (1918: 78) 'there are two accounts given as to the origin or derivation of this name. First:-An Indian officer who was with a party of "diggers", called the place Porepunkah - "pore" and "punkah" being two Hindoo words signifying respectively, "wind" and "blower". The name was given during a storm. Second:-Derived from a native name of somewhat similar pronunciation, signifying, "meeting of the waters", and having reference to the junction of the Buckland and the Ovens rivers'. O'Callaghan's source was Edward John Delany, Secretary of the Shire of Bright. Martin (1944), Blake (1977), and Gardner (1991) have accepted the Hindu explanation and Massola (1968) the Aboriginal explanation. The goldfield origin explanation may be suspect as the station name 'Portpunka' or 'Port Punka' (Billis and Kenyon 1974) or 'Point Punkah' (Lloyd and Nunn 1987: 7) was used from 1846, at least five years before gold digging commenced. Gardner notes that the run was taken up by William Walker and Co. in 1846; Walker was a banker and trader who spent much of his life in Calcutta. Indian coolies were imported in 1846 by Captain Robert Towns to work on Walker's stations and almost certainly worked here. The name is derived from the Hindi words for wind and blower, literally the name of a primitive cooling fan and almost certainly referred to the cold wind off the mountains. Also called Port Punkah and Point Punkah. Massola incorrectly has this as being of Aboriginal origins. (Gardner 1991: 17f)

Carol Sonogan (2011) suggests that Port Punkah may be derived from the Hindi term 'punka walla' which referred to a slave boy fanning a large rug to create a small breeze, or punka'. She postulates that given that the Port Punkah freehold provided the river-crossing place for a number of adjacent runs, the name may reflect its water association as well as the Indian connection. However, she believes it is more likely an 'attempt to assign personal meaning to the foreign sounds of an already-existing Indigenous name'. Sonogan (2011: 3) suggests a possible literal translation of Porepunkah is puwa pungga, head+stone, with an underlying meaning of 'man's head'.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: First known as Liardet's Beach after Wilbraham Frederick Evelyn Liardet settled there in 1839 and built the first jetty and established postal and ferry services to Melbourne. Lieutenant-Governor La Trobe later named it Sandridge to reflect the ridge of sand dunes along the foreshore. After the first land sales in 1850, Sandridge grew in importance as a port and was the terminus for Australia's first passenger railway, which opened on September 12, 1854. After some agitation, it broke away from the Melbourne City Council to become a municipal district in 1860. It became a borough in 1863, changed its name to Port Melbourne in 1884 and became a town in 1893 and a city on May 14, 1919.
Author: Jamie First
Page Title: The A-Z story of Melbourne's suburbs

Historical Information: The name is descriptive of role of the place, the port for Melbourne.  It was earlier known as Liardet's Beach after W.F.E. Liardet who settled there in 1839.  Lieutenant-Governor La Trobe later named it 'Sandridge' (descriptive of the beach frontage, which was an irregular ridge of sand).  'Port Melbourne' was adopted for the new borough in 1860.  See also Thomas O'Callaghan, Names of Victorian Railway Stations, 1918, p.79.

Historical Information: Name change was requested by the local school community after the Graham Street Primary School had become the only primary school in the Port Melbourne area.

The name was proposed in 2003 by the Mildura Rural City Council for an area then known as Mildura Wharf.  'Port of Mildura' was also a name in use  before Federation.  The proposal was referred to a Geographic Place Names Advisory Committee for approval following clarification of boundaries and liaison with NSW.

Port Phillip Bay was originally named Port King in honour of Governor King. Governor King later changed it to Port Phillip in honour of the first Governor of New South Wales. Prior to 1851 and the establishment of the colony of Victoria, the general area south of the Murray River was called the Port Phillip District of New South Wales. To clearly distinguish between the District and the Bay in general usage, one was called Port Phillip District and the other Port Phillip Bay. The name Port Phillip Bay has remained in general usage ever since. In 1970, the Hydrographer of the Royal Australian Navy suggested that the word Bay be deleted from the name Port Phillip Bay. The Place Names Committee contacted all the municipalities around the Bay and other interested bodies for their views. Historical Information:
In 1864, it appears Prahran Council purchased land west of Izett Street fronting Greville Street, allegedly for use as a market site, although this intention was never officially documented. Nothing further was done with the land until 1867, by which time the councils at St Kilda and South Melbourne had already set up local markets. A Market Committee of ratepayers and Councillors was convened to resolve the public debate about the best location for a market. People who argued that the Greville Street site was relatively remote and inaccessible, wanted a street market on Commercial Road between Chapel Street and the railway bridge to the west. Accusations of vested interests added heat to the debate. In mid-1867, Councillors spoke to market gardeners at Malvern, East Brighton, Cheltenham and Oakleigh to elicit support for the proposed market. The Market Committee recommended running the market in Greville Street in order to test public support for that location. The first market was held on Saturday 13 July 1867, and scheduled thereafter for Wednesdays and Saturdays between the hours of dawn and noon. The site controversy continued, so in January 1868 Council held a
referendum asking ratepayers if they wanted a market at all, and if so, to choose between the two sites.Only 480 people voted, with a majority voting for Greville Street. Greville Street was declared the permanent site for the market, a public weighbridge was installed and the animal pound moved to the other side of Grattan Street.
The open-air market continued to operate until 1881, when it was moved to the north of Commercial Road, close to its present site.
By 1890, the demand for stalls was greater than supply. Tenders for the erection of a building and an extension of stalls were invited in March 1890. The building works were carried out at a cost of about Ã¿Â£2,000. The new Prahran Market, designed by architect Charles A. D'Ebro, was opened in 1891.
The Market was extended in 1923 at a cost of Ã¿Â£80,000. Customers recall that it was cold in winter and hot in summer. Cart horses waited all day in the stables provided by the Council and their smells added to the odours of old fruit, vegetables, meat and poultry. It was not until the late 1920s that sufficient refrigeration was available for perishables. The old meat arcade, located on the eastern side of the Market was very primitive, with sawdust on the floors. The Salvation Army made a regular practice of marching down the Market aisles and regular Friday night concerts were held on the balcony above the Commercial Road shops.

Historical Information: The Prahran Crache is historically significant for its association with the nascent infant welfare movement in the late nineteenth and early to mid-twentieth centuries. It was an innovative response to the needs of working women and their children. The establishment and operation of the creche by middle and upper class women illustrates the philanthropic thinking of the time with regard to working class women and their children. The Prahran Crache was the second to be opened in metropolitan Melbourne, the first in the City of Stonnington, and the first in metropolitan Melbourne to have purpose-built premises. It has been operating in the same location since 1890. The 1913 building itself is architecturally significant as the first purpose-built crache or day nursery constructed in metropolitan Melbourne. The Prahran Crache is representative of an early twentieth century welfare institution. Its architectural form, with simple lines and domestic-type finishes and detailing which give a homely character to an institutional building meant to serve young children. Historically for its associations with the two honourary architects: Ernest H Willis and William Calder. Willis was a Prahran local, who designed a number of local landmark buildings, including the Prahran Club, Prahran Mechanics' Institute, Fawkner Mansions - early flats, and the Prahran Creche. He was also very involved in local political and community organisations. He was a member of the Prahran City Council 1908-20, serving as Mayor in 1913-14 and 1918-19. William Calder was the Prahran Council engineer and building surveyor from 1897 to 1913. He is best known in his role as chairman of the Country Roads Board, following his time at Prahran. The Calder Highway is named after him. The Prahran Crache is of social significance for its continuous use as a local centre for child care and welfare since 1890 in this location and since 1913 in the present building. Countless local residents have entrusted their children to this crÃ¿Â¨che, or been cared in it themselves, leading to high recognition of the facility to the local community.

Historical Information: In the Wake of the Pack Tracks suggests Pakenham is named after Major General Sir Edward Michael Pakenham (b.1788) who served with the Duke of Wellington in the Peninsula War and was killed in 1815 at the Battle of New Orleans. Blake, however, suggests that Pakenham was named for "General Pakenham who served in the Crimean War". This is probably Lieutenant- Colonel Edward William Pakenham (1819-1854) who was killed at Inkermann during the Crimean War. The Lieutenant-Colonel was the son of Sir Hercules Pakenham who was the brother of Major General Sir Edward Michael Pakenham. There are two other suggested sources for the name. Firstly, that   it was named for Catherine Pakenham, who was the wife of the Duke of Wellington. Secondly that it was named for "Rev Pakenham of Dublin". This is most likely the Very Reverend Henry Pakenham, who was Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin from 1843-1864. Catherine and Henry were siblings of Sir Edward and Sir Hercules. Their father was the second Baron Longford. Blake also suggests that the area was once called Longford. Pakenham was originally based around the Princes Highway and Toomuc Creek and the town that developed around the Railway Station from 1877 was known as Pakenham East. It was still referred to as Pakenham East well into the 1960s.

Historical Information: Named after 'Pearl' Iris Potts (nee Snell). Pearl came to Sunbury around 1938 and worked as a nurse at the then Sunbury Mental Asylum, locally known as The Hill. Pearl met and married Robert (Bob) Potts in 1939 and raised 8 children. She was an active member of the Sunbury Community being involved in the Parents Association of Our Lady of Mount Carmel School, the Co-operators of Rupertswood and a volunteer at the St Vincent de Paul Society. As a resident of Sunbury for almost 70 years, Pearl contributed to the wellbeing of many through her involvement with the support organisations and was a valued and respected member of the Sunbury Community.

Mount Pendergast cairn is built of unmortared stone. It is approximately 2m high by 2m in diameter. In 1960 it retained a centre pole with disks set into the stone cairn. A short distance away was a geodetic plaque set on a rock. The last inspection on 1997 revealed that the remains of the old beacon poles and metal vanes were now lying on the ground. During this inspection the cairn was dismantled to look for the ground mark, but it was not able to be located. Assumed to be associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The date of construction of the Mt Pendergast cairn is not known. Pendergast Lookout, a geodetic triangulation station cairn, is of local interest as
an example of the drystone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of five examples remaining in the alpine area of eastern Gippsland. The cairn has been completely rebuilt.
