Historical Information: Pleasant trig is an unmortared stone cairn approximately 1.5m high by 2m diameter with a timber centre pole. Comparing the recent photograph to the 1960 sketch of a conical cairn 2.4m, it appears that the top section of the cairn has collapsed or been removed. A geodetic plaque is located nearby, mortared onto the top of a rock several metres to the south of the cairn. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). The date of construction of the Pleasant cairn is not known.  Pleasant cairn geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of five examples remaining in the alpine area of eastern Gippsland. While the top section of the cairn has collapsed or been removed, it retains an old timber centre pole, and is more intact than three other surviving East Gippsland examples - Howe Hill, Mt Gibbo and Mt Pendergast.

Historical Information: Portland Bay was named by Lieutenant James Grant during exploration of Bass Strait in 1802. Grant's mapping of the coastline was approximate, scarcely showing the indent where Portland is situated, omitting much of the coast to the east, and picking it up near Cape Otway. That whole stretch was named Portland Bay, as a compliment to the Duke of Portland, English Prime Minister (1793) and Home Secretary (1794-1801). The French explorer Nicholas Baudin, explored the coast in 1802 and charted it more accurately. Unaware of Grant's visit, Baudin named the bay Tourville. Despite his superior mapping, the name Portland persisted.

A bridge was first built at this location in 1860. These early thoroughfares, and in particular river crossings contributed greatly in forming the shape of the city. Historical Information:
Ralph Goode enlisted on 16 August 1914, the first man from Lilydale to do so. He was allotted to the 2nd Field Ambulance to serve as a stretcher bearer and he travelled on the SS Wiltshire in the first convoy to Egypt. He was stationed there until he moved to Lemnos Island and then was at the landing at Gallipoli. He saw service at Anzac Cove and Cape Helles and was there at the Battle of Lone Pine. He was Mentioned in Despatches for his work here. After the evacuation, he was sent back to Egypt where his unit was re-organised and then moved to France.
Between 1916 and 1918 he served on the Western Front, experiencing all the horrors and heroism of those campaigns. He was a veteran of Pozieres, Bullecourt, Passchendaele, Ypres and Delville Wood. In 1918 he returned home to Lilydale, married, had a family and took up a business running a drapers store in Lilydale's Main Street. He also did community work and achieved an extraordinary amount for that township. His family believed his way of coping with what he saw during the war years was to keep himself busy with community work. He was awarded the MBE for his efforts for that community. He died in 1961.
Author: Anthony McAleer
Title: A Stretcher Bearer's War: the story of Ralph Goode MBE

Historical Information:
In the 17th century, the first Earl of Ranelagh built Ranelagh House just outside of London and in
1741 the Ranelagh Gardens were opened to the public. Ranelagh became a fashionable holiday resort and was the model for the development of the Mount Eliza Ranelagh in 1924. A number of Mount Eliza Ranelagh streets were named after London places. More specifically, the Mount Eliza Ranelagh was promoted as an area where people could build their holiday homes with recreational facilities, parks and internal reserves and a community focus. This approach was given full expression by Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Griffin who, consistent with their environmental and philosophical ideals, produced the 1924 plan.

The Estate's historical significance has associations with Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, leading figures in 20th century architectural and planning history and Saxil Tuxen who was an important town planning figure in Melbourne;

(610 m alt.), 3.7 km south-east of Caveat. A popular place for picnics in the 1920s; but the "eccentric old Aborigine who was said to have lived there" (Jones & Jones) is probably a myth. "Rantin, rovin Robin" occurs in the chorus of Robert Burns's song "There Was a Lad" [Elaine White] and reflects Scottish settlement in the area. The word rant in Scots implies happy celebration - quite different from its meaning in English.

Historical Information:
Following discussions with a Registered Planner it was determined that the name Rawbottom Gully Registered as a watercourse in the Register of Geographic Names is not appropriate. Upon reviewing the Map Source provided, along with the Place Names Committee (PNC) file index, the sources listed do not display the name Rawbottom Gully. The watercourse on a number of maps is unnamed.

Additional research undertaken by the Registered Planner, OGN and a local historical society found no reason why the name should exist in its current location. Research also found an alternative name, that being Rowbottom Gully, possible located further to the west. All correspondence and attachments have been printed and added to OGN file FOL/14/62172.  The original record was supposedly taken from a paper map in 1966. The date corresponds with other records which the PNC added to a register in 1966.

Based on the research and conversations between the Registered Planner, OGN and the Registrar of Geographic Names the record was un-linked from the Vicmap extent and the feature type was changed to Historic Site.
It was initially named Robertson after Alan Robertson, former Chief Engineer of the Board of Works. But, after local pressure, the name was changed to Rawson, honouring a pioneer family of the area.
Author: Victorian Places

The reserve was named Big Log Reserve in 1974 in recognition of the large log that was placed there as part of the Gembrook Centenary celebrations. It is renamed Remembrance Park to reflect the importance and significance of the memorial, particularly considering that the 100th Anniversary of the landing at Gallipoli will take place in April 2015.

Historical Information:
Richard (Dick) George Moss was a Councillor of the former City of Malvern (East Ward) from 1940 to 1963 and Mayor in 1946-47. For the majority of his period as a Councillor he was also Chairman of the Finance Committee. He was also a member of the Malvern Library Committee since its inception. Cr Moss died in office in 1963 prior to the opening of the Chadstone Library on 20 May 1964. 
Cr Moss had a distinguished war record from the First World War, being awarded a Military Cross for bravery in action in France. On his return he was a Lt. Col. in command of the 37th/152nd Battalion in the militia stationed at Caulfield. On the outbreak of WWII he was appointed to command camps at Balcombe, Watsonia and Royal Park. 
Apart from his Council duties he took a great interest in Legacy and was a member, past president and committee member of the East Malvern RSL, and was actively engaged in welfare work. 
On the professional side he was in the Victorian Police Force prior to WWI. On his return after the war he had a timber mill at Noojee then later returned to Melbourne and formed the Noojee Slipper Co Pty Ltd at Abbotsford. Among his other interests he was a Director of Olympic Cables Ltd. 
On a personal side he was married and had three daughters and a son. At least one member of his family still resides in Stonnington.

William and Helen Richards were two of the earliest settlers in Montrose, having selected Crown land near the location of the present reserve in Swansea Road in 1878, where they established an extensive orchard. One of their daughters, Jessie lived on the property until her death in 1964.

Kulin name: Quo-yung. Meaning: dead trees.

This name was recorded by A. W. Howitt, anthropologist, from conversations from sometime between 1897 and 1901 with William Barak, ngurungaeta (leader) of the Wurundjeri-willam, the traditional owners of what is now northern Melbourne, and Dick Richards, Barak's fellow Kulin countryman. The Kulin was an alliance of Aboriginal nations in central Victoria. Howitt jotted down Aboriginal names, mostly in the Woiwurrung language once spoken in the Melbourne area, corresponding to landmarks and municipalities that arose in Melbourne town during Barak's lifetime (c.1824 to 1903).

Barry Blake has noted that Kalatha resembles the Woiworung galada (or kalata), river, creek, and there was probably an identical or similar word in Taungurong. Kalatha also sounds like the Greek kalathos (???a???), Latin calathus, a basket, bowl, wine cup or the cup of a flower. Clem Earp has observed that early issues of the Yea Chronicle consistently printed this as Kalathea Creek, and this could certainly be Greek: kale thea (?a?? ??a), beautiful seat, view or lookout, except for the possibility of confusion with the Galatea Reef at Higinbotham! Historical Information: Robinvale was originally named Bumbang, the local Aboriginal word for the island in the Murray River. It was officially named Robinvale in August, 1924 after Lieutenant George Robin Cuttle, a local boy who joined the British (he had been rejected by Australian forces), fought in France and was killed, aged only 22, over the Somme in 1918. The name means "Farewell Robin".

Historical Information: The site of Robinvale was reserved for an agricultural college in the 1880s, but nothing was done because of the area's remoteness from transport and reliable water. The land was leased for farming in 1902, and the lease was transferred to Herbert Cuttle in 1911, a storekeeper at Ultima. Cuttle's son managed the property until enlisting in World War I. Cuttle purchased one square mile for a township, and in 1924 the railway line was extended from Annuello to Cuttle's private township. The name was given by Cuttle as a memorial to his son George Robin Cuttle, killed at Villers-Bretonneux while flying for the RAF. Robinvale formed a twin city relationship with Villers-Bretonneux in 1984.

Historical Information:
The locality is named after Capel Sound which is situated a short distance off the shore.

The historical entry for 'Capel Sound' reads as follows:

HMS Rattlesnake conveyed Capt William Lonsdale from Port Jackson to Port Phillip, arriving on 27 September, 1836. Taking advantage of the period required establishing a residence in the settlement for the Lonsdale family, Capt Hobson and his officers were able to survey the navigable areas of Port Phillip. In November, 1836 the ship anchored off Arthur's Seat to enable surveys to be made of that part of the coastline. It was during this time that Mount Martha and Mount Eliza were named by one of the lieutenants of the Rattlesnake, in compliment to Mrs.Lonsdale and Mrs. Batman, respectively. Although there is no available documentary proof to say that Capel Sound was named at this time, it was on the chart that was produced as a result of this survey that the name "Capel's/Capels Sound" first appeared. The Commander-in-chief of the East Indies Squadron of the British Navy was Rear Admiral Sir Thomas Bladen Capel, and it was him who sent the Rattlesnake to convey Capt Lonsdale to Melbourne. The following year, in 1837, HMS Victor named "Capel's Sound" in Victor Harbour, South Australia, after their Commanding Officer, Sir Thomas Capel. It is reasonable to conclude that Capel Sound in Port Phillip was named after Sir Thomas Capel, by the surveyors on board HMS Rattlesnake, in 1836.

Capel Sound was first named in 1836 during the survey of the Bay by HMS Rattlesnake. At that time the Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Navy's Far East Squadron was Admiral Sir Thomas Bladen Capel. Capel was an officer in the British Royal Navy whose distinguished service in the French Revolutionary War, the Napoleonic Wars and the War of 1812 earned him rapid promotion and great acclaim both in and out of the Navy. He was also a great friend of Admiral Horatio Nelson. On the 1836 survey it was shown as 'Capel's Sound' and on later charts as 'Capells Sound' and 'Capell's Sound'. By the 1860s it had stabilised in its current form of 'Capel Sound'.

Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: Rises near Lake Mountain and the Federation Range; flows into the Rubicon River at Rubicon; the confluence is called The Forks. Sometimes (as late as 1905) called the Left Branch (of the Rubicon River). The Royston was named much later than the Rubicon River, and Leonie Taylor has suggested that the Royston may have been named by the State Electricity Commission, which could well be the case, perhaps after an employee or Brigadier John Robinson Royston (1860 - 1942), a South African who led Australian troops in the Boer War and the First World War (ADB 11). John Stewart Royston was killed in a mining accident at Alexandra on 18 August 1904 [Alan Walker], but there is as yet no evidence clearly linking his name with that of the river.The name seems ultimately derived from Royston, Hertfordshire, known as Crux Roaisi[a]e (1184), Crux Roheis (1209), Croyroys (1262) and then Reyston (1280). It looks as if Roey, Roese, Rohesia or Royse's cross became her stone (or possibly town), as stone crosses on stone plinths were a common feature of mediaeval England. There is another Royston in North Yorkshire, with a quite different etymology, but it is a less likely source for the Victorian name.

A few fruit trees and a golden rain tree (Koelreuteria paniculata) just below the confluence of the Royston and Rubicon Rivers, at the junction of Royston (River) Road and Herbs Road, are the remains of Tin Hut, a tramway terminus and timber-milling settlement for which a church, public hall and other buildings were planned. It was named after a shelter shed, with a galvanised iron roof, built for tourists ca. 1900 (photo: Evans). The locality is now known as Rubicon, after the river. It was also the site of the Rubicon Junction State School, opened 1928, but relocated in 1935 to a site between Lower Rubicon and Rubicon "A". For the Rubicon State School, see Ruoak No. 1 Mill settlement. See also Lower Rubicon and other Rubicon entries.

Historical Information: (at first probably Rubicon Creek). Rises from the Blue Range; flows into the Goulburn River west of Thornton. Appears on Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847), and is listed by Wells (1848). Latin: Rubico, a reddish river (ruber, rubicundus, red, ruddy) in central Italy, perhaps the modern Fiumicino or Pisciatello, at the border of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy. (Italy, to the Romans, meant a smaller area than it does today.) By crossing the Rubicon in 49 b.c.e., Julius Caesar effectively declared war on the Roman Republic, hence the expression "crossed the Rubicon", meaning "made an irrevocable decision", or "began a hazardous enterprise". If Les Blake is correct about Ouseley Cockburn and Dr. Dougald Fletcher naming (or renaming) the Acheron River in about 1839, then they may well have named the Rubicon also. Other people who might have done so are John Christie Aitken (first licensee, 1840, of the Rubicon Creek pastoral run) or his neighbour Dr. James Dickson (Eildon run from 1838). William Leyden Ker, who liked classical names, probably arrived in the area too late (1848). See also Little Rubicon River.

The words 'rush' and worth' caught the fancy of the diggers, and the compound word, 'Rushworth,' was adopted.'

Historical Information: In September, 1860 gold was found near Rutherglen. A town named Barkly appeared overnight as prospectors poured into the area. Shortly afterwards another site was discovered 500 metres to the east. In October this second site was named Rutherglen after the Scottish birthplace of John Wallace, who established the Star Hotel on the new town site. It is claimed that Wallace, as the publican of the Star Hotel, was told "Shout the whole bar and you can call this town whatever you like." So he bought a beer for everyone in the pub and called the town Rutherglen.

Historical Information:
William Ruthven (1893-1970), soldier and politician, was born on 21 May 1893 at Collingwood, Melbourne, son of Peter Ruthven, carpenter, and his wife Catherine Charlotte, nÃ¿Â©e Bedwell, both Victorian born. He was educated at the Vere Street State School, Collingwood, and became a mechanical engineer.

Ruthven was employed in the timber industry when he enlisted as a private in the Australian Imperial Force on 16 April 1915. He left Australia in August with reinforcements for the 22nd Battalion which he joined in October on Gallipoli. Late in March 1916 the 22nd went to France. On 17 April, during his first tour of duty in the forward area near Fleurbaix, Ruthven was wounded. He rejoined his battalion in August on the Somme and was promoted lance corporal. On 26 January 1917 he was confirmed in the rank of sergeant.

On 19 May 1918 Ruthven took part in an attack near Ville-sur-Ancre. When his company commander was wounded, Ruthven assumed command but soon the advance was held up by heavy machine-gun fire. Unhesitating, he ran at the machine-gun post, bombed it, bayoneted one of the crew and captured the gun. Then, encountering enemy coming out of a shelter, he wounded two and captured six. Having reorganized his men and formed a post, he noticed further enemy movement in a nearby sunken road. Armed only with a revolver, he shot two men and captured thirty-two. He spent the rest of the day, under fire, supervising consolidation and encouraging his men. He was awarded the Victoria Cross.

On 11 June near MÃ¿Â©ricourt Ruthven was wounded again, and on 1 July was commissioned second lieutenant. He returned to Australia in October with several other Victoria Cross winners to assist recruiting and received a hero's welcome in Melbourne. He was promoted lieutenant and on 11 December his A.I.F. appointment ended.

Ruthven resumed work as a wood machinist and on 20 December 1919 married Irene May White at St Philip's Anglican Church, Abbotsford; they had a daughter and a son. In the mid-1920s the family moved to a soldier-settlement block at Werrimull. Bad seasons and poor health forced Ruthven back to Collingwood in 1931. He became a carrier and later worked with the State Rivers and Water Supply Commission. He was elected to the Collingwood Council and became mayor in 1945.

During World War II, from December 1941 Ruthven served with the 3rd Australian Garrison Battalion and other garrison units, including those centred at Murchison, Victoria's largest prisoner-of-war camp. In August 1944 he ceased full-time duty, as major. He sat in the Victorian Legislative Assembly during 1945-55 as the Labor member for Preston, then following a redistribution represented Reservoir until his retirement in 1961.

'Rusty' Ruthven retained close links with other Victoria Cross winners and the Returned Sailors' and Soldiers' Imperial League of Australia. In 1932 he was one of the pallbearers at Albert Jacka's funeral and he attended the 1956 Victoria Cross centenary celebrations in London. He was president of the Werrimull and Collingwood R.S.S.I.L.A. sub-branches, a life member of the Preston sub-branch and a trustee of Melbourne's Shrine of Remembrance and the St Kilda Memorial Hall. Ruthven was also official timekeeper for the Collingwood Football Club and a foundation member of its social club. The war, however, had severely affected his health; illness forced his retirement from politics.

Survived by his wife and children, he died on 12 January 1970 in Heidelberg Repatriation Hospital and was cremated with military honours.

The School closed in September 1951 and the children went to Pakenham Consolidated School. Rythdale is a coined name and doesn't have any particular meaning. Duncan McGregor was the owner of the 1618 hectare (4000 acre) estate Dalmore, part of which formed the Soldier Settlement subdivision.

Historical Information: Osborne Young built the original Young's hut at the old yards, which are up the hill from this site c1883. During this time he held the BUNDARMUNGIE (County of Bogong) run. where he ran cattle and horses on the High Plains. He was known to have mustered 1500 whalers (horses) in one season  (Carroll) Replacing the cattleman's hut, this Young's Hut was reputedly one of two built in 1928 for the SEC's early hydrological and meteorological survey of the Bogong High Plains (Lawrence (1993): 13f). The hut's components were thought to have been packed in from Mt.Hotham. However, the 1948  Department of Lands & Survey Feature Map of the area shows this hut south of Young's for the first time but the 1945 Kiewa Scheme Locality Plan and a 1933 tourist map do not show it. Rather than being built in the 1920s, this hut appears to have been erected on this site c1945. Peter McNamara, son of Charlie McNamara, confirms that the hut was erected in the 1940s (Carroll).

Historical Information: 'This place was originally known as 'The Sailor's Fall.'  In the early 'digging' days a runaway sailor was pursued by the police, and in eagerness to escape he endeavoured to pass down one of the steep walls of the gorge.  He fell to the bottom, and it was feared that he had been killed.  He was, however, only badly bruised and made good his escape.  In course of time the name was applied to the waterfall in the same gorge.'

Historical Information: The origin of St Arnaud's was the discovery of gold at a sandy knoll later called Bakery Hill, St Arnaud north, in January 1855. The resulting goldfield was known as New Bendigo, and mining spread into several hills and gullies. In 1856 a town was surveyed about 6 km east of the goldfield. It was named St Arnaud, after a French military commander in the Crimean War. Because of the town's distance from the goldfield the survey was cancelled and a township developed around the mining activity. The community readily adopted the proposed name, and sales of township lots occurred in 1858.

Historical Information: The origin of St Arnaud's was the discovery of gold at a sandy knoll later called Bakery Hill, St Arnaud north, in January 1855. The resulting goldfield was known as New Bendigo, and mining spread into several hills and gullies. In 1856 a town was surveyed about 6 km east of the goldfield. It was named St Arnaud, after a French military commander in the Crimean War. Because of the town's distance from the goldfield the survey was cancelled and a township developed around the mining activity. The community readily adopted the proposed name, and sales of township lots occurred in 1858.

Historical Information: It is named after a church built by Major Anthony Beale, who arrived in Port Phillip in 1839. His wife, the daughter of a Governor of St Helena, predeceased him in 1856, and he built the Rose Chapel in her memory.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner

Historical Information: One of the legacies of the extension of philanthropic activity in Fitzroy during the 1890s was St Vincent's Hospital, which was established in order to dispense aid during the Depression of the 1890s. St Vincent's provided a contrast to some of the other church-based charities operating in Fitzroy and the City of Melbourne at this time, since the institution was considered to be less discerning than many about the morals or respectability of those whom it chose to help. One writer remarked in 1905 that: 'there are charity organisations for assisting respectable people who are victims of misfortunes mourning by the current of adversity. But if one is to grade the various schemes for assisting distressed humanity, the premier position must undoubtedly be accorded to that noble institution, conducted by the Sisters of Charity, and known wherever established by them as St Vincent's Hospital.' St Vincent's was opened on 6 November 1893 by Janet, Lady Clarke. Despite fears that the hospital would not survive the depressed 1890s, the writer went on to point out that 'subsequent events have proved that the sisters were right when they realised that there was no such word as fail.' In 1905, it was reported that, 'the word success is branded on their efforts until now they find it necessary to complete the colossal establishment.'
Name adopted in 2002 for refurbished tram stop. Name refers to the nearby well known hospital.

Historical Information: 'The name was given to the lake because of its unusual depth amongst Mallee lakes.  Tradition relates that a 'Dago bullocky,' riding in search of his team came upon this strange sheet of water, and expecting it to be, as usual in such swamps, a foot or so in depth, he boldly urged his horse across it.  A few steps, and the water was up to the saddle flaps, for the lake, though of the smallest, is 13 feet deep.  Out he scrambled in great alarm and rode back to camp crying out he had found a lake deep as the sea - a Sea Lake.'
Author: O'Callaghan, Thos

Historical Information: The flat coastal plain was taken up by P.C. Buckley as the Coadyvale pastoral run in 1848. The homestead, named Prospect, overlooked the present town site. By the 1860s Sale residents were visiting the beach, which became known as Buckley's Beach. A reserve of 51 acres was set aside during the 1870s and known as Ninety Mile Beach Reserve. With an increase in size the area became known as Prospect Reserve. In 1915, the growing settlement was renamed Seaspray, the only suggestion put forward.

Historical Information: 'Settlers Square' notes the historical and contemporary interpretations of this name that relates to Dandenong's early pioneering history and recent migration.

River system and former pastoral run. Appears to be called Templeton's Creek in Thomas Ham's Map of Australia Felix (1847), presumably after James Templeton, licensee (1838-43) of the pastoral run. Wells's entry (1848) for Templeton's Creek provides additional corroboration. Seven Creeks is the principal drainage system for much of the Strathbogie Ranges. It rises south of Too-rour (west of Bonnie Doon Road), flows through Euroa and joins the Goulburn River south of Mooroopna*. Sections of the river provide a breeding habitat for the endangered trout cod (Macculochella macquariensis). Halsall (1980, 1: 48) mentions about three explanations for the name, none of them convincing. Seven Creeks is supposed to refer to Main Creek (another name for the trunk channel) and six other tributaries, though there are in fact more. Tributaries upstream of Euroa include Bald Hill Creek, Coach Road Creek, Hatchells Creek, Mountain Hut Creek, Sheans Creek, Shingle Hut Creek, two with the same name of Spring Creek (2 & 3), Station Creek (2), Surveyors Creek, Watchbox Creek and Wombat Creek (2). Magiltans Creek is an indirect tributary. The principal tributary downstream of Euroa is Faithfulls Creek. The Seven Creeks pastoral run (28,000 ha,  1838-80) was licensed (1851-67) to William Forlonge (1811-90), whose grazing empire at its height amounted to 932,000 ha (9,320 sq. km) of land in Victoria and New South Wales (see also Forlonge Memorial and Cropper's). For Seven Creeks State School see also Gooram Gooram Gong.

Historical Information:
This reserve is named in honour of two of Dromana's pioneering families: the Shaw family and the McKeown family.

The Shaw family (Benjamin and Elizabeth) arrived in Dromana in 1875 and established Kangerong Guest House. Their son Archibald Shaw married Maud McKeown, daughter of James and Catherine McKeown, and started the family connection. Archibald was elected President of the Flinders Shire Council in 1924. Archibald and Maud raised and educated five children in Dromana (Maurice, Ernest, Archibald, Elizabeth and John). Maurice was the long-term proprietor of the Shell Service Station in Dromana and Shaw's Motors on Nepean Highway for many years prior to his death in 1991 aged 87.

The McKeown family (James and Catherine) arrived in Dromana in 1864. James cut timber for the Dromana pier in 1874 and in 1889 bought Gracefield and land to the East, where they planted an apple orchard. That land covered the area on which the reserve is now located. From 1889 to 1891 they were caretakers at Heronswood and in 1892 the McKeowns built Aringa Guest House (Cnr of Clarendon and Foote Streets Dromana) which was managed by their daughters for over 70 years until after the Second World War. James and Catherine raised 12 children (five sons and seven daughters); one daughter, Edith, the source for the naming of Edith Place, died in Dromana in 1987 aged 100. Two further generations of the Shaw and McKeown families have since lived in Dromana.

The surrounding land and the land on which the reserve is located was subdivided by the descendants of the pioneering Shaws and McKeowns in 1977 and the reserve was transferred to the Shire of Flinders (and since Mornington Peninsula Shire) for use as public open space.
Author: McLear, Colin
Title: A Dreamtime of Dromana

Historical Information: It commemorates the service and sacrifice of all Victorians who have served and died in wars since World War I (1914-18). It embodies the devastating impact of that war on the Australian nation, and Victoria in particular, which lost the largest proportion of its young men in the country. When the project was conceived, Melbourne was the capital of Australia and the seat of Federal Parliament and this resulted in the grandest war memorial in Australia, until the Australian War Memorial was built in Canberra in 1941. Since World War II (1939-45) numerous elements, including a commemorative forecourt, trees, statues and memorials, have been added to the Shrine Reserve to honour servicemen and women and peacekeepers from 1939 to the present day. As the largest and most important war memorial in Victoria, it reflects the community's ongoing need for a public expression of grief and of commemoration for the sacrifice of life in war.
Author: Heritage Council Victoria

Historical Information: Rises at Snobs Gap, crosses the Goulburn Valley Highway (where there is a small settlement and a fish research institute) and flows into the Goulburn River. Named after a West Indian journeyman bootmaker, "Black" Brooks, who worked by the crossing of the creek and the main road. A shoemaker's anvil was called a snob, and the term also became slang for a bootmaker. O'Rourke mentions a character in the area called Jack the Snob. Aboriginal (Taungurong) name allegedly Snodpondue. Also called Cataract, Cobbler's, Snod-poor-dook and Snoop-Poor-Doop Creek, and Niagara Creek and Falls, after the Niagara Falls and River in North America (Iroquois: Ongniaahra, the strait, at the - or across - the neck) but very likely derived from Niagaroon (q.v.) nearby. Ned Kelly and his gang are said to have camped at Snobs Creek while considering a raid on the Union Bank in Alexandra (O'Rourke), but they abandoned the enterprise. (There is another Snobs Creek* in the Yarra Ranges National Park.)
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Sutherland, vol. 2, p. 149, gives the meaning as 'white sea bird or curlew.'  J. F. H. Mitchell, p. 20, says it means 'swampy plains, resort of native companions''

Historical Information: Spotswood (Scottish Borders, spelt Spottiswoode). The spelling of the name of this suburb was originally 'Spottiswoode', as in Scotland, having been named after Captain George Spottiswoode but was changed to Spotswood to honour John Stewart Spotswood, a prominent pioneer. Lay (2003, p. 58) notes that from the late 1840s to the 1860s, John Spotswood operated a ferry across the Yarra River near today's West Gate Bridge. The Spotswood family achieved prominence when in 1868 a daughter, Louisa Jane, married Richard John Seddon, who later became Premier of New Zealand. (Lancashire-born Seddon was half English and half Scots according to an article in the Te Ara Encyclopaedia of New Zealand.)

Historical Information: The town came about as a result of a land development scheme. The Cosmopolitan Land and Banking Company acquired numerous lots in the form of an original farm subdivision in 1886, comprising 512 ha either side of the railway line between Sunshine and Sydenham. The land company's manager, Alfred Padley, made an arrangement with the Victorian Railways for assistance with the building of the railway station. Padley insisted that the station be named St Albans, apparently derived from his grandfather's forebears (on his mother's side) having an association with St Albans Abbey, Herefordshire, England, since the 1500s.

Historical Information: The origin of St Arnaud's was the discovery of gold at a sandy knoll later called Bakery Hill, St Arnaud north, in January 1855. The resulting goldfield was known as New Bendigo, and mining spread into several hills and gullies. In 1856 a town was surveyed about 6 km east of the goldfield. It was named St Arnaud, after a French military commander in the Crimean War. Because of the town's distance from the goldfield the survey was cancelled and a township developed around the mining activity. The community readily adopted the proposed name, and sales of township lots occurred in 1858.

Historical Information: Parish, south-eastern Big River catchment (east of Youarrabuk parish), including the upper reaches of Oaks, Springs and Frenchman's Creeks. Locality, Warburton Woods Point Road, at the junction with Thomson Jordan Divide Road; also called Sinclair's Valley. Named after John Sinclair's St. Clair Hotel (the surname Sinclair is derived from St. Clair place-names in France). Other hotels in Yarra Track days included the Spring Vale and the Nonpareil (originally called the "Willie We Have Miss'd You"). St. Clair was a small village from 1862 until the 1870s. The Jessop (or Jessop Phoschek) Airstrip, a fire-bombing base, is in the Thomson State Forest* nearby. See also The Springs.

Historical Information: It is named after a church built by Major Anthony Beale, who arrived in Port Phillip in 1839. Beale had been Paymaster-General on the island of St Helena for the British East India Company. He acquired land in the Greensborough area, naming it St Helena Park, which he farmed until his death in 1865. His wife, the daughter of a Governor of St Helena, predeceased him in 1856, and he built the Rose Chapel in her memory.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: St Kilda was proclaimed a municipal district in 1855, a borough in 1863 and a city in 1890. Initially called Fareham in 1842, the locality was officially named St Kilda by Lieutenant Governor Charles La Trobe after the small vessel Lady of St Kilda, which in turn was named after an island off Scotland.

Historical Information: One of the legacies of the extension of philanthropic activity in Fitzroy during the 1890s was St Vincent's Hospital, which was established in order to dispense aid during the Depression of the 1890s. St Vincent's provided a contrast to some of the other church-based charities operating in Fitzroy and the City of Melbourne at this time, since the institution was considered to be less discerning than many about the morals or respectability of those whom it chose to help. One writer remarked in 1905 that: 'there are charity organisations for assisting respectable people who are victims of misfortunes mourning by the current of adversity. But if one is to grade the various schemes for assisting distressed humanity, the premier position must undoubtedly be accorded to that noble institution, conducted by the Sisters of Charity, and known wherever established by them as St Vincent's Hospital.' St Vincent's was opened on 6 November 1893 by Janet, Lady Clarke. Despite fears that the hospital would not survive the depressed 1890s, the writer went on to point out that 'subsequent events have proved that the sisters were right when they realised that there was no such word as fail.' In 1905, it was reported that, 'the word success is branded on their efforts until now they find it necessary to complete the colossal establishment.'
Name adopted in 2002 for refurbished tram stop. Name refers to the nearby well known hospital.

Historical Information: Nicknamed after Mr Baker who owned the land for many years prior to the Second World War and after. During the early part of the war, the land was used as an Army training Camp where soldiers assembled from all over Victoria. In 1943, American soldiers from the Pacific region used the land as a recreation camp. Towards the end of the Second World War the site was used as a P.O.W camp including Italian prisoners. The nickname 'Starlight' originated because of Mr Baker's tendency to roam the land at night. He may have used his property for hunting because in those days it was virgin bushland and very isolated.
The name originated from the rather infamous nickname given to one of the original owners of the area. The origins of the nickname remain obscure.

Historical Information:
Named after Jack Strachan, landowners with family descendants for approx. 58 years and respected legal practitioner in the Warragul are for 22 years.
John (Jack) Strachan was born in Hamilton in 1900. He completed his education at Melbourne University and then moved to Bairnsdale in East Gippsland to establish a legal practice. He moved to Warragul in 1946 and established a legal practice trading under JT Strachan, operating out of a first floor office in the old G & N building at 3 Smith Street Warragul. In 1960-61 he acquired the legal practice of BJ Dunn following the death of Mr Dunn (this practice was established by BJ Dunn in Warragul around 1900) and then the legal practice traded under the name of Dunn & Strachan. At the age of 68 JT Strachan sold his legal practice to Barry Armitage and from 1968 the legal practice was then known as Dunn Strachan & Armitage. The practice was again sold in 1971 to Wayne Hardie and it then became known as Dunn Strachan & Hardie and it traded under this name until the late 1990's. When the Strachan's came to Warragul the purchased the property, on the corner of what is now known as Princes Highway and Tarwin Street, known as 'Coolabah' from Mr Louie Clark. They established a dairy farm and with the assistance of dairy farmers it operated as such until 2005 when the property was sold out of the Strachan Family. The Strachans established a Friesian cattle stud and were regarded as significant breeders of Friesian cattle amongst his peers.
Jack Strachan died in 1972 at the age of 72 and the farming business was kept going by his wife Mrs Strachan. Eventually, as the Strachans had no children, Mrs Strachan moved to Queensland during the 1980's to see out her days in the care of her niece Valda Mason. The property remained in the Strachan estate until 1999 when it was transferred to Valda Mason. She kept it running in its then current form until it was re-sold to its current owners Baw Baw Developments in 2004.

Historical Information: 'In 1968, following an enquiry from the Art Gallery of new South Wales, the Committee identified the 'Murchison Falls' and the 'Strath Falls' on the Queen Parrot Creek as being the ones depicted by the Melbourne artist, Eugen von Guerard, in 1862.  Later, in April, 1975, the Forests Commission suggested that the name 'Murchison Falls' be changed to 'Strath Creek Falls'; and that the name 'Strath Falls' be changed to either 'First falls' or 'Little Falls': it seems that a Miss J. E. lade, a resident of the area (her family having lived in the vicinity for about 100 years), is of the opinion that the Murchison falls should properly be called the 'Strath Creek Falls'.  Miss Lade contends that the name 'Murchison' is a misnomer, as the squatter Murchison took up land between Murchison Gap and Kerrisdale.'

Historical Information:
Sumision Gardens is named after Eric William Sumision (1903-1988). He was a garden curator for Wodonga Shire Council. He worked on the area voluntarily permitted by council  later became Sumision Garden. He bought a house on Church Street adjoint to the park so he has more time to work on the garden. 

The park originally came into being when Paul Huon established his Wodonga Run on the banks of Wodonga Creek in 1834, and recognised the need for land to be available to people moving into Wodonga to use until they found permanent accommodation. The area became Wodonga's first settlement because it was close to permanent water. The Lagoon, Lake Huon, Belvoir Lagoon, Sumsion Gardens are names over the time for the park.

Historical Information: When the railways junction was formed the place was named Braybrook Junction.At Ballarat the McKay Harvesting Machinery Company was successfully selling H.V. McKay's combined stripper-harvester to wheat farmers in Australia and overseas. The Ballarat location, however, incurred uncompetitive transport costs for fuel and components and the company moved its Sunshine Harvester Works to a seaboard location by purchasing the Braybrook Implement Works. McKay resisted control by industrial arbitration (resulting in the Harvester judgment, 1908) but promoted the provision of housing and facilities for his workers. The rapid growth of the company dominated Braybrook Junction and in 1907 it was named Sunshine.

Historical Information: The park is located in Surrey Road South Yarra (part of the former depot site). The Surrey Road Depot was purchased by the Prahran Council in 1888 when the tipping of rubbish was then into clay pit holes around the municipality. In 1907 the new modem method of waste disposal was introduced with the construction of the municipal destructor and even produced electricity to the grid. The destructor was finally replaced in 1965 however the incineration of refuse decreased with environmental considerations and was finally replaced with a machine that baled the refuse in one tonne bales. This method finally ceased and was closed in 2007 with waste transported to a shared facility in Clayton. The Stables at the rear of the depot originally housed fourteen horses which were replaced by motor vehicles by the 1950s. The stables are heritage listed and were retained on the site when it was re-developed after the depot closure. The Council depot was relocated from Surrey Road into the new Council Depot in Tooronga Road in 2008. Part of the old site was sold with the front section retained for a park.

Historical Information:
The Sydenham Community Hub, at 1/1 Station Street, Taylors Lakes, officially opened on 10 May 2013. It is co-located with the Sydenham Library which opened in 2006, as well as the Sydenham Neighbourhood House, the Sydenham Customer Service Centre and a maternal and child health centre.
Although the Sydenham Community Hub is located in the locality of Taylors Lakes, not Sydenham, it is in an area that has been known to the local community as Sydenham for many years, and is adjacent to Sydenham Road and the former Sydenham Station (now known as Watergardens Station).
The Sydenham Neighbourhood House was formerly known as the Sydenham Community Centre and was previously located in the neighbouring locality of Sydenham, before moving to the new Sydenham Community Hub.

The Sanctuary is named for Sir William Colin MacKenzie (1877-1938), an orthopaedist, comparative anatomist and philanthropist. He was born in Victoria and studied medicine, becoming a well-recognised figure in the Melbourne medical community. After study in Europe in the early 1900s, he began to focus on the treatment of patients with poliomyelitis connected paralysis. During the First World War, he spent three years in England at the Royal College of Surgeons, working to catalogue war wounds and write on military orthopaedics. He also researched anatomy of Australian fauna. After his return to Melbourne in early 1918, he set up the Australian Institute of Anatomical Research and in 1920 founded the field station at Healesville. When he vacated the station he suggested the reserve be enlarged and made a national park; the Sir Colin MacKenzie Sanctuary officially opened in May 1934. In 1923 he offered his extensive college of specimens to the Australian Government; it was incorporated in to the new National Museum of Australian Zoology. He was a member of the Medical Board, second-president of Canberra-based Royal Society of Australia, and fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. He retired in November 1937, and died on 29 June 1938 at his home in Studley Park Road, Kew. He was survived by his wife. MacKenzie had red hair which earned him the sobriquet 'Bricky'. He had a great affection for children, which seems to have been reciprocated; his friends spoke of his modest, retiring nature and essential kindness, but he clearly also had great energy and determination. He disliked controversy but was often involved in it. He was inclined to jump to theoretical conclusions with great conviction on little evidence. This can be instanced by his ideas on the importance of Australian fauna for the understanding of human health and disease, on which the institute was founded, and by his controversy, with Wood Jones, Elliot Smith and others, on the antiquity of the Jervois skull, which he considered to pre-date Peking Man. On the other hand, he was a pioneer in orthopaedics in Australia and a dedicated practitioner. He energetically espoused the conservation of Australian fauna and was very generous with his time and money, both in his efforts to advance Australian science and in the care of his poorer patients. Former students have spoken with warmth and gratitude of the personal help and inspiration he gave them. He had a love of things Australian including Australian Rules football, which he considered the best form of human exercise. His wife borrowed Wren's epitaph for the commemorative plaque in the institute: 'Si monumentum requiris, circumspice'.
Author: Monica MacCallum
Site Owner: Australian Dictionary of Biography, Australian National University

Historical Information: Smeaton is a large stone cairn constructed of mortared field stone. The cairn has a square base. A sketch made in 1966 noted that the cairn did not have a centre pole. A memorial stone inserted into the cairn recorded "Captain Hepburn Koorootvnch 15 April 1838". Photographs in 1976 show loose stone piled onto the mortared stone base. The 1997 photograph may indicate the upper section of the cairn has been repaired and mortared. Smeaton cairn was erected in its current form by local residents c1938 to celebrate the townshp's centenary. The cairn is very close to the location of the 1864 cairn. The centre pole and discs were placed by RASC in 1940. Coordinate values indicate that the present cairn is coincident with the position of the OG trig. point. It can be readily suspected, but not proven that the remains of the original cairn were utilised for the present one.
'The Victorian 'Scarsdale' was, probably, named after 'Harry Scarsdale,' a prospector who camped near a water hole on Woady Yallock Creek.'

Historical Information: The origin of St Arnaud's was the discovery of gold at a sandy knoll later called Bakery Hill, St Arnaud north, in January 1855. The resulting goldfield was known as New Bendigo, and mining spread into several hills and gullies. In 1856 a town was surveyed about 6 km east of the goldfield. It was named St Arnaud, after a French military commander in the Crimean War. Because of the town's distance from the goldfield the survey was cancelled and a township developed around the mining activity. The community readily adopted the proposed name, and sales of township lots occurred in 1858.

Historical Information:
Unmortared circular stone cairn 1.2m high by 3m in diameter. The top of the cairn is roughly formed, suggesting it has been partially demolished. The remains of an old sighting pole survive in the centre of the cairn. The cairn is located amongst a group of other structures: old forestry lookout tower, a more recent SEC tower and building, and another tower. No information is available on OSG files on repairs to the cairn. The Stanley (or Mt Stanley Geodetic station) was replaced with a new station in 1960. The new station was built due to the condition of the old geodetic cairn, confirmed as being partially demolished and unstable in 1969. Mt Stanley is noted as an important "first order station". Stanley geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local interest as an example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), the only example remaining in north-eastern Victoria outside the alpine area, and of interest as a first order or primary station. The cairn has been
altered, reducing its significance.

Historical Information: Rises on Lake Mountain; joins the Steavenson River N.N.E. of Marysville (Vic Oak Picnic Area). Note that the Taggerty River does not flow through the township of Taggerty. Aboriginal (Taungurong): taggarty. "Natives used to gather a blue pigment or clay on its banks with which to stain their bodies" (Saxton). Because the Taggerty River must have been named about twenty years or more earlier than the Steavenson River, it is likely that the lower part of the Steavenson, from its confluence with the Taggerty at Vic Oak to its confluence with the Acheron at Buxton, was originally regarded as the Taggerty River. This would also make better sense of the origin of the name of the Taggerty pastoral run.

Historical Information: Strathbogie Ranges: parish, locality, former settlement. Aboriginal (Taungurong): Les Blake gives drinking place, from tallang, tongue, and ook, of the body; Barry Blake records djalang as tongue, but regards -ook (as a suffix) as more likely meaning his or her. Also -allook could be the Taungurong equivalent of Woiworung yaluk, river, creek; Clark & Heydon (M) concur. (Compare Doogallook.) If so, the name may well refer to the Hell Hole Creek ravine, which might have reminded the Taungurong of a tongue in an animal's muzzle. Historical Information: Parish, town, railway station, pastoral run and state forest. Listed in 1848 by Wells. A settlement, to be called Tallarook, was surveyed on the other side of the Goulburn River, but never built. The present township was at first known officially as Dabyminga, after the nearby creek. The settlement was soon renamed Tallarook, after Tallarook House and the Tallarook pastoral run. The railway station was the junction with the main line to Melbourne for the former lines to Alexandra and Mansfield. The Tallarook pastoral run (11,000 ha, est. 1837) became part of Sunday Creek* and Tallarook in 1843. This was subdivided (1853) into Sunday Creek B*, the Tallarook Sheep Run (q.v.) and the Tallarook run, which was subdivided again (1859) into Tallarook (until at least 1876) and Tarwell (q.v.). (There was another Tallarook* run in the Wimmera*.) Aboriginal (Taungurong): wattlebird (Massola, 1968); wattlebird or honeysucker (Reed, 1970); Les Blake derives Tallarook from tooloorook, brackish creek or wattlebird. See also Dabyminga Creek and Mount Hickey.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information:
The Survey section of the Royal Australian Engineers was created soon after Federation and given the task of compiling contour maps of selected areas near capital cities to as part of defence planning. Initial survey work in Victoria
included a large topographic triangulation covering the area between Ballarat, Bendigo and Werribee. Their work became a high priority during the Second World War due to its closeness to Australia. Most of the surviving army beacons date from this period. The Tara beacon was built around 1941 by the RASC. Of regional significance as only one of only 5 known remaining examples of an Australian Army Survey Corp beacon, providing evidence of this important phase in the national coordination of the land survey system, the role of the Army survey corps, and the planning response to the anticipated need to defend
Australia during the Second World War.

Origin and meaning unclear.  'Tara'  could be derived from the name, Charlie Tarra, one of the Aboriginal guides who accompanied Paul Strzelecki, James Macarthur and James Riley during their overland trip to Western Port in 1840.  Or 'Tara' could be a reference to the 'Hill of Tara', and ancient meeting place of Irish kings.  [Research by I.D. Clark and D.A. Cahir, University of Ballarat, 2005.]

Named by surveyor W.S. Urquhart in compliment to Sir Roderick Murchison, a great European geologist who first predicted the existence of gold in this country.  Gold was discovered in July 1852. Tarradale in Ross Shire, Scotland, was Murchison's birthplace.  See also letter W.S. Urquhart to Andrew Clarke, Surveyor-General, 24 November 1853.

Historical Information: Highlands. Former pastoral run (about 16,000 ha, 1840-78 or later), originally  known as the Vale of Tempe. Parish; settlement on Ponkeen Creek near its confluence with Hughes Creek. The origin of Tarcombe is obscure: Clark & Heydon (D, M) give it as Aboriginal (Taungurong); but it could also be derived from Old English, Welsh or Gaelic. There is a Tarcoon in Scotland, and Saxton says there is a Tarcombe in Cornwall. Tempe (??µp?) or Tempea (??µpea) is a Greek valley between Olympus and Ossa, through which the Riber Peneius flows into the sea. The Hughes Creek or Tarcombe state school (1884-88, 1890 - 1915, 1925-43) was "near Bungleboor estate" (VR).

Historical Information: Formerly known as German Town and Hochkirch. Shortly after the turn of the century, when the town was still named Hochkirch, there was a German printing office, a German bookseller, a German Young Men's association, and a weekly and a fortnightly newspaper (both German language). As a result of strong anti-German feeling in the Victorian community during World War I, the township name of Hochkirch was changed in 1918 to Tarrington, the name of a nearby property owned by S.G. Henty with memories of the Sussex village of Tarring from whence the Henty family originated.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: Drung Drung is the name of one of three lakes some 16 km south-east of Horsham. Samuel Wilson (in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 178) confirms that Drung Drung is a native name, but he does not provide a meaning. Saxton (1907: 22) considers it a native name meaning 'spoiling'. According to Martin (1944: 32) it is an Aboriginal name meaning 'much spoiled'. Massola (1968: 20) extends the meaning to 'spoiling, spoiled, ruined'. Blake (1977: 85) also notes that Drung is the name of an Irish village in County Donegal. Les Blake is the only source for the dissonant etymology, and it may be disregarded as speculation on his part.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: The suburb's name reportedly comes from William Taylor, a 19th-century land owner who created a gully on the Keilor-Melton Road to provide water for his household and garden.
Author: Jamie First
Page Title: The A-Z story of Melbourne's suburbs

Historical Information: Jenny Keating, writing for the Encyclopedia of Melbourne (Brown-May & Swain, 2005, p. 709) states that the suburb's name "reputedly comes from the action taken by William Taylor, 19th-century owner of the large property Overnewton, to dam a gully on the Keilor-Melton Road to provide water for his household and garden." Overnewton Castle, with its Scottish baronial style turrets, was built in 1849 and is located in the nearby suburb of Keilor. Since Taylors Hill is adjacent to Taylors Lakes, it is a reasonable assumption that the name of this new suburb is an indirect reference to William Taylor.
Author: Ian Kendall

This bridge was able to be constructed by the generosity of Ted Gearon who donated all the steel and the platform for the bridge, which came from GMH factory in Melbourne. He carted all the materials to the site. By his generosity the Oxley Shire was able to construct the bridge. 
Ted Gearon arrived in the valley about 1972-73 when he bought a farm on Top Plain Lane. He was involved in the earth moving business. He was one who could see the value in many items he acquired at clearing sales and the demolition of buildings. He donated many of these items to Greta Football Club Clearing sales and the Moyhu CFA. On numerous occasions he lent his fire truck to the area when Moyhu CFA truck was away. He also donated a static roller to the Oxley Shire, this roller is still used by Rural City of Wangaratta. 
In 1984 he donated the toilet facilities for the Moyhu Youth Club.
Named to honour Redvers Edwin Jeffs (1900-1974), President of the McLoughlins Beach Progress Association in the late 1950s, a saw-miller and a long-time active member of the local community.

Historical Information: originally the Blacks' Spur. Forested ridge west and south-west of the Dom Dom Saddle (q.v.). The name is also used for the section of Maroondah Highway from Fernshaw (q.v.) to the Dom Dom Saddle (where it crosses the Great Divide) and a little beyond. There had long been an Aboriginal trail here, and it (or one close to it) was opened up as part of the early packhorse track to Woods Point. Massola says the name was adopted after some of John Carter and William Phillippe's teamsters met John Green (inspector for the Central Board to Watch over the Interests of Aborigines), William Barak, Simon Wonga (the elder) and a long line of Koories at the spur. Barwick writes that "Green had secured Board permission to cut a new track through the bush in a direct line from Yering* to the headwaters of the Goulburn River - to 'benefit the miners' who were now moving into this district in search of gold." E.E.H. (quoted by Mitchell), writing in 1934, said that Aboriginals guided some of the early miners over the spur. See also Acheron Aboriginal Station and Mount Dom Dom.

Historical Information: Pastoral run first held by George Curlewis, then taken up by John Foster in 1843.  C.J. Tyers referred to it as 'the heart of Gippsland'.  Name origin possibly relates to the story of a shipwrecked Scottish woman who joined or was capture by a group of local indigenous people. In 1841, settlers in the area found a recently abandoned encampment with a heart cut into the soft earth and a line pointing to dense tea trees.  Search parties sent out on Government orders were not successful in inducing the woman to join the settlers.  The mystery of her identity was never solved.  See Victorian Historical Magazine, Vol.3, p.175.

Commemorate the current land owner's grandfather, Thomas Patrick Millett, who was born in 1856 and who died on 5 December 1918. Thomas Patrick Millett was one of 12 children to George and Susan Millett. He was well known and highly regarded in the local community. He was once a butcher in a shop that was located next to the current Olive Tree Hotel in Evans Street, Sunbury, and a publican of the Royal and Rupertswood Hotels in Sunbury. He was also the first of the Millett family to farm the land at Rosenthal.

Thomas Alfred Thomas - Alf or Tom, was born on the 12th October 1912 in Happy Valley Ballarat. He would ride his motorcycle to pharmacy college in Carlton. When he qualified he worked in a family chemist shop in Chapel St Prahran before buying Bain and Co at Fitzroy St St Kilda. Pharmacies in Chapel St and Croydon followed as well as a chrome plating works in High St. He was the youngest of 3 brothers, Vivian, Edmund and Arthur and 2 sisters Joyce and Amy. He was raised by his mother when his father died in a mining accident when Tom was one year old. He met Nola Myra Madden while playing golf at Rossdale in Aspendale and married her on the 27th of November 1945, then had 2 sons Douglas in 1946 and Russell 1953. He was a social person, loved gambling, horse racing at Cranbourne, was a keen golfer at Elsternwick and Waverley, hunting and fishing at Mathoura NSW as well as flying at Moorabbin. His greatest passion however was the Prahran council, serving as mayor in 1951 and 1959, supporting many council activities and charities including the rebuilding of the fire ravaged Prahran market. There is a great deal of material recorded on the council website including many excellent photos. He also enjoyed driving his Austin Healy six sports. He died suddenly on the 11th of May 1961 at his residence in Lansell Rd Toorak.
Wodonga Shire was created in 1876 and Thomas Reidy was one of the first Councillors in 1876 along with John Woodland, Rowan Lockhead, George Street, James Bambrick and Owen Maher.
Thomas Reidy established the Carriers Arms Hotel and was one of Wodonga's first shire councillors.

Historical Information: Parish, township, pastoral run. The parish is on the south side of the Goulburn River, from near the confluence of the Goulburn and Delatite Rivers (a portion of Darlingford parish was at the confluence) west to the parish of Acheron. Eildon parish is on the north bank. Most of what used to be called Upper Thornton is now regarded as Eildon, and the site of the Upper Thornton state school (1875 - 1901) is under the wall of either the Sugarloaf Weir or the Eildon Dam. Lower Thornton township became known simply as Thornton in the late 1920s. The Thornton pastoral run was created in 1860 by subdivision of the Rubicon Creek run. Thornton was subdivided in 1865 into the Torbreck run (q.v.) and a smaller Thornton run, cancelled in 1877. The name is ultimately derived from one of about twenty places in Britain called Thornton, but three possible reasons have been advanced for how and why. (i) After D. Thornton (Saxton) or Dr. Thornton, settler, 1848 (Martin; Les Blake), whose full name appears to have been lost. Leonie Taylor of Thornton suspects the doctor may be an historical mistake or myth, and she is very likely right. (ii) From a name perpetuated by the Aitken family (e.g. Fanny Thornton Aitken). John Christie Aitken also had a property called Thornton on Darebin Creek*, Heidelberg*. (iii) After Thornton, Fifeshire, Scotland, original home of John Christie Aitken (first licensee, 1840-70, of the Rubicon Creek and Thornton pastoral runs), according to Peter Tossol of Thornton (Vic.) [Leonie Taylor]. Old English: þorn tun, thorn-bush enclosure.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Timor is the name of a creek and a farming district north-west of Maryborough. Flett (1975: 83) notes that the town of Coxtown on the Bet Bet Creek was surveyed in 1856 by Hugh Fraser and named 'Timor' 'although the new name went unknown for a long time'. Blake (1977: 257) fails to add to Flett's information. P.C. Crespigny (in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 180) lists Timor as a native name of 'unknown meaning' of a 'creek running through Adelaide Lead into the Bet Bet Creek'. At first glance it is tempting to draw parallels with the Island of Timor and the Timor Sea, north-west of Australia, which is a variant of the Malay word 'timur' meaning 'east'.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Toolangi was transferred from the shire of Yea to Healesville in 1924, but became part of the shire of Murrindindi in 1994. Historical Information: In the 1850s the Buchanan brothers set up a sawmill on Muddy Creek near present day Toora. A small settlement began at Muddy Creek, but by the 1870s falling prices had cut back timber production. Later in that decade farm selections were taken up. The name 'Toora' was given to a property east of Muddy Creek in 1876 and by 1880 it was the name of the survey parish. It is thought that 'Toora' derives from an Aboriginal expression referring to a woman keeping a fire alight.

Historical Information: During the 1840s William Thomas, Assistant Protector, recorded the existence of an Aboriginal campsite known as Tuuruk, situated by the Yarra River and covering the present day areas of Como Park and Thomas Oval. The people camping on this site were members of the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung and Daungwurrung language groups. Tuuruk is a Kulin word, meaning 'reedy grass' or 'weed in a lagoon'. Toorak is a variation of Tuuruk. Much of the area belonged to the Yalukit-willam clan, one of six Boonwurrung language clans. Yalukit-willam is belived to mean 'river camp' or 'river dwellers'. A small area east of Gardiners Creek belonged to one of the Woiwurrung language clans, the Wurundjeri-balug, a name that means 'white gum tree people'. The boundary between the Yarra River and Gardiners Creek, approximates the original boundary between the Boonwurrung peoples and their northern neighbour, the Woiwurrung. They camped regularly along the banks of the Yarra River and Gardiners Creek, where they could access the rich resources of aquatic foods and a diverse range of fauna and flora such as murnang or yam daises, eels, fish, mussels and waterfowl. Gatherings for social, ceremonial and trading purposes occurred regularly between the Boonwurrung and Woiwurrung people, while marriages were arranged between these two groups and the Daungwurrung, Wathawurrung and Djadjawurrung people. The settlement of disputes was also a very important part of inter-clan relations. In April 1842 the Woiwurrung and Boonwurrung clans, along with the Wathawurrung balug, Warring-ilum balug and fellow Daungwurrung clans gathered at Tuuruk. The purpose of the gathering was to resolve inter-clan grievances, but the intervention of the Native Police and Assistant Protector Thomas disrupted and cut short the proceedings and a resolution was not reached.

Historical Information: Land was selected in the district, known as Narracan, from 1875. In 1878, the railway into Gippsland was constructed and the railway station became the focus of a settlement. As there was already a township of Narracan about 13 km to the south, a new name was sought. The next town to the west was named Waterloo, so Trafalgar, also commemorating a great British military victory, was chosen. Several streets in the town are also named from British military history.

Historical Information: The Rev. George Langhorne was appointed as government missionary to Aboriginal people in Port Phillip in December 1836, and he arrived in 1837 from Sydney with a mission to ''civilise the blacks at Port Phillip''. According to Langhorne, in the late autumn of 1837 Robert Hoddle called at his camp, seeking a list of Aboriginal words to present to the government. Langhorne provided the names of some 'fine boys' from the local Wurundjeri tribe who were in camp with him and said, '...you may call on Parish, 'Kulbundora', other 'Kerbukena', 'Yall Yall', 'Tullamarina', 'Tallanghata' 'Tarook' (black crow)'. The name is a corruption of the original Woiwurung word 'Tullamarina' would almost certainly have been accented on the first syllable and the initial 't' would have sounded more like the English sound 'd'. Twelve years after the failure of the mission in 1839, Langhorne was walking down Collins Street and met Yall Yall. The latter told him that Tullamarina and the other boys were 'all dead and gone'.
Author: Alan West
Title: Tullamarine - what it means

Historical Information: From the Aboriginal word for "plenty of fish" Tynong State School, No. 2854, opened in teh4 Mechanic's Institute in August 1887. It closed in 1892 and then re-opened in the Tynong Hall in May 1905. In 1908 the School moved onto its own site into a building relocated from Cardinia School, No. 2139. This building was replaced in 1915 and the School was closed in April 1951 and the students went to Pakenham Consolidated School. This was also the fate of the Tynong North School which opened in June 1930 and closed in Decemver 1951.

Historical Information: The name Tyntyndyer (Tyntynder) has become commonly referred to as a translation of the local Wadi Wadi peoples' term for 'the flight and twitter of birds'. According to L Kostanski in 'Spurious Etymologies: Toponymic Books and Town Name Identities of the Murray River', the name is a translation of the original name of the locality on the Murray River used by the Wadi Wadi people. Chief Protector, George Robinson, noted in his journal in 1846, that there was a tribe of Aboriginal people in the area, the Tindinee, who referred to the area as Tin.tin.dare.re, the translated meaning of which is 'acrid lichen'.

Tharra, the quail hawk.
Bunjil, also spelt Bundjil, is a creator deity, culture hero and ancestral being, often depicted as a wedge-tailed eagle in Australian Aboriginal mythology of some of the Aboriginal peoples of Victoria.
In the Kulin nation in central Victoria he was regarded as one of two moiety ancestors, the other being Waang the crow. Bunjil has 2 wives and a son, Binbeal the rainbow. His brother is Palian the bat. He is assisted by 6 wirmums or shamans who represent the clans of the Eaglehawk moiety: Djart-djart the nankeen kestrel, Tharra the quail hawk, Yukope the parakeet, Lar-guk the parrot, Walert the brushtail possum and Yurran the gliding possum.

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Stone cairn with a base of 6 metres in diameter and 2.1 metres, then a second level 3.6 metres high. The stepped form is unusual, as is its overall size. A metal beacon on tripod legs was placed on top of the stone cairn, but later moved to an adjacent site. The cairn is thought to have been originally conical in shape, with the stepped appearance being a later adaptation. Associated with the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72). Said to have been built by Pinniger in 1866-67. Torbreck geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an example of the dry-stone cairns built as part of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), one of only four examples to survive in Central Victoria. This cairn is of particular interest due to its overall size and the stepped form, apparently a later adaptation.

Historical Information: Underbool is the name of a railway station on the Ouyen to Pinnaroo line in the Mallee region of north-west Victoria. According to O'Callaghan (1918: 92), from information he obtained from A.S. Kenyon, it is a native name, 'probably from 'wimbool', the ear, 'bool' means 'water', native name of waterholes'. Martin (1944) accepts O'Callaghan's interpretation. Massola (1968: 50) renders the name 'Undera-bool' meaning 'abundance'. Hercus (1986: 261, 290) confirms that the local word for 'ear' was 'wirimbul', and 'water' was 'gadjin'. Blake (1977: 264) suggests that on '30 October 1861 surveyor Dr Neumayer camped there and district received German n. Underbolt'.
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information: In the middle 1890s the part of the locality was divided into ten-acre blocks as part of the 'Scoresby' village settlement scheme, which extended northwards to Ferny Creek. Notwithstanding the Scoresby appellation, Upwey was known as Mast Gully, after several ship masts had been cut from a gully in 1850. In 1897 three sisters, the Tullidges, bought a homestead and named it Upwey, after the English village on the River Wey.

Historical Information: Named after former resident, Val Boyd, who made a significant contribution as a community worker over many years in the Ferntree Gully area.

Born in Germany of Ukrainian parents, Valentina arrived first at Bonegilla in 1951, then moved to South Australia.  She returned to teach at Wodonga South Primary School and was a councillor for Bonegilla ward from 1985 to 1993.  She was Mayor of Wodonga in 1989 and was inaugural chairwoman of the Albury-Wodonga Regional Arts Board.

Historical Information: Named after the Van Cleef family, who were long standing residents of the Venus Bay district. French name (Baie de la Venus) was given by French explorers.  They named the bay after the ship 'Venus' in which George Bass sailed to Pacific Islands to obtain supplies for the Sydney settlement.  On his return, Bass sold some supplies to the French who were in Port Jackson at the time.

Title: French placenames on the Victorian Coast

Historical Information: The bay, after which the township takes its name, is thought to have been named after Venus, the morning or evening star, by George Bass on his coastal voyage of discovery in 1798. Venus Bay is on Bass Strait, and Anderson Inlet is like an inland bay, fed by the Tarwin River on its east and emptying into Venus Bay on its west.
