Historical Information: The park was created as part of the residential development on the former Haig Street Primary School site. The park is named in honour of Vin Heffernan OAM, Councilor - City Of Heidelberg (1966-1985) Mayor (1979-80), State Member for Ivanhoe (1985-1996) and Minister for Small Business and Youth Affairs (1992-1996). There is a strong local connection to Vin Heffernan in Heidelberg Heights with the former Haig Street Primary School library, which stood on the site, named in his honour.

The park was formerly known as Vin Heffernan Reserve. It was renamed in 2016 in order to free up the name 'Vin Heffernan' for use in a more suitable location.
Community consultation to rename the reserve occurred in early 2016. The name Radio Park is in recognition of a radio relay tower which was formerly located near the site prior to its development.
Council Minutes: Banyule City Council, Ordinary Meeting of Council Minutes 18 April 2016

Historical Information: 'The mines ' Department map, 1901, shows it as Baron's Creek.  The Military map, 1942, shows it as Von Mueller Creek.  The Lands Department map, 1957 shows as Von Mueller Creek.'  The parish plan of Wongarra shows it as Von Mueller Creek.  The occurrance of Baron's Creek on the geological map of 1901 makes me believe that the creek is named after Baron Von Mueller - the early Botanist and curator of the Melbourne Botanic Gardens.  Why and when the name Flatbottom arose I cannot say - possibly during the anti-german feeling during the Great War - but this is a guess.'

Historical Information: Viewbank (Aberdeenshire and Perth & Kinross). The suburb evidently takes its name from the property established by James Williamson in 1839-40 (Brown-May & Swain, 2005, p. 750). According to the Parliament of NSW website, James Williamson (1811-1881) was born in Edinburgh. He purchased Viewbank in 1839, was an Elective Member of the first Legislative Council 1843 - 1856 for the District of Port Phillip and moved to NSW in 1858.

Historical Information: Former shire (1895 - 1994). Included Boho South and Marraweeny. Historical Information: It is widely accepted that the town got its name from Major Thomas Mitchell, the first European to pass through the district. On his Australia Felix exploration in 1836 he noted that the swamps and marshes in the area seemed to have a profusion of violets and named the district Violet Ponds. When the government laid out the village they called it Violet Creek. Some of the early settlers thought there was more evidence of Honeysuckle than Violets and, for a time, the settlement was known as Honeysuckle Creek. Violet Town, however, persisted.
Author: Aussie Towns

The locality was originally known as Waratah Bay, named after S.S. Waratah which put in there for shelter in 1854. The captain of the ship reported the bay as a good, safe anchorage. In 1875 the manager of the Yanakie pastoral station on the Wilsons Promontory isthmus discovered limestone deposits at Waratah Bay. In conjunction with Melbourne shipping agents, the manager built lime kilns and a jetty on the western side of the bay. The business was sold to a partnership which included William Walker, Collector of Customs, in 1880. Walker's name may have been the origin of Walkerville, which was known as Waratah Bay until 1892.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information: The name Wallermeryong was given to the Creek on Commander H.L. Cox's Charts of the area after he surveyed it in 1865, although the Bunurong People, who walked the Creek, already used this name. The name Main Creek appears on a Certificate of Title issued in 1872. A map of the Parish of Wannaeue from 1949 shows 'Main Creek' but a map of the Parish of Fingal printed in 1961 shows 'Wallermeryong or Main Creek'. The 'meryong' part of Wallermeryong means 'happy place' and the 'Waller' part of the name is the name of an animal species. The Bunurong Land Council is still researching what kind of animal. www.mornpen.vic.gov.au/Files/Governance_Minutes/031905om.pdf

Historical Information: Walter Cottrell lived his whole life in Wodonga.  His main transport was his bicycle. He became a drover of sheep and cattle, then worked for Albert Schlink who owned the first store south of the railway line.  He cut wood for the quarry boilers during the construction of Hume Weir.  His last job was with the Army at Bandiana.  He was a champion shooter and a life member of the Wodonga Show Society.  He kept pigeons and was in demand all over Victoria as a show judge.

Author: Blake, Les
Title: Place Names of Victoria

Historical Information: It was named after the Wando Vale pastoral run which was taken up by John G. Robertson in 1840. Robertson was an associate of the Hentys at Portland, and like them pushed north with sheep to settle on land described by Thomas Mitchell, the Surveyor General of New South Wales, as highly suitable for grazing and agriculture (1836). Mitchell also named the Wando River, which is a tributary of the Glenelg. He understood the name to be Aboriginal for stream.
Author: Victorian Places

Historical Information:
In recognition of the club's commitment to the park dating back to 1989. Examples of the efforts of the club as follows:
1989 - a double BBQ, shelter, drinking fountain, playground and some fencing was installed with some assistance from Council.
1995 - in partnership with Council and a DEET program a new toilet block was built.
2006 - a BBQ shelter, a double BBQ and a memorial rock were installed. The shelter was unveiled and named the Peter Seargeant Memorial BBQ Shelter. The memorial rock was unveiled and dedicated by Bishop David Farrer to deceased Lions and Lions Ladies for their selfless service to the community.
2012-2013 Council replaced the existing playground at Batchelors Green with new equipment depicting the K191 steam locomotive that was installed at Wareena Park by the Lions Club in 1968 and later removed.
2013-2014 the Liberty Swing was the Lions Club's major project funded through an Australian Lions Foundation grant. The Variety Club of Australia donated the swing to the Lions Club and Council provided the soft fall and path to the swing.

Historical Information: Parish. Pastoral run (12,000 ha, est. 1847, originally part of Watson and Hunter's Run) on the Delatite River, partly submerged by the Sugarloaf Weir, and further inundated by the Eildon Dam. Burial place of Baalwick, head of the Yeerun-illam-balluk band of the Taungurong; for many years the home of Scottish-born John Bon (1805-68) and his wife Ann, who gave the Taungurong people sanctuary here until they were resettled at Coranderrk (q.v.). Wappang was a Taungurong name probably for the Delatite River ("that part of the Devil's [sic] River on which the run was formed" - Noble). Clark & Heydon (D) suggest that Yallermeerrangan (Yallermeourung), mentioned in George Augustus Robinson's journal (1840) was the Taungurong name for the Wappan area. See also Mrs. Bon Bay, Point Tehan, Taungurong Creek and Wappan Block.

Historical Information: This is the name of a town in the Wimmera region of Victoria that takes its name from a local pastoral station. District surveyor, Philip Chauncy (in Smyth 1878 Vol. 2: 208), recorded the original native word as Wurranjibeel', referring to Warracknabeal station on Yarriambiack Creek, and gives it the following signification: 'Wurra, lip; ngi, its; beal, flooded gum tree - ie., lip of a flooded gum tree'. He noted that he obtained this information from native speakers at the Wimmera. Howitt (1904: 54) interpreted it as 'plain of red gum tree'. Saxton (1907: 66) notes that it is a native name meaning 'large gum trees'. O'Callaghan (1918: 94) reproduces Chauncy's information. Martin (1944: 85) translates the name as 'large gums'. Massola (1968: 51) renders the name 'warrak, plain, na, of, beal, red gum tree (Eucalyptus rostrata)'. Priestley (1967: 3) in a history of Warracknabeal translated it as 'redgum trees shading the creek'. Linguist Luise Hercus (1986: 214; Clark and Heydon 2002) analysed the name as Wurungi-bial 'mouth of creek with red gum trees'. Blake (1977: 273) notes that 'although in 1932 Mrs G.H. Warrack of Edinburgh claimed n. came fr. her family and nabeal (Gaelic), of the ravine, the Abor. origin is usually accepted: fr. word for fringe of gum trees about hollow, or flooded red gum trees; in 1878 spelt Werracknebeal'. The Warrack family claim seems to be spurious. The pastoral run was named 'Werracknabeal' by Andrew Scott in 1845 with his sons Robert and Andrew (Billis and Kenyon 1974: 137).
Author: Ian D. Clark, Luise Hercus and Laura Kostanski
Title: Indigenous and Minority Placenames Australian and International Perspectives

Historical Information:
Djilang was the traditional Wadawurrung name for Geelong. Djilang meaning a "Tongue of Land".

As Bunjil, our Karringalibil Murrup (Creator Spirit) flew over this country, his eyes looking down on country, he saw the water coming into the bay and the tongue of land - Djilang.

Djilang was a rich cultural landscape for the Wadawurrung, a place of plenty. From our wetlands, coastal country, rivers and inland country, the resources were used by our people to live a rich and sustainable life and as valuable trading materials. Significant cultural landscapes feature surrounding Djilang include: Wurdi Youang, meaning Big Hill and now known as the You Yangs, Corio Bay, meaning Sandy place, Lake Connewarre coming from the Wadawurrung word Kunawarra - the Black swan, and the Moorabool and Barwon Rivers, a connected system between the mountains and the sea. These significant cultural land features show how our land still speaks to us of our language, Wadawurrung Ancestors and their connection to this Country.
Author: Rebecca Famlonga - Wadawurrung Traditional Owner
Page Title: Reconciliation Action Plan - Wadawurrung Aboriginal history

Historical Information: Named after a local park. Previously owned by businessman and Mayor of Melbourne Orlando Fenwick and then by Eliza Welch, the 137-acre block was secured by the Hawthorn Tramway Trust in 1917 as a destination for its Riversdale Rd line. The adjacent suburb, developed for housing from the 1920s, came to share the name Wattle Park.
Author: Jamie First
Page Title: The A-Z story of Melbourne's suburbs

Historical Information: Wattle Park is the only Australian example of a comprehensively developed pleasure park established, owned and operated by a transport authority with the dual aim of promoting its transport services and providing a recreational facility for the public. The layout of the park and its buildings and structures remain intact in their original 1920s form. The name and theme of the park reflect the strong national fervour of the early decades of the century - the wattle is Australia's national floral emblem. It has a historical association with two prominent Melbourne identities, Orland Fenwick, a former lord mayor and Eliza Welch, widow of the co-founder of the retailing firm Ball & Welch, before it was purchased by the Hawthorn Tramways Trust.
Author: Heritage Council Victoria

Mainly in the Maroondah Catchment. Rises north of Mount Donna Buang; dammed to form the Maroondah Reservoir; flows into the Yarra River* south-west of Healesville. The Watts River Falls are in the headwaters, by the crossing with Road Seven. The river was first made a water catchment in 1872. Named after George Watts, stock rider drowned in 1837 (about 1843 according to Saxton). Watts is a diminutive of Walter. Aboriginal (Woiworung) name: Broong-ku-galk, rotten logs (Massola, 1968); Brun-ker-zalk, "rotten log creek" (Symonds). Barry Blake lists brun-guit, rotten, bunkun, buang, stinking, and galk, stick, tree, wood. Renamed the Maroondah River in 1891, but without lasting effect. See also Maroondah Dam and Maroondah Weir.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: The lake was originally known as Yuille's Swamp, forming part of William Yuille's Ballarat pastoral run (1838). Yuille's Swamp was used to supply water to Ballarat (1852) until better reservoirs were built in the 1860s. Until then the lake was alternately a water storage or dust hollow, depending on rainfall and the amount drawn off. During the 1870s improvements were made to the lake as an aquatic venue, and the City and Wendouree rowing clubs raced there. It appears that the name Wendouree was given at about the time of the improvements. The name apparently is derived from an Aboriginal expression.
Author: Victorian Places

In 2011 Ian Wacey and Ray Barber (authors of 250 Victorian Waterfalls) submitted the name Birringun Falls to be included in the data set. On the consequent 1:50,000 Yinnar map instead of this new drop being added as another waterfall near West Tarwin Falls (on a tributary) it over wrote the name West Tarwin Falls and as a consequence all the signage at the site now refers to West Tarwin Falls erroneously as Birringun Falls. To clear up the confusion future Vicmaps need to include both West Tarwin Falls and Birringun Falls. N.B. Only West Tarwin Falls is in Ian and Rays book not Birringun Falls, this name was circulated to other waterfall enthusiasts and Vicnames privately.
Author: Ian Wacey & Ray Barber
Title: 250 Victorian Waterfalls

Historical Information: Named after the Wieland family.  Carl Ferdinand Wieland (1827-1902) was an immigrant from Prussia who arrived in 1872.  He established the first orchard in the district with his wife Caroline.  He named the settlement of Heathmont after the heath growing on the low hilly slopes.  His grandsons, Norman and Stanley helped construct Heathmont's first railway station which opened in 1926. Stanley and his wife Thelma had an orchard in the area 1930 to 1950.  The reserve was formerly their horse paddock and dam.
Wiggy Jackson came to Wodonga in about 1920.  He worked for various road gangs and later in Albury as a garbage contractor. His family has significant links with Wodonga.

Historical Information: Proposed by Suzanne Canning, a descendant of the late William Canning. This Council owned reserve consists of 2 adjoining parcels of land, which are believed to be part of properties that were owned by William Canning.  The parcels of land are located at 33 Sycamore Crescent Campbellfield and 40 Fordson Road Campbellfield. William Canning bought and sold several parcels of land in the Parish of Will Will Rook. In January 1860 he purchased approximately 215 acres of land which he named 'Highclere'. William and Lucy Canning built their family home on this property, where it remained until demolished in 1963. In 1900 the property was transferred to their son Walter Moses Canning. A Moreton Bay Fig was planted by the Canning family which is still standing today. William Canning was a Trustee and Secretary of the Will Will Rook Pioneer Cemetery from 1858 to 1893 (35 years), a highly respected member of his church, and a person who was considered a pioneer in the area, having lived in the Campbellfield district for 61 years. William Canning and his wife Lucy are buried at the Will Will Rook cemetery.
Footscray local and Indigenous leader.

Historical Information: The first lighthouse was built at Point Gellibrand, Williamstown, in 1839-40. This timber structure was replaced with a square bluestone lighthouse tower, designed by Henry Ginn. The bluestone section has battered lower stories featuring rusticated masonry with smooth string courses and originally had a castellated parapet with mast and spherical, copper plate Timeball above. The masonry was quarried and worked by convict labour. Four lamps were shining in May 1849; a larger lamp was installed in August 1849. Angles of the base of the Tower were set to the cardinal points of the compass and a bench mark was cut into the sill for use in the hydrographic survey of Victorian waters. Williamstown Time Ball tower was the first bench mark established in Victoria and served as the bench mark for all Victorian height measurements for many years. It also provided the longitude datum for the original Geodetic Survey of Victoria. The geodetic survey started with the marking of meridians and parallels to form a network of geodetic squares. The first meridian surveyed was the 145th meridian in west Melbourne, chosen because of its close location to the Williamstown Observatory. The time keeping service was part of a larger undertaking which was the setting up of an Observatory at Williamstown. Interestingly, R.L.J. Ellery, Superintendent of the Williamstown Observatory was transferred to the Surveyor General's Department in 1858 to start the preparations for the proposed geodetic survey. The Williamstown Observatory was closed in 1863 and its Observatory functions were taken over by the Melbourne Observatory. In 1932, the height of the Timeball Tower was increased to 98ft by the addition of a circular brick tower 30ft in height.

Historical Information: The surveyor Philip Chauncy recorded this name (cf. R. Brough Smyth 1876 vol 2:211). He also recorded that it meant 'where is it?' The place is in Djadjawurrung country and this language is very close to the neighbouring Wembawemba. The Wembawemba word wintya means 'where' (Hercus 1992). It looks like an obvious example of lack of communication, and as Tully (1997:92) suggests in his dictionary of Djadjawurrung: 'It appears that the informant was not sure where Chauncy meant'.

Historical Information: At the point where the Wodonga Creek and the Sydney road intersected with the Murray River, a town was surveyed by the Victorian government surveyor in 1852. It was named Belvoir, after Charles Huon's homestead. The formation of other official townships along the Sydney road in the next few years marked the road as the main inter-colonial freight route, and Belvoir's position immediately before the river crossing made it a stopping-off place. During the 1860s Belvoir became known as Wodonga (thought to be an Aboriginal word meaning bulrushes), and a gazettal on 7 August 1874, confirmed the change of name.

Historical Information: Supplanted the small settlement of Cherry's Point* (980 m alt.; named after Thomas Cherry, who built a shanty there ca. 1861) 2 km to the east on Clarke Spur*. First called Woods Junction in 1862 after a settlement grew up around the general store of Henry Gibson (Harry) Wood [Brian Lloyd] (Lloyd, 2002) by the Goulburn River. Access was at first from Mansfield and Jamieson to the north until the Yarra Track provided a link with Marysville and beyond. By 1866 Woods Point was a bustling mining and shopping centre with an immediate population of more than 2,200, a hospital (Upper Goulburn District Hospital), numerous hotels, three breweries, two newspapers and suburbs such as Gooley's Creek* (after prospector William G. Gooley, who found gold there in May 1861; see also Gooley's Bridge), Killarney, Morning Star Hill, Piccadilly, Richmond and Waverley.  The boom known as "Woods Point Mania" was followed by decline in the 1870s. After being burnt out on 13 January 1939, the town was extensively rebuilt, but declined after the closure of the Morning Star Mine in 1963, and is now a fraction of its former size. Camping is available at the Scott and Comet Flat* reserves north-west and south-east of the town. See also Morning Star Creek.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: This outer western municipality was created in 1994 to replace the former Shire of Werribee (less Balliang East, Exford and Laverton). Wyndham was the original name for the shire, having been used from 1864-1909. Werribee's first publican had fought alongside a fellow officer named Wyndham at the Battle of Waterloo.

Historical Information: Wyndham Park is a central park located in the Werribee CBD, the name is readily identifiable within the community.

In 2011, the State Government Department of Education & Early Childhood Development approved the naming of a new school entity formed by the merger of Glen Orden Primary School and Glen Devon Primary School as Wyndham Park Primary School. The School is located next door to the new community centre, and it is Council's understanding that the School intends to construct a pedestrian entrance that would align with the community centre.
Name aligns with nearby primary school name.

Wyndham Park was previously underutilised due to its remote location and lack of visibility from the CBD. The new pedestrian bridge was built to address these key issues. Therefore, the name of the bridge is linked to the name of the park.
Name adopted following the merger of Glen Devon and Glen Orden Primary Schools, and consultation with the local school communities.

The station was named after the locality it was situated in, that being Wyndham Vale.
The creation of Manor Lakes (gazetted 17 March 2016) as a locality sees the station now being situated in Manor Lakes versus Wyndham Vale.

Historical Information:
The Wauka mark is a concrete pillar or obelisk, approx. 1.32m high placed over the earlier cairn foundation. Associated with the survey of the NSW - Victoria State Border. Conference Point was the point agreed by the Victorian and NSW representatives in 1868 as being the seaward terminal of the Black- Allan line. This point was triangulated to enable the necessary computations for the azimuth of the line to be effected. When the line was run through to Cape Howe by Alexander Allan, the surveyed position appears to have been marked as Wauka (effectively replacing the
original Conference Point mark). Conference Point mark was reported lost in 1897 by NSW surveyor, but Wauka was extant. It is surmised that Allan may have used the materials from the Conference Point cairn to build the Wauka cairn. The Wauka cairn was described in 1919 by E H Lees as "having a diameter of 10', height of 10'6" with a pole of galvanised pipe (2" diameter and 16' long). The cairn is centred over the bottom of a glass bottle placed there at the time of the original survey, and undisturbed at the time of the construction of this cairn". This cairn was an unmortared stone cairn. This cairn survived until at least 1967 when a new central pipe was placed down the centre of the remains of the old pipe. A new cairn was built in May 1978, comprising a pillar 1.32m high placed over the cairn foundation. It was built by NSW Lands Department surveyor Dave Vincent.

Historical Information:
The South Base and North Base marks both consist of a solid bluestone base set into the ground, capped by a heavy stone. A plug of gun metal with a platinum centre is set into the stone base. The capping stone at South Base has been broken in the recent past. North Base was last inspected by the Office of the Surveyor General in 1989, soon after it was gazetted as an 'area of historic interest' (23/8/1988). The mark was covered by piled stones covering the stone cap and marked by four posts. Three permanent marks are associated with the establishment of the Victorian Geodetic Baseline at Werribee in 1860 by Robert Ellery, Government Astronomer and Supervisor of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria: South Base, North Base and Green Hill extension.
Located on the east side of the Werribee River, north of the railway, the baseline was five miles in length. It was extended north-west to a total of nine miles to Green Hill by triangulation. The baseline was measured using three ten-foot iron rods made in Victoria against the NSW standard originally obtained from the Ordnance Survey Department of South Hampton in England. The north and south ends of the five mile baseline 'were permanently marked with sunken masonry piers, having in their upper surfaces a piece of brass carrying a platinum dot indicating the termini of the measure. These marks were then covered with heavy cap stones'. The third mark, at the end of the extension to the north, on Green Hill, 'consists of a sunken bluestone block with a projecting iron spike. The South and North Bases, and the location of the third mark on Green Hill are shown on a 1915 Army Ordnance map of the area. Examining this map it is possible to follow the course of the baseline from the present day location of Hoppers Crossing, across the Tarneit Road to the North Base south of Sayers Road and close to the Werribee River, and then across the Werribee River to Green Hill within Staughton's Eynesbury Estate. The South Base is possibly the best known of the three permanent marks because of its location close to the Princes Highway and the various campaigns to ensure its preservation. The South Base and North Base marks both consist of a solid bluestone base set into the ground, capped by a heavy stone. A plug of gun metal with a platinum centre is set into the stone base. The capping stone at South Base has been broken in the recent past. North Base was last inspected by the Office of the Surveyor General in 1989, soon after it was gazetted as an 'area of historic interest' (23/8/1988). The mark was covered by piled stones covering the stone cap and marked by four posts.  Three permanent marks are associated with the establishment of the Victorian Geodetic Baseline at Werribee in 1860 by Robert Ellery, Government Astronomer and Supervisor of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria: South Base, North Base and Green Hill extension.
Located on the east side of the Werribee River, north of the railway, the baseline was five miles in length. It was extended north-west to a total of nine miles to Green Hill by triangulation. The baseline was measured using three ten-foot iron rods made in Victoria against the NSW standard originally obtained from the Ordnance Survey Department of South Hampton in England. The north and south ends of the five mile baseline 'were permanently marked with sunken masonry piers, having in their upper surfaces a piece of brass carrying a platinum dot indicating the termini of the measure. These marks were then covered with heavy cap stones'. The third mark, at the end of the extension to the north, on Green Hill, 'consists of a sunken bluestone block with a projecting iron spike. The South and North Bases, and the location of the third mark on Green Hill are shown on a 1915 Army Ordnance map of the area. Historical Information:
Wheeler Hill geodetic cairn is located close to the highest point of this lightly timbered hill, with the more recent trig nearby. The cairn is built of local stone, unmortared and with a central pole. Its condition was recorded in 1963 as excellent, and recent photographs confirm this. The cairn is approximately 1.8 m high, conical in shape. Associated with early phase of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-72), the survey of Geodetic Squares. Probably built around 1864 by Thomas Pinniger,
Geodetic Surveyor. Pinniger undertook substantial survey work on the
Geodetic Squares in Central and Noth-eastern Victoria. Wheeler Hill geodetic triangulation station cairn is of local significance as an
example of the dry-stone stone cairns built as part of an early phase of the Geodetic Survey of Victoria (1858-1872), the survey of Geodetic Squares. It is one of four examples of geodetic survey cairns remaining in Central Victoria. The cairn retains its centre pole and appears substantially intact, a rare surviving example.

Historical Information:
Williamstown Timeball Tower is a bluestone tower, square in section. A later cream-brick circular tower, built to convert the timeball tower into a lighthouse, has been recently removed and a replica timeball added.
The first lighthouse was built at Point Gellibrand, Williamstown, in 1839-40. This timber structure was replaced with a square bluestone lighthouse tower, designed by Henry Ginn. The bluestone section has battered lower stories featuring rusticated masonry with smooth string courses and originally had a castellated parapet with mast and spherical, copper plate Timeball above. The masonry was quarried and worked by convict labour. Four lamps were shining in May 1849; a larger lamp was installed in August 1849. Angles of the base of the Tower were set to the cardinal points of the compass and a bench mark was cut into the sill for use in the hydrographic survey of Victorian waters. Williamstown Time Ball tower was the first bench mark established in Victoria and served as the bench mark for all Victorian height measurements for many years. It also provided the longitude datum for the original Geodetic Survey of
Victoria. The geodetic survey started with the marking of meridians and
parallels to form a network of geodetic squares. The first meridian surveyed was the 145th meridian in west Melbourne, chosen because of its close location to the Williamstown Observatory. The time keeping service was part of a larger undertaking which was the setting
up of an Observatory at Williamstown. Interestingly, R.L.J. Ellery,
Superintendent of the Williamstown Observatory was transferred to the
Surveyor General's Department in 1858 to start the preparations for the
proposed geodetic survey. The Williamstown Observatory was closed in
1863 and its Observatory functions were taken over by the Melbourne
Observatory. In 1932, the height of the Timeball Tower was increased to 98ft by the addition of a circular brick tower 30ft in height. The Williamstown Timeball Tower (Lighthouse) is of state significance as a rare example of a Timeball Tower in Australia, and as a monument to the Colony's development of marine aids around the coast of Victoria and the early economic development of Melbourne. It has also played an important role in relation to land surveying, and is of also of State significance serving as the original Observatory, providing the datum for all height measurements throughout Victoria for many years, and the longitude datum for the Geodetic Survey.

The names means strong heart, and represents the following values:
- A centre such as this can become the heart of the community - both the local Wyndham Vale community, and the Wyndham-wide Aboriginal community.
- Strength of identity, strength of culture, strength of families, and strength of community will be outcomes of this centre, and the "strong heart" name reflects this.
- Uncle Bryon Powell, Wadawurrung elder, shared a story on the 'soak' located on the site, the importance of that to cultural practices and being a place where clans would have gathered for food. 
- It can serve as a reminder that the Wyndham Aboriginal community's heart continued to beat strongly, even when that community was disrupted, dispersed and without a specific home to meet in.

Historical Information: From the Aboriginal word for "creek stream or river". Yallock was the original name of the Koo-Wee-Rup Railway Station. There have been two schools called Yallock. The first, No. 2629, opened on the corner of Bayles Road and Bethunes Road in 1884, changed its name to Koo-Wee-Rup in 1903 and was moved into the town of Koo-Wee-Rup in 1911. The second school, No.3420, started in 1902 as the Yallock Village Settlement School and later changed its name to Yallock. The Yallock Village Settlement was based around Fincks, School, Hall and O'Briens Road off Koo-Wee-Rup Longwarry Road. The Bayles Railway Station, which opened in 1922, was the station closest to Yallock.

Historical Information: From the Aboriginal word to "to walk about". There have been four schools called Yannathan. Yannathan, No.2422, opened in 1883. Yannathan Upper, No.2492, began its life as Lang Lang North in 1883, changed its name to Yannathan Upper in 1906 and closed in 1912. Yannathan South, No.2510, operated between 1882 and 1890. In 1895 Protector's Flat School, No.3225, opened at Lang Lang East, it was relocated in 1914 to a more central site, and became known as Heath Hill and then changed its name again in 1951 and became Yannathan South. The Yannathan Railway Station opened June 29, 1922 and closed April 1950.

Historical Information: Parish, settlements, former railway station (1890 - 1978). Because the parish of Yarck extends from the Maroondah Highway to Spring Creek Road, Yarck as a locality or settlement name has "wandered". In 1889 two communities, one on Home Creek (1) and another on Spring Creek (1), were both claiming to be the township of Yarck! A map of 1893 shows a settlement of Yarck along Spring Creek Road, 3 km N.N.E. of Fawcett, and Yarck Station (and the south part of Kanumbra) where the township of Yarck is now: by Home Creek (1) and the Maroondah Highway. Yarck Primary School (1870-73, 1874 - 1993) was known as Home Creek School until August 1903. "Name of an old cattle station, which at one time occupied that locality" (AES 1931); if so, not a pastoral run. Aboriginal (Taungurong): yaruk, swamp grass (Massola, 1968) or long river (Les Blake, Noble, Reed 1970). Barry Blake lists a Woiworung word yaruk, meaning magic. However, Brough Smyth (1878) gives Yaruk, long river, as an Aboriginal name for Narrawong*; and Clark & Heydon (M) mention a parish of Yarak* in Gippsland*. The Scots dialect word yark, jerk or tug, has been suggested [Rex Tate], but it does not seem to have generated a place-name in Scotland, and there is no plausible connexion with Yarck. See also Godfrey's Creek and Kanumbra.
Author: Sinnott, Nigel
Title: Place-Names of the Alexandra, Lake Eildon and Big River Area of Victoria

Historical Information: Lying on the flat plain of the Moe River, the district was known as Little Moe. During the late 1860s and 1870s the country south of Yarragon was selected, extending into the steep Strzelecki Ranges. The construction of the railway from Melbourne into Gippsland further encouraged settlement. The railway station, opened in 1878, was named Waterloo after the British military battle. However, the existence of another town of that name caused confusion with mail. In 1883, the town was renamed Yarragon after the adjoining parish. According to Bunce's Language of the Aborigines of the Colony of Victoria (1859), Yarragondock is an Aboriginal word meaning mustachoes, which may relate playfully to the name Little Moe.

Historical Information: Parish, town, former shire (1873 - 1994), former railway station (1883 - 1978). Gold was discovered in the area in late 1851. State school Yea No. 699 was in Yea, but Yea No. 1433 (eventually renamed Homewood) was at Gill's Gully and Mount Charlotte. Yea was originally called Muddy Creek after the nearby river; surveyed 1855-56 by Thomas Wilkinson Pinniger (commemorative cairn and plaque in High Street; see also Mount Pinniger); renamed (1855) after Colonel Lacy Walter Giles Yea (1808-55) commander of the 7th Royal Fusiliers, who served with General Windham in the Crimean War and was fatally wounded at Redan near Sebastopol. (The surname rhymed with saw, the place-name now rhymes with say.) Harvey Blanks reckons the name change was proposed by surveyor-general Sir Andrew Clarke (1824 - 1902) and implemented after surveyor Pinniger had discussed it with William Leyden Ker and Anna Maria Ker of the Killingworth pastoral run. (See also "Antiquarian", Alexandra Times, 23 June 1868.) The new name was ironically appropriate as Yea - a variant of the Devon and Somerset surname Yeo - comes from the Old English ea, stream, river. See also Marshmallow Hill, Providence Bridge, Sebastopol Creek, Windham and Yea River.

Historical Information: The township of Yellingo was gazetted in March 1896 however, Helen Coulson, said the area was originally called Claxton, then Parslows Bridge. J.Claxton operated a store, Post Office and a wine saloon near the Woori Yallock creek. When Claxton's daughter and her husband took over the store, the area became known as Parslow's or Parslow's Bridge. Helen Coulson says in her book, published in 1959, that 'in recent times' the area became known as Yellingbo after the last Aboriginal known to have frequented the area, however the evidence suggests that the name was in use for much longer than that. This is another example of the fluidity of town names in the early days of European settlment. Yellingbo means "today" or "this day".

Historical Information: A family group of the Wathaurong Aboriginal people known as the Yawangi balug enjoyed a rich lifestyle in the You Yangs for thousands of years. The name You Yangs comes from an Aboriginal word 'Wurdi Youang' or 'Ude Youang' meaning big mountain in the middle of the plain. Explorer Matthew Flinders and three of his crew were the first Europeans to see the You Yangs. They climbed to the highest point on 1 May 1802. Flinders named it Station Peak, but this was later changed to Flinders Peak in his honour.

Historical Information: Osborne Young built the original Young's hut at the old yards, which are up the hill from this site c1883. During this time he held the BUNDARMUNGIE (County of Bogong) run. where he ran cattle and horses on the High Plains. He was known to have mustered 1500 whalers (horses) in one season  (Carroll) Replacing the cattleman's hut, this Young's Hut was reputedly one of two built in 1928 for the SEC's early hydrological and meteorological survey of the Bogong High Plains (Lawrence (1993): 13f). The hut's components were thought to have been packed in from Mt.Hotham. However, the 1948  Department of Lands & Survey Feature Map of the area shows this hut south of Young's for the first time but the 1945 Kiewa Scheme Locality Plan and a 1933 tourist map do not show it. Rather than being built in the 1920s, this hut appears to have been erected on this site c1945. Peter McNamara, son of Charlie McNamara, confirms that the hut was erected in the 1940s (Carroll).

Alexander (Alec) and Patricia (Pat) McGregor were unable to have children of their own, but were extremely dedicated to the community. Their input went above and beyond the normal assistance offered by other community members and volunteers. Both Alec and Pat are the only life members of the Junior Football Club (of which the reserve is home to), and they have been heavily involved in all community groups over their respective lives. Pat had also been the local kindergarten assistant for over 30 years, and they were both well known and adored in the community. The couple bequeathed a large amount of money to all of these groups. The name change is in their honour as thanks for all of their generosity.
